Man, I really want to like this game. I have a ton of respect for From Software and the worlds they have built over the years, though this is my first time actually playing one of their games (besides armored core VI, which I loved). I have watched countless lore videos on every single one of their games over the years. I really want to dive deep into the world of elden ring, but what holds me back from both playing and being able to recommend this game for mouse and keyboard players such as myself are the downright ATROCIOUS controls/camera design, that have no options for changing. 

Why does left click cause me to swing my weapon on the RIGHT side of torrent, and why does right click swing my weapon on the LEFT side of torrent? Why does a heavy attack actually swing on the correct side of torrent in regards to if you do a left or right heavy attack?

Why does the camera lock feature constantly lock me onto enemies I don't want to be locked on if it detects the slightest input from my mouse? Why cant I just lock onto a single enemy, and only unlock from that one enemy by dragging my mouse away, disengaging target locking as a whole? Why am I forced to hold my mouse 90 degrees relative to my computer desk to stay locked onto a single enemy while my camera goes haywire tracking it inside of a small room as it jumps around like crazy? Even fighting outside especially in the case of trolls, I am constantly fighting my mouse to stay locked onto a single leg instead of locking on to like 3 other body parts constantly, all the while trying to stay under/behind it to avoid its attacks, while my camera is spinning all over the place like crazy. 

Why cant I rebind dodge and sprint to different buttons? In helldivers 2 for example, I love being able to dive with the left alt key. In every game that has a dodge or dive feature, I always rebind that action to alt. It is extremely convenient to hit with your left thumb and it instantly eliminates the possibility of accidentally performing an action you didn't intend. Which in this game, an unintended button press is usually a death sentence. 

Also the fact the game is locked to 60 fps really blows. Sorry for being a pc gamer chud about this but c'mon guys. 

All in all, MAYBE I can fix these clear and present issues with mods. But the extreme depth of the world in combination with little to no explanation of what to do or where to go to get better loot/gear/become stronger (without watching hours of YouTube videos) might have been bearable if I wasn't fighting my controls the entire time. For me, I can't recommend this game for mouse and keyboard players, but I am sure plenty others will still enjoy the game who have more patience than me. I just don't have the time or energy in my life anymore to constantly fight against a video game in order to enjoy it. I just want to enjoy the video game.

Elden Ring – A Masterpiece with Some Flaws

I first bought Elden Ring in 2022, but despite spending over 200 hours on Steam, I never managed to finish it. Part of the problem was my approach: I relied on walkthroughs that explained almost everything, which made the experience unnecessarily slow and, eventually, boring.

Later, I decided to give the game another chance on PlayStation, this time with a different goal: completing it and collecting all the trophies. That approach worked much better for me. After spending another 100 hours on PlayStation, I finally achieved the Platinum trophy.

Now that I've completed the game, I can confidently say that Elden Ring is a masterpiece. It's beautiful, ambitious, and filled with incredible details. However, even a masterpiece isn't without flaws.

1. An Excessively Large World

Elden Ring's world is enormous, and while exploration is one of its main attractions, its sheer size can become exhausting. Some players may enjoy getting lost and discovering things along the way, but for others, constantly wandering around without a clear sense of direction can become frustrating. I have nothing against open-world Souls games, but I think Elden Ring sometimes takes this concept too far.

2. Overcomplicated Level and Path Design**

In traditional, linear Souls games, finding hidden paths, discovering shortcuts, and struggling to reach a particular item or boss can be a rewarding part of the experience. However, in a massive open world like Elden Ring, this design philosophy can sometimes become more frustrating than enjoyable. The combination of an enormous map and complicated paths doesn't always work in the game's favor.

3. Unbalanced Boss Difficulty

I feel that FromSoftware struggled to find the right balance between freedom, accessibility, and genuine difficulty, particularly when it comes to boss fights.

The difficulty curve can feel inconsistent. You might spend hours struggling against one boss, only to defeat the next one surprisingly easily. It's almost as if the game can't decide whether it wants to be extremely challenging or relatively accessible.

Of course, difficulty is subjective, and different players will have different experiences. But for me, the inconsistency between boss encounters was noticeable.

Final Thoughts

Sometimes, it's simply impossible to satisfy everyone with a single experience, and Elden Ring is a good example of that.

Despite my criticisms, I believe the game deserves every bit of praise it receives. FromSoftware did an excellent job with its storytelling. The cutscenes are captivating, the major bosses have their own identities, and I would even argue that Elden Ring represents a significant evolution in storytelling compared to Miyazaki's previous works.

Its art direction is simply outstanding. It's the kind of artistic vision that makes a game memorable for years, something that graphical fidelity alone cannot necessarily achieve.

Interestingly, as I'm writing this review, I'm completely exhausted by Elden Ring. Its enormous world, constant exploration, and lack of straightforward progression sometimes made the experience frustrating. Its open-world design was both one of its greatest strengths and, at times, one of its most exhausting weaknesses.

Nevertheless, Elden Ring is worth your time. It's more than just a video game; it's an artistic achievement that offers an experience you simply cannot get from watching a movie or reading a book. Interactive worlds have their own unique way of telling stories and creating memories.

Give it a try. It's an experience worth having.

Wow, what a game. Probably the best open world game I’ve experienced. My first playthrough was well over 100 hours and I still missed some of the content. This world is absolutely full of things to see and explore, and it is absolutely beautiful. The world and aesthetic are peak fantasy and is what makes this game a masterpiece in my opinion. There’s so many options for weapons and builds, it's insane. Incredible boss fights and soundtrack as well. The storytelling is vague but I think that’s what the Souls-like games do best, you feel like you are experiencing this story as a real and insignificant part of this larger world, the story doesn’t revolve around you as the protagonist. 

The biggest thing that bothered me was the quests. You genuinely could not complete most of these quests playing the game blind, characters would disappear, die or lock you out of parts of a quest because you took one step in the wrong direction, or didn’t do some hyper specific action related to that quest. This game does not hold your hand at all but I feel it goes a bit too far in that aspect, a lot of important details will be missed. There’s also the difficulty at times, and things will feel unfair but persevering is worth it. 

The DLC had more of what I enjoyed, but also the things I didn’t. Trying to navigate the DLC map was an absolute headache, and different regions would have wildly different difficulty that didn’t seem to follow a coherent pattern like the base game does. 

Despite that I consider this game a master piece and easily sits within my top 3 favourites, and I pray for more Elden Ring content some day.

I may return to this game later, because giving it a negative review feels unjust (I wish I could vote somewhere in the middle). 

On a good note the gameplay is engaging, if somewhat initially unwelcoming in it's difficulty. But one's persistence pays off, and soon you'll be winning those unwinnable battles. Consumables feel a little useless but that may be a build-craft issue on my part. It's a little strange that the game is hard capped at 60fps but honestly you barely notice. Enemies look absolutely great too, especially some of the nighttime-only field bosses.

On a VERY good note mounted combat in this game feels wonderful. I did not expect this and was pleasantly surprised. While it would've been nice to have a little more going on with mount(s) via stats or items, compared to most games this actually feels like you're twice as dangerous from atop a horse rather than just using it to cover ground.

It also must be said that the logistical design of the open world is a feat of great technical and artistic talent. The world blocks and guides you in ways that feel organic and natural. The fact that this is the first time FromSoft has made an open world game almost defies belief. To the world designers at FromSoft: congratulations! A debut of this quality is a generation win.

Sadly Elden Ring's storytelling style does not suit me. I can't connect to any character as they all feel extremely hollow and everything about the world and setting feels empty and boring. This lack of characterization and the absence of meaningful relationships is where the game lost me. 

The player character is kind of just a emotionless murder puppet who says next to nothing and has basically no motivation aside from "You're Tarnished, so go become Elden Lord". I found the open world to be painfully empty of anything to do other than kill kill and kill some more. 

Going out to fight an enemy or explore the open world felt as though I was only doing so to level up my stats and find better items, not because the story has provided me a reason to do so. "I'm just playing a game" versus "I'm doing something this character needs or wants to do."

There are no moments of beauty or peace to offset a persistently depressing tone. Elden Ring is joyless in a way I've seldom encountered. I found it to be overwhelming monotonous and with the story being very obscure I was starving for a relatable goal and yearning for a purpose that felt remotely human.

Elden Ring is one of the better action RPGs of all time. However, there are not that many role playing elements in the game, to be honest. There is a lot of build variety and some different endings you can pick from, but very limited NPC interaction or real decision making from the player character. FromSoft continues their storytelling style, which is to say vague, abstruse, and limited, with little in the way of player character motivations to be doing anything that you’re doing. To be frank, we got more world building from the 4 minute story trailer that came out three years before the game than we actually got in the game itself. The quest design continues to suck with NPCs declining to tell you where they will be going next in order to continue their quests, and usually declining to give you names of places to go when telling you what to do. If you want to complete most of the quests in the game, you will likely need to look up the steps online. FromSoft is a big AAA studio at this point, so there is little excuse for the continued poor storytelling and quest design. They proved with Sekiro that they can create compelling plots and characters while still leaving a lot up to player interpretation. Sekiro kept the good parts about the writing and world building of the Souls games and excised the bad. Unfortunately, FromSoft regressed with Elden Ring. The overall lack of plot and the style of story telling here is incredibly disappointing. 

From a gameplay perspective, the exploration is handled well. You are constantly given new weapons, spells, weapon skills, and talismans when clearing dungeons or just exploring the open world. From a world building perspective, it falls very flat. Where did all the people live in this world? There is one city, a handful of towns, and one sorcery school. The Lands Between is not a believable or immersive place. Many games have done a better job with this. I don’t hate it overall, as I find the open world to be a nice change of pace between delving into the catacombs, caves, and legacy dungeons. With your summonable mount always at the ready effectively lowering the risk of death close to zero, the open world acts as a tension break and pacing contrast compared to the linear areas. I do wish there were more legacy dungeons in the game though, as these areas are consistently excellent. They are dense with compelling combat set pieces and rewarding exploration. I think areas like Stormveil Castle, Leyndell, Haligtree and the Shadow Keep are as good as any area in any of FromSoftware’s games. Having three or four more of these in the base game would have elevated the experience for me. 

The actual gameplay, though, is a big improvement on the Souls formula. The game is much more polished from a mechanical perspective and much faster paced. Almost all of the bosses in the game are fun challenges to master (Gargoyle Duo and Consort Radahn being the big exceptions for me). The flexible weapon skill system is excellent and the wide variety of build options is a lot of fun to play around with. The awful checkpoints of previous Souls games have been tempered tremendously with modern checkpoint design in the form of Marika Statues. This does not make the game easier, but does immensely decrease the tedium from previous games. The enemy design is quite good and enemies are more aggressive and mobile than past Souls games, however, they are probably easier to deal with due to the fact that you have much more room to maneuver in Elden Ring. A lot of the difficulty in Souls and Bloodborne came from the cramped environments you fight in and Elden ring simply doesn’t have this issue. This is an unequivocal positive for me. Elden Ring rarely feels unfair or tedious and the challenge is a lot more satisfying because of it. 

The mechanical design of the gameplay is well done and has more depth than previous Souls games. Instead of 2 to 3 swing light attack combos you have 3 to 6, and instead of 1-2 swing heavy attack chains, you have 2 to 4. Weapons have two different running and jumping attacks instead of one each. The addition of a dedicated jumping mechanic led the devs to design many attacks that can be jumped over and oftentimes are better to be jumped over rather than dodged through. All of this increases the mechanical depth of FromSoft's combat design. It still doesn't come close to other styles of action games, however. Games like Devil May Cry and God Of War and Ninja Gaiden are just much more complex and have vastly higher skill ceilings. I am sure if you set those games to Easy they are probably easier than Elden Ring, but I know for a fact that on the hardest difficulties those games are drastically harder than Elden Ring or any FromSoftware game. In the end, the main thing you have to “git gud” at in Elden Ring or any Souls game is just timing your dodge rolls. It’s just not that complicated. The way that the difficulty of FromSoft’s games gets overhyped and overstated is pretty strange. The discourse around Malenia’s supposed difficulty is especially bizarre. It might be the most overhyped thing in the history of gaming. I was already aware of the legend of Malenia before fighting her, so I was definitely more locked in than average for a boss, but I beat her first try. I have beaten her 4 times more with a different build each time and never lost to her more than twice. I do think she is a very enjoyable and well designed boss, but not especially harder than a dozen other bosses in the game. I thought the Duo Gargoyles were harder, tbh. PCR was legit a very hard boss, but it felt distinctly unearned to me. He was such a big difficulty spike over anything else in the game, that his design felt a bit obnoxious.   


Conclusion: 9/10

Even with the poor storytelling Elden Ring is a beautiful and massive game that is fun to explore. The combat is fundamentally simple for such an action focused game, but the enemy design and encounter design is so well done that you don’t even notice how basic the mechanical design is. The bosses are the highlight of the game and almost every one of them is fun to fight multiple times. The game is very well paced and the dungeons are fun to fight through. It is a game that I have continued to come back to, and will continue to come back to until another game of its ilk matches its scope and quality.

At this point it's a little silly to write a review for this game given how famous it is, but I want to put something out there regardless since I already made a review about shadow of the erdtree. 

This game is phenomenal. I played all of the souls games (except the PS exclusive ones) before this, and think that Elden Ring is a natural culmination, evolution, and expansion on many separate aspects of those games coming together. I don't want to go very far into details because there's too much to cover in a review (and a lot of it would technically be spoilers), but a few things I really liked:

- Ashes of War. The Ash of War system makes the Weapon arts introduced by Dark Souls 3 much more appealing by allowing you to customize them. Some weapons still have unique skills that cannot be changed, so it's not fully unrestricted either. This massively increases the usage of weapon skills both for better and worse, allowing more niche ashes a way to shine but also allowing many players to spam weapon arts as their only form of attack (imo, boring).

- Difficulty. Partially resulting from the previous point, Elden Ring is the easiest souls game to customize your own difficulty in. Want an easier experience? Use an arcane build and bleed bosses faster than they can attack. Want a harder experience? Try an off-meta weapon, like the halo scythe or straight swords without square off. The DLC also has a system that assists in this. What I really liked about this particular aspect is that it also applies to the REALLY hard challenges, like rune level 1 runs, where you can find many tools (stat boosting, damage reduction, etc) to make the experience easier despite RL1 not really being intended.

- Spells. While I dislike that pyromancy as a spell subdivision was consumed by miracles to create "incantations," I much prefer the spell system that Elden Ring uses over Dark Souls 3 (DS1 and DS2 systems have their advantages since they don't use an fp bar). Attunement no longer exists; instead pickups (and one talisman) determine your spell slots. Casting speed is determined by Dex (and can be boosted by a talisman and a staff). Spellcasting builds are no longer strained for every level of attunement they can get for spell slots, and instead can casually level mind if they want more FP. This leaves more room for building unique spellcasters and generally making them less frail. On top of all this, the variety of spells is staggering. As a result, my favorite spellcasters have been built in Elden Ring, and I find them much more enjoyable here than the other souls games.

- The open world. I thought the open world was neat, but the repetition of structures and puzzles is very noticeable, particularly in the catacombs and other mini dungeons. In comparison to many other open world games, however, Elden Ring does pretty well. When you see a ruin, there's usually something in it that's useful or interesting. When you see a catacomb, there is a boss in it (though it's usually the same erdtree watchdogs you fought 4 other times). There's usually something in every building you see, and sometimes there's something out in the middle of nowhere. I don't mind that some of these are boring, since the scale of an open world kinda necessitates that not every reward can be mind-blowing, but the base game does relatively well.

There's also some stuff I didn't like, most notably crafting (very half-baked system that hardly anyone uses) and status effects like sleep and madness (almost entirely useless outside of npc invaders or pvp). I think a lot of my gripes, however, come from me playing this game too much and the valid gripes I do have aren't worth a paragraph like the things I listed above.

This game is definitely an improvement over the Souls trilogy in many ways. The bosses are more aggressive, leaning closer to Bloodborne or Sekiro, and the game generally feels more hardcore. Most of the NPC questlines are excellent (especially those for Millicent, Ranni, Patches, and Diallos). However, the open world feels redundant. The core of the Souls experience has always been exploring interconnected locations with limited healing items and challenging bosses. That exploration loop remains in nearly all the previous games (with the exception of DS2, to some extent), but Elden Ring’s quasi-open world breaks that core design. The individual areas - like Stormveil Castle, Volcano Manor, the Academy of Raya Lucaria, and Leyndell, Royal Capital - are still quite interesting to explore, but they are no longer seamlessly connected. The gaps between them are wide, empty spaces filled with repetitive activities. I completed all the dungeons, caves, and loot practically everything across the map, yet I can barely remember anything about the "exploration" of the open world. I can only recall three unique and interesting dungeons: Auriza Hero’s Grave, the Leyndell Catacombs, and the War-Dead Catacombs. I also remember the creepy dancing Celebrants (who turn out to be part of a cult) and the cursed lobsters- that’s basically it. The open world also makes completing NPC quests much harder without guides, as some characters literally teleport to the other side of the map with no warning. In previous Souls games, I was interested in clearing all mobs in a single area in one run. In Elden Ring, I don’t give a shit about killing anything in the open world; I just want to grab loot on Torrent and get out of there. That said, it’s still a very good game.

EDIT: My review was a little too ranty so I'm revising it to be more comprehensive.

Before I get into why I'm leaving this as a thumbs down, the positives:

The Start: The early and mid game is extremely addictive. Deciding on a build, working towards improvements, findings items that make it better, exploring the map, all genuinely top tier. 
Leveling: Leveling stats feels impactful from the very beginning. Your bars get longer, your damage numbers go up, a hit that used to kill you no longer does, a weapon you couldn't efficiently wield is now stronger, etc.
Weapon variety: The amount of variety is so high it's bordering on coming full circle and being too much. Each weapon type has it's own feel, you can mix and match with your off-hand, switch on the fly to holding either one with both hands for certain benefits, the fluidity and sheer number of options available is genuinely impressive and I deeply respect the modelling and animating work that went into all these choices.
The World: Theme, music, sound design in general, armor designs, NPCs, they are all great too. I have gameplay issues with the world and NPCs, but as a theme, they are A+.

Now the bad, starting with:
The World: More does not always equal better, and this open world is a good example. Many times it feels like things are extremely large just to pad out the game. At first, the scale of all the architecture is awe-inspiring and fills you with wonder as to what is out there. As I said, the visual design and the world building is amazing. But, as the newness wears off and you focus more on the gameplay aspect, the obnoxiously long ladders, elevators and sprinting from A to B for literal minutes, gets old. There are fast travel locations, but a lot of areas are perfectly inbetween those spots, especially if you're trying to do NPC quests. More on that after bosses.
The Bosses: This ties into the above about the world feeling padded. Bosses are reused so much it's actually silly. You will fight the same bosses over, and over, and over, and over. The first time you fight them, you may die a lot trying to learn their moveset. Imagine how it feels to finally beat them, just to encounter them again in another part of the map. And again, and again, and again. More does not equal better.
NPCs: While their designs are top tier, the execution of their questlines is genuinely terrible. So much love and care clearly went into their aesthetics and story, only for at least half of them to be hidden behind some of the most obscur pathing I've ever experienced. You will absolutely need to follow a checklist guide to do them, and I think that undermines the fun and the quality of it all. I don't need or expect a quest marker floating in front of my eyes at all times, but having an ingame list with genuine hints on where to head to find an NPC and talk to them more is noticebly missing here. On a lesser note, most of the questlines ending in 'loot xyz from their corpse' is wild. We have become loot goblins for sure.

The combat: While the animations and weapon/skill designs are all genuinely impressive, there is a jank underneath it all that is persistent across FromSoftware games. Attacks are well telegraphed, but sometimes the hitbox just doesn't line up with what you can see. Areas where you fight often have stuff on the ground for you or your attacks to hit/get stuck on. Enemies jump around, going up and down depending on where their body is, or their limbs. It can be quite frustrating to watch and try to interact with in a consistent manner. Ranged is also heavily favored almost all the time, which becomes a problem for enjoying a variety of builds when up-close melee emphasizes the jank.

Lastly, the pricing structure: I'll give just one example to make my point. Sekiro has gone on sale for 50% off, 4 times in the past 12 months alone. Elden Ring on the other hand has been 35% only twice. This doesn't sound that extreme, but add in the fact that the DLC, which costs as much as other soulslikes, has literally never been on sale, and you can see the issue. It is a flawed game, so the price just doesn't make sense after all this time.

In conclusion, it's hard to hate Elden Ring even with all it's issues. But after spending a good amount of time with it, I can't honestly say it's worth full price, as much as there is to like here. There's an equal amount of fun to be had elsewhere these days, for less money. So unless it's on sale, I'd pass.

Elden Ring is an extraordinary gaming experience, and one that's difficult to put into words. Its world-building and level design are nothing short of outstanding. 

The map is massive and constantly subverts your expectations. Just when you think you've reached the end, it keeps expanding with new regions and massive underground areas. Every location feels distinct, and the art direction is phenomenal. The graphics are solid, too. I played this completely blind, exploring and clearing almost every corner of the map over 180 hours, and I was constantly mesmerized by just how beautiful the environments looked. It doesn't rely on heavily cinematic set pieces to impress you; the sheer scale and design of the world do that on their own. It's undoubtedly a game that will go down in gaming history.

The difficulty might seem intimidating at first, but the open-world design gives you plenty of freedom to tackle its challenges your own way. Whether it's experimenting with different weapons, trying out magic, or making use of Ashes of War, there's no shortage of ways to approach combat. Personally, I stuck to a single weapon and a shield, focusing on mastering the core melee combat with strength build. 

The bosses are mostly fantastic, with Malenia being an absolute standout. However, I do have one major complaint: the delayed attacks. Some bosses hold their swings for an absurdly long time, seemingly just to catch you mid-dodge. It feels more like an artificial way of increasing difficulty than a genuinely challenging attack pattern. Normal enemies also get a bit repetitive, but it never really bothered me.

Story-wise, it follows the classic FromSoftware formula. You're not spoon-fed the plot, but if you pay attention to the world, its characters, and the environmental clues, it's fairly easy to piece things together. The questlines are fun to figure out, although the clues about where to go next can sometimes be frustratingly vague. The deep lore is brought to life through excellent voice acting and an amazing soundtrack that perfectly complements the scale of the world. As for the ending, I understand and appreciate FromSoftware's minimalist approach to storytelling, so I wouldn't call it a major disappointment, but it did leave me wanting more. I save-scummed to experience all six endings, and getting a short cutscene felt like a bit of a letdown after investing 180 hours in such an incredible journey. 

Despite these minor complaints, the sheer freedom, beautiful art direction, and solid performance far outweigh the flaws. Whether you want to master a single weapon or replay the game ten times with ten different magic builds, there's plenty of room to experiment and enjoy yourself. Elden Ring lives up to the hype and is easily one of the best gaming experiences I've had. 

*Note: This review covers the base game only and does not include the DLC.*

Elden Ring is more than just a game; it's an unforgettable journey through a breathtaking world. Every corner of the Lands Between has something special to offer, from its stunning landscapes and mysterious ruins to its incredible atmosphere and hidden secrets.

The world feels alive with beauty, mystery, and danger. Exploring it is an experience unlike anything else. The art direction, world design, soundtrack, and attention to detail are simply outstanding. There are moments when you just stop playing, look around, and admire the beauty of the world FromSoftware has created.

What makes Elden Ring truly special is how it makes you feel like a small part of a vast, ancient world waiting to be discovered. Every journey, every discovery, and every challenge feels meaningful.

Thank you, FromSoftware, for creating such a masterpiece. Elden Ring is an experience I'll never forget, and one of those rare games that stays with you long after you've finished playing.

elden ring was a game that took me an embarrassingly long time to get into, thanks to its overwhelmingly large world, the absurd difficulty of the bosses and enemies, and a complete lack of any exposition whatsoever. I had no motivation to push further into the game, to give it the time necessary to understand what made it special, and i regret not getting into it sooner. elden ring is one of the best games I've ever played, it uses a colossal open world and a completely hands-off approach to the player's exploration and development of strategies/builds to let you grow and take on its daunting obstacles and challenges by any means necessary.

i had assumed for the longest time that fromsoft games were just harsh challenges that asked the player to meet an uncompromising obstacle and tackle it exactly as it is, and to some extent thats true. bosses in elden ring have a fixed difficulty in the way that their health, attack patterns, and damage dealt cannot be changed, they exist as they are, and you have to find a way to defeat them. the change in difficulty instead comes from the player and your own progression, with complete freedom in what level you tackle the boss at, and what kind of items, spells, or spirit ashes you'll use for the fight you can almost always find a strategy to counter any boss, and a way to take an impossible fight and make it something manageable. i barely struggled any more than i needed to, and always found myself taking on bosses that i would be evenly matched with and able to reasonably beat (most bosses took maybe an hour tops, with the toughest taking multiple sessions but rarely more than maybe 4-5 hours total (except for the valiant gargoyles)). 

due to a lack of a strict narrative or proper exposition, the game allows the exploration to become the main point of the game, with whatever knowledge you gain as you wander forming your primary understanding of the world, letting the experience vary drastically from person to person. vague spoilers for the endings: [spoiler]it's only fitting that the choices you make and the endings of the game end up being heavily symbolic and vague, you wander a ruined and decaying world, so of course when it hits a breaking point, you get to decide what direction it goes into, whether to maintain the status quo with you on top, to simply burn it all down, or the most popular choice: to bring about a change so radical that the world will be unrecognizable from what it was before[/spoiler]. that exploration and deeply personal narrative and decision making allows for a level of investment and attachment that really make the game unforgettable. my first playthrough took a solid 160 hours and for the entire duration i was excited to keep pushing forward, the world stayed mysterious and dangerous and interesting, there is honestly nothing like it. i think its worth checking out. to say the least.

Now sure, the bosses are very hard. But that's where the fun comes in. This game made me a much calmer person in general. I understand this game might not be for everybody, but if you're someone who's looking for a beautiful and challenging game, where you can choose your destiny and how you get there, this game is for you.

One of, if not the best game you will ever play. Do not hesitate, or listen to the people who try to stray you. 
Here is the main things you should know and consider:

1)The difficulty. This is the main reason people either love or hate this game. Theres no selection from easy,normal or hard. Theres one difficulty and I have to say, if youre new to gaming, know youre not the best , or have no patience this will be a struggle. But I promise you, one that is worth it. 
Do not listen to souls veterans telling you its watered down compared to the older souls games, they simply improved things that made the previous games agitating to play (sites of grace being closer to boss arenas, drops that randomly kill you etc.). Another thing you might hear is that its the easiest, which isnt true either, the game just gives you the option to be played in an easier manner, which you dont have to do. As the last thing, I know it might make many dislike the game when you first jump in and get mauled by the "weakest" enemies right out of the gate. However, the feeling of thriumph after dying over and over and succeeding at the end because you kept trying and improving is purely ecstatic.

2) The value for your buck. I have over 400 hours on elden ring (on this account, I have 1 more as well) and I have still not explored all of this game, nor did every quest or fought every enemy. My first playthrough (without the DLC and where Ive missed like 40% of the game) took 140 hours. You can either immerse yourself and not look at the guides (Id recommend some however, later on with that) and just slowly pace through the game or you can look up all the info online, either way youre going to enjoy the game. The replayablilty is amazing, the options of builds you can run is immense and the DLC is amazing letting you do even more.

3) The confusion. If you go into this game blind, like I did, youre going to run into some big suprises. Theres no one to hold your hand through exploration, quests, fighting. All you get is "the cave of knowledge" at the beggining explaining some basic keybinds and combat. To be frank, I quit the game when I first played because of this and I returned after a few months. If I can bend your ear , my advice would be to not let it discourage you. Theres always the internet to help you out, and the satisfaction of figuring something out yourself is amazing. Especially given how due to this internet age were handed everything immediately and your brain cant handle waiting and thinking.

4) The game overall. I cant describe how beautiful this game is. Whether story wise, the combat, the way it looks, boss design or the dialogue. Its picturesque and the music is perfect, the sights from mountains, the hidden cities, the underground dungeons, the speeches of foes or friend. Its divine at the very least.

Given all this. I highly recommend the game. If you enjoy it , the DLC is definitely worth it, some would argue its as good if not better than the base game.

[h2]To figure out if you will like game or not, here's a simple question.[/h2]
Imagine playing a videogame, and coming across some obstacle. Some friction, some issue. What is your thinking process? Is it "[i]I should try better next time[/i]"? If so, this is game that will bring you some joy, and ALOT of misery and grief. I advice sticking to Dark Souls series in this case.
On the other hand, if at this moment you think "[i]How can I utterly break this game, what option I have to completely invalidate whatever opposition I'm facing?[/i]", then you will have alot of fun, and maybe some dissatisfaction when things fold in front of you a bit [b]too[/b] quickly. Go for it, I suppose.

[h3]If you want my opinion on the game, it can be found below.[/h3]
On one hand, this is a very good game. It's high quality, it's most beautiful open world game out there, and you MAY get hours upon hours of fun out of it (as long as you comply with certain unwritten, unexplained rules that go beyound just clicking buttons at right times). At it's worst ER is still above plenty other games of simillar genre.

On other hand, it's a display of complete lack of control and self-restrain in chase of some nebulous ideas and ideals that end up running contrary to what elevated studio to heights it's enjoying now. It's a game that shows that sometimes "more more more" doesn't equal "better". A silly comparison - think of a person who does so many plastic surgeries that they look nothing like person they used to be, all to end up looking utterly ghastly, even though lots of money, care and skill went into creating the look they now sport. That is Elden Ring and it's DLC "Shadow of the Erdtree".
I'm confident that ER2, or whatever else game will be next in Elden's Soulsborne pseudo-series will shock everyone, and not in positive way, unless From Software finally stops and rethinks their approach.

**Elden Ring – Ein gutes Souls-like, aber kein gutes Open-World-Spiel**

Die Open World von Elden Ring überzeugt mich nicht. Es fehlt ein Questlog, NPCs sind teilweise kaum wiederzufinden, und ihre Dialoge geben oft zu wenig Hinweise darauf, wie ihre Quests weitergehen. Erst im dritten Durchlauf konnte ich Rannis Quest vollständig abschließen. Dass man für solche Quests teilweise externe Guides benötigt, empfinde ich als schlechtes Questdesign.

Abseits der Bosskämpfe gibt es für mich wenig, was die offene Welt wirklich interessant macht. Katakomben und Bergwerke bieten gelegentlich spannende Erkundung, aber vieles andere fühlt sich wie Beschäftigungstherapie an, um den Charakter für die nächsten Bosskämpfe vorzubereiten. Die eigentliche Geschichte bleibt dabei erstaunlich banal: Man besiegt mächtige Gegner, um selbst Eldenfürst zu werden.

Die Bosskämpfe sind dagegen anspruchsvoll, fordernd und teilweise hervorragend gestaltet. Hier liegen die größten Stärken des Spiels. Die Kämpfe verlangen Geduld, Ausdauer und die Bereitschaft, aus Fehlern zu lernen.

**Mein Fazit:** Elden Ring ist für mich ein sehr gutes Souls-like, aber kein überzeugendes Open-World-Spiel. Die offene Welt wirkt eher wie ein Mittel zum Zweck, um die Bosskämpfe miteinander zu verbinden. Wer herausfordernde Bosskämpfe liebt, kommt auf seine Kosten. Wer eine gut erzählte Geschichte, nachvollziehbare Quests und eine lebendige Open World erwartet, wird dagegen enttäuscht.

​"I have no idea what I’m doing, but I refuse to stop."
​As my first-ever Soulslike game, Elden Ring has been a total trial by fire. It is brutally hard, punishing, and completely unforgiving—and yet, I am so hooked to it.
​The Good:
​Atmosphere & World: The world design is breathtaking. Moving through new areas, discovering underground cities, and much MUCH more makes exploration insanely rewarding.
​Punching Demigods: at first i went with Uchigatana but then...found the BALLS! I went with a Strength build using Star Fists, and running up to terrifying bosses to hit them with spiked iron knuckles. This is peak gaming satisfaction. Landed stance-breaks feel incredible.
​The Bosses: The spectacle is unmatched. The Radahn Festival has been my absolute favorite moment so far—charging across a red desert alongside summonable allies against a cosmic demigod felt straight out of mythology.
​Verdict:
If you’ve never played a FromSoftware game before and are scared of the difficulty: jump in anyway. You will die a ton, but the world, ambience, and triumph of finally downing a boss make every second worth it.
​10/10 — Would punch a demigod with spiked gloves again.

Literally THEE BEST action RPG to ever be made. Calling this game a souls-like is an under statement. The gameplay in this game is beyond great, it's an entire league of its own. I'v never played a game that offers as many weapon varieties and combinations as Elden Ring. Wanna duel wield whips or cross bows? OK Wanna be a spell sword with a staff and axe, or a staff and hammer? How about a staff and shield, or duel wield shields? The builds you can make and types are insane, I went in my first playthrough with a high Dex backhand sword build and it was crazy teleporting around bosses with how fast i was, but sad all of them almost 1 hit killed me with how low my other stats were (if thewy caught me :>). All kinds of cool armors as well but stat wise they didn't really change much other your weight class.    

On top of that this game has the most BEUTIFUL scenery if ever witnessed in a fantasy game. I'v taken over 100 screenshots of just the sights you see because of how jaw dropping they are.  Your thrown in the game just gazing at how mighty the Erdtree towering in the sky is compared to the forest size of Limgrave, like going to Manhattan as a rural kid for the first time and seeing the twin towers (spoilers).  than you cross into Liurnia and see the academy across the swamps miles away. Then when you think you've seen it all you go up to Altus and see the Great Walls of Lyndell and just image what its going to be like to enter the city, a parallel that of a young mexican coming to the Arizona border dreaming of crossing the MAGA wall to see the USA.

Other than the gorgeous sights and awesome gameplay that game wasn't too hard overall. I wen through an beat every boss in their relative skill order and killed a few on my first try with others taking a hand full of attempts. The only bosses that took MANY trials to beat for me where Melania, Consort Radahn, and Twin Gargoyles. But even if you do struggle with the games difficulty you have tons of areas to grind mobs and beta side bosses or mini bosses to level up to fight harder ones. On top of that summoning makes the game 10x easier and if that doesn't work you can co-op summon another player who might be cracked and carry the boss alone for you. 

The only down sides of this game is the story telling is pretty bad with short narrations that are hard to paste together to figure out what the games over arching story is about (other than kill bosses get Elden Ring). The "side quest" are hard to navigate with noting what's going as you explore areas, and I literally forgot to return to NPC's for like 90% of quest since they are super forgettable. Also the fact that ENTIRE SECTIONS of the games are hidden behind secret doors or puzzles is FRUSTRATING. There's literally a massive castle in the base game with hours of exploration what is literally all hidden behind single hidden doorway. 

Other than that this is probably the best action RPG of all time. There's enough content in this game to make an MMO, it took me 250+ hours just to clear every boss and area ONCE.

As of today, October 24, 2026, I have played over 155 hours (Level 109 Wretch) with the Elden Ring Tarnished Edition on Switch 2 and another bunch of hours with the Shadow of the Erdtree edition on Xbox Series X. I only play on PC when I have to, I prefer not having to waste time on graphical and performance settings and FPS counters - and that's basically all that I did with the PC version of the game; and that tells me all anybody needs to know about PC gaming and how ridiculous is that?

That being said, the game itself is the same on all platforms (but as far as I am concerned, the Switch 2 version feels the best - there, I said it).

Just like the first sip of Islay Whiskey like Laphroaig, you WILL hate this game when you first play it. And you will uninstall it in rage.

Then you will re-install it a bit later. And uninstall it in rage again.

When you re-install it for the third time, you're testing positive for having caught "the Elden Ring bug".

This is one of the most frustrating games in the history of gaming, if not THE most frustrating game ever created.

In a nutshell: You will burn 12 hours or more on trying to beat a "boss" that is so ridiculously overpowered and unfairly designed that you can successfully claim temporary insanity for even playing this nonsense.

And then you beat this boss.

You might have had to take long detours in the game to level up your character or find items or weapons or summons that help you beat him or her, but eventually you got there.

Strangely enough, when you finally succeed, you will feel nothing.

No rush of victory.

No satisfaction.

You just move on.

And then there will be a regular guard waiting for you around the corner who will kill you with one blow. Not a boss, just a puny little guard.

Once more, "YOU DIED" takes the center of your screen.

That's the Elden Ring experience in a nutshell.

This is not a game anyone can recommend to any sane person.

Elden Ring does not have a story. It has lore that's being told through the environment. But this game does NOT have an actual story. 

It's a brutal and broken world that drove everybody insane and turned all living or undead creatures into murderous lunatics.

It only has a fistful of NPCs that actually speak. Almost everything in this world is just out to kill you - without even saying a word.

The game has a gigantic amount of catacombs, tombs, tunnels and dungeons that LITERALLY (!) use copy and paste design. Apparently, this world only had one old socialist architect who reused the exact same design all over the country.

The music tries to be Richard Wagner's PARSIFAL, but fails miserably. It is a depressing soundtrack that only adds to the constant frustration and this game is so much better when you just turn off the music and only listen to the wind and rain in the game.

The graphics are not as good as everybody says they are. But what they deliver unbelievably impressive environments. That extremely long elevetor ride down to that underground city alone makes it worth playing the game. These are the moments when Elden Ring feels like pure genius, when you know that you are playing something truly unique and special despite its astronomical amount of design flaws.

This is when you love the game.

A second later, you will get one-hit-killed again and hate the game and might even throw your controller into your screen, screaming and shouting and hitting the desk with your fist.

Then you keep on grinding, leveling up, exploring and picking the next fight until you win it - usually by using your brains instead of your brawns, because your brawns will never be powerful enough in this game.

That insanity of a game is Elden Ring. I will NOT recommend it to any sane person who wants to find an escape, entertainment or merely a few moments of fun when playing a game. Because that is NOT what Elden Ring is.

But if you are a defiant, grinding and ambitious type of gamer, then Elden Ring will be the hill you die on.

Wonderful game. I only have 6 hours on pc but over 900 hours on console. This game is a great introducer for those who have never played anything from the Souls franchise and is also a wonderful game for veterans of the category. The bosses are wonderfully crafted, each holding their own unique move sets with their own unique weaknesses and strengths that tie to the lore of each foe. Speaking of which, by God is the lore perfect. The whole family-tree dynamic with each branch having their own separate branches that also branch off into other branches, creating a beautifully complex system of who relates to who and what caused what. The scenery is gorgeous, from the moment you step foot into the Lands Between all the way to the end of the game and even into the DLC; no matter the playthrough, the sights will always remain breathtaking. The real attention grabber and the reason I even have 900+ hours on this singular game are the builds and their complexity. Each class - that being strength, dexterity, faith, intelligence and arcane - can be mixed into larger classes, of which can be broken down into smaller micro-classes such as dex-faith incantation caster or an arc-strength bleed build means that you can go through endless playthroughs and still find new ways to play the game. The resources are also plentiful and each fulfill either a niche or broad use, such as spirit summons spawning an ally or poison stones being used to inflict poison from afar, meaning even the most novice of players can still enjoy the game without being stumped for too long. This is further aided by the larval tears allowing you to fully re-spec your entire build into something else - something that can aid you better against a certain boss with their own specific weakness. However, no perfect game is truly perfect and this game does contain some flaws. First, we still have the issue of limited resources, especially max upgrade materials. The amount of max upgrade materials are plentiful enough, however, to not be too cumbersome meaning you'll always have enough even for a single NG playthrough to max out your favorite weapon without needing to enter NG+. Of which, by the way, is its own flaw. NG+ is still as boring as ever, just being a slightly more difficult campaign with nothing new added. I wish they had another Dark Lord system like in Dark Souls 1 or more enemies just like in Dark Souls 2, however, none of that is present meaning NG+ is just a challenge for those who want to face it or those who want extra weapons for PvP builds. A small nitpick would be the grinding that feels almost required to achieve resources and a reasonable level to enjoy your builds at their peak power and for PvP. If I were to guess how much of my 900+ hours I spent on this game was spent grinding, I would say ~24 hours, which is low compared to the 900+ total hours but, in my opinion, is still too long. However, as stated before, this is just a nitpick and not something to be considered, in my opinion. In summery, this game is a wonderfully crafted and written Souls-RPG that can appeal to the most novice of the franchise, to the most experienced with hundreds of hours worth of builds and content not including the DLC.

[h1]100+ Hrs in the Lands Between, and My Journey Still Isn't Over![/h1]

[h2]My First Souls Experience[/h2]

Elden Ring was my very first Souls game, and honestly, what an experience it has been! I enjoyed it a lot, but at the same time, I struggled quite a bit throughout my journey. There were moments when certain bosses made me question my life choices, haha. But finally defeating them after countless attempts was incredibly satisfying.

Since this was my first Souls game, everything felt new to me, especially the combat, difficulty, and the way the game encourages you to figure things out on your own.

[h2]Exploration & World Design[/h2]

One of my favourite things about Elden Ring is definitely its beautiful world. The scenery, atmosphere, and overall world design are simply breathtaking. Every new area feels different, and there's always something interesting waiting to be discovered.

I especially loved [b]Leyndell, the Royal Capital[/b], and [b]Crumbling Farum Azula[/b]. Leyndell's architecture, atmosphere, and sheer scale were absolutely stunning, while Farum Azula's ancient ruins and storm-filled skies gave it a completely different, almost otherworldly feeling. Both are easily among my favourite locations in the entire game. Sometimes I just wanted to stop exploring and admire the surroundings instead of progressing further.

[h2]Combat, Weapons & Boss Fights[/h2]

Getting used to the combat definitely took some time. Some bosses were genuinely frustrating, and there were plenty of moments when I had absolutely no idea what I was doing, haha.

One thing I really appreciated was the [b]huge variety of weapons and builds[/b] the game offers. From massive swords and fast-paced katanas to magic and different hybrid builds, there's so much freedom to experiment with your playstyle. You can approach the same fight in completely different ways depending on your weapons, abilities, and build, which makes the combat even more interesting.

The boss fights were definitely some of the most memorable parts of my journey. Learning their attack patterns, figuring out different strategies, and finally overcoming a difficult encounter gave me a kind of satisfaction that very few games have managed to offer.

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]

Looking back, it has been a journey filled with frustration, excitement, exploration, and some truly unforgettable moments. Despite all the struggles, I genuinely loved my time with the game.

I finally completed and platinumed Elden Ring on [b]October 17, 2026[/b], and I'm currently making my way through the [b]Shadow of the Erdtree DLC[/b]. Even after spending over 100 hours in the Lands Between, there's still plenty left for me to discover. I'll be sharing my thoughts on Shadow of the Erdtree separately in its own Steam review once I've finished it.

For my first Souls experience, I honestly couldn't have asked for a better introduction to the genre. Definitely one of the most memorable games I've played, and I'm really glad I gave it a chance!

Cyberpunk 2077 is phenomenal. The story, combat mechanics, progression, and graphics are top tier. As someone who no longer has the time or energy for 100% achievement runs or grueling difficulty after a long workday, playing on Easy just to enjoy the ride was completely worth it.

Combat & Build:
I started with stealth, but found it too slow. Re-specing into a maxed Reflex/Tech "run-and-gun" build changed everything. Combining legendary ARs, SMGs, dual-wield revolvers, Mantis Blades, dashing melee combos and double-jump parkour made combat felt like DOOM where I was locked in a room with enemies, and they had nowhere to run.

Story & DLC:
The story choices give off great Fallout: New Vegas vibes, which can impact multiple endings. I was able to finish all cyberpsycho sightings and almost all the main companion arcs. The Phantom Liberty DLC felt like playing Skyrim’s Dragonborn or Fallout 4’s Far Harbor. It's like a full standalone game rather than just an expansion.

Ignore the Online Comparisons:
Don't listen to short-form videos comparing small details to RDR2 / GTA V or any other games. Missing tiny details doesn't make Cyberpunk any less impressive.

Minor Drawbacks:
- No TPP: The strict FPP gave me eye strain and dizziness, limiting sessions to around 4 hours. A Third-Person option would be a huge game changer.
- Progression Glitch: Hit a minor bug during Cyberpsycho: Letter of the Law (couldn't interact with a computer prompt), but loading a recent save fixed it.
- Endgame Wait: Waiting days in-game for Reed’s call after Phantom Liberty last main mission felt stalled (or maybe even bugged), so I decided to wrap up my playthrough here and move on to a different game.
- Forced Character Orientations (LGBTQIA+-<>{}1234567890ABCXYZ): Restricting romance options based on fixed orientations felt a bit forced for an RPG. Honestly, why? It doesn't make any sense.

Recommending it now even after all the fixes and QoL updates feels like we're just letting other developers know it's okay to "sell broken and fix later" OR makes them feel like they can lie in their marketing and sell a different product as long as it's good enough.

I feel like if you're the type of gamer who loves Skyrim and Fallout 4, then this game is going to blow your socks off. Graphics are still great. Driving around the city is fun. I love spending money on the cyberware (upgrades) - being able to choose parts that allow me to super jump like Hulk, deal extra damage with my fists like I'm Baki, or even slow down time is extremely satisfying. Side quests are fun - I had a great time doing the basic "kill em" contracts because of the investment in my cyberware. The story is very engaging and has some super cool set pieces. The perk system add some cool abilities but cyberware is definitely the way to go if you want the really cool abilities. Attacks feel good and weapon variety is great. 

BUT if you love very choice driven RPGs where choices matter (Fallout NV comes to mind), then this is not gonna  scratch that itch. Only 30 hours in but the promises they made about this having branching storyline are not delivered in the game. Choices matter A BIT in the sense that you'll get access to different weapons or vehicles depending on your choice but the story doesn't really change. The game is VERY polished but CD Red still have not delivered on 3 out of 4 of the promises - and they should be remembered:

1) Story for mature audiences (delivered)
2) Gripping non-linear story (not delivered)
3) Advanced RPG mechanics based on Pen&Paper RPGs (NOT AT ALL)
4) Different character classes (Classless system like Skyrim where you can do most things or specialize in a specific playstyle)

So, I played this game on Linux. Decent performance for playing what's still a benchmark game on a laptop running an officially unsupported OS. The game isn't all that bad nowadays if you don't turn ray tracing or path tracing on.

BUT... yeah, this game is not great. It's also not bad, in case that was your immediate thought. It's mediocre or just above. A 6 or 7 at best, on a strict 1 to 10 scale.

I finished it AFTER doing every sidejob, gig, police call, and cyberpsycho. That includes the recent Edgerunners season 2 content and Phantom Liberty. Before this week, I would have probably scored the game above a seven... but honestly, I can't do that now.

[b]The Illusion of the Open World[/b]
Over the past week, I spent a while stealing Rayfields from the yacht club parking lot and driving them around the city. And you know what? I wasn't stealing them. I was *borrowing* them. Because I can't keep the cars, and I can't sell the cars. I can just go on a joyride. And nobody calls the cops on me. They might if I kill someone or hit another car, but very rarely. 

That made me realize that once the map is devoid of gigs, sidejobs, NCPD dispatch calls, and cyberpsychos, the game is a lot less of an open world than it looks at first glance. Speaking of which, driving in this game sucks. You do get used to it, but the requirement of car fights forced CD Projekt Red into making some questionable choices about the actual driving physics. You're either going to love it... or, like everyone else playing the game, grow to tolerate it.

[b]Pacing and Player Agency[/b]
One Phantom Liberty path leads you into a pseudo-horror game that removes your agency and forces you into playing it like a horror game for a mission. I didn't buy the game for that, and I didn't appreciate having my V's power stripped away for story purposes. That was the first red flag.

Now, all that being said, this still wouldn't really kill the game for me. I didn't play the buggy edition that came out; I played the most complete edition available, and it's fairly bug-free. No, what drops this to a 7 is how badly the game fumbles the ball just before the goal line.

[b]The Endings (Minor Spoilers Below)[/b]
The endings suck. Most people dislike the endings because of what happens to V. I dislike them because they waste my time. 

[spoiler]Even the suicide ending ends up wasting your time with a giant wall of credits text that takes forever if you actually want to show some respect to the people who made the game. Every ending is somewhat different, but in each, you end up doing jack shit in a barely interactive cutscene. It's not quite a cutscene, but it's not actually real gameplay either.

I did the Phantom Liberty ending first, then I went to meet Hanako at Embers. I refused to redo Reed's ending again from a different point, so I did the suicide one, then I did the secret one, then I did the Arasaka one. And you know what? I'm not going back for the Rogue and Panam ones. The amount of disrespect the devs showed toward the player's time is disgusting. It's basically a soap opera episode with forced interactions each time to make sure you are still paying attention, but with no actual choice. When V gets angry in the Arasaka ending and breaks his necklace... I realized I wasn't feeling anything. I wasn't empathizing with V. I was just bored. And that right there is why I uninstalled the game instead of getting the last two ending achievements.[/spoiler]

I spent several hours stealing Rayfields and driving them around the city in a game whose driving mechanics I don't even like, and the f***ing *endings* are what made me bored. The literal last dozen or so meters before the marathon's end, the game decided it wanted to suddenly be "high art," and peak gameplay became following Hanako and picking from a number of meaningless choices.

[b]The Verdict[/b]
The game is decent and worth a single playthrough, but don't bother with the alternate endings. Enjoy whatever ending you get naturally and ignore the others. Seeing the Aldecaldos and Reed say the exact same thing a second or third time for a different ending just breaks the magic.

Cyberpunk 2077 is one of gaming’s greatest comeback stories. After a disastrous launch marked by ridiculous bugs, broken promises, and disappointed fans, CD Projekt Red managed to turn things around, delivering an experience that finally lives up to its enormous potential.

Night City is an absolute visual treat. While exploration feels somewhat limited, and the AI still has (major) flaws, simply wandering around the city is a pleasure. Combat has evolved into an absolute playground, offering a wealth of different builds and playstyles, backed by gunplay that feels snappy, responsive, and ridiculously fun. The soundtrack is fantastic, not to mention the voice acting (Keanu Reeves, anyone?).

The character writing is nothing short of outstanding, introducing deeply human, morally ambiguous individuals who are simply trying to survive or leave their mark on such a merciless world. Customization is quite disappointing, particularly when it comes to character creation and clothing. Thankfully, the modding community has stepped in to fill many of these gaps.

This ability to tell compelling stories through its characters and morally complex situations is also what makes Phantom Liberty such a fantastic addition, an outstanding spy thriller filled with political intrigue, paranoia, unforgettable characters and emotional moments. The darker atmosphere and soundtrack make the expansion feel like a whole new experience, arguably even more mature and compelling than the base game.

Overall, Cyberpunk is an unforgettable experience, that finally delivers on its promises, rightfully earning its place among the greatest achievements in video game history and holding a special place in my gamer’s heart.

I like Cyberpunk, but I'm struggling to finish it. Hype can't hide the enormous wasted potential. Six years of patches and there's still rebinding issues, unfinished textures, broken animations, floaty physics, rampant clipping, etc. 

Keep in mind, this is a looter shooter, not an RPG. Exploration and lore are the highlights. Clearing inventory clutter and grinding gear stats is the game loop. Story choices rarely matter. You'll slaughter cops, civilians, and gangsters indiscriminately with no consequences.  

Gameplay is a little disappointing. The weapons are great. Everything else is subpar. Melee in first-person POV looks goofy. Stealth is generic and unrewarding. Slo-mo, x-ray vision, tagging, and invisibility, you know the drill. Character builds are deep, however combat encounters are not, consisting of simple trash mobs or kiting bosses. Enemies are aggressive but dumb. While you're in vehicles, enemy AI deactivates when V drives within two meters of their personal space. Which explains why you never get yanked from vehicles. Nice QA-testing, CDPR.

Hopefully updates finally fix the AI and implement basic open-world features to breathe some life into the shallow map. As of the 2.5 patch, foes cannot hijack cars to pursue you or perform real PIT maneuvers like in GTA IV. Nor is there a functioning APB/bribe/bounty system that made Mafia 2, Elder Scrolls, and RDR games immersive. Unlike the Saints Row series, gangs serve no purpose. Even Thief: Deadly Shadows had a more fleshed out faction system than Cyberpunk, ffs.

"Is Cyberpunk 2077 a 'head pat' simulator?"

- "headpat simulator" refers to the player being automatically rewarded as the hero for accomplishing simple mundane tasks or on screen prompts as opposed to solving a puzzle with genuine critical thinking and potential risks for attempting the content. - 

Under that specific framework, yes, Cyberpunk 2077 heavily exhibits these "headpat simulator" design flaws.
While the world is structurally mature and violent, the underlying mechanical loop frequently treats the player exactly like that. If you are looking for a true tactical or mental challenge where a failure to think critically carries real consequences, Cyberpunk entirely fails to deliver.

Why Cyberpunk 2077 Fits This Critique

• The "GIG" Checklist Loop: The open world is packed with markers and "gigs" where you show up, follow a yellow dotted line on your mini-map, press a prompt to download data or neutralize a target, and immediately get a phone call from a fixer giving you cash and calling you a mercenary legend. The mental load is practically zero.
• Frictionless Brain Dances: The investigative "Brain Dance" sequences present themselves as a high-tech detective puzzle. In reality, the UI literally highlights the exact visual or audio layer you need to look at, color-codes the timeline bar to show you exactly where the clue is, and rewards you for simply scrubbing back and forth until the prompt fills up.
• Zero-Consequence Failures: Outside of failing an explicitly timed quest objective (which is incredibly rare), you cannot truly "fail" a puzzle or a conversation in a way that derails your progress or forces you to deal with a catastrophic, unscripted crisis. The game actively protects you from the consequences of poor planning.
• Overpowered Power Fantasy: Because of how the scaling and cyberware systems work, even on the highest difficulties, a basic build quickly trivializes any tactical risk. You aren't solving a dynamic combat puzzle; you are clicking a button to wipe out a room through a wall via Quickhacks while the game rewards you with massive XP drops.
It hands the player a massive checkbox of mundane tasks, holds their hand through the execution via aggressive UI markers, and immediately rewards them with the "hero" validation without forcing them to take any genuine analytical risks.


Of the characters;

Cyberpunk 2077 heavily relies on flatter, archetype-driven writing where characters are built out of predictable, edgy tropes rather than genuine human complexity.

Because the game is constantly trying to project a cynical, "gritty" corporate dystopia, almost every NPC is funneled into a highly stylized, tropey version of a fixer, a rebel, or a corporate sociopath. Instead of navigating nuanced relationships or unpredictable personalities, you are largely interacting with a checklist of predictable, flawed and deplorable caricatures.

By flattening the characters into these predictable, edgy templates, the game removes any actual social or psychological puzzle-solving. You never have to truly study a character's unique motivations or risk misinterpreting them because they wear their hyper-stylized stereotypes directly on their sleeves.

On failing to produce an expected native 3rd person perspective;

The absence of a native third-person perspective is often cited as a massive missed opportunity, as a well-implemented third-person mode could have introduced the very structural friction, systemic risks, and narrative weight that the first-person checklist loop lacks.

By forcing the player exclusively into a first-person perspective, the game leaned entirely into a hyper-immersive illusion that its mechanical depth simply can't back up.

[b]Cyberpunk 2077[/b] has an incredible amount of potential, but I struggle to understand how such an interesting universe can feel so average in its execution. I first tried it in 2020 and disliked almost everything, from the story to the gameplay. Returning several years later, I can recognise the improvements, but many fundamental problems remain. Night City is beautiful, its architecture and visual design are impressive, and the universe has enormous potential. Unfortunately, a beautiful city filled with NPCs does not automatically become a living world.

One of my biggest problems is how superficial the world feels. Too many NPCs exist simply to fill the streets. Most stand around doing practically nothing, staring into the distance or repeating basic animations. You occasionally see characters talking, but these interactions rarely develop into anything meaningful. I am not asking for every NPC to have a complex routine or storyline. I mean basic everyday life: people interacting, recognising familiar faces, following routines and reacting naturally. Night City should feel like a place that exists independently of the player. Instead, it feels like a backdrop. Fewer NPCs with meaningful interactions would have been better than streets full of characters that barely do anything.

Other open-world games handle this better. The Witcher 3 makes Geralt feel connected to the world, with people recognising him as a mutant. Bethesda games also use conversations and NPC reactions to acknowledge the player's presence and actions. In Skyrim, even a bard singing about your achievements makes your progress feel relevant. Cyberpunk rarely creates that connection. Mission characters may know V is a mercenary, but the rest of the world barely acknowledges who you are or what you have accomplished. You experience Night City without feeling that you belong there. I had a similar feeling in Hogwarts Legacy: you visit an interesting universe without becoming properly integrated into it.

The narrative has similar problems. The three life paths suggest that your background will matter, but they eventually converge into practically the same direction. The game also does very little to establish who V actually is, offering little personal history about their family or circumstances. The relationship with Jackie Welles is another missed opportunity. We are expected to care about a friendship that has already developed before we get to experience most of it. Skipping that important period makes the emotional connection harder to establish and the experience feel even shorter. For a game with this much potential, the narrative feels shallow, with little suspense or weight.

Exploration and side content contribute to this problem. Missions and activities are scattered across the map, sometimes requiring ridiculous distances between objectives without natural progression through the districts. Unlike GTA, where progression can gradually open up areas, Cyberpunk throws activities everywhere from the beginning. I barely found a reason to use the metro, and once I discovered fast travel points, driving became increasingly unnecessary. Many activities feel like they exist simply to fill the map. Exploration should offer more than another weapon or piece of equipment. A world this interesting should reward curiosity with meaningful discoveries.

The police and general AI systems are another major disappointment. The police feel incredibly weak. NPCs can attack the player without meaningful intervention, and I rarely saw convincing pursuits involving other NPCs. Gang-controlled areas also fail to communicate the danger they are supposed to represent. Meanwhile, ordinary NPCs panic over the smallest contact. Some run directly in front of your vehicle or refuse to move when you are leaving an alley. In some situations, NPCs run into my car and the police somehow decide that I am the problem. At three wanted stars or more, police officers also start appearing directly in your field of vision. This is not how a convincing police system should behave.

Vehicle pursuits are particularly bad. They are among the weakest action sequences I have experienced in an open-world game. Vehicles feel strangely slow, and you cannot properly ram enemy cars or force them off course. Enemy vehicles behave like indestructible objects following predetermined routes. It becomes even more frustrating when the narrative protects certain characters or vehicles because they must survive until a specific point. The game creates the illusion of a dynamic chase while restricting what the player can actually do. If you cannot meaningfully influence the encounter, why create that illusion?

Adam Smasher is another example of the gap between presentation and execution. He is presented as an absolute monster, a massive cybernetic killing machine who should feel intimidating. After seeing his portrayal in Cyberpunk: Edgerunners, I expected something much more memorable. Instead, the boss fight was embarrassing. Using a shotgun and landing headshots made the encounter surprisingly easy. He fired missiles and used his other weapons, but I could withstand everything he threw at me. For a character with this much importance, the actual confrontation is incredibly underwhelming.

Johnny Silverhand also feels like a character whose potential was not properly developed. His identity as a musician, his history with Samurai and his role in the destruction of Arasaka Tower could have been explored much better. The game never makes his music feel as memorable as it should. I never found a track that made me interested in Samurai or gave Johnny's musical identity the impact the story expects. *I Really Want to Stay at Your House* gained a much stronger emotional association through Cyberpunk: Edgerunners, especially with David and Lucy. The anime gave the song a memorable context that the game never managed to establish. It is a shame, because Johnny could have had a much stronger musical identity.

Then there are the technical problems. Despite years of updates, I still encountered a ridiculous number of bugs. Some character storyline finales and expansion-related quests became completely stuck, preventing progression. I sometimes had to load an earlier save. It is disappointing that progression blockers still exist, with some situations apparently requiring mods to work around them even in a vanilla playthrough. I also encountered NPCs walking through walls, vehicles spawning on top of each other and creating pile-ups, collisions and flying cars. In two locations, my character suddenly accelerated backwards, as if a time-rewind ability had activated, before getting attached to a random wall like Spider-Man. Character models sometimes rendered without hands, and objects disappeared during cutscenes. I even have video clips of some incidents. I understand that bugs can be inconsistent between players, but these were part of my experience.

I can recognise the improvements since launch and appreciate what Cyberpunk 2077 does well. Night City is visually impressive, and its universe has enormous potential. That is precisely what makes the experience so frustrating. The game constantly gives you glimpses of something greater without delivering on it. A large open world is not automatically immersive, a huge number of NPCs does not create a living city, and a collection of activities does not make exploration meaningful. The narrative, world simulation, AI, police systems and major action sequences all feel underdeveloped. Cyberpunk 2077 is an average experience built around an extraordinary universe. I wanted to experience Night City as a living world, not simply walk through a beautiful backdrop. Unfortunately, that is exactly how much of the experience felt to me.

However, after watching Cyberpunk: Edgerunners and getting more invested in its universe, I slowly felt the urge to return to Night City. And honestly, I'm glad I did.

Coming back to the game after all this time feels like rediscovering an old place. Every time I explore Night City, walk through its neon-lit streets, or simply take in the atmosphere, I get hit with a sense of nostalgia that reminds me of Edgerunners. That connection between the anime and the game makes the experience even more enjoyable and keeps me coming back without getting bored.

The story is incredibly well structured, the world-building is amazing, and the characters make Night City feel alive. There's something special about the way this game tells its story and makes you feel connected to its world.

And, of course, my absolute favorite character has to be Johnny Silverhand. His personality, attitude, dialogue, and overall presence make him one of the most memorable characters in the entire game.

Overall, it's difficult for me to give Cyberpunk 2077 an exact rating, especially because my appreciation for it is also influenced by my connection to Edgerunners. But one thing is certain: this game deserves a score well above 8/10.

The characters are memorable, the storytelling is fantastic, and the world is full of things to discover. Whether you're exploring, fighting, making difficult decisions, or getting yourself into situations you probably shouldn't be in, there's always something interesting happening.

The combat system is incredibly satisfying, especially if you enjoy strategy and turn-based combat. There are so many different ways to approach encounters, and experimenting with different builds, abilities, and party combinations keeps things fresh.

What really makes this game special is how much freedom it gives you. It doesn't force you down one path or punish you for thinking outside the box. It lets you create your own adventure, and that's something not many games manage to accomplish this well.

If you enjoy RPGs, fantasy worlds, meaningful choices, and incredible storytelling, Baldur's Gate 3 is an absolute must-play.
