I think Baldur's Gate 3 has handily taken that title and ran away with it. There may not be another game on the same caliber as BG3 for years to come. It's a truly special experience, to be so free as to choose from so many different branching paths and know that your choices do actually matter, and will lead you to an ending you may not have ever seen otherwise. Few video games can truly claim to do such a thing, and Baldur's Gate 3 does it better than any other video game ever made.

Baldur’s Gate 3 is a remarkable RPG, filled with memorable characters (Shadowheart and Astarion FTW!), fantastic moments, and an incredible sense of freedom. It's arguably the closest a video game has ever come to capturing the magic of tabletop Dungeons & Dragons, giving players countless ways to approach situations and shape their own adventures.

At the same time, it often feels like a jack of all trades, but a master of none. Its ambition is both its greatest strength and its biggest weakness, something that becomes especially apparent in Act 3. While packed with content, the final act feels like the game's scope grew beyond what the developers could realistically manage, leaving parts of the experience unfinished, uneven, or lacking the polish they deserved. The numerous bugs certainly don't help either.

Yet, despite all its shortcomings, BG3 is one of those games where the highs overwhelmingly outweigh the lows. Its freedom, creativity, and sheer number of unforgettable moments make it easy to forgive its rough edges. It may not excel at every single thing it attempts, but this was a truly special adventure that I'll hold close to my heart.

Lots of impressive technical and artistic work in this, but I never got around to finishing it because it's so repetitive and grindy. I was really hopeful at the start of the game, because it throws you into an insane set of gameplay segments/cutscenes blending esoteric D&D lore w/ H.R. Giger-style horror, plus a compelling multi-planar crash sequence. However, after that point it becomes bog-standard narrative-wise and the combat can be very tedious. The inclusion of the  dice roll mechanic in particular indicates a fundamental misunderstanding of the medium. Random dice rolls work well in D&D because failing checks can be just as interesting as succeeding (for instance, failing an important deception check against the king and then being sentenced to death--what will our intrepid heroes(?) do?), since the DM can creatively adapt as the situation evolves. In Baldur's Gate, however, the flow of the game is more or less fixed. Which means, with no DM to turn a flubbed role into a comedic or dramatic opportunity, low rolls are almost exclusively a source of frustration. If there has to be randomness, it should at most be Pokemon-style, where (very) occasionally someone can get a crit or whiff an attack. Also, the fact that you can't pick off enemies without initiating combat is really annoying. Before writing any review, I wanted to finish the game properly. And that took me over 150 hours; 150 absolutely AMAZING hours of adventure, filled with unforgettable moments and so many positive emotions.

When I first started playing and got into my first battle, I wasn't exactly impressed. The turn-based combat system didn't convince me at all. I guess nostalgia for the good old combat system from Baldur's Gate 1 and 2 was simply too strong. But I decided to give it a chance, and once I got used to it, I realised it actually adds a whole new dimension to the game.

The same goes for the party size. Having only four characters instead of the six we had in BG1 and BG2 was initially a bit disappointing. Again, nostalgia talking. But after spending some time with the game, I realised just how brilliantly balanced the four-character party actually is. It adds another layer of complexity, forces you to think more tactically, make better use of every character's abilities, and really get the most out of your party.

And then there's everything else... The depth of the game. The seemingly endless possibilities. The decisions and their consequences. The dialogue. The incredible characters and their personal stories.

And this is where the game truly shines. Every major character you meet, especially your companions, has an incredibly detailed story of their own, one you can gradually uncover and become deeply involved in. But what makes it so special is that you're not just watching their stories unfold. You're actively shaping them. Depending on your choices, their personalities, relationships, beliefs and ultimately their fates can change dramatically. Who they become and where their stories lead is, to a remarkable extent, in your hands.

And those decisions don't exist in isolation. They have consequences, sometimes immediate, sometimes much later when you least expect them. They shape your companions, your relationships, the dynamics of your party and ultimately your entire gameplay experience. It's this incredible sense that your choices genuinely matter that makes the world feel so alive and every playthrough so personal. And, of course, a wonderful dose of nostalgia when Jaheira and Minsc showed up. Seeing those two again was something special... #corememoriesunlocked. :)

I put off playing Baldur's Gate 3 for years because I didn't believe it could possibly live up to the hype. All I'd seen from it were clips of dialogue or exploits. I didn't expect it at all to be the most unique RPG I've ever played for one reason that stands out above all others: the sheer flexibility. Many single-player RPGs either don't allow you to bend the rules or the narrative, while others let you bend them so far that they break. Baldur's Gate 3 lets you bend every quest to the point where you expect it to break, but it never does. I cannot emphasise enough just how much the game accounts for every action you could possibly choose to take in every situation, so I'm not going to try.

An aspect I hadn't seen much (if any) of was the combat, so I had no idea what to expect. I'm coming at this as someone who has zero experience with D&D mechanics. I very wrongly assumed that the inherent randomness of "dice rolls" determining every move would make the game feel random and unfun, but that's almost precisely what makes it so engaging. Your character builds all influence the bonuses your dice rolls get, so you actually have a lot of control. There are moments where you feel like the rolls are BS, but they're so rare, and they can make fights feel much more intense. Also, the fights can be LONG. I'm talking 10 minutes for basic encounters and upwards of 20 minutes for big ones.

Another expectation I had that was completely wrong was that it's an open world. The game is broken up into three "Acts", which can be anywhere from 30–60 hours each in a single run. Each act takes place on a fairly big map, but it's by no means an open world. This isn't a bad thing, and I really enjoyed exploring each area of every map to find encounters ranging from small scuffles to treasure hauls. They're very distinctly different from each other, too, so I never felt as though it was a repetitive cycle.

One thing I was slightly let down by was the fact that some builds just aren't viable long-term, so you can easily end up with characters who are frustratingly weak and others who are borderline broken, without intending any of it. Each class has multiple subclasses, and it's very intimidating at first to choose one based on its initial description, so you end up choosing something that sounds cool only to find out it sucks either in the short or long term. You can respec at any point, so it's not the end of the world, but it is a shame that I felt the classes aren't as balanced as they could be.

Without getting into spoilers, the main narrative focus of the journey you go on is more about getting to know each of the characters you end up having in your gang. The overarching goal is more of a motivator to keep the journey going rather than the main hook that will keep you invested. If I had to sum up my thoughts on each of the characters, they would be:

[spoiler]Astarion: Funny most of the time, but I found him to be too on the nose and in-your-face in terms of being a borderline villain. He has the funniest dialogue scene in the game in Act 1. I won't say what, but if you know, you know. I do like the conclusion to his quest a lot, but he feels very disconnected for most of the game.

Gale: Nerd emoji wizard. He feels more connected to the main story, and I did like having him in my party. No strong feelings towards him.

Lae'zel: Feels the most connected to the main narrative for most of the game, and is also one of the top contenders for my personal favourite. Her evolution as a character is definitely the most dramatic. I found her ignorance of the world and fight-or-die mentality very charming.

Karlach: Initially, I couldn't stand her. She talks like a modern-day, quippy millennial, and I hated it. She does have some of the most dramatic dialogue and a seemingly high-stakes story, but she doesn't have much to do for most of the game in terms of a personal story. I like her more dramatic moments, though, and she did end up growing on me.

Shadowheart: The other contender for my favourite of the gang. She is also very much tied to the main story in every act in the most significant way. Weirdly, she seems like the most normal and pragmatic of the bunch and is very easy to get along with.

Wyll: I found Wyll to be the polar opposite of Astarion, in that he's a goody-two-shoes, sometimes to an obnoxious degree. I liked his character, though, and the dilemma he finds himself in is a very cool twist for a hero-type character.
[/spoiler]

There are others who can join that I didn't mention, but they're not as deep as the main six and to be honest I didn't use them in my party so I can't comment. Each of the characters in your party reacts to your decisions in dialogue, and you actually learn a great deal about each one of them purely from the "X Approves/Disapproves" pop-up when you're in dialogue.

I honestly think Baldur's Gate 3 is a little overhyped, but that doesn't mean I don't love it. If you are a diehard RPG fan who wants the truest RPG experience possible, this is your game. Everything it tries to do, it succeeds at exceptionally well. One of the ending cutscenes is one of the most jaw-dropping things I've seen in a game. I won't say in what way.

If CD Projekt Red gave us The Witcher 3, then Larian Studios gave us its CRPG equivalent with Baldur's Gate 3. And I mean that as one of the highest compliments possible.

I was never into turn-based combat. In fact, I avoided the entire genre because I thought it wasn't my thing. Boy, was I wrong.

The combat and mechanics can feel overwhelming at first. I actually started on the lowest difficulty because I was so invested in the role-playing that I just wanted to keep the story moving. But here's the beauty of it: the game grows with you. In Act 1, you're figuring things out. In Act 2, you're discovering mechanics you didn't even know existed. By Act 3, you're still learning new tricks. And somehow, it never stops being rewarding.

But the real magic? The freedom.

Imagine the freedom of a CRPG combined with the cinematic presentation of a AAA RPG. Fully voiced conversations, incredible cutscenes, memorable companions, and a developer that seemingly thought of EVERYTHING.

Think of a ridiculous way to solve a quest? There's probably a way to do it. Wonder what happens if you betray someone, save someone, kill someone, or simply walk away? There's probably a dialogue, consequence, or entire story branch waiting for you.

This is ROLE-PLAYING in its purest form. Your companions, decisions, relationships, and even the smallest choices can shape your journey.

And by the time the credits roll, you're not thinking about uninstalling. You're thinking:

"What if I chose differently?"

"What if I brought another companion?"

"Wait... I could've done THAT?!"

The branching possibilities are practically an Elden Tree of their own, except every branch makes you want to start another 100-hour playthrough.

If turn-based combat is the only thing stopping you from playing Baldur's Gate 3, don't let it.

This review has spoilers.
Let me paint you a picture:

You're abducted by aliens and get probed. A little while after you escape, a voice inside your head that wasn't there prior to probing starts encouraging you to seek out other probes to shove inside yourself. Much literature is written about how bad being probed is, every medical professional you speak to agrees you should deprobe yourself pronto otherwise you'll die, and you start to suffer nightmares and have hallucinations.

You now have a choice:

a) listen to all of the information presented to you and attempt deprobing / do not engage with further probing

b) listen to the new voice in your head and continue collecting probes to insert into yourself in exchange for neat magic powers. When you use the probes, a little visual pops up of your brain turning to goo, but don't worry about that.

This is the core conundrum the game presents. Sell your body and soul for power, or abstain. Guess where it leads?

Nowhere. There's no negative outcome for sacrificing your humanity outside of a single pass/fail roll that you can reattempt via save/reload. If you fail, the worst that happens is a minor cosmetic change in the last leg of the game. Your choice to take the game's negative presentation of "probing" at face value actively makes your gameplay less varied by locking yourself out of a useful skill tree, and it has little to no bearing on the trajectory of the plot or the ending you receive.

This is BG3 in a nutshell: a strong opening that stumbles so hard in the final lap that it actively undermines everything that came before.

The combat is initially fun, but the encounter design and AI vulnerabilities frequently reward repetitive chokepoint kiting and leans heavily on initiative, leading to interesting encounters having a handful of solutions. 

Companions start interesting, until you find that each one you meet past the 4th got less and less dev time.

You get the point. 

The game is frontloaded, and the accolades it's had heaped upon it have set an extreamly high bar that it doesn't quite hit. It's a 7.5 out of 10 if you're cool with the plot kneecapping both itself and your agency in the final leg, a 6/10 if you value your cerebrum.

A final story: there's an eldritch chair a companion can sit on that is supposed to remove the probe. You can make a series of choices that result in the companion getting multiple permanent debuffs. The only way to cure the debuffs is convincing the companion, who is dogmatically opposed to probing, to accept a probing. If you don't, these debuffs will cripple them until the end of the game.

The length of time you allow a companion to sit in a chair has stronger ramifications than offering chunks of yourself up to a hive mind alien. That's BG3.

I've owned Baldur's Gate for just less than a year, and the first few times I tried the game it just didn't click. However, like many other titles this year I gave it another shot, and I really loved it this time around. The combat took a little getting used to, I've played so many other RPGs that the idea of frequent long rests was foreign to me (gotta keep the loot til you roll credits), but once I got past those obstacles I could finally get into the meat on the bones.

The best part of the game is easily the cast of characters, both in your party and spread throughout the world. Whilst at first very few of them really appealed to me, by the end of the game I loved almost every last one of them. Astarion, a character I heavily disliked initially, somehow ended up being my favourite character by the time I rolled credits - the writing is just really good when it comes to their development (depending on your choices, I'd assume), and of course the incredible voice acting only does further wonders (looking at you Samantha Béart). Of course, there's a few instances where dialogue doesn't account for some situations, and it can take you out of it (e.g., Astarion and Gale would pretend like they helped defeat the goblin camp in Act 1, yet I hadn't even recruited them until I was on my way back to the grove), but that's a small nitpick.

The story, whilst nothing special, is the perfect vessel for giving you both these incredible characters and their individual quest lines, and also allows for so much freedom of choice. It's truly remarkable how much you can truly unlock or miss all dependent on your choices and attributes. Of course, sometimes it might be frustrating to fail a roll and miss something, but once you get used to it you can really start enjoying it more. Save scumming is of course an option (though sometimes the terrible autosave is enough), but I found that it really just disrupts the flow of the game and I only ever used it if I was really getting sick of a quest.

As previously mentioned, the combat is quite fun but has a learning curve for sure. Spell slots and healing are all things that take some getting used to whilst you learn to rely more on short and long rests, but by the halfway point of act 1 you'll likely get the hang of it. That said, the combat does falter heavily in act 3, where encounters become these bloated hoards of enemies which are more frustrating than they are challenging, with lots of mechanics which just generally aren't fun to fight against no matter the build. It really takes you out of it, which isn't helped by the broken enemy AI you will typically encounter at this stage of the game - where enemies (including bosses) will freeze up and not do anything, dragging out fights and just ruining the moment completely.

There is one final complaint, and this one is the major one for me, but the autosaves just aren't good. It's too infrequent, and you will often find yourself loading a save about an hour old or longer when your party dies. It's frustrating, ruins the flow, and makes you care less and less about the quest you're doing. And boy did this happen a lot. F5 will be your most pressed key by the time credits roll, that I can assure you. You might also think you can save yourself the trouble by downloading an autosave improvement mod, but then you lose access to your achievements - which is a stupid rule for such a minor QoL mod, and I hate it every time games that do this, Cyberpunk now included as of update 2.5.

Despite my long rants about what I disliked, the game does offer so much that I really do recommend - a beautiful world full of so many interesting and unique characters, with thousands of possible ways to make your next play through different from the last.

I was going through my history of games I've played but never reviewed, and I honestly couldn't believe I never wrote anything about Baldur's Gate 3. I don't even know where to begin with this game. I genuinely can't put into words just how amazing the entire experience was.

The story, the gameplay, the characters, the world, the music, the exploration. Everything. It's one of those rare games where everything just comes together to create something truly special.

The amount of freedom you're given is incredible. Your choices actually matter, the world reacts to your decisions, and there are so many different ways to approach situations that it almost feels impossible to experience everything in a single playthrough. The writing is phenomenal, and the companions feel like actual people with their own personalities, struggles, and motivations. You genuinely become attached to them.

The combat is fantastic, too. Every encounter feels like a puzzle with multiple solutions, and the game constantly rewards creativity and experimentation. Even after spending countless hours playing, I was still discovering new things.

But what really sets Baldur's Gate 3 apart is how it makes you feel.

It's one of those games where, when the credits finally roll, you almost feel depressed because it's over. You've spent so much time in this world, getting to know these characters, making decisions, fighting battles, and experiencing this incredible adventure. And then suddenly, it's done. You sit there staring at the screen, not knowing what to do with yourself or what game could possibly come next.

Very few games have ever left me with that feeling. It's almost like saying goodbye to a group of friends after an unforgettable journey.

As much as I want to jump back in and experience it all over again, I'm actually going to give it a few years before I replay it. I want to forget as much as I can about the story, the characters, and all those little moments that made the game so special. I know I'll never be able to experience it for the first time again, but maybe if I give it enough time, some of those memories will fade just enough that I can rediscover a little of that magic. That's how much this game meant to me.

I could probably write pages about everything I loved, and it still wouldn't do the game justice.

Baldur's Gate 3 isn't just one of the best RPGs I've ever played. It's one of the greatest games I've ever experienced, period. I wish I could erase my memory of it just to experience it all over again for the first time.

[u] Negative remark [/u]
Yet, there is a major flaw, which poisons the thing - [b] Act 3 [/b]. Act 3 is a complete disaster, unless you are an assasin or stacked with void bombs from very first nautiloid location (these dismantle invisibility with ease).

[u] Details [/u]
Act 3 has quite serious issues with:
1. Gameplay - you came to city to kill. To kill a lot. Game doesn't allow negotiations there. Thus all perception and persuasion stuff are wasted points. 
1. P.s. I wonder if Orin was a right choice for a Bhaal chosen, as MC simply outperforms her. And if you are in tough situation - you are still supposed not to reason, but be stealthy and pick apart people one by one. 
1. P.p.s. At certain moment I was thinking I am playing turn-based Titan Quest.

2. Enemies invite you to cheese out the game and completely ruin the immersion. Your enemies are frenzy beggars with knifes, who survive simply by abusing invisibility (your potion of "see invisibility" is straight useless here, that's why use the void bombs) and having ablative armour (each layer of unstoppable nullifies all kind of damage, even psychic one). And there are lots of them of such kind. 
2. P.s. They grind down everything in matter of couple of turns - I have tried once to unleash beholder on them and bring in the steel watcher - it was very sorry sight.

3. Gale story breaks here, useless you pick a correct answers like in exam. "Let's be careful for a while and withhold information from Mystra" = "Gale, please become a god". That completely ruins all interactions with Raphael and his only meaningful quest "Fulfill the Deal". I guess the author, who was arranging it, wanted player to resort to P.1 and go kill him as well. Blood for the blood god I guess.

3. P.s. I defeated Brain without Gale. MC could have taken the crown. But "No, Gale gets it, cuz screw you, that's why." And thus I had to wrap up the game at the moment where he pops up out of nowhere and looks in the water. Softlock in its finest form. For first 90 hours I am thankful. But last 50 - I really regret them. 
3. P.p.s. (Tho, to end up on high note - Iron Throne heist, Gortash and Shadowheart act3 storybits were very decent... Let's agree then on 45 lost hours of my life).

A True RPG Masterpiece

After 70 hours, Baldur's Gate 3 has given me one of the most immersive RPG experiences I've ever had. The freedom to make choices, the consequences of those choices, and the incredible variety of ways to approach each situation make every playthrough feel unique.

The companions are one of the game's biggest strengths. Their personalities, personal stories, relationships, and interactions make you genuinely care about the characters traveling alongside you. The combat is also incredibly satisfying, rewarding strategy, creativity, and experimentation rather than simply having the strongest equipment.

The game isn't perfect, and the turn-based combat and overwhelming number of choices might not appeal to everyone. However, the storytelling, voice acting, world-building, and sheer freedom more than make up for it.

This game is simply amazing! It offers an incredible number of possibilities and storylines. Every character you create can experience a completely different adventure, and you can replay the game over and over in so many different ways that it never really feels like you're playing the same game twice.

The graphics are fantastic, the dialogue is clear, well-written, and, most importantly, changes depending on your choices, your companions, and the main character you decide to play. Every decision can have consequences throughout your adventure, making the game incredibly rich and immersive.

There is an enormous amount of content, countless places to explore, and so many different situations to experience. The sheer depth and variety of this game are truly impressive.

And let's not forget about the multiplayer experience, which is just as incredible! Playing with friends adds an entirely new dimension to the adventure. Everyone can make their own choices, approach situations differently, and sometimes create completely unexpected or hilarious moments. Whether you're exploring together, fighting side by side, or dealing with the consequences of someone else's questionable decisions, multiplayer makes the experience even more memorable. It's almost like discovering a whole new side of the game, and it makes every playthrough even more unique!

On the technical side, I haven't encountered any major bugs, or at least very few, and those were easily fixed. And if you've already spent countless hours enjoying the game, mods are there to help you rediscover it and experience what can sometimes feel like a completely new adventure!

This is a game with so many different layers. Even though the turn-based combat might seem unusual or even off-putting at first, it actually turns out to be one of the game's greatest strengths. It encourages you to think, experiment, and approach every battle in multiple ways.

I honestly can't wait to see what a potential Baldur's Gate 4 could bring, even if that probably won't happen anytime soon!

The game is absolutely worth its price, and I genuinely have nothing to complain about. Even when I try to be pessimistic and look for flaws, I struggle to find any.

An absolutely exceptional game that lives up to every expectation and deserves to be experienced by every gamer, even those who aren't usually fans of turn-based RPGs. Whether you play solo or with friends, you're in for an unforgettable adventure!

To be honest the hype around this game when it was released is what mostly got me so curious and made me add this game to my wishlist. Not to mention I like turn-based games too. However seeing the steep learning curve of its mechanics and the DND system (which I have ZERO idea of btw) made me put off buying the game until 2 years later. Bought the base game when it went on Steam sale but still did not play it until another year later (you know how it is). Finally decided to give it a try recently but I prepared myself first by watching no-spoiler gameplay tutorials on YT (which helped A LOT). I made sure to finish all of ACT 1 first 120 hrs later (I know, I like to take my time guys) before making this review, and now I realize how foolish it was of me to not have played this game sooner with everybody else! This game is awesome! I think I would best describe it as like playing turn-based Skyrim. It's like embarking on an adventure where you have no idea of the dangers that lies ahead - if people you meet along the way would be hostile or friendly; where caves or dungeons or even houses with hidden passageways will take you; if your choices will lead to good or bad consequences, etc. I also never expected the story to be this rich. Even the characters have very interesting backstories. I didn't even really like how they looked in the game posters or trailers but when I got to know them in game, I found myself liking all of them - and I mean all them that I don't want a single character to die in the journey. And don't get me started with the battles and the magic and all that good stuff. I always find myself torn on which among the party members I will take with me on the next mission (you can only take 3) or the next boss battle because all of them have different skills and strengths that you really can't go wrong with whoever you pick. Battles are so fun. My jaw would literally just drop when my Vengeance Paladin kills an enemy with a single blow, or if a character like Karlach lands 3 hits consecutively, killing the enemy in the process without even able retaliate. I can go on and on about how great this game is but I'm still a new adventurer. I'm just certain the battles will be harder and the story will get even better as I progress. But let me tell you right now, this is indeed a legit LABOR OF LOVE. You can just tell the scale of work, effort, and dedication that Larian Studios have poured into this game to make it the masterpiece that it is. It deserves the GOTY it won. It deserves the Overwhelming Positive reviews it continues to get to this day. As a small token of my appreciation I purchased the DLC at full price even when I didn't need to. I know it's not much, but it's my way expressing my gratitude to the team. I hope all developers set the bar high like you. I hope you have more success in your future games. And to the gamers still thinking of picking this up, JUST DO IT. Learning the game will be challenging at first especially if you have not played a DND title like myself, but it will all be so worth it once you get around all that. See you all in Baldur's Gate! More Than Just a Game — The End of a Legendary Era (1,100+ Hours Played)

I was only 4 or 5 years old when my dad let me play Grand Theft Auto V for the very first time on the PS3, and to this day, I still haven't forgotten the exact moment I hijacked a city bus and got into a fistfight with the bus driver in the middle of the street. Back then, the game felt so unbelievably massive, advanced, and hilarious that it completely blew my mind. Calling GTA V "just a video game" feels like an understatement. Without exaggeration, this is easily one of the most important, culture-defining milestones in the entire history of gaming—the ultimate dream game that every single kid grew up talking about at school and daydreaming of getting their hands on.

Nothing will ever quite replicate that magic of stepping into Los Santos for the first time. Loading into that sun-drenched metropolis felt like crossing into a living, breathing world that had no limits. Whether it was experiencing the iconic story of Michael, Franklin, and Trevor, cruising down the highway at sunset with the radio blasting, or exploring every single street corner from Vinewood Hills to Blaine County, this map holds countless core memories.

Don't let the 100 hours on my Steam profile fool you—that is just the victory lap. Before moving over to Steam, I poured a massive 1,000 hours into the Epic Games version. Across more than 1,100 hours in total, Los Santos has been more than a map; it has been a second home.

A huge part of those hours comes down to GTA Online—the ultimate sandbox for pure, unfiltered chaos. Some of the funniest, most unforgettable moments I've ever had in gaming came from just messing around in lobbies with friends late into the night, failing heists in the dumbest ways possible, launching cars off Mount Chiliad, or starting all-out wars on the streets for no reason at all. Even when playing completely solo, just hopping in to tune a car, test out ridiculous stunts, or cause five-star mayhem across the city was effortlessly entertaining every single time.

What makes writing this review today so surreal and bittersweet is knowing that this era is practically coming to an end. From my dad letting me fight a bus driver on the PS3 as a little kid to putting in over a thousand hours on PC—and with my dad now having GTA VI and an Xbox Series X waiting for the next chapter—Los Santos has truly been the ultimate playground for an entire generation. Now, as we stand right on the edge of leaving it all behind for Vice City, it finally hits you that these streets will soon become history.

If you were there for it, you know it wasn't just a game—it was an entire chapter of our lives. One last drive around the highway before the sun sets on Los Santos for good. 9.5/10 — A Generational Masterpiece.

Looking at my profile, the numbers lay out a 13-year journey: over 1,288 hours poured into the original Legacy edition, and another 114 hours spent in Enhanced. But no stat counter could ever capture what this world truly meant to me.

I picked up Grand Theft Auto V on the PS3 back in 2013 as an 18-year-old kid. Moving across three hardware generations—from PS3 to PS4 Pro, and finally to mouse and keyboard on PC—this game wasn't just entertainment running in the background. It became the soundtrack to my entire late teens and 20s.

I started at Level 0 with empty pockets. I made a promise to myself early on that I would never buy a single Shark Card, choosing instead to earn every dollar through pure hustle and heavy grinding. I worked my way up from stealing cars off the street all the way to Level 363. By the end, I built an empire from the ground up: the highest-end penthouses and properties, thriving businesses, a fully upgraded Nightclub, the galaxy super yacht, and garages packed with the finest vehicles in the game. Knowing that every single dollar, property, and car was bought with genuine sweat and hours of work made it all mean so much more.

Yet, the true soul of those 1,400+ hours was never about the assets—it was about the community. I ended up forming a tight-knit anti-griefing and grinding crew, introducing and bringing together a group of over eight amazing friends. We became an absolute force. I dedicated myself to mastering thermal scope sniping, perching high on urban rooftops to lock down entire blocks, dismantle jet grievers, and cover our flank from incredible distances. We fought intense, lobby-wide wars for the sole purpose of defending innocent crew members and securing high-stakes business sales so everyone could make their cash in peace. Those late-night sessions turned random usernames into genuine, unforgettable friendships.

Time moves on, life shifts, and the old squad has gone quiet. Today, after streaming one final peaceful ride, I gave the game the ultimate send-off. I took out my fireworks launcher and set off rockets over Franklin’s house, Michael’s mansion, and Trevor’s trailer out in Sandy Shores to pay homage to the story that started it all. Then, I climbed into my Hydra, took off, and flew one last low-altitude sweep through the skyscrapers of Downtown, banking over the mountains, and soaring out across the countryside.

No weapons drawn, no chaos, no grinding—just the jet engine roaring, the radio playing, and watching the sunset hit San Andreas one last time before parking the fleet for good.

To the squad who covered my flank, to the friends who rode shotgun, and to the city that watched me grow up: thank you. The story is complete. 10/10. End of an era.

[h1]Grand Theft Auto V Review[/h1]
[h3]★★★★[/h3]
[h2]Main Story[/h2]

[h3]Act 1: Jewelry Store Heist & Introductions[/h3]
GTA V starts off strong and throws us straight into the action with the prologue mission in North Yankton. This mission is filled with action and does a great job at introducing us to the game mechanics and also I have to say that I just absolutely love the snowy environment of this prologue mission. It is truly breathtaking and I wish we got to see more of it. Right after we finish the prologue mission we are introduced to my favorite character Franklin and we get to see how he and Micheal meet each other and throughout this first Act we get to see them grow closer. The relationship between Franklin and Micheal is honestly one of my favorite parts of this game and I think it is only second to the relationship between Franklin and Lamar. The big mission that this Act builds up to is the jewelry story heist and it does not disappoint. For being the first real heist we undertake in the game it is in my opinion the second best in the entire game. My one issue with this heist is more so an issue with all the heists in this game and that is that the heist setup missions can be kind of annoying at times and don't really intrigue me that much. They can kind of feel like a roadblock to the real fun stuff at times that being the actual heists. Even then though this first heist was an amazing experience and definitely a great way to introduce us to the heist mission structure. Right after the heist we take a step away from Micheal and Franklin and instead are finally formally introduced to Trevor Phillips. When it comes to Trevor's section there is only really one major thing that I didn't like and that was the setting. Other than that though Trevor’s section was really engaging and I liked almost all of his missions in this Act and the moment where he finally meets Micheal again is just so cool. Overall this first Act is extremely engaging and does a great job at setting up future plot points and really getting the story going. If I am being honest this first Act is probably my favorite overall, not because it has the coolest missions in the entire game but because it is such an amazing introduction to these characters and because it has the best average missions.

[h3]Act 2: Merryweather & Paleto Bay Heists[/h3]
The Second Act of GTA V is the worst one in my opinion. This Act follows Micheal, Franklin, and Trevor(Now a trio) as they are forced to work for the FIB Agent’s Steve Haines and Dave Norton and this act also includes the expected criminal shenanigans. Before I get into what I didn't like about this Act let me go over some of the positives. I loved that we finally got to see Micheal, Franklin, and Trevor work together to do jobs and we get to see the group dynamic rise and grow. I also liked most of the FIB agent stuff and I found Steve Haines to be a good Antagonist. Other than that thought I found the things in this Act to be either fine or bad. My main problem with this Act is the Trevor missions. I absolutely hated the whole Flyod plotline and doing the setup for the Merryweather heist was boring especially that one cargo mission. When it comes to the actual Merryweather heist my feelings are the same, this heist is by far my least favorite in the entire game. The reasons for this are because one we don't get anything out of this heist so all of the hard work he put in on the setup missions are useless, and two because the heist just feels like a filler heist to expand the runtime of the game. I honestly think that the writers were struggling to give Tevor something to do in Los Santos so they just created this heist and everything with Floyd. Thankfully there is the Paleto score to kind of balance out because that was a pretty good heist. Overall though this Act was just a downgrade for me and most of the big stuff that happened in this Act felt insignificant but on the bright side there were a lot of little pieces that were laid in this Act.

[h3]Act 3: Bureau Raid & The Truth[/h3]
I liked this section of the game. I would say that it is pretty good overall but it also has some high highs. This Act follows our trio as they are blackmailed by Steve Haines and Dave Norton into doing dirty high risk operations against their rival agency the IAA. We also get to see Trevor finally uncover the truth and confront Micheal in this Act but first lets talk about the FIB shenanigans. The FIB forces the group to go only many different raids, my favorite of which being the Bureau Raid. This is one of the only big moments in the game where the setups for it weren't that annoying mainly because they involved mopping floors. The actual Bureau raid itself though is just amazing. I took the explosive approach and I loved how the building looked when it was on fire and having to gun down men as you try and escape the burning building was the coolest action moment in the entire game for me. There is also the whole Devin Weston plotline which I found to be okay but sometimes I kind of wished it would just get to the point. I liked the character development of micheal and how he realized that he wanted his family. Then there is one of the best moments in the story which is when Trevor discovers that Brad is buried in Micheals grave and we see Micheal get kidnapped while Trevor starts to hate him. Prior to that though the characters also start scoping out the Union Depository. Overall this Act was a good continuation of the story and I enjoyed seeing tensions rise and our characters grow. 

[h3]Act 4: Ending[/h3]
GTA V’s final Act is where we get to see a lot of the previous setup be paid off and I would say I am mostly satisfied with its final Act but at the same time I don't have much to say about it. We get to free Micheal as Franklin and we get to see what I consider the climax of the whole government storyline at the Kortz Center where Trevor steps in to save Micheal. Then the trio decides to hit the Union Depository which is my favorite heist in the game even though some of those setup missions were annoying me. Then after we hit the UD we got the choice and for me there was only really one choice and that was C. The final mission of this game can only be described in one word and that is ICONIC. I will never forget the feeling I had when Trevor, Micheal, and Franklin pushed Devin's car off and then that music started playing and honestly I can't hear that song without feeling a little nostalgic. My one big issue with the Final Act of this game is that the ending does feel a little rushed with how they just kill all of the games Antagonist in one day like it was nothing but I am able to overlook that because of how much I enjoyed this final mission. Overall I think GTA V has one of the most iconic stories in all of gaming and for me whenever I hear GTA I will always think of this masterpiece. 

[h3]Online[/h3]
The vast majority of my playtime has gone to GTA online and I don't regret it because this game has one of the best online modes out there. It is pretty simple: you do missions and heists and work your way up from broke to rich. Most of said missions and heists are good but replaying them so many times for money does cause them to lose some enjoyment. GTA online has so many hours worth of content that at times it felt endless to me and honestly I just wish I was able to make more progress then I did before GTA 6. I will never forget my first 50 hours on this game just running around in online robbing gas stations and beating up NPC's. I kept trying, hoping that somehow, something would work. But eventually, I had to accept that it just wasn't going to happen. Honestly, my eyes are watery as I'm writing this. It might sound silly to some people, but this game meant a lot to me. I didn't need the best graphics or the highest frame rates. I just wanted to experience Los Santos, even if it meant playing at the lowest settings possible.
I even bought a controller just for this game. I was so excited to finally play it, and now I have to uninstall it without even getting to properly experience it.

I will mainly be talking about the single-player, so up to this day the GTA I liked the least among Vice City, IV and San Andreas I am not taking into account the 2D era. To begin, the story is heavily inspired by heist movies like Heat. You take control of three criminals who have to carry out a marathon of robberies against a backdrop of conflicts and unspoken tensions. The gameplay in the chase sequences is completely scripted. The story is simple and not memorable; the writing is decent, but we're still looking for iconic characters with cheeky lines. I wonder where Rockstar Games' humor has gone. The characters are all bland and lack personality; it's more hipster writing than what we're used to seeing.

The fact that you can play as three characters simultaneously is something I didn't like because it breaks a certain dynamic, and the characters are less developed. I'm not interested in playing as Franklin, who isn't developed at all. I was really disappointed by the lack of missions in his neighborhood and with his gang. He has an immeasurable lack of charisma. [spoiler]He's practically erased from the story. If I'd had the choice to kill him at the end, I would have chosen him without a doubt.[/spoiler] Trevor, on the other hand, is a good character that I wish I hadn't played as, but rather visited for missions. I compare him to Phil Cassidy, a bit of a crazy guy. Trevor was added during development, according to Dan Houser, there was no intention of controlling him. That shows how underdeveloped the story is. The real and best-developed character is Michael (inspired by Tony Soprano's life), the most interesting because he has a connection to the ghetto through Franklin and to the desert/country through Trevor. It's Michael who connects people; he's the most charismatic character and the one who truly carries GTA V, in addition to having impeccable voice acting. A GTA without DLC, with far less missions (79 missions) than San Andreas (101 missions) and GTA IV + DLCs (136 missions), a little over 10 more missions than Vice City (67 missions), a game from 2002. Isn't there a slight problem considering we play as three characters?

The late 2010s, with Rockstar Games and Take-Two influencing the video game world, marked the beginning of an era where studios focused on online play, where fewer and fewer people played single-player games. As a result, we ended up with games where single-player was neglected in favor of online mode, as perfectly exemplified by GTA V. In the 2000s, multiplayer appeared in the menu after the single-player campaign; today, games shove online mode right in your face. Studios that have become focused solely on online play, a lack of single-player DLC, microtransactions, endless updates, and an over-exploitation of online mode given the profit it generates. Red Dead Redemption 2 is the exception, but keep in mind that it's the only Rockstar game developed for 4th-generation consoles. The online mode was cool in the early years because it focused on creating lasting memories. You can't take that away from them.

But the writing is gone, the online experience has become terrible, and the people in charge of the script are a disgrace. It's worth noting that they censored original content from the solo; if you want to see the list, it's amusing. They believe they have the right to change the game because it is offensive. The fact that GTA is the most played and best-selling game of all time attracts people who don't intend to play a game, but to control it. So I'm asking for all the grafitti to be removed from the game because I feel bad against. Seriously, no jokes, this is getting ridiculous. It's the same reason I'm not playing the remastered versions of the 3D trilogy.

Rockstar Games has lost many people since its creation who were part of its DNA. I'm thinking of Dan Houser, Leslie Benzies, Jamie King, Terry Donovan, Lazlow Jones, Michael Unsworth, Rupert Humphries, David Jones, Obbe Vermeij ...

Grand Theft Auto V is essentially a "Tourism and City Planning" simulator, provided your idea of tourism involves stealing a jet from a military base and your idea of city planning is seeing how many fire hydrants you can knock over in a single block.

The game offers a touching story about three men who clearly need therapy but decide to commit multi-million dollar heists instead. You have Michael, a retired criminal who is essentially a grumpy dad in a fancy house; Franklin, the only person in the city with a functioning brain cell; and Trevor, a human hurricane who looks like he was raised by a pack of caffeinated coyotes.

The real magic, however, is the AI. There is nothing quite like the joy of driving a supercar at 120 mph through a crowded street, only for a random pedestrian to step in front of you, survive the impact, and then scream at you as if you were the one being unreasonable.

It is a masterpiece of open-world design that asks the important question: "How many different types of vehicles can I possibly crash into a swimming pool?" 5/5 stars. I have committed several thousand felonies and I feel great.

A Masterpiece That Made My Childhood - GTA V Review
GTA V has always had a special place in my heart. As a kid, I remember endlessly watching GTA V videos on YouTube, dreaming of playing it myself. Back then, I could only jump in occasionally through an old shared account just to mess around in GTA Online and do a few heists with friends.

Now, years later, I finally bought the game on my own Steam account and decided to complete the main story for the very first time before GTA VI arrives. It took me 26 solid hours to beat the campaign—I rushed through it a bit because I already knew most of the cutscenes from watching videos so many times over the years. But experiencing it myself was a completely different feeling.

Even though it’s been years since its release back in 2013, and even though I played the Legacy version, the graphics still look absolutely incredible to this day.

I love all three main characters—Michael, Trevor, and Franklin. The dynamic between them is unforgettable. Even though Trevor and Michael fight like an old married couple half the time, they always have each other's backs when it matters most. That’s why choosing Option C (The Third Way) was the only right decision for me. Seeing all three of them stand together until the end was pure satisfaction.

I could write so much more about this game, but I’ll leave it at this. No matter how many games with insane graphics come out in the future—even when GTA VI finally drops—GTA V will always hold a unique place for me. The ability to seamlessly switch between three main characters during missions, planning your own heist approaches, and controlling each character in different tactical roles—like Franklin on the sniper, Michael handling the heavy action, Trevor flying the helicopter, or Franklin controlling the traffic lights—made the gameplay mechanics truly special. Those seamless transitions made the action scenes feel like an absolute movie—at times, I genuinely couldn't tell if I was playing a game or watching a blockbuster film. Combined with the nostalgia, excitement, and pure happiness it brought back from my childhood, GTA V will forever remain irreplaceable.

[h1]GTA V — Crime Pays. Apparently, So Does Great Storytelling.[/h1]

A game where you can rob banks, outrun the police, cause absolute chaos, and turn some poor driver's commute into the worst day of their life. And somehow, underneath all that glorious criminal nonsense, there's a genuinely great story.

[b]THE STORY — THREE PSYCHOPATHS, THREE ENDINGS, ONE HELL OF A RIDE[/b]

What I love most about GTA V is its single-player campaign. The three protagonists give the story a fantastic dynamic, each bringing their own personality, problems, and questionable approach to conflict resolution.

The campaign is long enough to really sink your teeth into, without feeling like it's dragging things out just for the sake of playtime. And having three different endings depending on your choices gives the finale some real weight. You actually have to decide how you want things to end.

Well, sort of. This is GTA, after all. The line between a thoughtful moral decision and shooting your way out of another disaster is remarkably thin.

[b]THE GAMEPLAY — A MASTERCLASS IN BAD DECISIONS[/b]

The gameplay is just plain fun. Whether you're following the story, exploring the world, or spontaneously stealing someone's car and running them over with it, there's always something to do.

Is it morally questionable? Absolutely.

Is it entertaining? You bet.

Sometimes the most poetic form of storytelling is punching a man out of his own vehicle and turning him into a speed bump. Shakespeare could never.

[b]THE GRAPHICS — OLD, BUT STILL HOLDING UP[/b]

GTA V has certainly aged, but its graphics are still good. Not breathtaking by today's standards, but the world remains convincing, detailed, and enjoyable to explore. It doesn't need to look cutting-edge to deliver a memorable experience.

[b]THE ONLINE MODE — NOT MY CRIME SCENE[/b]

GTA Online never really clicked with me. I know plenty of people love it, but it simply isn't what I came to GTA V for. The single-player campaign is where the game truly shines for me, and that's where I spent my time.

[b]THE VERDICT[/b]

GTA V delivers a fantastic story, memorable characters, satisfying gameplay, and a lengthy campaign with choices that make the ending feel personal. Even years later, it's still an absolute blast.

I swear to fucking God, this game is not a shooter. It's a psychological experiment conducted by Valve to find out how much human suffering one person can take before their brain starts leaking out of their ears.

You wake up. You make coffee. You feel good. Maybe today is the day. Maybe today you'll finally have a normal match. You launch CS2, queue Premier, and within 30 seconds some guy with 4 hours in the game is already explaining how your mother works.

First round: teammate dies in 3 seconds.
Second round: another teammate disconnects.
Third round: some 14-year-old starts screaming into a microphone that sounds like it was manufactured inside a washing machine.
Fourth round: you get headshot through smoke by a guy who apparently has the fucking CCTV footage of your entire apartment.

And the cheaters. OH MY FUCKING GOD, THE CHEATERS.

Sometimes I wonder if I'm playing Counter-Strike or attending a convention for people who downloaded their reflexes from a suspicious Russian website. You check the demo and suddenly the enemy knows your exact location, your plans for tomorrow, and what you had for breakfast. VAC is there, of course. Watching. Thinking. Probably taking a fucking nap.

Then there's hit registration. You shoot a guy 14 times, hear the bullets connect, see blood, and somehow he survives with 100 HP. Meanwhile, the enemy looks at your general direction and you instantly get sent back to the main menu. Very realistic. Very competitive. My bullets are apparently decorative.

Your teammates deserve their own documentary. One guy is AFK, one is playing with his feet, one is screaming at everyone, and the last one has 3 kills after 20 rounds but keeps telling you how to play. You lose 13-2, everyone blames everyone, and somehow the guy who bottom-fragged is the first one to type "ez".

And Premier? Beautiful. A magical place where matchmaking brings together people with completely different skill levels, mental conditions, and definitions of the word "teamwork". You can win five games in a row and then get matched against a squad that looks like they have been training for the CS Olympics since birth.

The penalties are another masterpiece. Your internet disconnects? Cool, enjoy your cooldown. Your teammate kicks you for fun? Cool, enjoy your cooldown. Something goes wrong with the match? Somehow, congratulations, you're the criminal now. Apparently leaving a broken match is a greater offense than making the match unbearable in the first place.

But hey, at least we have skins! Beautiful skins. Expensive skins. Shiny skins. I may have lost my sanity, my rank, my friends, and my will to live, but at least my AK-47 has a nice paint job. Priorities, gentlemen.

And the worst part? The game itself is actually fucking brilliant. The gunplay, the maps, the clutch moments, the sound of a perfectly timed headshot. Nothing feels quite like winning a 1v3 and hearing your teammates suddenly remember how to speak English.

That's why I keep coming back. Not because I'm having fun. Not because I enjoy it. I think at this point I'm just emotionally attached to the suffering.

Los gráficos son buenos, las mecánicas son increíbles, el balance es discutible y tu salud mental es completamente irrelevante para los desarrolladores.

Lo mejor: Es gratis.

Lo peor: También es gratis, así que no tienes excusa para escapar.

Veredicto final: 10/10. Lo odio con toda mi alma. Mañana vuelvo a jugar.

Dota 2 is a great MOBA that's being held back by nothing more than its player base and mediocre management.

Before you're allowed to play ranked, you're forced to endure 100 hours of unranked matchmaking. Doesn't sound too bad in theory, until you realize that unranked is essentially a free-for-all with absolutely no standards.

You'll be matched with players who can barely manage to breathe without choking on their own saliva, as well as players with over 7,000 games under their belts. You'll encounter smurfs and players who don't care about winning. Not necessarily because they don't want to win, but because they refuse to learn, hiding behind the classic excuse: "It's unranked, bro."

While unranked isn't something you're supposed to take particularly seriously, when you're still grinding through those 100 hours, you don't really have a choice. You're effectively being held hostage by people who have absolutely no respect for your time.

Furthermore, there isn't a single good region to play in, as each one comes with its own unique brand of toxicity.

Play on EU East, and you'll be greeted by four egotistical morons suffering from main character syndrome, who refuse to play support and wouldn't buy a ward to save their lives.

Play on EU West, and you'll be met with four misfits who refuse to communicate in English.

Play on NA, whether East or West, and there's a 50% chance your match will contain bots. And no, I'm not talking about Valve's bots. I'm talking about mediocre, third-rate scripts that run down lanes and die repeatedly.

"Are you sure they're not just new, bad players?"

Yes, I am. Every single one of these bots follows the same naming conventions and behavioral patterns: "AdjectiveName####", usually accompanied by a QR code or a picture of a girl as their profile picture. They also constantly spam chat wheel emotes, making them about as subtle as a brick through a window.

And the saddest part of all this is that the game itself is genuinely fantastic.

When you find yourself in a match with nine other like-minded individuals who have even a shred of competitive spirit and genuinely want to win, there's no other game that comes close to the satisfaction of winning an intense, hour-long match of Dota.

The hero design is amazing, the mechanics are smooth and satisfying, and the items are meaningful, often fundamentally changing how you approach and play the game. There's an incredible amount of depth here, and very few games can deliver the same experience.

People often say that Valve doesn't care. Personally, I think Valve is ashamed of its own creation and, more importantly, the community it has cultivated.

I would pay every cent I have, and every cent I will ever earn, just to gather the entire player base into one gigantic trebuchet and launch them into shark-infested waters.

Welcome to the Never-Ending Game.

Dota 2 is a strange place.

You enter looking for entertainment, spend hundreds of hours trying to understand it, thousands more trying to master it, and eventually realize that you might never truly understand it.

It's a game where five strangers are expected to work together like a perfectly coordinated team, where one tiny mistake can destroy a 60-minute match, and where the difference between an absolute genius and a complete fool is sometimes just one decision.

Every hero has a story. Every item has a purpose. Every match has its own chaos.

You can experience the most incredible comeback of your life, followed immediately by a defeat so ridiculous that you start questioning your existence.

There are beautiful moments hidden between all the madness. A perfectly executed team fight, a game-winning Black Hole, an unexpected Rampage, or that one teammate who actually knows what they're doing.

And then there is the other side of Dota 2...

The toxicity, the endless arguments, the questionable decisions, the matchmaking, and the occasional feeling that the entire universe is personally against you.

Yet, somehow, you keep coming back.

Maybe it's the complexity. Maybe it's the competition. Maybe it's the satisfaction of finally pulling off something you've been practicing for weeks.

Or maybe we've all just lost our minds.

Dota 2 isn't a game you simply finish. It's a journey with no final destination, where even after thousands of hours, there is still something new waiting to surprise you.

You don't always win. You don't always improve. Sometimes you don't even enjoy playing.

But when everything comes together, there is nothing quite like it.

**A beautiful disaster. An endless obsession. A game unlike any other.**

Would recommend. 10/10.

Dota 2(도타 2)는 밸브 코퍼레이션(Valve Corporation)이 개발하고 유통하는 PC용 AOS(MOBA) 장르의 멀티플레이어 온라인 전략 게임이다. 워크래프트 III: 레인 오브 카오스와 그 확장팩 더 프로즌 쓰론의 유저 제작 지도(유즈맵)인 'DotA(Defense of the Ancients)'를 정식 후속작으로 계승하여 제작되었다.

게임플레이

각 매치는 5명으로 구성된 두 팀이 맞붙는 방식으로 진행된다. 플레이어는 각각 고유한 능력과 능력치, 플레이 스타일을 가진 120여 명의 '영웅(Hero)' 중 하나를 선택해 제어한다. 한 팀은 빛의 진영인 '레디언트(Radiant)', 다른 한 팀은 어둠의 진영인 '다이어(Dire)'가 되어 경기하며, 게임의 최종 목표는 자신의 기지를 방어하면서 상대 진영의 본진 중심 건물인 '고대 요새(Ancient, 한국 내 유저 호칭: 본진/네서스)'를 먼저 파괴하는 것이다.
플레이어는 경기 내에서 미니언 역할의 컴퓨터 캐릭터(크립)나 적 구조물, 적 영웅을 처치하여 경험치와 골드를 획득하고 영웅을 성장시켜야 한다. 획득한 골드로 영웅의 스탯을 올리거나 특수 능력을 부여하는 아이템을 구매할 수 있다. 도타 2는 완전한 무료 공개(Free-to-Play) 모델을 채택하고 있어 모든 영웅을 처음부터 무료로 플레이할 수 있으며, 유료 결제 요소는 게임의 밸런스에 영향을 주지 않는 캐릭터 외형 꾸미기 아이템이나 패스 상품 등으로만 제한된다

It's basically the exact same thing that happened with War Thunder. They kept loosening things up until the whole game turned into a complete circus. From the perspective of a picky online gamer, the game is simply shit.

I've played PUBG since before its full release. I have over 4,000 hours on both accounts.

That number means something. It means I didn't just try PUBG and move on. I stuck with it. I came back to it. I played it through bad patches, bad performance, cheaters, bugs, questionable decisions, and years of frustration. A lot of those hours were with friends, especially over the last three years after taking a long break.

And honestly? That is the part that hurts.

Was PUBG good when it first came out? Not really. It looked rough, ran badly, and often felt like it was barely holding itself together. But it was fun. It had something special.

Did it get better when it went free-to-play? A little, maybe. But not enough. The bugs stayed. The cheaters multiplied. The game kept finding new ways to disappoint you. And still, I kept playing, because despite everything, I was having fun with my friends.

Over the years, I watched PUBG slowly turn more and more into a cash grab. Season passes, collaborations, skin boxes, endless cosmetics, monetization everywhere. The soul of the game started to feel buried under all of it.

But I still played.

Not because the game deserved endless forgiveness, but because the moments with friends were worth it.

Every few matches, you run into someone who is very obviously cheating. Not “maybe they’re just good” cheating. I mean the kind where everyone in the squad goes quiet because we all know exactly what just happened. Did that make me quit? No. We complained, we sighed, we queued again.

And the worst part? That anti-cheat still doesn't seem to stop the most blatant cheaters. But somehow the people ruining matches every day are still there.

I tolerated a lot.

Cheaters? Fine, queue again.

Bugs? Annoying, but whatever.

Bad performance? Been there before.

Greedy monetization? Disappointing, but not surprising anymore.

I kept making excuses for this game because I wanted to enjoy it with my friends.

But now I can't even reliably open it.

That is where it finally breaks me.

Sometimes I get lucky and reach the lobby. We queue, we play a match, maybe we win, maybe we lose. And then the real game begins trying to get PUBG to work again. My friends sit there waiting while I restart, relaunch, crash, fail to load, get stuck, or hope that this attempt will be the one that actually lets me back in.

Thirty minutes can disappear just trying to enter the lobby of a game that is almost ten years old.

And what makes it even worse is that this does not seem to be some brand-new, isolated issue. You can find people talking about this on Reddit, Steam, and other platforms for months now. Around three months of players reporting the same kind of problem, and still there has been no real acknowledgement.

Not a fix. Not a workaround. Not even a simple message saying, “Hey, we know something is wrong and we’re looking into it.”

Just silence.

That silence is what really kills any remaining goodwill. Bugs happen. Technical problems happen. But when a game has been around this long, and when players are clearly struggling just to launch and play it, pretending the problem does not exist feels insulting.

PUBG has been around long enough. It has made enough money. It has had enough time. And somehow, after all these years, it still feels like the developers never managed to turn it into the game it should have become.

I didn't quit because I stopped caring.

I quit because I cared for too long, and PUBG made that feel pointless.

I play PUBG with my friend to relax my mind after a long day.

And somehow this game has managed to turn “relaxing with a friend” into a full-time anger management course.

Nothing is more peaceful than dropping into a city, spending 15 minutes looting, finding absolutely everything except the one gun you need, and then getting sent back to the lobby by a guy sitting in a bathroom since 2014.

The aiming system deserves a special award.
The aim does not aim.

You move your mouse 2mm and your crosshair decides to explore the entire map. Trying to control the aim feels less like playing a shooter and more like negotiating with a wild animal.

Enemy: standing completely still.
Me: 640 hours of experience.
My crosshair: “Interesting. I think I’ll look at the sky.”

And recoil? Absolutely beautiful. I shoot at someone and my gun immediately applies for a NASA internship.

The best part is when you finally get good loot, good positioning, full health, perfect attachments and enough confidence to believe you're actually good at the game...

BOOM.

Dead.

From somewhere approximately 17 kilometers away by a player whose entire strategy was apparently “sit down and wait for someone to have fun.”

Teammates are another amazing feature. My friend and I queue together for some peaceful gaming, only to spend the next 30 minutes arguing over who stole whose ammo, who drove us into a tree, and why neither of us has a first-aid kit despite looting an entire hospital.

Then comes the circle.

Because apparently walking peacefully toward the safe zone would be too enjoyable. Instead, the game watches you carefully calculate your route and says:

“No.”

Now you're sprinting across an open field while 14 people are shooting at you, your teammate is 800 meters away looting a frying pan, and your character has decided that climbing a tiny rock is apparently impossible.

Cheaters? No no, they're just incredibly talented professional athletes.

Getting one-tapped? Skill issue.

Bullets not registering? Internet issue.

Aim going everywhere except the enemy? Feature, not a bug.

Dying after 25 minutes? Free meditation session.

And somehow, after all of this, I still launch another game.

That's the real achievement of PUBG: making me hate the game while simultaneously making me press “Play Again.”

I don't play PUBG because it's relaxing.

I play PUBG because apparently my brain believes getting shot by a 14-year-old hiding behind a bush is cheaper than therapy.

Playing with my friend is the only reason this game survives on my PC. Without him, I'd probably uninstall it.

With him, I uninstall it, restart Steam, stare at the desktop for 30 seconds, and reinstall it.

10/10. Terrible game. Fantastic memories. Would suffer again.

Apex Legends is one of the greatest battle royale games ever created. Since its release in 2019, it has captured the attention of millions of players around the world. Developed by Respawn Entertainment, Apex Legends offers an exciting combination of fast-paced action, teamwork, strategy and unique characters. What makes the game so special is that it is not just another battle royale where players simply run around and shoot each other. Instead, it creates an experience where every match feels different, every decision matters, and every victory feels rewarding. From its amazing movement mechanics to its memorable characters and competitive gameplay, there are countless reasons why Apex Legends is such a fantastic game.

One of the biggest reasons Apex Legends is so great is its movement system. Unlike many other battle royale games, Apex Legends allows players to move around the map quickly and smoothly. Sliding down hills, climbing walls, jumping across buildings and escaping dangerous situations makes the gameplay incredibly enjoyable. The movement mechanics give players the freedom to approach fights in different ways and make every battle exciting. Learning how to move effectively can take time, but once players understand the mechanics, the game becomes even more satisfying. There is nothing better than successfully escaping a difficult fight using clever movement or outplaying an opponent with a perfectly timed slide and jump.

Another reason Apex Legends stands out is its huge variety of unique Legends. Each character has their own personality, abilities and playstyle, meaning that players can find a character that suits them. For example, Wraith is excellent for players who enjoy moving quickly and escaping dangerous situations, while Gibraltar is perfect for players who prefer protecting their teammates. Pathfinder allows players to travel across the map using his grappling hook, while Bloodhound helps the team locate enemies. These different abilities make the game more interesting because every team can have a different strategy. The characters also have entertaining personalities, interesting backgrounds and memorable voice lines that make the Apex Legends universe feel alive.

Teamwork is another major part of what makes Apex Legends such an incredible game. Unlike games where players can easily succeed on their own, Apex Legends encourages players to work together. Communicating with teammates, sharing equipment, reviving fallen players and planning attacks are all important parts of winning. The ping system is especially impressive because it allows players to communicate without needing a microphone. Players can mark enemies, point out useful equipment and suggest locations with just a few clicks. This makes teamwork easier and creates a more welcoming experience for people who might not want to use voice chat. Winning a match with friends after working together as a team is one of the most satisfying feelings the game can offer.

The weapons in Apex Legends also deserve recognition. The game includes a wide selection of guns, each with different strengths, weaknesses and firing styles. Whether someone prefers using an assault rifle, shotgun, sniper rifle or submachine gun, there is something for everyone. Weapons such as the R-301 Carbine, Peacekeeper and Wingman have become favourites among many players because of their unique designs and satisfying gameplay. Learning how to control recoil, aim accurately and choose the right weapon for different situations adds another layer of skill to the game. The weapon variety also means that players must constantly adapt depending on what equipment they find during a match.

Furthermore, Apex Legends has some incredibly well-designed maps. Locations such as World's Edge, King's Canyon and Olympus each provide different environments and opportunities for players. Some areas encourage intense close-range fights, while others are better suited to long-distance battles and strategic positioning. The maps contain interesting buildings, hidden areas, open spaces and different routes that players can use to their advantage. Over time, map changes and new locations help keep the experience fresh. Exploring these environments and discovering new strategies makes every match feel like a different adventure.

Another fantastic feature of Apex Legends is its competitive nature. The ranked system gives players something to work towards and allows them to test their abilities against opponents of similar skill levels. Climbing through the ranks requires patience, practice, communication and determination. Every match provides an opportunity to improve, whether that means getting better at aiming, learning when to attack or understanding when it is smarter to retreat. Although ranked matches can sometimes be frustrating, achieving a new rank after hours of hard work makes the experience worthwhile. The competitive scene also gives talented players an opportunity to showcase their skills through tournaments and professional esports competitions.

Apex Legends is also an enjoyable game because of its constantly changing content. New seasons introduce different updates, balance changes, events and sometimes entirely new Legends. These updates give players reasons to return and experience something different. The developers have continued to expand the game since its release, helping it remain an important part of the battle royale genre. Seasonal events and cosmetic items also allow players to customise their experience and show off their favourite characters. While not every update is perfect, the ongoing development helps keep the game interesting.

Of course, one of the best things about Apex Legends is the unforgettable moments it creates. Whether it is winning a match with only a few seconds remaining, getting an incredible squad wipe, reviving a teammate at the perfect moment or defeating an entire team against overwhelming odds, the game constantly creates exciting memories. These moments are what keep players coming back. Even when a match ends in defeat, there is usually something to learn or improve before the next game. Playing with friends makes these experiences even better because every victory, mistake and hilarious moment becomes something to remember.

In conclusion, Apex Legends is an outstanding game because of its incredible movement, unique characters, exciting weapons, detailed maps, competitive gameplay and emphasis on teamwork. It offers an experience that is difficult to find in other battle royale games. Although it can sometimes be challenging and frustrating, these difficulties make winning even more rewarding. The combination of skill, strategy and teamwork ensures that no two matches are exactly the same. Whether someone is a casual player looking to have fun with friends or a competitive player trying to reach the highest rank, Apex Legends has something to offer. Its exciting gameplay and unforgettable moments are what make it such a brilliant game and one of the best battle royale experiences available.

I am suprised that this game is still going 7 years after release. Like, I haven't met anyone mention this game just casually and yet this game is the 25th most played game on Steam! I played Apex Legends AGES ago, back when they still had gold armor and helmets. So when this game started appearing on my Instagram showing clips of people clutching the most unclutable fights, pulling some random bullshit movement tech that just breaks everyones ankles, or rizzing up japanese baddies? I knew I had to redownload and give this game a proper go!

It was quite suprising for me when I got into my first game back as a lot of things had been added or changed/reworked so I did have to spend some time learning new mechanics, but they were explained pretty well and or pretty simple to use. I remember struggling on the mantle boost but after a few games I had it down to a T and felt pretty good whenever I was able to hit it. So was I able to hit some crazy clips? YES SIR!! I've had a few clutch moments and let me tell you the dopamine high was immaculate, I swear my brain shortcircuited at least once during my time playing this game due to how crazy these fights get. I didn't really get much movement tech down but what I was able to achieve was pretty fun, and I wasn't able to rizz up any japanese baddies, so no tsundere girlfriend for me. But that doesn't matter that much.

I think Apex Legends does a pretty good job at achivements, as a majority of them insentivise you to give each Legend a proper go, and the rest are just unlocked naturally through playing the game. Which was great, as I didn't feel like I was doing a chore and instead was enjoying the game. The only achievement I had to go out of my way for was [b] Decked Out [/b] which is a lot harder to get due to gold armour and helment not existing anymore, but after that? It was just smooth sailing. I felt like I gave every Legend a good chance and got to try a variety of diffrent weapons to see what I liked/didn't like. Speaking of weapons, the gunplay in this game is so satisfying. Each weapon sounds so crisp and you can feel the feedback of each bullet hitting your target. The sound effects are also really good too and you can easily tell what is happening (sometimes) during a fight. My personal favourite weapons are the R-301 Carbine, Volt, Prowler, EVA-8 Auto, Peacekeeper and Triple Take. Each of these weapons both sound good and feel good to hit someone with.

Apex Legends was definitely a suprisingly fun experience for me, from wiping out squads solo to winning games, no matter what happens you will definitely have a good time. The acheivements although quite boring in nature, were pretty much perfect and to me, felt like an obligation to try out each Legend at least once. I even got a heirloom too! Which was the last thing I was expecting to get while playing this game LMAO. So I do think that I was able to experience everything that this game has to offer and I wouldn't mind playing this game again sometime. On a small note, I won the last game that I played as I hit level 50 which feels like the perfect end to my journey for now. Great game, great gunplay, great movement, no tsundere girlfriend.
