This title used to be spectacular around the release period, and for the first year-ish of support, it seemed like they had something that could really stand up to Fortnite.

Around the time of the Loba update, cracks started to show, and I fear it's only gotten worse since then.  The game feels like the developers are sort of directionless... with the worst feature creep I've ever seen in a live-service title, bloated UI/UX, and a storefront tab that's dishearteningly massive.

Playlists are split in 4-5 different directions, and getting a successful match takes a bit of time... which wouldn't be a problem if the TTK wasn't so low.  At first, this trait of the game was what drew me to it, but now it only serves to FRUSTRATE, as the game bombards you with post-match info, several click-through boxes, and multiple button presses to just RETURN TO THE LOBBY.  Oh my god, please, just let me go back to re-queuing solo as fast as possible.

In a match itself, it's a cluster of things /happening/, constantly.  You have EVO Harvesters.  You have upgrade stations.  A ton of different ways to gear up... but all this does is confuse me and make me feel lost.

The skill floor is very high, too.  This wouldn't really be an issue if the game tracked MMR in a reasonable way, but it's still using statistical data from when I was playing it actively in 2019-2021.  It's been five years.  It's still matching me in a rank far beyond what I'm capable of now.  Trying to re-enter it is an exercise in utter frustration.

Due to these factors, getting +2 friends together to /try/ and play it is impossible.  Nobody wants to come back to it.  Even as they fix broken systems and other bugs, it feels like the game is desperate for your money & your attention.

I can only see myself coming back if they reduced the amount of systems bloat.

Rockstar Games: Beautiful Worlds Ruined by Frustrating Game Design

Rockstar has become exceptionally good at creating beautiful, believable worlds, but somewhere along the way, it seems to have forgotten what makes an open-world game enjoyable to actually play.

GTA V and Red Dead Redemption 2 are impressive technical achievements. Their environments, attention to detail, animations, characters, and environmental storytelling are incredible. But all of that effort is undermined by one enormous problem: the games constantly fight against the player instead of allowing the player to enjoy and interact with the worlds they've created.

The biggest issue is the complete disconnect between what the world visually communicates and what the game actually allows you to do.

You see something interesting and want to investigate it. You find an object and reasonably expect to interact with it. You encounter a situation and naturally come up with a solution. But instead of allowing you to participate organically, the game throws arbitrary restrictions in your way.

A perfect example is seeing a shovel sitting five feet away from something you need to dig. Any reasonable person would pick it up and use it. But Rockstar's design philosophy often turns something that should be a simple interaction into an unnecessarily complicated sequence involving specific mission triggers, designated objects, scripted dialogue, or some predetermined mechanic that you have to discover before the game will let you proceed.

Why?

Why create a world full of objects, characters, buildings, and environmental details if the player can't interact with them in ways that make logical sense?

This problem becomes even worse during story missions. You can understand the objective perfectly, know exactly what you want to do, and still fail because you didn't approach from the correct direction, follow the exact route, trigger the correct dialogue, or perform the action in the precise sequence the developers scripted.

At that point, you're not playing an open-world game. You're following stage directions.

It's especially frustrating when the game creates a cinematic situation that looks like an opportunity for natural player interaction, only to turn it into a restrictive, heavily scripted experience. You spend more time figuring out what Rockstar wants you to do than actually enjoying the scene.

And then there's the obsession with contextual animations. Every little interaction becomes a drawn-out process. Picking something up, opening something, moving through an environment, interacting with characters. The animations might look impressive, but when responsiveness and player control are sacrificed for cinematic presentation, the experience becomes tedious.

Realism should enhance gameplay, not become an excuse for making basic interactions unnecessarily frustrating.

This is what makes the whole thing so disappointing. Rockstar clearly has the talent, technology, and resources to create extraordinary worlds. But they repeatedly undermine those accomplishments by restricting the player's ability to experience them naturally.

Compare that with Cyberpunk 2077. Night City makes me feel like I'm actually participating in a living world. I can explore, investigate, interact, approach situations differently, and feel like my character belongs there. The experience feels much more accommodating to the player rather than constantly demanding that the player accommodate the developers' scripting.

A beautiful world is worthless if interacting with it feels like a chore.

I don't want every interaction to be a cutscene. I don't want every objective to have only one acceptable solution. I don't want to spend my time fighting arbitrary mechanics, memorizing scripted sequences, or looking up how the developers intended me to walk, talk, blink, and breathe.

I want to play the game, not negotiate with it.

Rockstar needs to understand that immersion isn't just about realistic graphics, detailed animations, impressive NPC routines, or cinematic storytelling. Immersion also comes from freedom, responsiveness, logical interactions, and the ability to make decisions without constantly being punished for not following an invisible script.

If I see a shovel, let me use the damn shovel. If I find a reasonable way to accomplish something, let me try it. If I want to explore something interesting, don't make me wait until some arbitrary mission unlocks the ability to interact with it.

Stop building worlds that look alive but constantly remind the player that they're trapped inside a scripted video game.

Rockstar's worlds deserve better gameplay than this. And frankly, so do the players.

The developers of RDR2 focused much on achieving a realistic, breathing world. Sometimes to the point of being boring... since we don't want to play games to see our (sometimes) "boring" own world reflected back to us. Still, most of the time it's fun to see a person being thrown back realistically when you run full speed towards them or to stalk prey that is approaching the bait you put out - and consequently skin and roast it.

The story for me seems a bit dull - a typical bandit gang story - despite many folks praising it. Also it is unbelievably dragged-out, to the point of leading to none of the people I know finishing it. After playing for 48 hours, I'm somewhere at the half of the story, albeit playing slow and exploratively. The physics and world simulation again are very good and you sometimes discover that you spent half an hour playing around with stuff, lassoing animals or learning about new game that you just killed.

And, of course: gunfights. No western is full without the good ol' revolver and dozens of bodies hitting the floor. To the demise of the game, it stops there: most shootouts are repetitive and become stale quick. It also doesn't help that most of the missions involve the good old GTA1-2-3-4 formula: go to point A, kill some bastards, then go to point B or home. To be fair, it's still much more enjoyable than in the aforementioned games, due to the realistic world physics, ragdolls and somewhat realistic shooting mechanics. Also, you can switch between 1st and 3rd person any time.

Luckily, RDR2 is one of the most modding friendly games, and some of its cons can instantly be redeemed while expanding gameplay.

All in all, for me it would have been a near perfect game if the story was shorter and less dragged-out, with more unique missions and a little more interesting gunfights. In its defense, this is set in 1901 and not in the 2000s where you have flamethrowers, laser guns and rocket launchers (GTA6?).

Verdict: a solid 8,3/10

My god. Where do I start. Every part of this game is just.... it's just perfect. First of all, this game has the most insane graphics I think I've ever seen. Every tree, every leaf, every thread of grass, every sparkle of water was crafted with the most delicate sense of beauty. I couldn't even tell you how much time I spent simply riding my horse Otis and admiring the world around me. For a game pushing a decade old I cannot fathom how wonderful simply the sight of the atmosphere is. I couldn't begin to express how beautiful the world building is. It's truly gripping, reeling me in to explore every cave, every shop, every character, every body of water. Rockstar crafted such a unique take on 1899 America during the Wild West era. Every single town, from Blackwater to Saint Denis was incredibly special and unique in their own ways.

The main story itself, from the robbing missions to simply going into town for supplies was an absolute blast. Every single mission felt like it had the utmost effort put into it, even the ones some may consider 'boring'. As a Kingdom Come: Deliverance and Witcher 3: The Wild Hunt lover, this game takes the cake. Even the side quests, from Hamish the Veteran to Albert's photography missions, each set of side stories developed their own ideas and sense of progression that further developed nuance and character depth for Morgan and the characters he interacted with. Even the challenges, traversing the vast world in hopes to study every animal and weapon to add it to your compendium is simply extradorinary. There is so much to do beyond the main story that I could live in the world of Red Dead forever. 

And Arthur Morgan, oh Arthur Morgan. His complex and deep nature make him a truly special protagonist. Seeing him change throughout the story as he suffers in different ways creates such a beautiful experience for the player, he makes the game feel alive. Like it's not just a game. Seeing his relationship breakdown with his once brother Dutch is a truly special experience to endure. Seeing them grow apart as their natures begin to change emphasise the beauty in personal morals, and how Dutch's loss of self made Arthur realise what he truly cared about. His final acts of selflessness will truly stick with me forever, as he put everybody before him, even until the very end (I hate Micah so much). Seeing him slowly suffer more and more from his tuberculosis was proved to be so much deeper then people may realise. Knowing his time was almost over helped shape his final acts as he urged to make things right with those he cared about, ensuring they didn't suffer the way he would.

The ending. I can't get over it. Even now I think about the final scene as he saves John and sacrifices himself (Yes I got the high honour ending). And the epilogue was just the cherry on top. Killing Micah and being saved by Dutch was an absolute shock to me, and the act of redemption by Dutch (I haven't played the first game yet) I will never forget. Charles and Sadie returning was absolutely amazing, I can't get over how unique each person was in the Van der Linde gang, and how each had a different role in influencing Arthur as a character.

This game will truly go down as one of the greatest of all time, and, as of right now, my favourite single player experience of all time. 120 hours I will never forget, nor regret.

I will continue to thrive in the heart of Rockstar's North America as I traverse the world as John Marston as well as my unique character in the online experience. 500 hours here we come.

Thankyou Arthur Morgan. You will live in my heart for as long as I live.

Red Dead Redemption 2 is easily one of the most immersive open-world games I've ever played. The world feels incredibly alive, from random encounters and wildlife to the small interactions between characters. Rockstar really put an insane amount of detail into this game.

What I love most is the story and character development. Arthur Morgan is such a well-written protagonist, and watching his journey unfold makes the experience even more memorable. The story is emotional, sometimes heartbreaking, and definitely one of the strongest aspects of the game.

The gameplay can feel a little slow at times, especially with the animations, traveling, and certain activities. It's not a game for everyone, and the slow pacing might put some players off. But personally, I think that's part of what makes the world feel so immersive.

The graphics, soundtrack, atmosphere, and attention to detail are still incredible. Even after spending dozens of hours in the game, there's always something interesting to discover.

Overall, Red Dead Redemption 2 is more than just an open-world cowboy game. It's an unforgettable journey with an amazing story and a world that feels genuinely alive. Definitely worth experiencing.

[h1]I came for the cowboy stuff and stayed for the feelings[/h1]

[b]Verdict: Recommended.[/b] Red Dead Redemption 2 isn't just a game, it's a whole world you can get lost in. It's slow, it's detailed, and it's one of the best things I've played.

[b]The good stuff[/b]
[list]
[*][b]The world feels alive.[/b] Towns, wildlife, weather, and random strangers on the road all make the frontier feel real. I once got distracted by a random encounter and forgot my mission for an hour. No regrets.
[*][b]Arthur Morgan and the gang.[/b] The writing and acting are outstanding. The camp feels like a real family, with all the jokes, arguments, and tension that come with one, so the story hits harder than I expected. (No spoilers from me.)
[*][b]The little details.[/b] Your horse bonds with you, your gear gets dirty, and the animals react to what you do. Every small thing adds to the feeling that you're actually there.
[*][b]Hunting, fishing, and just riding around.[/b] Some of my best moments weren't missions at all. A quiet ride at sunset is hard to beat.
[/list]

[b]The not-so-good stuff[/b]
[list]
[*]The pacing is [i]slow[/i] on purpose. Looting, skinning, and long rides are part of the experience, but they can test your patience.
[*]The controls take time to get used to, and some missions are strict about how you complete them.
[*]It's demanding on PC, so check your hardware before buying.
[/list]

[b]Who should buy it[/b]
If you like story-driven games, open worlds, and taking your time, this is a must-play. If you want fast, nonstop action, the slow pace may not click for you.

[b]Final word:[/b] Some games you finish. This one you live in for a while. Easy recommend.

That's really all there is to say.

From the opening scene to the final moments, this game is as close to perfection as I've ever experienced.

The graphics were revolutionary at the time, and even in 2026, this game remains my benchmark for what looks good, what plays well, and above all, what makes a truly unforgettable story.

Of all the Rockstar titles, RDR2 stands above the rest. You can genuinely lose yourself in this world. My first playthrough took me over a year, simply because I couldn't bring myself to focus on the story when there was so much to explore and experience. I've logged 118 hours on Steam and countless more on PS4, and somehow, it never gets old.

My only real complaint is that Rockstar seemingly abandoned Red Dead Online. It's a shame they put so little effort into something with so much potential. But I suppose when you can milk GTA Online for every last dollar, why bother?

Anyway, this was the first game in a long time that made me feel a genuine emotional connection to its characters. The characters you love, you *truly* love. You feel compassion for them, grow attached to them, and even mourn them. And the characters you hate? Well, I'll let you decide how you feel about those bastards.

It's rare for a game to make you feel like you've actually lived through something rather than simply played it. RDR2 does exactly that.

Red Dead Redemption 2 is not just a game. It's an experience that stays with you long after you put down the controller.

The world is absolutely breathtaking. Every corner of the map feels alive, every interaction feels meaningful, and the attention to detail is something truly extraordinary. The pacing might feel slow for some players, but that's exactly what makes the journey special. This isn't a game you should rush through. Take your time, explore the world, enjoy the little moments, and let yourself become part of it.

Even after finishing the story, the world still makes you want to come back.

Rockstar didn't just create a game. They created a world worth getting lost in.

Praises: 
for a game from a triple A studio this game is filled with a dang good surplus of unique interactions, small details and Easter eggs to explore. 
The honor system allows different players to experience the game differently and gives good replay ability. 
Story is great with a good share of twists and good buildup, characters feel grounded and real. Lenny, Sally and Kieran are some of my personal favorite characters. and seeing the people slowly change over time as a response to the in game events is very fun. 
Also a good aspect of the game is that you can kill members of the KKK and the game rewards you with honor for doing that. 

Critiques:
I do think it struggles a bit from having to many mechanics that aren't fully utilized outside of one or two quests to introduce them. But those introduction quests are at the beginning and all placed really close to each other making the mechanics feel crowded and overbearing to the new player. Satchel upgrades give incentive to engage with hunting but it never really felt that needed, I beat the game without a single one. 
 Another critique is that like many other triple A games it suffers from a lot of character over crowding, Its another game where your character is already a member of a group and has been there for a long time, for that reason all of the individual members are thrown at you one after another and because your character is already canonically acquainted its hard to introduce the player to them in a natural way. Quests don't give time to expand on these characters individually instead having each mission play hot potato on who its focusing on and so most characters are hard to remember especially during the first half of the game.

⭐ Not Recommended – One of the Most Overrated Games I've Ever Played

I genuinely refuse to believe people enjoy playing this game. At this point, I'm convinced the 10/10 reviews are part of some elaborate social experiment.

Let's start with the horse. Apparently, riding a horse requires a fucking PhD. Why does something as simple as travelling from A to B feel like I'm trying to land a Boeing 747? The horse has the intelligence of a potato and controls like it's actively working against me.

The controls are an absolute fucking joke. There are approximately 7,000 different keybinds, none of which seem to have been designed by someone who has actually used a keyboard before. Every five seconds I'm having to Google what button does what because apparently remembering 400 different inputs is now a core gameplay mechanic.

And the tutorial? What tutorial? Apparently Rockstar expects you to absorb the entire control scheme through psychic communication.

Controller aiming is somehow even worse. Trying to shoot something feels like attempting brain surgery while wearing boxing gloves. I want to aim at an enemy, not negotiate a peace treaty with the right analogue stick.

And the graphics? Don't get me wrong, they're decent, but holy shit, you'd think this game was rendering the actual universe with the amount of resources it consumes. My PC is working overtime to deliver an experience that looks nowhere near worth the performance hit.

I keep hearing about this incredible masterpiece, but so far I've experienced:

A horse with the handling characteristics of a shopping trolley.
Controls designed by someone who clearly hates human hands.
Aiming that makes me question whether my controller is broken.
An unnecessary amount of keybinds.
Performance demands that would make NASA reconsider its budget.

Apparently, the story is amazing. Fantastic. Unfortunately, I have to PLAY the game to experience it, and playing it feels like an unpaid administrative job.

I don't care how beautiful the sunsets are or how realistic the horse's testicles supposedly are. If I need a fucking instruction manual to get on a horse and shoot someone, something has gone horribly wrong.

Red Dead Redemption 2: 10/10 cinematic experience, 2/10 actual gameplay experience.

I wanted to play a cowboy game, not become a full-time horse technician with a minor in keyboard memorisation.

The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered: Still a Benchmark, Still a Masterpiece

Years after its original release, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt remains the gold standard for open-world RPGs. The Remastered edition, released in September 2026, proves that a game can age gracefully without losing its soul.

A Huge Thank You to CD PROJEKT RED

I want to take a moment to thank CD PROJEKT RED for this update. They could have taken the easy route — a simple resolution bump and a new price tag — but instead they delivered over 90 improvements: a reworked skill tree, new combat finishers, improved animations, a revamped mount system, cross-platform mod support, and a stunning visual overhaul with native DirectX 12, path tracing, and updated tone mapping. Most importantly, they didn't touch what made the game special in the first place.

The Essence Remains Intact

This is what matters most. The Remaster does not dilute the experience. The world still feels alive — the side quests still carry real emotional weight, the characters still linger in your mind long after you've moved on, and the sense of consequence in every decision is unchanged. The story of Geralt, Ciri, and the Wild Hunt hits just as hard as it did a decade ago. The remaster polishes the surface without sanding down the character.

Visually Stunning

The visual upgrades go far beyond a texture swap. The new shading model, improved foliage lighting, subsurface scattering for more natural skin, and the updated tone mapping make the world of the Northern Kingdoms feel richer and more cinematic than ever. The expanded photo mode makes it easy to capture the breathtaking landscapes and memorable scenes that define this game.

Perfect on Linux via Steam

A special note for the Linux community: the game runs perfectly on Linux through Steam and Proton. No fiddling, no workarounds — just launch and play. It's a testament to how far Proton has come, and a reminder that Linux is a first-class gaming platform.

Final Verdict

If you played the original, this is a free upgrade you shouldn't skip. If you're new to the series, there has never been a better time to jump in. The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered is, and remains, the reference point against which every other open-world RPG is measured.

The good aspects of the game:
An absolute masterpiece that feels like pure cinema, especially experienced through the remaster on a 2K OLED screen using high-end hardware setup. The visual attention to detail is staggering: from the armor, spell effects, and dynamic weather to the stunning skyboxes and environmental interactions. The atmosphere is 100% on point, backed by an elite soundtrack that shifts dynamically during combat to hook you right into the action, while Geralt's sheer aura shines through every frame. 

The storytelling and side quests are phenomenal. The world feels completely alive, and side content is integrated so organically that it never feels forced or like a checklist. CDPR proves to be absolute geniuses at micro-details, character writing, and complex relationship dynamics: from unforgettable narrative clashes like Yennefer vs. Triss (or entertaining the chaotic option of pursuing both, chain-bed included), to choices that genuinely matter and make your actions feel impactful rather than a linear railroad. 

Exploring the world is so breathtakingly immersive that fast travel becomes entirely optional, preferring to ride Roach or sail across the map just to soak in the atmosphere. The combat system shines brilliantly when leaning into a Sign-heavy magic build. Even coming from a Souls-game background where heavy swordplay might technically be more optimal, building around Signs and magic adds a layer of absolute satisfaction that makes the combat experience uniquely rewarding.

And the 'ish-negative' ones:
Minor gripes include feeling slightly overwhelmed by the sheer volume of side quests, sometimes causing you to stall the main story (or hilarious delays in saving Ciri because you were busy doing everything else). The alchemy system can feel a bit underutilized once you automate oil applications to streamline gameplay. Roach's notorious habit of spawning anywhere except right next to you is a classic quirk, and the economy/gear loop can feel unbalanced: either you're constantly replacing weapons every 2 levels and hoarding gold, or wondering how to spend it all. 

Overall, a legendary gaming milestone that leaves an unforgettable footprint, made infinitely better by experiencing it in its ultimate remastered glory.

Previously I would have given this game a 10/10. But the remaster is plagued by visual errors and bugs. The main game was still an enjoyable experience, but the DLCs have been a chore.

Main issues encountered
- Lighting is off, especially in the blood and wine expansion. I couldn't say exactly why but saturation feels too high at the very least. Going back and forth from Velen to Tousaint is night and day.
- Throughout the course of a full playthrough I have experienced about 7 crashes to desktop. Fortunately they didn't occur at key moments.
- Geometry, especially in caves, is very off. Geralt and enemies will start walking into thin air, or an open patch of ground will behave like a solid wall.
- A follow on for geometry but honestly Roach feels like she gets stuck on even more random things than before.
- Models for characters will break after ~2 hours of play time, their bodies will de-tatch from their eyes/hair and T pose.
- Far off hills seem to be lacking any detail now.
- Enemies, especially horde ones like wolves or drowners, will constantly run away. They used to be aggressive but now I have to waste time running them down.
- Boss fights, sometimes at the end of a boss fight (including the final one in blood and wine) the boss will freeze in place and become un-killable, meaning you have to do the whole fight again

That last one is the kicker really. The boss fight is fun. but very hard and filled with near instant death moves. So finally doing it on the hard difficulties and then knowing you have to do it all again because of a bug ruins everything. My desire to finish blood and wine just evaporated.

I will say for the most part the remaster does look good. But as noted above there are regressions in the games visuals which feel very odd and frankly a bit lazy.

Unfortunately I can't recommend the game in its current state. Stick to the pre-remaster editions by changing the preferred version, the remaster simply wasn't fit for release. I'll change this back if it gets fixed.

There's a lot I genuinely love about The Witcher 3. The writing, characters, atmosphere, worldbuilding and some of the side quests are excellent. I wouldn't have spent so much time exploring and completing everything otherwise.

But the more thoroughly you play, the harder it becomes to ignore how unpolished and occasionally downright stupid the actual gameplay can be. Even after all these years and updates, I've encountered broken geometry in caves, quest scripting issues, stuck loading screens, awkward movement and interactions, and all sorts of ridiculous animation bugs.

And then there's the quest design. Some objectives are genuinely interesting, while others feel like nobody bothered testing whether they made sense. Veni Vidi Vigo, where you're expected to identify one particular ship and underwater anchor in a hostile fleet with almost no useful guidance, is a perfect example.

It's a fantastic world with some remarkable storytelling, but the technical quality and consistency of the gameplay are nowhere near the same level. After this many years and another remaster, I expected better.

"The most outstanding game of its era." The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered delivers a world of unmatched immersion, setting a benchmark for storytelling and character writing that remains unmatched.

--- PLOT ---
You play as Geralt of Rivia, a witcher (mutated monster slayer for hire) searching for his adopted daughter Ciri while fleeing an otherworldly threat known as the Wild Hunt. What sets the narrative apart is how meticulously every single character is crafted. From major allies down to random villagers and minor NPCs, everyone possesses distinct personalities, clear motivations, and believable human emotion. The developers treated every side quest with serious narrative dedication—there are no generic fetch quests here. Each side story is written with depth, weight, and fascination, ensuring your daily choices ripple across a living, reactive world.

--- GAMEPLAY ---
Gameplay focuses on tactical third-person sword combat, magical signs, alchemy preparation, and open-world exploration. Combat requires balancing fast and heavy strikes, dodging, parrying, and casting five distinct magical Signs (Igni, Quen, Aard, Axii, Yrden). Preparation is key: consulting enemy weaknesses in the Bestiary allows you to craft tailored oils, potions, and decoctions before engaging deadly beasts. Beyond combat, exploration spans massive regions filled with settlements, ancient ruins, and hidden treasures, while the legendary in-game card game, Gwent, provides an extraordinarily addictive tactical side activity.

--- SUMMARY ---
The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered takes an absolute masterpiece and elevates it with modern visuals, quality-of-life additions, overhauled skill progression, and unmatched world-building.

PROS:
+ Unmatched Character Depth & Emotion: Every character—even background NPCs—feels uniquely alive, driven by distinct motivations, clear personalities, and genuine emotional weight.
+ High-Quality Side Quests: Zero filler content. The developers crafted every side quest with serious dedication, making each side story just as engaging and memorable as the main campaign.
+ Outstanding Masterpiece Status: Widely considered one of the most outstanding RPGs ever made, setting the gold standard for immersive dark fantasy.
+ Excellent Performance & Optimization: Visuals look stunning while staying well-optimized for smooth performance on low-to-mid tier systems.
+ Enormous Content & Value: Includes the massive base game plus both full-length expansion DLCs (Hearts of Stone & Blood and Wine).

CONS:
- Map Icon Fatigue: The sheer volume of question marks and points of interest (especially in maritime areas like Skellige) can feel tedious to clear.
- Steep Inventory & Mechanics Curve: Managing alchemy ingredients, armor crafting, bestiary weaknesses, and skill trees can feel overwhelming to casual players initially.
- Minor Open-World Quirks: Occasional physics glitches like Roach's pathfinding or minor terrain collision bugs can still pop up.

* This game is a great match for gamers who:
- Want to experience what is arguably the most outstanding RPG period, packed with emotional NPC writing and deeply serious side-quest design.
- Love narrative-rich open-world RPGs with deep lore, moral choices, and massive world-building.
- Want a modern, feature-packed edition with upgraded skill systems, transmog options, and streamlined looting that runs great on PC or handheld devices.

* This game might NOT be a match for gamers who:
- Prefer fast, linear hack-and-slash action without inventory management, alchemy crafting, or long dialogue trees.
- Get easily exhausted by massive open-world maps packed with dozens of icon markers.
- Want a short, light-commitment game with minimal mechanics.

# The Witcher 3 Review

## 1. Atmosphere & Level Design — 10/10

**World — 10/10:**  
With the remaster and what my rig can offer, I feel like I'm getting the best of everything this game has to offer visually. This remaster is exactly how I remember this game aging in my head. It is just as beautiful to play today as it was when it first came out. Every zone feels unique, and every location feels like it has a reason to exist.

**Level Design — 10/10:**  
From swamps to cities, islands and Vikings, to France-inspired regions and wine country, every environment builds upon the world with masterful storytelling. Every area feels worth exploring and taking the time to appreciate.

**Exploration — 10/10:**  
This game is a completionist's dream. So much to do, so much to discover, and so much to explore.

## 2. Characters & Companions — 9.33/10

**Main Character — 10/10:**  
Geralt is one of my favorite fictional characters. Even though we're constantly told he has no emotions, I think he displays more meaningful emotion than most characters. He's witty, sarcastic, and ultimately tries to be a force for good in a world filled with cruelty and horror.

**Companions — 10/10:**  
There is so much lore behind every companion and character you meet. Honestly, the romance options are fantastic too. It's always difficult to choose, and that's a good problem to have.

**Character Development — 8/10:**  
Probably the weakest point of the category. It's not necessarily that these characters evolve or develop dramatically. Many are already established, and I think there's something special about seeing them remain true to who they are. The score is an 8 because your choices can still lead to some pretty bad outcomes. That's part of what makes it an RPG.

## 3. Story — 9.67/10*

**Main Story — 10/10:**  
I love the hunt for Ciri. Having read the books, played the other games, and watched the shows, the story feels incredibly compelling.

**Writing — 10/10:**  
Even the DLCs are masterpieces in writing. So much of the storytelling is built around relationships, right and wrong, and the moral grounds you're willing or unwilling to stand on.

**Pacing — 9/10:**  
The story has great pacing. As a completionist, though, F the Skellige island markers scattered across the ocean and getting stuck in the swamps. Haha. The story keeps you engaged, and there's always something to keep a completionist busy.

**Ending:**  
The main ending is great. Hearts of Stone is amazing, and Blood and Wine is perhaps the best DLC ever made.

## 4. Combat & Gameplay — 9.75/10

**Combat — 10/10:**  
This is my favorite RPG combat system in any game. The modern controls and quick casting refresh were amazing. You can do so much without it feeling like a hassle, and the new finishers are fantastic.

**Gameplay Loop — 10/10:**  
I'm a completionist. There's plenty to do. Enough said.

**Progression — 9/10:**  
Leveling feels fair, even starting fresh on Death March. My only complaint is that I found it nearly impossible to acquire all the ability points needed for the additional mutagens and slots, even after completing the main game and both DLCs. I also wasn't able to craft every Grandmaster gear set, only the two I was testing builds with.

**Variety — 10/10:**  
I never really felt bored playing this game, with the exception of those Skellige question marks out in the ocean.

# Final Score

Atmosphere & Level Design: 10/10  
Characters & Companions: 9.33/10  
Story: 9.67/10*  
Combat & Gameplay: 9.75/10

**Overall: 9.69/10**

**Final Thoughts:**

"4 against 1, and there's no way you have another unit card to play, I HAVE this." you think to yourself, another false hope. The old man plays a ranged unit card, but he plays it to your side. 5 against 1 now... which would almost be a comfort, if you didn't know what comes after that is. As fast as a blink, the old man draws 2 cards from his deck... You don't manage to catch a glimpse of either one, yet you still feel the dread. The old man plays a second siege card, it's worth 1 point, but it has a boost to other siege units. He has 12 points to your 5. You lose, and it's all your fault for your ignorance. Buyer beware: Frustrating mechanics mar a beautiful remaster.

Where do I even start? I am only five hours into the game, and I have to ask: what game in 2026—or even back in 2015—does not have a working autosave feature? While the game does remind you to save often, my experience was completely derailed when I kept receiving an "unable to save at this time" error.
The movement is slightly better than Blood of the Dawnwalker, but it still suffers from that same sluggish, unresponsive feel. Because of this, the combat suffers tremendously. I know the common refrain is that this game is "all about the story," but it is incredibly difficult to immerse yourself in a narrative when the core movement and combat mechanics feel this poor.
Case in point: I died in what should have been an easy area against a few basic mobs. The combination of a clunky lock-on system and frustrating movement left me struggling until I went down. Because the manual save failed and no functioning normal autosave feature the game sent me almost all the way back to the very first starting point—wiping out four completed side quests of progress. As a Souls veteran, I am perfectly fine with difficult gameplay and "gotcha" moments. I am not okay with bad mechanical design.
On a positive note, for an 11-year-old game, the remastered version looks spectacular. Running on Ultra+ settings with path tracing and DLAA, I am getting a smooth 100 FPS. Aside from some rough-looking character hair physics, the visuals are gorgeous and the game runs incredibly well.
Ultimately, great performance can't save a game that holds back your progress. Proceed with caution.

PROS :
- The aesthetics. I loved most of the parts i've traveled to, Skellige probably being my least favorite, but everywhere else was great. Loved the ambiance, from the creepy Crookback Bog to the city center of Novigrad.
- It feels very immersive, wherever you go. The music, the atmosphere, the NPCs ("Think i pissed me trousers" is my favorite NPC line).
- Nothing you do really feels boring, it's good to not have a feeling of doing the same thing over and over.
- The storyline is pretty good, I got invested a lot. The fact that you can make certain choices to shape it is also great (SPOILER : F**k Dijkstra).
- The combat system is good enough to enjoy the fights.

CONS :
- At times the Navigation system to go to certain places for the quests is really clunky, missleading even.
- The terrain is weird at some places, you need to escalate invisible elements, Geralt can't seem to climb even small steps and other shenanigans like this.
- The ending felt a bit rushed, some characters completely vanished and didn't get involved at all in the last chapter.

Side notes : Roach is a dingus. Triss >>> Yennefer by a HUGE MARGIN. Big Boss move from CD Projekt to give the DLCs for free to those who already owned the base game.

I am a firm believer that this is the video game equivalent of The Lord of the Rings in terms of scale, weight and grandeur. It is hard to put into words just how great this game truly is, but I think that comparison points in a direction that other fans of this masterpiece will understand and perhaps agree with. This was my third time playing through The Witcher 3 and by far the most emotional one. It truly became an adventure and having a goal of unlocking all achievements made it all the more fulfilling. It took me five months, partly due to me really wanting to take my time, and partly because of finding little time to actually sit down and play. I started on May 27th, incredibly surprised to see the announcement of Songs of the Past. It was almost like a sign. Now, almost exactly five months later, the journey is over. The path has been walked, and what a path it was...

My personal experience aside, it is hard not to place TW3 among the all time greats. In my not so humble opinion, this is the greatest game ever made. Nothing that I have played before or since matches it and I think that is due to one very simple reason. There simply is nothing about this game that is lackluster or half-arsed. I will admit that it is not perfect, but no game is. However its lowest lows are still miles above most other games and the highs are above anything else in gaming. It's a game that somehow manages to be greater than the sum of its parts, while also being made of the greatest parts ever put together in a game. And just calling it a game almost feels like a disservice, for this is nothing less than pure art. The praise that CDPR has received through the years is so incredibly well deserved. They built something absolutely spectacular here, while also building upon the works of Sapkowskis books and universe.

I could go on talking about all the aspects of this amazing journey that I came to fall in love with, but I think it would make for an all too long review. So much has already been said and I do not wish nor feel the need to add to that echochamber. What I will say instead is that this game truly stuck with me and has in a sense ruined gaming a bit for me, since nothing else seems to be able to live up to The Witcher 3.  The characters that the game introuduced and the stories it told are so, so memorable and sticks with you long after one puts the game down. And I think that is a true testiment to the games greatness. 

I feel like there is so much more to be said, but there is neither space nor time for such a long review. So let's just end it by saying thank you so much to the fantastic people that put their hearts and souls into this masterpiece. You made one for the ages. I cannot wait to see what you will let us experience in Songs of the Past and so look forward to walking the path, one last time...

I have never been this fond of an open world RPG. The world of Witcher 3 feels incredibly lively and vibrant even 11 years after its release. The architecture, soundtrack, characters, dialogue and everything else in this game create a somewhat warm atmosphere that keeps you hooked.

Then there are the DLCs. Hearts of Stone felt like a fun little adventure in the map you've already gotten used to. It also added a bunch of new features to the base game. Blood and Wine, on the other hand, introduced a completely new area to the game! Toussaint and the new faces it brings feel fresh after the base game and HoS. It almost feels like a completely new game.

All in all, I would recommend The Witcher 3 to anyone. Yes, to anyone. You can't go wrong with this game. It will hook you in and keep you hooked for hours.

I am definitely not a fan of RPGs, and this was the first one I have played through. While it definitely has a lot of things that I do not like or enjoy, it has ten times more things I love and can’t get enough of. 

Let me start with the negatives. This game has so much unnecessary bloat that my eyes just rolled. +2% chance to cause bleeding or +3% resistance to slash damage? Who cares about such insignificant stats in a singleplayer game? Hundreds of types of crafting ingredients. Completely unnecessary mechanics, such as vendors always having very little money to buy your junk, so you sell few things, then meditate for five days so their budget restores and you can sell more. Or, almost always, you have to return to the quest's original assigner so he can tell you, “thanks for letting me know, here is your reward”. Things that are supposed to feel more realistic just add more grind and repetitiveness and feel like a chore. But those things are very typical for RPGs, so thank god that it is not required to embrace them, especially on lower difficulties or with some accessibility options turned on. Kudos for that.

But the positives highly outweigh the negatives. With the remastered version and path tracing turned on, this game has jaw dropping visuals. Lighting is perfect in almost all scenarios. World design is truly realistic - city design, foliage, and character density feel truly authentic. Combat is really great and offers a huge variety of options. Side quests and contracts offer a lot and bring a lot of value to the overall package. The main storyline is great and engaging, delivering a lot of memorable moments. But I did not enjoy it as much as I could simply because it relies a lot on the expectation that you have played previous entries, which I have not. I understand that it is a third entry into a series, but I think higher emphasis could be given to introducing characters to newcomers.

[h2] Gameplay and Mechanics [/h2]
The control scheme is simple and the combat system has a great implementation in responsiveness and variety with the various combat strategies or character builds that are available as options to me. 
For the difficulty and balance aspects, there are 4 difficulty modes story, story and sword, blood and broken bones and death march.
The mechanics of oils, potions and decoctions with resulting increase in toxicity is unique to this game and brings more depth to what would be a souls like monotonous RPG without these components.

[h2] Story and Worldbuilding [/h2]
The story has a lot of depth and the worldbuilding is pretty good however some areas of the map feel underutilized from a player perspective as in there could have been much more. The secondary quests play a major role in how the game unfolds and the decisions you make in the secondary quests have consequences on the main quest.
The worldbuilding is impressive to say the least as the amount of player immersion it brings is the biggest factor in this game being so good.

[h2] Performance and Optimisation [/h2]
The developers have optimised the game very well in my opinion. Even without DLSS and frame gen I am able to get 80+ fps on 1080p max (no ray tracing, version: remastered).

[h2] Audio and Graphics [/h2]
Given I play the game at the ultra+ preset, the graphics are impeccable. Audio is great with a few amazing soundtracks and the voice actors have a done amazing with the portrayal of the characters (language: English).

VERDICT: 10/10

[h3]There is something quaint about leaving a review for a game that has been soaked in a Niagara of critical acclaim.[/h3] 

In any case, the Remastered doubles down on what makes the game great: The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt is more than a video game, it is a simulation, no less than a novel or screenplay. Like any good book or movie, it asks the players' patience as the story unfolds and complex systems are introduced. But soon, you will find yourself scrounging for every alchemy recipe you can find, pining for the best version of your armour, rushing to the next thrilling contract—and, as I am currently doing, hoarding mutagens for the next overpowered ability.

[h3] To me, the Witcher 3 is not one of the greatest game ever made for its systems or gameplay. Its true accomplishment is capturing the feel of "living" in the world like few other open world games do.[/h3]

When I arrived in Velen, the despair of the region was palpable. 
When I arrived in Novigrad, I felt like a small fish in a big, breathing, living pond. 
When I received the deed to Corvo Bianco, I wanted nothing more than for Geralt to live out his days tending to the vineyard and local Nekkers. 

When the player is immersed in the world, they begin to act—and, most importantly, [i]think[/i]—like the protagonist. Faced with a dangerous fight, they carefully choose their potions, change their gear, and reconsider their skills. Approaching a moral dilemma in the story, whether friend or foe, they feel the stakes. There is something beautifully harmonious when game systems and world logic collides, leading to one of the most immersive experiences in the industry. 

In short, once you get it, Witcher 3 gets its claws in you not unlike its trademark monsters. 
From there, you're hooked. 

One issue, though. Too many portals. I hate portals.

While I have enjoyed my 2nd playthrough after a decade, there are is significant amount of bugs I'm surprised remains after all this time.

Most notably, I could not complete the "Collect 'Em All" achievement without enabling the in-game console, which is exclusive to PC players and required editing game files. Zoltan's Gwent Card, which can be won either during the Gwent Tutorial at the Start of the Game or below a Hanged Man's body later on if you missed it (which was my case), never spawned. I thoroughly researched my issue online and found dozens of online posts describing the exact same issue, both from the original and Remastered Game. Ultimately, I had to manually add the card to my inventory via the in-game console, which finally completed the Side Quest for me after 200h+ of playtime.

Eredin Commander of the Red Riders, which is a Leader Card of the Monster Gwent Faction, is permanently locked and unplayable both while checking your Gwent Decks or playing a Match, despite the game registering all Gwent Cards collected, the "Collect Em' All" achievement being completed, and the related merchant usually selling the card no longer selling it.

I have experience numerous crashes during my playthrough from basic interactions such as Fast Traveling to a different region, looting chests or selling items at Merchants.

Even on a 4070super, AMD Ryzen 7 5700x and 32GB DDR4 configuration, I had to lower the "Number of Background Characters" do Medium and even Low for big cities like Oxenfurt and Novigrad, as NPCs would slowly start being half-loaded and T-Posing. 

While this game is beautiful and still worth playing, it's baffling that there are still so many game-breaking bugs after so much time that SHOULD have been fixed for the Remastered. It's unacceptable for players to be unable to complete Quests and obtain Trophies because of issues persisting 12 years past.

Hogwarts Legacy: Brilliant Magic, Hollow Schooling

As a fan of both the movies and books, finally getting to explore the Wizarding World firsthand was a major draw. Hogwarts and its surrounding world look great, the art direction is pleasant, and discovering familiar locations helped bring to life the mental images I'd built up over the years. I didn't even mind the liberties taken with the source material, especially considering the inconsistencies between different adaptations.

Unfortunately, the things I enjoyed also came with plenty I had to endure over those 50 hours.

For a game called Hogwarts Legacy, I spent an awful lot of time feeling like a tourist with a student ID. There's never really a sense of belonging. Starting as a fifth-year student is an odd decision in itself. You're essentially a late arrival who somehow turns out to be an extraordinary prodigy, destined to save the world from generic villains with next to no personality. Another overused chosen-one trope. BORING.

Character interactions are superficial and bare-bones, usually amounting to someone asking me for help with yet another generic fetch quest. The main storyline was painfully uninteresting, and I never developed any attachment to the characters. I simply couldn't bring myself to care about who they were or what happened to them. The classes consist of sitting through overly drawn out dialogues and cutscnes so much that I ended up fast-forwarding through most of these. Seriously, WHY are some of these scenes so damn long?

The only time I could tolerate them was when I was rolling a joint and letting the dialogue play as background noise. Otherwise, straight to the skip button.

Making the primary villain a goblin was equally underwhelming. Where are the other dark wizards, competing magical factions, and genuinely compelling conflicts? I wanted choices that could determine my allegiances, or a morality system that actually shaped the story and ultimately determined the characters' fates. Instead, there was very little in the way of unpredictable twists or meaningful consequences. So much storytelling potential wasted.

Thankfully, exploration was incredibly immersive. Wandering through Hogwarts and visiting locations I grew up reading about brought back lots of nostalgia. However, why weren't there more secrets to discover? Come on, this is HOGWARTS! Where are the secret passages? Where are the prefects roaming the corridors at night? What about a proper curfew or nighttime stealth mechanics? Even the portraits feel like little more than background decoration. So many opportunities to deepen the immersion, yet so much was left unexplored.

Aside from the exploration, the combat is truly where this game shines. Chaining spells, blocking, countering, dodging and repositioning made me feel like an absolute badass. This is exactly the kind of dynamic magical combat I've always wanted to experience, a massive step up from the simplistic spell-trading in the movies.

In fact, I enjoyed the combat so much that I'd frequently abandon whatever tedious mission or objective I was supposed to be completing and head straight into the Forbidden Forest to blow off steam. I was practically roleplaying as a dark witch, swooping in on my broom, unleashing unforgivable curses and chaining spells to obliterate anything unfortunate enough to cross my path. Emptying that forest of life became my favourite pastime for much of those 50 hours. Forget the main storyline, forget the fetch quests. Just let me loose in the forest and let me duel.

Other frustrations worth mentioning include:

Meaningless dialogue choices.
Tedious Merlin Trials (couldn't be assed to do more after the initial discovery phase).
Repetitive fetch quests that I practically autopiloted through and barely remember.
Occasionally ridiculous difficulty spikes, particularly when the camera locks at the worst possible moments.

Ultimately, I loved exploring this world and fighting in it. I just wish I cared about the story and characters as much as I enjoyed the gameplay.

This is a beautiful recreation of the Wizarding World, with an enormous amount of untapped potential.

Recommended for its exploration and combat, NOT for its storytelling or character development.

My rating: 7/10.

Here's hoping the sequel builds on this foundation and delivers the experience this world deserves.

**Overall Rating: 84 / 100**

**Pros:**

* Outstanding visual representation and architectural fidelity of Hogwarts Castle.
* Immersive, magical atmosphere and strong initial nostalgia during the first 15 hours.
* Dynamic, fluid, and enjoyable spell-casting combat system.
* Engaging beast care and Vivarium customization inside the Room of Requirement.
* Exceptional side storyline featuring Sebastian Sallow and Ominis Gaunt, offering genuine emotional tension and darker themes.
* Great overall entertainment value for a maiden title (offering over 40–45 hours of fun).

**Cons:**

* Complete absence of a New Game+ mode, rendering endgame gear and power unusable for a second playthrough.
* Severe lack of genuine role-playing choices, creating a frustrating ludonarrative dissonance where scripted cutscenes overwrite player achievements and power.
* Flawed loot and gear progression system: static wand mechanics with no stat upgrades, relying absurdly on cosmetic gloves and clothing for offensive stats.
* Poor economic balancing with low monetary rewards for high-tier chest exploration versus exorbitant shop prices.
* Shallow social dynamics that fail to evoke a realistic adolescent school life (lacking rivalries, bullying, house pranks, or meaningful romance).
* Predictable, overly black-and-white main plot centered on ancient magic and repetitive trials, missing potential for deeper political intrigue, corrupted faculty, or morally complex threats.
* Companion NPCs act as passive spectators during puzzle-solving and exploration rather than active partners.
* Open-world activities outside the castle feel repetitive and formulaic, lacking the graphical polish and charm of Hogwarts itself.

---

### Full Review: A Magical First Step Dragged Down by Structural Boundaries

*Hogwarts Legacy* stands as a remarkably solid debut for a potential new franchise, delivering a magical atmosphere and dozens of hours of pure entertainment. On the surface, the recreation of Hogwarts Castle is nothing short of a masterpiece. Exploring its moving staircases, hidden corridors, and grand halls provides an intoxicating sense of wonder that easily hooks you for the first fifteen hours. Coupled with responsive spell combat and the charm of managing magical creatures in the Room of Requirement, the core gameplay loop provides genuine fun. For a price point under full retail, it delivers exceptional value.

However, once the initial magic settles, significant structural flaws and conservative game design choices begin to surface, leaving a noticeable aftertaste of missed potential.

#### 1. Shallow RPG Progression and Broken Economy

The most baffling design decision lies in the itemization and gear system. In a world defined by spellcraft, the player's wand remains entirely static from start to finish, offering zero statistical progression or combat customization. Instead, offensive power is inexplicably tied to gloves, cloaks, and hats—treating a wizard's core weapon as a cosmetic afterthought while assigning combat stats to apparel. Furthermore, the game’s economy is poorly balanced: late-game dungeon chests often reward a meager handful of coins after arduous exploration, forcing players into a tedious cycle of hoarding and selling gear at Hogsmeade just to afford basic upgrades and seeds.

#### 2. The Illusion of Choice and Ludonarrative Dissonance

While marketed as an open-ended RPG, *Hogwarts Legacy* suffers from a frustrating lack of player agency. Dialogue choices rarely alter the narrative, and major story beats rely heavily on rigid scripting. This creates severe ludonarrative dissonance: after grinding to build an invincible witch or wizard, scripted cutscenes repeatedly force your character into passivity or incompetence to let scripted NPCs take action. The game constantly teases moral freedom—even allowing the use of Unforgivable Curses—yet the world exhibits zero reactivity. Instructors and peers react to dark magic with total indifference, stripping your choices of any weight or consequence.

#### 3. Missed Social Potential and Predictable Narrative

For a game set in a boarding school filled with teenagers, the social dynamics feel sterile and unnaturally detached. Aside from the excellently written and emotionally grounded arc of Sebastian Sallow and Ominis Gaunt, most student interactions (such as with Natsai Onai) are flat and lack organic development. There are no rivalries, no romantic tensions, no house pranks, and no systemic representations of adolescent peer pressure or bullying.

This predictability extends to the main storyline. The central conflict—revolving around Ranrok, Victor Rookwood, and four ancient portraits—remains a basic "good versus evil" narrative. It completely passes up opportunities for complex intrigue, such as faculty corruption, internal school betrayals, or a darker resurrection plot reminiscent of classic high fantasy. Moreover, the castle itself—by far the best-crafted asset in the game—takes a backseat in the second half as missions push the player into repetitive, copy-paste open-world camps and caves.

#### 4. Endgame Frustration and Missing New Game+

Perhaps the most disappointing aspect hits right at the finish line. Players unlock the most devastating spells (including *Avada Kedavra*), high-tier traits, and legendary mounts only in the final hours of the campaign. Yet, the moment your character reaches peak power and completes the Vivarium, the game simply ends. Without a **New Game+** mode or a meaningful endgame loop, all accumulated strength and gear sit idle, leaving players unable to carry their hard-earned progress into a fresh playthrough.

### Final Verdict

*Hogwarts Legacy* earns a very strong **84/100**. It is a fantastic first chapter that succeeds in fulfilling a long-held fantasy, proving that a high-budget Wizarding World RPG can be immense fun. Nevertheless, it remains constrained by safe, traditionalist open-world design. Had the developers embraced true co-op puzzle mechanics with companions, deeper gear progression, and a more courageous, reactive narrative, it could have been a timeless masterpiece. As it stands, it is a highly enjoyable journey that leaves you wishing it had taken a few more risks.

A Victorian Setting with a Modern Soul

Hogwarts Legacy is by no means a bad game. Quite the opposite: its recreation of Hogwarts, its architecture, atmosphere and attention to visual detail are genuinely impressive. However, I find its worldbuilding somewhat contradictory.

Despite being set in 1890s Britain, the world often feels more like modern-day Britain with everyone dressed in Victorian clothing. The demographics, social attitudes, dialogue and general character interactions frequently feel distinctly contemporary, creating a disconnect between the historical setting and the society being portrayed.

My issue isn't with representation in itself, but with the apparent lack of consideration for historical and cultural consistency. There is a difference between making a setting inclusive and making it feel as though it belongs to an entirely different era.

Ultimately, the game does a good job at recreating the appearance of Victorian Britain, but considerably less so its social and cultural character for its time. It doesn't ruin the experience, but it certainly takes away from the immersion.

Sometimes it feels less like exploring 1890s Britain and more like playing in 2040 Britain where everyone is LARPing as Victorian wizards and witches.

[h2] Hogwarts Legacy is an unremarkable, formulaic open-world experience whose impressive castle recreation and decent combat mechanics are undermined by how little substance the rest of the game offers [/h2]

The castle is big and beautiful, but in practice it feels lifeless. Nobody actually seems to inhabit it. Nobody goes to class outside of cutscenes or appears to lead a life of their own. The world doesn't feel like it operates independently of you. NPCs seem to just stand around somewhere, in reality they probably do move around the castle but perceptively it would not make a difference if they were frozen in a fixed position. For a game set in a magical boarding school, it's impressive how little of the experience actually involves being a student and doing student things. The school ends up feeling like a transit hub or a collection of a few useful rooms for a freelance monster hunter rather than a place people go to for the sake of learning. Missions actually introduce arguably cool mechanics, like [spoiler] a night sequence introducing a stealth-and-distract phase involving hall monitors [/spoiler]. This makes it all the more disappointing when, upon completing the mission and going back to the very same hallway, this mechanic is seemingly nowhere to be found ever again.
Exploration, the hallmark of open-world games, is also not much better. The developers made extensive use of invisible walls to the point where you literally cannot even jump over railings half the height of your jumping animation. There are a few kinds of puzzle copy and pasted 50 times around the castle, collectibles are largely found by spamming [i] Revelio [/i] every 2 steps everywhere you go rather than relying on observation and search. Leaning on it is a passable fix if your game is failing to motivate the player into actual curiosity and exploration, coming at the cost of not actually fixing the underlying issue and also making traversal annoyingly slow. There's a lot of superficial "interactivity", like globes you can spin, but nothing of it makes the world more interesting to inhabit or explore.
Oh right, there's an entire open world outside of the castle? I almost forgot, because it feels like there's barely a reason to explore it. It's mostly just wide open terrain dotted with a few villages or structures, alongside endless copies of the same handful of unexciting activities. If someone told me Ubisoft secretly made it, I would not question it. In all fairness, Hogsmeade is pretty well-done though.
Progression is possibly even worse, though I can't speak for most of the game definitively because this is what ultimately broke my playthrough. Spells are locked behind arbitrary-feeling busywork and fetch quests for the professors, which is a particular shame because the spell-based combat system is actually one of the strong suits of the game. It manages to make spell combinations and counters reasonably satisfying and rhythmic, even if there's nothing particularly groundbreaking about it. In practice you end up spending your time hunting down [spoiler] the one kind of chest that gives you a useful amount of money [/spoiler] or collecting truckloads of generic equipment to sell, just to afford the item you need to use for professor XY to teach you a spell. And usually, the assignment barely even relates to the spell you're learning. Again it's remarkable how in a game set in a school of witchcraft and wizardry, learning magic manages to resemble just about anything [b] but [/b] learning. After struggling through a main mission where I had the required spells but lacked some of the useful ones, I tried to progress to prepare for the next one. Instead, I found myself buried in hours of repetitive errands just to learn [b] something [/b] new, and ultimately dropped the game entirely.
The writing is also not exactly helping the experience. The story, or what I saw of it, is serviceable, although you're still a new student moonlighting as a creature exterminator. But the character dialogue is so sanitized, so thoroughly bleached of any discernable personality, that every conversation takes on an obnoxiously hyper-polite tone straight out of a Teams chat. The voice acting, let's say it doesn't help things.  The cast is noticeably diverse, but written so devoid of any memorable character traits that their backgrounds end up feeling more distinctive than anything they actually say or do. It feels like a world where hallmarks plot points in the actual movies and books, like bullying and interpersonal hostilities, have been made illegal. Even when someone [b] is [/b] openly hostile towards you, they still manage to sound like they're writing an e-mail to HR.

Ultimately, Hogwarts Legacy has a decent combat system and a nicely recreated castle, but it seems to mistake that for having an engaging gameplay loop and open world design.

The games from the 2000s have a charm that this latest game simply never manages to capture. Because it just doesn't feel... believable.

You don't really get to be a Hogwarts student here. You don't collect Bertie Bott's Every Flavour Beans as currency, gather Chocolate Frog cards, hang out with your housemates in the Gryffindor common room, rush to class to avoid losing house points, or sneak around the corridors at night under your Invisibility Cloak, trying to avoid Mrs Norris, Snape or Filch. And where are the four giant house hourglasses, gradually filling up with each house's points throughout the school year? ⏳️

Careful, I'm not saying I wanted to find those exact same mechanics again. Not at all. But I did want mechanics that could do just as much to convince me that I was part of a believable, immersive universe.

Honestly, it's as if the developers had never read a single book and had only watched a few clips from the movies.

Because in Hogwarts Legacy, we're basically a thief, a mercenary and a poacher who kills other poachers because, well, we're the good poacher. 😳 And we can even add dark wizard to that list if it isn't long enough already.

We don't follow Hogwarts' rules. We ARE the rules. We can leave school, kill pretty much anything that moves, and people are actually quite happy about it and pay us for it!

Even the caretaker encourages us to sneak around at night and steal Demiguise statues all over the region. And sure, we're taught Alohomora to unlock doors, but then we still have to pick the locks like some random Muggle. Remind me, what's magic for? 🪄

I spent most of the game wearing my house's default outfit, just to preserve what little role-playing immersion I could in a world that seemed far more interested in feeling like Diagon Alley, or even Knockturn Alley, than Hogwarts itself.

And that's precisely where the older games did so much better. They understood the importance of immersion, something Hogwarts Legacy seems perfectly happy to replace with ridiculous hats and outfits. ✨

If you (still) love Harry Potter, I genuinely recommend giving the older games a try if you haven't already. Especially the PC versions, which are absolutely brilliant, and the PS1 games, which may be clumsy, but have an undeniable charm.

And if the developers really wanted to give us that much freedom, why not let us leave Hogwarts behind altogether? Let us play as an Auror or a dark wizard in 19th-century London! Don't force us to stay at Hogwarts when the gameplay clearly seems better suited to something else.

By the end, I'd even developed a theory: Hogwarts must have been a pretty lax school back in the day. It was only after our little visit in 1890, and all the trouble that followed, that the school was forced to introduce the strict rules we know today. Because honestly, we left behind one hell of a mess! 💀🪄🔮

[h1] A Building Block for the Wizarding World [/h1]

[b] Overall [i] Hogwarts Legacy [/i] is unambitious but fun, beautiful and entertaining building block towards future Hogwarts games. The main story is somewhat shallow and gameplay isn't anything spectacularly innovative but there are some fantastic side quests with plenty to keep different types of gamers occupied. [/b]

[h3] Gameplay/Difficulty [/h3]

[b] World [/b]

The world of [i] Hogwarts Legacy [/i] is chalk full of activities, puzzles, places to explore and bad guys to fight, while not quite an RPG there is substantial amounts of character customization, freedom to choose spell loadouts, decoration, potion making, plant growing and magical beast care. There are only two voices to choose from for your character (male and female) although you can pitch tone up or down. Also your name is irrelevant with no nickname that you can choose to be referred to by NPCs; your character will only ever be called "Our New Student" in recorded dialogue.

[b] Combat [/b]

Combat is quite fun with a substantial variety of enemies that make for distinctive types of combat and difficulty. While not particularly difficult on the normal difficulty there are elements that require average reaction times and there are different (non mechanical) combos that can be learned to accelerate fights although they are unnecessary and the even boss fights can be completed without much skill. 

[b] Puzzles [/b]

There are a plethora of different puzzles, some optional, some required in nearly every quest and mission in the game. Most of the puzzles range in difficulty from easy to medium, although there are so many different types of puzzle parts that sometimes you can miss something obvious and take a while to figure it out. There are a few side quests and areas that have Hard level puzzles but they are not essential to the main story.

[b] Time [/b]

I finished the main story of my main save in about 32 hours with around 60% total completion. Those 32 hours included side missions and puzzles as well as combat and crafting although I probably did slightly less than your average player. I would expect the average gamer gets 35-40 hours out of the game. I am not sure if I am going to go for 100% but if you want to really go for completion the level of depth and size of the map will cause playtime to scale exponentially as you get closer to 100% unless you are very intentional about completing everything from the second you install.

[h3] Intended Audience [/h3]

[b] General Thoughts [/b]

[i] Hogwarts Legacy [/i] was clearly designed to be palatable to a broad audience. Even if you haven't read any of the books or seen the movies, this game has lots of context and world building (although revealing might be a better word as it mostly uses existing creations in the [i] Harry Potter [/i] universe. The writers and developers didn't want to take risks as this game is clearly a market test to evaluate sales from a game with a new story from the IP.

[b] Representation/Politics [/b] 

Despite being set in Victorian Britain there is quite a bit of minority representation and even a trans character (despite J.K. Rowling's highly publicized views on Trans issues) but there is not major focus on identity politics or virtue signaling and the main story is mostly apolitical.

[b] Age Group [/b]

[i ] Hogwarts Legacy [/i] Is intended for the same general age groups as its source material. The story does not involve particularly complex or mature themes and violence is generally kept pretty PG. Anyone from 10 and up can easily appreciate and enjoy this game although those especially scared of light horror elements might want to steer away from opening their own shop in hogsmeade ;)

[h3] Design, Graphics and Bugs [/h3]

[b] System Requirements [/b]

Running this game is not particularly difficult if you tweak the settings. Using FSR 2 frame gen I was able to get a consistent 45 FPS with very very infrequent stutters and drops on a Steam Deck OLED. If you do want to crank the resolution and graphics without frame gen however you will need towards a top of the line PC. You also need a sizable 85gbs of space although it took up only 72.2gbs of storage on my PC.

[b] Art and Graphics [/b]

Although it is the universal UE art style this game is absolutely beautiful even on lower graphics settings. The different environments in the game have incredible detail and feel very immersive and the developers also included lots of different pieces that really add to the atmosphere of the locations across the map, creatures and enemies have interesting and unique looks that pay homage to the original movie series style.

[b] Bugs and Issues [/b]

I experienced few bugs or glitches, there were a few times where I managed to mess up a puzzle by dropping an item out of my character's vision and once glitching an item into a wall that required me to reload from a previous checkpoint. The only consistent issue was doors frequently loading for a second. This partially was probably due to the hardware limitations of my Steam Deck but also due to the fact that this game was designed and optimized for the 9th generation consoles. As such the game is not built to utilize desktop CPUs, instead using fast storage which limits the PC experience. Also the game should definitely be played on a controller due to the console focused design.

[b] Music and Sound [/b] 

The music in [i] Hogwarts Legacy [/i] is fantastic and pays homage to John Williams' movie score while building its own unique sound that is new. It doesn’t feel repetitive (although this is mostly because there are so many different places that the character is visiting on the map). The SFX are excellent and feel realistic and fun. The voice acting across the board is pretty well done although it definitely isn't perfect, common actions and spells typically have only one or two different recordings and conversations often don't have creative introductions.

[h3] Story and Missions [/h3]

[b] Main Story [/b]

The main story of [i] Hogwarts Legacy [/i] follows a new student at Hogwarts joining the school new in his 5th year without any previous magical training. We learn that the new student has a special ability to use and see a special type of ancient magic that is being sought after by dark wizards and goblins. Unfortunately the whole story feels very contrived at every moment and honestly leaves a lot on the table. Lots of elements are poorly thought out and essentially ignored.

[b] Side Missions [/b]

The side missions and quests in this game are spectacular. Feature side quests have fantastic cutscenes and some are far better than the main story especially the quests with Sebastian which arguably could have been transformed into the main story for the game. Many side quests encourage exploration and discovery of new mechanics or areas that would not be required in the main line.

[b] Immersion and sandboxing [/b]

The real casualty of the console focused and proof of concept style design was the immersion of [i] Hogwarts Legacy. [/i] As a massive fan of the [i] Harry Potter [/i] books I had high expectations for what you can do at Hogwarts and in game. Unfortunately the world feels somewhat dead as you can only interact with NPCs that are engaged in a quest with you and random interactions do not really exist. All of the magical aspects of the world feel very contrived and structured as opposed to the whimsical nature of the books. Also despite all the magic you learn little of the world can be transformed or moved outside of the room of requirement. Hopefully this is something that will be improved on in future games when the developers have a base to work from.

[h3] Final Thoughts and Verdict [/h3]

[b] Ultimately I highly recommend [i] Hogwarts Legacy [/i] and although it definitely has a lot to be improved upon it is well worth your time. 8/10

It affects the girls the most. My daughters (one is grown) just wanted to play as a pretty girl, but had to settle.

Game Story
This is where it gets divided. I wasn't interested in it and skipped most of the dialogue. The main story didn't feel compelling to me. However, my kids liked it, especially my oldest. She would go around and eavesdrop on other students and complete all the dialogue and tell me about what they said.

Controls
They made some strange decisions with the default. I didn't check if I could change it because that is a global setting and I didn't want to confuse my kids if they already had it figured out. You can do a target/ focus mode and for some reason, it will swap the sticks. Keyboard play is just contorting you fingers, but my kid cant get used to the controller.

What the Game is
This is essentially a scavenger hunt in the HP universe. There is a badguy, but mostly its a scavenger hunt, exploration, and light puzzle game. There are some combat events, but it seems like you have to go looking for it to find it. It may happen more often, but there are literal level locks to certain areas so I can't be sure that there is much more combat.

Weird Observations
There is a woman bartender with a gruff man's voice.
