After 192 hours and two playthroughs, one on easy and one on hard, I’ve thoroughly enjoyed Hogwarts Legacy. Given enough of a break, I could easily see myself playing it again.

I like the gameplay and the open world, and the story is interesting and engaging. But a lot of the enjoyment comes from all the little side activities. Potion-making is probably my favourite, regardless of how often I actually use what I brew. I simply enjoy doing it.

I didn’t find the game particularly difficult, even on hard. Completing all the collections is another matter: you need to be meticulous and more or less comb through the game. Still, that’s more about my desire to collect everything than a complaint about the design.

My biggest frustration has been technical. Getting close to water, or even mist, sometimes made things go completely haywire, despite my setup meeting the requirements. There’s also a side quest with a particularly intense fight and a sequence where the world turns upside down, which repeatedly crashed my system. Those issues interrupted an otherwise enjoyable experience.

The gear and money could also have been more rewarding. You collect plenty of legendary gear, but much of it ends up being sold. I tended to stick with one set until something better came along and change its appearance when I wanted a different outfit. Eventually, I had plenty of money and little I wanted to spend it on. Once you get comfortable with the combat and earning money, neither presents much of a challenge.

There’s very little I dislike about the actual gameplay. The technical problems were frustrating, and I would have liked more reasons to use the gear and money I collected, but neither outweighed how much I enjoyed exploring, following the story and getting sidetracked. Two completed playthroughs probably say that better than anything else.

The work of the 3D artists and designers deserves the highest praise. From the animations to the meticulous detail of every asset, this game is a true masterpiece. They were given a beloved, iconic universe, and they succeeded brilliantly in showcasing this world in all its glory.

However, the quests and many of the storylines can be summed up in one phrase: missed opportunities. Take the lock-picking quests, for instance—how cool would it have been to pull off a daring scheme or break into somewhere, only for the entire school of Hogwarts to end up talking about it? As for the quests to learn new spells, they could have incorporated mini-narratives—much like the scene in the film where Harry uses *Wingardium Leviosa* to defeat a troll. While the stories within the quests are generally interesting, and the dialogue is well-written, the gameplay often boils down to simply walking around, killing enemies, or fetching items.

The game suffers significantly from a desire to "offend no one," which has led to a great many missed opportunities. Still, it is well worth playing—if only for the puzzles and the visuals.

The combat system is also well-executed, reminiscent of a light hack-and-slash game. That said, it could have benefited from more combinations and refined combat controls; it had the potential to be far more engaging. Once again—missed opportunities.

**Hogwarts Legacy** is essentially a "Wizarding World" vacation simulator where you get to attend school without the crushing pressure of homework, unless you count "finding 50 hidden pages in a damp cave" as homework.

The game does an incredible job of building Hogwarts. Walking through the halls feels like a dream for anyone who spent a decade imagining they’d get a letter in the mail that never arrived. The castle is gorgeous, the magic feels snappy, and flying a broom is exactly as exhilarating as it sounds—until you accidentally fly head-first into a stone tower because you were trying to look at a particularly interesting gargoyle.

However, the "Legacy" part of the title is a bit funny because you have the freedom to be a model student or a complete menace. You can spend your time helping classmates with their problems, or you can spend your afternoon casting *Confringo* on every potted plant in the common room just to see what happens. The combat is a flashy dance of spells that makes you feel like a prodigy, though the AI enemies sometimes have the tactical awareness of a confused potato.

The open world is lovely, though it occasionally feels like a checklist of "Go here, clear this camp, collect these weird plants." It doesn't reinvent the wheel, but it polishes the wand perfectly. **7.5/10. A magical experience that almost makes you forget that you're basically a glorified errand boy for the professors.**

**Hogwarts Legacy is a beautiful game that captures the magic of Hogwarts, but struggles to make that magic meaningful.**

The first few hours are genuinely wonderful. Walking through Hogwarts, discovering its secrets, visiting Hogsmeade, flying around the Scottish Highlands, and simply existing in the Harry Potter universe is something I've wanted from a game for years. The developers absolutely nailed the atmosphere and visual identity of the wizarding world.

Unfortunately, once that initial wonder wears off, the cracks become increasingly obvious.

**The biggest problem is that Hogwarts feels more like a theme park than a living school.** Classes are barely relevant, house choices mean very little, friendships lack depth, and the world rarely reacts to your actions. I can casually cast Unforgivable Curses in front of people, and nobody seems particularly bothered. Are you kidding me?!

Exploration suffers from a similar problem. The castle itself is fantastic, but the enormous open world is filled with repetitive Merlin Trials, generic caves, and meaningless collectibles. There's plenty to explore, but surprisingly little worth discovering. I'd rather find one genuinely mysterious location with interesting lore than another twenty identical puzzles.

And the loot! Finding a legendary robe should be exciting, not an exercise in comparing slightly bigger numbers. Most equipment feels cosmetic, and progression rarely changes how you actually play. In a universe filled with magical artifacts, enchanted objects, and legendary equipment, how did we end up with such uninspiring itemization?

Combat is enjoyable, and chaining spells together can be incredibly satisfying, but enemy variety is limited, and there's little consequence to becoming an extraordinarily powerful wizard. The story also never quite delivers the emotional weight or memorable characters that make this universe so special.

**Hogwarts Legacy gets the fantasy of visiting Hogwarts right, but not the fantasy of actually belonging there.**

For the sequel, I hope the developers focus less on making the world bigger and more on giving it depth. Meaningful choices, memorable characters, and whats with the damn stereotyping what the hell??!!, actual school life, unique discoveries, rewarding magical progression, and a world that remembers what you've done.

There's an incredible game hiding underneath Hogwarts Legacy's beautiful presentation. I just wish there were more magic behind the magic.

**Recommended for the atmosphere and the experience of exploring Hogwarts, but don't expect the depth that this universe deserves.**

If you're a Harry Potter fan who has waited decades to explore Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry, this is the game for you. Exploration is easily the highlight, and nothing is quite as satisfying as stumbling upon a location you recognize from the books or films. In fact, you aren't just limited to the castle. You can explore the entire surrounding valley, including Hogsmeade Village, the lake, and the many communities and dungeons dotting the countryside. For me, flying a broomstick around the castle walls was enough to justify the price of this game.

Unfortunately, the rest of the game is half-baked. Combat is spammy and tedious, the puzzles are short and repetitive, and the storyline merely serves its purpose, nothing more. There are ambitious ideas, such as the ability to decorate your own room, capture magical creatures, grow plants, and brew potions, but there isn't enough variety to make these activities particularly rewarding. The Quidditch pitch stands ominously beside the castle, and you spend plenty of time flying your broomstick. All the pieces are there, yet you can't even play Quidditch! That seems like an apt metaphor for the entire game.

Even though I got my money's worth and lived out my dream of wandering the halls of Hogwarts, I can't help but feel a bit disappointed. Perhaps a sequel will build on this solid foundation, but until then, this will have to do.

Could've been the perfect Harry Potter game if only the Hogwarts castle didn't function as a base camp, like a hub filled with friendly NPCs that give you quests and allow you learn new skills. The game starts off with exploring the castle for a fairly long time, but then it just fades into the background. The open world map is huge, and after the first couple hours, you will barely need to go back to Hogwarts, except for some mandatory dialogues to progress with the current quest. Spells feel good to use in combat admittedly, chaining them together is fluent. Story-wise it is a huge question why every NPC in this world is okay with a fifth-year student roaming the wilds ending the life of everything in sight. The Forbidden Forest is not so forbidden anymore, except for a wooden sign that says stay out. As a Harry Potter world based RPG, it's pretty solid, the environment is a bit of a lackluster, basically every region looks the same with some hills, a few different colored tree models, and a river or lake occasionally. Grinding is far too present for completionists who want to get every achievement. [h1]⚡ [i]Hogwarts Legacy[/i] — My Letter to the Wizarding World[/h1]

As an avid Harry Potter fan who has read the books more times than I can count and watched the movies an equally embarrassing number of times, I went into [i]Hogwarts Legacy[/i] with some VERY high expectations.

And honestly? From the very beginning, I was hooked.🥹💌

[h2]✨ The Magic Begins[/h2]

The opening sequence is a fantastic introduction to the game. It eases you into the gameplay mechanics through a story that feels natural, rather than throwing a tutorial at you and expecting you to get on with it.

And that sets the tone for what I loved most about [i]Hogwarts Legacy[/i]: [b]it understands that Harry Potter has always been about more than magic. It's about being transported to a world where magic feels real.[/b]

The story is central to the experience, and I'm so glad it is. The familiar names, references, and historical connections to the books make the world feel like a genuine part of the Wizarding World rather than a separate fantasy game wearing a Harry Potter skin. I especially appreciated how the developers used established characters and names to give us a sense of the timeline. 

[b]And most importantly, the game manages to tell its own compelling story without stepping on the toes of the original books.[/b] It introduces a powerful antagonist, gives us a meaningful purpose, and brings its central narrative to a satisfying conclusion while leaving the established canon intact.

[h2]📖 A Story Worth Staying For[/h2]

The main storyline is excellent, but I also really enjoyed the individual storylines involving our fellow students. They give the world more personality and allow us to connect with characters beyond our own journey.

Sebastian's storyline, in particular, stands out to me. I appreciate that the game gives us some meaningful choices along the storyline, especially [spoiler] when it comes to the choice of learning the Unforgivable Curses.[/spoiler]

I would have loved even more opportunities for our decisions to shape our character's journey, but I understand how difficult it is to build a game where dialogue choices genuinely alter the narrative, particularly one with such an established setting and history.

Still, it leaves me hoping that a future instalment might explore this idea further.
Because let's be honest: [b]the idea of deciding what kind of witch or wizard you want to become is far too good to leave unexplored.[/b]

[h2]⚔️ Spellbinding Gameplay[/h2]

The gameplay is fantastic. The spell animations, the sound design, the way spells interact with enemies, and the ability to improve your abilities as you progress all deserve a standing ovation.

I also appreciate the level requirements for the main story. They encourage you to explore, complete side quests, and grow stronger before moving forward, rather than letting you rush through the entire narrative without engaging with the rest of the game.

The difficulty options are another big plus. There's Story mode for those who primarily want to enjoy the narrative, followed by Easy, Normal, and Hard for players looking for more of a challenge.

And I can assure you: [b]Hard mode is ACTUALLY hard.[/b] 😂 Defeating enemies is no small feat, and you really need to understand your spells, timing, dodging, and combinations if you want to survive.

I have a love-hate relationship with the enemy variety, though. For instance, fighting trolls? Fantastic. Having several different troll variants that ultimately require the same approach? Repetitive.

The side quests, on the other hand, were a pleasant surprise. I genuinely enjoyed around 98% of them. Yes, a couple felt a little forced or underwhelming, but most gave me an excuse to meet characters I wouldn't otherwise have encountered or explore places I might have missed during the main story.

And flying? OH, THE FLYING! 🧹

Taking off on a broomstick and soaring over the Hogwarts grounds never gets old. Flying on a hippogriff is equally wonderful, and the dragon-related side quest is nothing short of majestic.

I also loved being able to rescue and care for magical beasts. Creating a little sanctuary for them is such a lovely addition. My only disappointment? We can care for all these incredible creatures, but we can't choose our own owl! How am I supposed to feel like a proper Hogwarts student without one? 🦉

[h2]🏰 The Developers Didn't Just Cook. They FEASTED.[/h2]

Now, let's talk about the world itself.✨

Hogwarts is absolutely breathtaking. Every corridor, every classroom, every staircase, every courtyard, every garden, every little hidden corner feels lovingly crafted.

I have spent HOURS simply walking around the castle, exploring rooms, admiring the architecture, and discovering little details that make the place feel alive. There are so many moments when you stop to look at something and think, "They really didn't have to put this much effort into it... but I'm so glad they did."

To everyone who has uploaded hours-long Hogwarts walkthroughs to YouTube: [b]I hope your pillow stays cold on both sides forever.[/b] ❤️ You are doing a public service.

And it's not just Hogwarts. Hogsmeade and the wider map are equally beautiful, with plenty of places to discover and reasons to venture beyond the castle walls.

The freedom to explore is wonderful. But it also brings me to one of my biggest criticisms.

[h2]📚 I Wanted to Be a Hogwarts Student, Not Just Its Most Talented Visitor[/h2]

For all its beauty, [i]Hogwarts Legacy[/i] doesn't quite deliver on the fantasy of actually *living* as a Hogwarts student.

We start as a fifth-year, but we never really get a proper explanation of why we're joining Hogwarts so late. Given how unusual that is in the Wizarding World, I would have loved a little more background.

More importantly, there's very little sense of an actual school routine.

We don't have to attend classes according to a schedule, follow school rules, or return to our common room by curfew. We can wander around the castle at practically any hour and spend our nights exploring the world without much consequence.

Now, that's wonderful if you're a rebellious Gryffindor, but as a Ravenclaw, I have to question what kind of educational institution allows its students to disappear for hours, break into people's homes, and return carrying half their belongings without anyone batting an eye. 😂

I understand why the developers prioritised freedom and accessibility, but [b]I didn't just want to explore Hogwarts. I wanted to experience what it felt like to belong there.[/b]

[h2]🏆 The Road to 100% Completion[/h2]

And finally, a word of warning for anyone considering 100% completion.

Prepare yourself. Bring snacks. Clear your schedule. And perhaps make peace with the fact that a small part of your sanity will not survive the journey.

You will eventually have to convince yourself that breaking into someone's house, rummaging through their belongings, and walking away with their valuables is perfectly acceptable behaviour.

You're not a thief. You're a witch or wizard on an important collecting mission. There's a difference. 😂

The sheer number of things to find can become exhausting, especially when you're chasing that final missing item and have absolutely no idea where it is.

I love the world enough to explore it for hours, but even my love for Hogwarts has limits when I'm hunting for one last collectible.

[h1]❤️ Final Verdict[/h1]

Despite its shortcomings, [i]Hogwarts Legacy[/i] is my favourite game.

It brings that magic, the charm, the world that I wish would come true, and the game gives me just enough hope to still look forward to my Hogwarts acceptance letter.

[b]9.5/10 — A beautiful world, unforgettable memories, and a game I'll always come back to.[/b]

[i]Thank you, [i]Hogwarts Legacy[/i], for giving me a little taste of the magic I've dreamed about for years. 🪄✨[/i]

Open-world roleplaying game.  You are a student of magic, entering Hogwarts University as a seventh-year, having been discovered late and given independent training.  Before even reaching Hogwarts, you face danger and are exposed to grave secrets.  Find answers to the questions that arise.  Attend classes.  Meet students.  Explore the countryside.  Pet cats.

Set many years before the events in the Harry Potter books, this game makes me think of Skyrim, English Countryside Edition.  It's big.  It's loaded with detail.  It's open-world: you can wander the countryside, exploring every inch of the wizard-compatible land around Hogwarts, on foot, broom or, eventually, critter.  It's completely voice-acted, including the casual conversations you overhear in the corridors and hamlets.  It has the main story line along with side quests.  You can craft, decorate, enhance gear, breed critters, compete in spell use and flying, fight bandits and hostile animals, and solve puzzles scattered across the land.  Did I mention it's big?

I can't help but call it "completionist crack."  It seems like you keep discovering new things to do all of, like solve all the puzzles, breed all the critters, find all the locations, and so on.  Shortly after arriving at Hogwarts, you're given a book, the pages of which fly off in all directions; you're tasked with finding them all and learning about the different locations in the process.  Things like treasure locations, critter breeding grounds and puzzles appear on your map as you pass by them in your wanderings. and not only next to the roads you walk; you sometimes need to go off-road, or swimming, or climbing, or even flying, to cover every inch of terrain.

There's what they call "relationship quests," but there's no romance in the game, merely storylines that follow certain characters.  Unlike Skyrim, you don't find yourself a spouse...you're essentially a high school student, after all.

Some issues I did have with the game:

- Initial load time seemed horrendously long, feeling like it took as much as five minutes each time, though that sped up remarkably after I finished the main story line.  I don't know if this was a patch that came far too late for me, or if tracking the main story line was just that much of a drag for it.

- It triggered my motion sensitivity at times.  Prolonged play, running across the countryside, uphill and downhill, sometimes in twilight, clambering up rocky ledges or running up an down stairs could set off dizziness and nausea for me.  Not as bad as some games, but enough to make it hard to play past 60 to 90 minutes at a time.

- Sunlight was occasionally an issue.  Catch the sun at the right angle, and you're suddenly in a room flooded with light and can't see anything.  In most cases, you could go to the map and hit a key to wait for nightfall, but it's still annoying to be suddenly blinded.

- You eventually get access to a room that provides everything you need in one place.  Everything, that is, except any kind of storage or a vendor.  If your inventory gets full, which is an increasingly occurring event, you can only sell things outside of Hogwarts or drop them on the spot.  This gets awkward inside a complicated dungeon.

- Flying was awkward.  By default (I didn't play with keymapping, and I'm not sure there was any), you used spacebar to go up and ctrl to go down.  This is awkward while you're mashing W to go forward and using your mouse to steer.  Using the mouse for up and down as well as steering would be much more intuitive.  Plus, it wasn't possible to look up or down while flying, making it hard to spot things on the ground or in the air.

On the whole, though, I liked the game.  I got most, but not all, of the achievements; I completed most, but not all, of the challenges; I Beat the Bad Guy; and in the end I was satisfied with the experience I took away from it.  I think I would happily play a game with similar mechanics, scope and production value with a totally different setting.

Bought it directly while it was on sale.  The Steam list price of US$60 is a lot for a game, more than I would normally pay, but I can understand the developers wanting that much; however, at this writing, the game is on sale for US$6.00, which is easily a price to snatch it up at.

Don't forget to pet the cats.

I absolutely love this game. If you grew up watching and or reading Harry Potter you will love this game. I'm so excited for the sequel however I can't give the game a perfect score and it's mainly because of missed opportunities. 

The biggest missed opportunity are that the houses and wand types could have changed the gameplay so much and added so much replayability! At the moment (hopefully this will change for the sequel) the houses and wand types mean nothing but there could be so many possibilities. ( I understand this is the first game and a lot of experimenting was already taking place.)

Let's start with the wands as this would greatly affect combat. Rowling has gone into detail that the core, wood and length of the wands matter. For example Fir wood is good for transfiguration magic while Yew is good for dueling and curses, larger wands tend to favor "dramatic" magic where slender wands focus on refined spell casting (this would be more of a cosmetic thing but still would be neat.) Certain wands are better at casting charms or jinxes while others are better at overall combat. Think of the different play styles this could produce! I have a wand that's better at casting charms, well if have a spell that let's me summon an ally then I could play support and casts buffs on my summon or jinxes on the enemy. So basically depending on the wood type, core and length could change how combat goes for the player and in turn players could share their opinions with each other. This could also be solely based on player discovery and encourage the sharing of information. 

Next is the houses. I'd like to see some sort of benefit and detriment to the houses to spice things up. An example will be support items. Your house will determine what items you can get and how to get them. Crafting and buying are available for all players but you'll find some that in some houses things are easier to get than others. Also I'd like certain simpler quests to be repeatable and in turn you will have to be careful of storage. It would also be nice if the house of the quest giver played a role in the rewards, like a Hufflepuff is more likely to give you a fully grown chomping cabbage or a Ravenclaw giving you a spell or potion. Obviously there will be exceptions, but the most common quests could be like this.

Gryffindor, let's have students exchange rumors or secret locations that can lead to secret passageways or hidden items. Or maybe you can have access to more advance spells an upperclassman could teach you provided you proved yourself. The downside would be these areas are patrolled by NPCs that can catch you if spotted. Or you can have access to certain missions earlier but the difficulty goes up. Afterall only the brave can get the good rewards. Maybe also have more students from other houses ask for help, a Gryffindor would definitely help me. Support items will be given as quest rewards and Gryffindor's can repeat certain quests and will have the biggest variety. You will still have access to crafting, but there will be more quests that give out completed items like potions. Gryffindor's will have the largest list of combat spells.

Ravenclaw: I would give them a larger spell pool from the other houses and put these behind academic based quests. "Find the hidden book and learn a new spell" kind of a thing. It will be up to the player to remember what they have and how to use it. The player could even have other students asking for the player to teach them spells and even have more teachers giving out quests. In return they can hit road blocks with some of the missions having to come back later if there is a certain spell that's needed that the player doesn't have.

Hufflepuff: They will have access to a lot of support items and spells. Not that there isn't a way to get any of these things outside of Hufflepuff but they will be easier to get and they will have the most craftable options. Hufflepuffs will get the most variety of NPCs asking for quests, like house elves and other non-human races. I'd also like to see Hufflepuff have access to summons earlier than the other houses and have them get a slight bonus for gathering items. Now the downside would be the quests. Hufflepuffs will have a larger group of resource quests. For example: "gather this material for me" and for later "make me x thing" type of quests. The Hufflepuffs aren't known for being adventurous so these quests will be harder to come by. Also they will have a smaller list of combat spells.

Slytherin: This one was hard to come up with. I'm thinking a lower variety of student given quests. Slytherins will have an easier time making money (example other houses won't always have a money as part of the rewards but Slytherins will always receive some money.) Slytherins will have access to darker more destructive spells and can learn the unforgivable curses earlier than the other houses. While other students aren't too comfortable sharing rumors with Slytherins this can be solved with money. Shops will sell things at a higher price but will have access to more items and materials. 

These are just some of my ideas, I'm hoping for feedback in the comments as well as anymore ideas and balancing. My hope is that between the different wands and houses players can have a large variety of ways to play. Can you build a Slytherin who plays support, yes! But you better know who to talk to and what you need in order to make that happen. Can you play a Hufflepuff that uses the dark arts? Of course! I want to make each playthrough unique not to limit the options too much. Afterall no one wants to discover a different playstyle halfway through the game and be forced to start over if they would rather play that. My goal is to make the game easier in some areas and harder in others based on the player's choices. I personally think we'd get an amazing game!

It really captures the Hogwarts experience from the perspective of an aspiring student. Though a late starter at Hogwarts, you learn earlier on in the campaign that your skills are above ordinary. 

This game makes you earn every skill, potion and ability. It's easy to forget sometimes that there is a main story, since there are a generous number of side quests and points of interest littered across the map. 

PROs:
+ The graphics and animations are top-notch. It looked great playing on an OLED screen.
+ The ability to mix and vary spells brings out some interesting options for wand-based combat. 
+ Some really well designed companion quests.

CONs:
- Inventory management is an inconvenience. Once you pick up a handful of items you will max out your inventory space, at which point you either have to discard or sell.
- The final campaign can often be finished much earlier than the end game if you don't pace yourself. This can leave you with several hours of grinding afterwards to see the true finish.
- A few of the quests have bugs, with voice cues activating incorrectly or spell effects not triggering cutscene. 

Overall it is a great game if you like casting magic and exploring.

I don't want to sound like 'well this game isn't what I would have done, so I don't like it' but it is missing what I would have thought would be BASIC elements of a Hogwarts RPG. For instance, you don't get an owl. You get mail, there's a snowy owl by your bed that is probably yours, but I didn't get to PICK my owl or name it or anything. Classes are done in MONTAGE cutscenes. The sorting hat? It asked me ONE question that was basically 'are you brave or loyal or smart or ambitious' which made my jaw drop it was so lazy. And you "make friends" by being forced into quests with students you may or may not actually like, but the game MAKES you like them. For instance, I gave basic responses to one girl the whole time and never expressed much for her, but at the end of the game she said that my friendship was one of the most important relationships in her entire life. Most reponses that you choose between are just VERY positive anyway, so you can't get around calling people 'my friend' or singing their praises to other characters without meaning to. It DRAGS you out of any hope of an RPG experience because you're really just on rails. If you wanted to play as a bully or a jock or a nerd... You can't. Your character has no personality other than 'the people I meet are my friends'.
There is ONE real choice near the end of the game and it is the least complex choice you could ever make in your life with one very obvious moral answer. If the game had taken its time, made things more grey, or even let you RP as a character that might not want to make the most moral choice- then I'd be more understanding. But you're on rails as a goody-good and then the game asks you to REALLY think about if killing is wrong. Yes, it is. But also the game has you killing people all the time for minor crimes so whatever it's just weird that it was the only time you're really allowed to choose something.

The world visually oozes with charm from every nook and cranny. The castle itself and Hogsmeade especially are a treat to just wander around to take it all in. The classes and storylines with the students were a particular highlight for me.

The rest of the game is... fine. Serviceable combat. Predictable but enjoyable writing. Once you leave the castle and the story moves into the open world, all the charm and magic seems to leave it, and it turns into a bog-standard Ubisoft-style copy-pasted collect-the-map-tokens-a-thon. The story and visual appeal was enough for me to slog through, but when I thought I was almost at the end, [i]another[/i] equally uninspired-looking open world opened up, and I quit.

I feel this would've worked better if it focused on being a student at Hogwarts and building relationships with your fellow schoolmates. It starts off like that with strong character introductions and storylines, but after the first few hours there's really very little left to do at the school itself. Classes dry up. Relationship development with named characters are left hanging. The world goes from vibrant, engaging, and rich to dry, dull, and static, both visually and in the writing.

It's enjoyable and I recommend it to fans of Harry Potter, but it hurts to see how close it came to being truly magic.

As of the time I’m posting this review, I’ve already put 298.8 hours into the game, so I think I’ve spent more than enough time with it to give a proper opinion.

First, I’ll give credit where it’s due: the recreation of Hogwarts is excellent. The school and the overall Wizarding World atmosphere are beautifully done.

But honestly, that’s about it. To me, this game is only really suitable as a Wizarding World sightseeing simulator — something you enter just to walk around, explore, and experience the setting.

Now for the problems. There are so many that I honestly don’t even know where to start.

1. There are way too many bugs.

For a multi-platform game that has already been out for several years, it’s ridiculous that bugs from the launch period still haven’t been fixed. And I’m not even talking about mod-related issues — some of these bugs still happen in a completely unmodded game.

2. Basic clipping issues are the least of the problems. The really serious problem is how badly some quests are designed and tracked.

This is supposed to be an open-world game, yet if you pick up a quest item too early, rescue an animal before the related quest starts, or open a certain door while exploring before you’re “supposed” to, the game can fail to register the quest properly and prevent you from progressing.

When that happens, your only option may be to reload an earlier save and do everything again.

There are also situations where your character can fall into a deep pit or off a cliff inside a dungeon and become completely unable to climb back out, leaving you with no choice but to reload.

3. Your character can also get stuck inside objects, fall through the map endlessly, or get trapped in broken areas — yet the game doesn’t even provide a proper “unstuck” or rescue option in the menu.

The most ridiculous part is that sometimes when you’re stuck or falling endlessly, you can’t even open the menu. That means you may not even be able to reload your save normally.

Conclusion:

I VERY, VERY, VERY strongly do not recommend buying this game.

Honestly, even if it were free, I wouldn’t recommend adding it to your library.

There are simply too many serious bugs that can completely ruin the experience: getting stuck in the environment, quests failing to progress, completion states not being registered properly, shop equipment refresh problems, collection bugs, achievement bugs, and many more.

In the worst cases, dozens or even hundreds of hours of progress can be wasted.

DO NOT BUY THIS GAME!!!

For such an expensive game, are we really paying this much just to walk around and admire a Wizarding World simulator?

As an actual game experience, it is absolutely unacceptable.

- This is what Pokemon could have been long time ago if they didn't intentionally lag behind and rely on lawsuits for profit. Now another group of japanese simply provided and became popular. If you want more fun and more modern mechanics, you don't need to play any Pokemon video game anymore: Palworld got your desires covered. Comparing to Pokemon the bad part is that Arena in Palworld is very boring, lackluster. But that issue pales to what Palworld has to offer. And most importantly: Palworld runs on PC.
I hope the devs of Palworld don't get cocky from all this fame now, ruining this wonderful pearl.

GOOD THINGS
- For a very fair price you get 150+ hours of things to do. There's so much content. I've yet to finish the game. Just do what you like, don't rush. After the end there's nothing to do, except make YouTube videos for the new players...
- Not an "Early Access" dump and run garbage - no crashes, very rare bugs out of which none break the game, it's detailed and rather well polished. Except the visual performance ofc.
- Made in Japan - the game has a cutesy feeling.
- Not a meme, it's actually well balanced game - you can play on normal difficulty without needing to change any world setting at all. The game will provide you anything you desire, just explore the world. The only setting you might want to change is replace the hold to interact with toggle.
- If you've binged The Elder Scrolls IV - Oblivion night and day, you'll also binge this game.
- It's not grindy - if it does start to feel like that and you truly hate grinding, just consult YouTube. Once you search for one thing, the platform will be very generous in providing all of the top Palworld videos that will help you get somewhere. The game is so popular there are even dedicated websites.

MEH THINGS
- Visuals are average, there's not much to see. Balloon animals with plastic skin, some with simple cute faces and a couple with extra effects. No idea why they added all of the modern visual gimmicks under the visual settings.
- - Save your GPU's lifespan and power bill, start the game with DirectX 12 and set the visual settings preset to Medium and enjoy a quiet PC and stable FPS.
(See how nice the video game Alan Wake looks while requiring almost nothing from the hardware? That's all you really need, anything else is an irrelevant gimmick just serving the material interests of the hardware monopolies...)
- The UI could use a bit tuning - some panels react to Esc only when you make the panel active. Arena's transition screens are annoyingly long and unskippable. And some other minor gripes.

- Chests to have a few more item filters.
- Better object snapping and grid positioning.
- Arena to be way less boring and allow all transition screens to be skipped.
- NPCs to have voice.
- Quick reset button outside of filter settings panel to reset the filter.
- Palpedia to properly indicate which pals are marked as new - current faint yellow diamond is very hard to see.

- - Wild pals spawned near jagged objects make them rotate violently for a few seconds, but long enough to make your PC fans go vroooom - the sound the wild pal would make if it rotated so fast, ha.
- - When you take food out from tier 3/4 cooking device the food item just disappears. This luckily happens very rarely and doesn't break anything.
- - The most annoying bug is that the summoned pals and the ones floating nearby the player can't get down from certain elevations. The player can just walk down the slope but the pals just stand there as if there's an invisible wall. Sometimes they take the long way around the invisible blockage.
- - If you have any "floats nearby the player" pals in your party and you go to an Alpha battle in an instance separated by a portal, the floating pals disappear/don't spawn or take some time to appear or just one spawns.
- - The machine that retrieves all items behaves weirdly and ignores key combinations.
- - Wild pals running through your base don't recognize boundaries of your buildings so they are stuck running forward until they either slide or you terminate them. Putting my thoughts on Palworld is quite difficult. There is a lot to say, more than a Steam review allows. It came out at the right time when a certain other creature game was at a decline in quality, and it has reignited my obsession with these kinds of games in ways that other franchises haven't in a very long time.

Palworld is a great game. It's an open world survival game that's very ambitious, but knows how to reign it in and not go over the edge. Palworld is often compared to Pokémon in the sense that they both have creatures to catch, train, fight other creatures with, breed to optimize stats or transfer skills or to just pat them on the head occasionally for doing a good job. It also features type advantages and disadvantages, you catch them with a ball and store them in a box. Most Palworld fans would deny the comparison and liken the game more to something like ARK, but I specifically chose to play this game because of my love for creature/monster games that came from Pokémon and the Digimon Story games, and the game satisfies in that aspect to a degree I find commendable. I've never played ARK. I played this game specifically for its comparison with Pokémon and found that it exceeded my expectations in nearly every category.

Palworld's story is very simple. You're a stranger on an island unfamiliar to you. You're told to seek out a settlement while becoming a Pal Tamer. You're made aware of different factions on the island that all fight for survival, to enrich themselves, as well as other reasons unique to each faction. While journeying to fight these factions, you fight their respective leaders, the Tower Bosses. Each of them have personal reasons to do what they're doing, and while you're explicitly told in some ways and less so in others, the game showcases one of its strengths right here: Palworld is a lighthearted game with some dark and cruel themes about survival and greed, but the game is never beating you over the head with it. In fact, the game's story is extremely light and you never even really have to engage with the story at all. Finding out more about the state of the world is cool and it happens on its own, just by playing the game. The games' longest cutscene is the ending, and its not even really that long. This is a believable and rich world with bits of lore here and there that you can sink your teeth into, but it will never be in your way. This unobtrusive way of delivering the world and lore is appreciated in a world where other creature battle games absolutely frontload you with a bunch of dialogue that you have to mash through every single time you start a new save. This game has a story, a decent story too, and it will never make you waste your time for it.

The gameplay is where Palworld shines and becomes truly addictive. I am not a fan of many open world games. Traversal is often annoying and exploration can be unsatisfying. Other open world games have exploration just for the sake of it, with the only reward being self-satisfaction. In Palworld, you have to gather resources, catch more Pals, get stronger, fight better and bigger monsters and then return home to upgrade or sort out your loot. This gameplay loop is enjoyable and the open world serves the gameplay well. Exploration is rewarding, expanding the map and finding fast travel points gives you EXP and more access to different Pals and materials. Combat in the game is fun and requires player input depending on your build. You fight alongside your Pal for the most part using your own weapons that you crafted. Just from having to climb everywhere to being able to fly in the level 14-20 area is already such a massive and rewarding change that will make any player yearn for more. Fighting the bosses is fun - you'll have an easy or a hard time, depending on your loadout, but playing completely blind on Hard World settings has often had me take a while until a boss was defeated, and it felt like a good time.

Speaking of World settings: the game gives you the freedom to play however you like. You can choose spawn rates, work speed, damage to/from players/pals and the game even offers Multiplayer, so you can play with (or against) your friends. This freedom of choice is what ultimately makes me keep coming back to this game over every other creature game, even those I enjoyed, because you can play the game in many different ways and its fully customizable.

The gameplay has many mechanics and systems to a degree that people might find far too ambitious at first glance, but its much more well balanced than you'd expect. The game gives you a lot of freedom with how you build your base. Want a little nice house? No problem. Want to build a futuristic skyscraper? Also no problem. Want to build a satanistic dungeon and spray a cross on the floor? No problem. Similar to games like Minecraft, you can choose walls, floors, roofs of any material you like. Some people have created wonderful structures in this game, and if you love base-building, this game is perfect for you. The game has a GTA-style wanted system, giving the world some added depth with the PIDF as a faction that acts as this world's police force. Fighting them can be a lot of fun, but its often also somewhat buggy, but never to a degree that is detrimental to my enjoyment though. All of these things can be safely ignored if you don't care for them, which is another strength of the game. It offers so much and you can pick and choose what exactly you want to do with it, and each mechanic offers its own depth. Instead of a horribly bloated "jack of all trades, master of none"-type game, it has a decent amount of depth to everything. The base building, combat and exploration are certainly more fleshed out than the GTA, economy and crafting are, but none of it feels like it's obtrusive or shouldn't be in the game.

Interacting with your Pals is better here than it has ever been in Pokémon. You can cuddle with them in bed, pat them and directly feed them with any random food you find. The Emote menu even gives you special animations if performed with a Pal. You can ride Pals, each Pal is unique and has a unique passive skill and moveset. This is not too strange to see in a game like this, but the amount of depth and interactivity that the Pals offer is superior to other games of its kind, which is surprising considering how creature games are often about the creatures themselves, yet Palworld set a new standard in how much you can interact with them.

If there is one thing I would criticize about the game, it's the games' lack of meaningful difficulty. I played on Hard World settings, but I've felt that, rather than expand on the game with different attack patterns for bosses or changing the way I think about approaching exploration and combat, Hard World settings just make the game very tedious. Everything takes far longer to achieve in a way that doesn't really equate with "being good" at the game. With a game as big as this, I didn't mind it too much, but as someone who enjoys games for their combat gameplay, Hard World settings don't actually make it all that much harder. Enemies just become more spongey and gathering resources becomes more annoying, that's it. That said, once you've defeated all the Tower Bosses, the game lets you fight them again in a "Hard" mode: THIS is when the bosses change things up, choose different patterns and ways to attack, and even receive additional help, giving you more enemies to fight. I found them to be a lot of fun and they satisfied by desire for difficulty. This is to say that Hard World settings aren't really the KH2FM Critical Mode you might think it is at first, but the postgame tower bosses are fun.

This game rocks, and I will probably play it for many more years to come. I'm also interested in all the spin-offs, merch and trading cards. Keep it coming, Pocketpair, consider me converted. I'm a huge fan.

I originally purchased Palworld following its 1.0 release, after hearing all of the positive reception it had gotten, and I couldn't be any happier with the experience. At first, I was drawn to the creature collecting aspect, having been a longtime fan of Pokemon. However, I quickly feel in love with the sense of freedom you get from the exploration and base building.

Before Palworld, I had never tried playing a survival game, as I didn't really see the appeal. So having the option to customize the overall difficulty and the intensity of the survival mechanics, made the entire experience that much more enjoyable.

I would easily recommend Palworld to just about anyone, especially those who are already fans of creature-collecting games or exploration-centric games. Plus, if you are looking for a good game to play with friends, Palworld supports full crossplay between platforms.

This game has a lot of opinions on it from a lot of different sides, and that's before you factor in the corporate politics surrounding it, so I ended up going in not really sure what to expect. What I got though was actually pretty dang fun, especially with friends.

If you're a longtime Pokemon player like me poking your head into this game for the first time, I think what'll stand out to you the most is how much survival crafting is in it. I dunno what I was expecting -- I guess more of a traditional Pokemon adventure -- but no, this game really tries to be half monster catcher, half survival crafter, and honestly, the mix works really well. Base logistics in particular are a highlight in the way it marries the two halves, where different Pals have different aptitudes for different kinds of work, and you organize and arrange your base to automate all sorts of different tasks. It makes you feel smart for engaging with the game's primary two mechanics. All these little flourishes dot the overall gameplay, making it feel familiar and new at the same time.

The Pal designs are overall rather hit-or-miss, but the highlights I find myself liking as much or even more than some Pokemon. The quality is less consistent, but good enough to get the job done; you'll probably find at least a couple dozen Pals you'll like and want to stick with. Special shoutout goes to Chillet because weasel-wyrms are something I never knew I needed in my life until this game introduced me to them.

The story was... A little difficult to wrap my head around, and I guess that's on me for not finding enough codex entries to fill in the gaps. It was hard for me to feel invested in the game until it was already almost over. Finding those codex entries wasn't the most intuitive thing for me to do either, as there aren't very many systems in place to help you find collectibles. Of course, some people prefer to not be given that sense of direction, but I like having something optional to give you a hint.

It is also pretty funny how Palworld doesn't shy away from topics that Pokemon usually does -- Pals as food, slavery, the line between human and Pal, all of them are played around with in amusing ways ranging from making your Chikipi commit cannibalism when you feed it a roast leg, to making a misinput and accidentally throwing your Ancient Sphere at your bounty target, capturing and enslaving them instead of killing them. It does feel a little refreshing coming off of how squeaky-clean Pokemon tends to be in this regard.

What I'm trying to say with all this is that Palworld isn't a Pokemon clone, and that's its strongest suit: It forges its own path, finds its own compelling gameplay formula, and i think that's what made it strong enough to actually challenge the king of monster catchers to begin with. Definitely recommend it, especially if you're playing with friends, as multiplayer lets you divvy up work in a base and tackle bosses together.

Pros:

• Massive Progression: You start naked on a beach with a wooden club and end up riding a dragon while firing a rocket launcher.
• Massive Content: The 1.0 update added massive new areas, flying islands, and hundreds of unique Pals to collect.
Cons:
• The Grind: Late-game tech trees require heavy resource gathering if your base isn't fully optimized.
• Building Jank: The base-building grid can still feel a bit stiff compared to other survival games.
• Dark Humor: The game's satircal take on monster labor might not be for everyone.
Verdict:
If you like Ark, Factorio, or Pokémon, buy it immediately. Easily worth the price for hundreds of hours of chaotic fun.

I remember when Palworld first came out and everybody called it "Pokémon with guns."
Which... yeah. I can see how we got there. 😂
But after actually playing it, that's selling the game pretty short.
You can spend one night building a huge house/base because apparently that's what you're doing now. Next thing you know you're exploring the map, finding new areas, catching Pals, taking on Alpha Pals, going through dungeons, upgrading your gear, breeding Pals, unlocking new technology and preparing to go fight one of the tower bosses.
Then you get distracted halfway there because you spotted a Pal you haven't caught yet.
There goes another hour.
That's probably what I like most about Palworld. I can get on with a plan and almost never actually stick to the plan.
"I'm going to beat that boss tonight."
Three hours later:
I have not fought the boss.
But I DID rebuild half my base, hatch 37 eggs, catch something I didn't have, find a dungeon and somehow end up on the complete opposite side of the map.
Productive night.
There's actually a lot more going on in the world than I expected too. There are different factions, bosses and bits of story/lore to find, so exploring actually feels like you're working your way through something instead of just wandering around collecting creatures forever.
It's not perfect. Pals occasionally make some... interesting life choices around the base, and there are definitely moments where the game reminds you it's Palworld.
But I've had a ridiculous amount of fun with it.
If Pokémon ever made you think, "This is great, but I'd also like to build a mansion, fight a giant boss and carry a rocket launcher," Palworld might be for you.

After relatively positive first impressions, the longer I played the more they faded away.

Game is too grindy. Catching pals, getting resources and crafting all feel like tremendously tedious tasks.
You will especially feel it after leveling slows to a crawl. And don't get me started on crafting itself. The resources needed are ridiculous. To make a single handgun you need 62 ingots. 62! 

Managing pals is a pain. Pals themselves have awful pathfinding - don't build their beds or food baskets in the interiors because they will get stuck in the doors unless they're really small. Glitches related to pathfinding are plenty.

But probably the biggest issue is the exploration. For a game that puts so much emphasis on it, it sure is extremely unfun to explore. 
The world feels empty and uninspired. It has barely any interesting spots, it's just open areas with some pals/gangsters here and there. There is nothing fascinating to see or discover. After couple hours, it all feels very bland and boring. Dungeons are copypaste, ugly and feel pointless. Bandit bases are much the same, offering almost nothing of value. [b]Everything Pokemon does, Palworld does better.[/b]
If you've heard of Palworld, you've probably heard that Nintendo is frothing at the mouth and chomping at the bit trying to get rid of it-- And for good reason. There's a million other games out there that take "Weird elemental monsters that you catch in your balls" for their own little spin, but NONE of them do it like Pocketpair. My partner described it as being "more mature" than Pokemon, and frankly, I agree-- Nintendo's afraid of growing up, and Palworld's overwhelming success proves it.

But why is Palworld so overwhelmingly successful?
First of all, the game is SO much more immersive and refuses to hold your hand through a bullshit storyline that ruins the first thirty or more minutes of gameplay [i](looking at you, Legends Arceus.)[/i] before dropping you in a blank slate of a world with nothing going on that you can't even freely explore [i](STILL looking at you, Legends Arceus!)[/i] 

There IS technically a storyline and lore after Palworld 1.0, but Palworld almost never locks you in a cutscene or forces you to talk to people. I'm pretty sure you could just do all the towers on your own without ever advancing the main story. And while there IS a "story" after 1.0, I think it's rather shallow and is my only real gripe with the game-- Palworld didn't need one. The NPC dialogue lacks any sort of depth and it would have been better off without it. But regardless, that is a very MINOR gripe and everything else in this review is plated in glowing positivity.

Punch trees. Punch rocks. Get stuff. Build stuff. Punch a chicken. EAT a chicken. Catch a chicken. 
No starter? No problem! 
Palworld's combat differs wildly from Pokemon in the fact that every wild encounter is, in fact, a wild encounter. You must dodge around left and right to avoid the enemy Pal's attacks, switch out your pals, and try to catch it in REAL TIME. It's much more exciting that way, and best of all, you are not only allowed, but ENCOURAGED to deal damage yourself. (See: Guns! Many of them!) The Pals do NOT run away for no reason-- If you fail an encounter, it's most likely because you Have A Skill Issue and Died. However, the same pal you were trying to catch often is much easier to find again than in Pokemon-- They have set spawn areas, and if its a boss or a field boss, they often have somewhere else on the map they spawn regularly too.

You can climb, glide, dodgeroll, crouch, and slide-- Every inch of the Palapagos islands is intended to be explored, even far out over the ocean where you'd THINK a world border would be are dozens of little islands with secrets and surprises waiting upon them. Getting to Whalaska made me feel like i was about to drop into the void!

Just like ARK: Survival Evolved, you can build your own base with modular parts and equipment that you unlock with player levels in the tech tree. Enemy factions will raid you every once in a blue moon-- But that's just a wonderful opportunity to watch your Pals mop the floor with them and come back grinning as they continue to work. The base-building isn't really anything to write home about, but you can paint the walls and floors and add various sets of furniture to make it feel just that much more like a home. Did I mention the pals work for you?

There ARE in fact types in Palworld, but there's a lot less of them than in Pokemon and they're much easier to understand. There's also work suitabilities-- A Fire type pal will most likely have a certain level of Kindling suitability, and can help you cook or smelt ingots at a furnace. [spoiler]The Eye of Cthulhu[/spoiler] doesn't do much of anything but Transporting, but by god, he does it well, at a glistening LEVEL 7 suitability. Each pal also has a partner skill-- These can do anything: increasing your damage, an early game mercy hit, being able to be ridden, increasing your carry weight, increasing loot from Fishing, increasing base pals' efficiency... Or nothing, if you've decided to catch a Human.

Yes. You can catch humans. Almost all of the NPCs in Palworld can be caught-- There are a few I'd like to mod into that list, such as the [spoiler]Wildlife reserve attack drones[/spoiler], but you can catch a full team of Humans and even get the cops to come after you for it. And then you can catch the cops, too, because fuck the police. There are also mods that give the humans genders and make them breedable, if you're that much of a freak. 

Did I mention mods? You can mod this game, and people have done that to... make some awfully suspicious things. Go get 'em, tiger.

Speaking of being a freak, and not a Game Freak might I add, the paldex entries do not spare you any sort of couth when it talks about the shit pals tend to get into. Lovander is probably the most popularly incriminating example. I'm surprised the PIDF didn't put that one in jail...
There's a lot more mature themes going around that are not just the guns-- Death, depression, assault, counterfeiting, animal abuse... It's rough out here, man. But I respect it. Too many games and communities nowadays are worried about being sanitary and "kid safe" (read: boring, censored, and having an excuse to steal your personal information.) Palworld is NOT that, whatsoever, and in my book that gets it a load of good boy points for being itself. There's no blood or anything, and the defeated Pals ragdoll with swirly eyes, but they drop MEAT, and hell, just look at Splatterina. You can even do evil and suspicious surgery on your Pals. You can put them in a giant blender to make one of them stronger. lIke what the fuck.

Multiplayer is also a thing, with public lobbies (ew) and private invite codes (YAY).

I could probably go on and on about how awesome Palworld is and how obsessed I've been with running around getting into places I'm 10 levels below, barely managing to survive and scrounging up high tier Palspheres along the way, but at this point you just need to try it for yourself. 
You're a big kid now. Ditch the Pokeball, and come play in the big leagues! Get Palworld today.

There is so much to sink your teeth into Palworld, even when I beat the final boss it felt that there was still more to discover.

I completed this with two friends, and most of the time spent was either building some elaborate bases, designing and decorating rooms for all the base Pals. On occasion, I had to tweak with the world settings a little to speed up our progress (there's just been a plethora of new game releases the last few months), but otherwise, the experience was thoroughly enjoyable.

The progression systems put in place to level up and power up your Pals is so deep, that almost any activity you engage with, whether roaming dungeons, the items you collect from chests, exploring and reaching watch towers, all culminate to some sort of progression for you and your Pals.

It's always fun to roam about and find a cool Pal that you might want to have in your main squad, or that occasional rare legendary Pal hatch from an egg. The tech tree is expansive and offers a lot of weapon types to suit your style of combat.

The game does suffer from a handful of issues - its user interface being a pretty cluttered experience. It did get the job done for the most part but when managing Pals within a base there are names, health bars and other UI elements overlapping with each other making the HUD appear incredibly messy. Additionally, the Palbox interface suffers from a search bar in some screens vs. others which is quite inconsistent. The art style and direction feels a bit conflicting when you look at the Pals and the detail of the environments and buildings. And while there's alot of quality of life done for inventory management, it would be nice to have a way for Pals to prioritise moving items to certain containers over others. There are a few boss fights that showed some impressive creativty in affecting the battle arena and environments which is great to see - but would've been nice to see more of in the majority of the boss encounters.

With all that said, these issues in no way stopped me from enjoying the heck out of this game because exploration is fun, the progression systems are deep, the tech tree is expansive, and most importantly, the character designs of the Pals are awesome.

Looking back, multiplayer with friends probably would have been a superior experience. It's fun but half-baked. That's as concisely as I can put it. It has a lot of issues:

 - Most of the difficulty in the game will come from the game itself being as counterintuitive as possible in every aspect and expecting you to spend dozens of hours throwing shit at the wall until something sticks (or reading/watching tons of third-party content to learn what the game refuses to teach).

 - Instead of balancing their game, the devs threw in a bunch of damage/time multiplier sliders and said "balance it yourself loser." As a result, the difficulty is deeply schizophrenic; the boss required to access the final world area is an order of magnitude more difficult for its level than the actual final boss of the game, and a lot of that difficulty is mechanical (it stays so far away your weapons receive massive damage falloff and you can't even order your pals to attack it from the center of the arena because the damn raycast doesn't reach that far).

 - Rather than letting you specialize like a good role-playing game would, Palworld demands that you spend the time to fully exploit every single one of its often nebulous mechanics. To succeed in harder battles you'll have to maximize player stats, equipment tech level, pal passive attributes, pal condensation level, pal elemental matchups, and pal soul boosting (I'm sure I forgot something), and getting any one of these things maxed out takes hours of grinding, but the game doesn't respect your time in the slightest.

 - Half the environments look like a four-year old's show and tell diorama, with prefabricated terrain elements copy-pasted haphazardly around with seemingly no consideration for appearing natural.

In spite of all that, the bits of game strung between the massive glaring deficiencies are really quite fun. I recommend it but would also suggest you wait for a sale unless Pocketpair actually come back and finish Palworld, which seems unlikely given their history of leaving game(s) unfinished.

[h2]Deep Dive[/h2]
There isn't a true storyline in this game, which I think is where it falls down dramatically, forcing the player to hunt down journal entries that are hidden around the world to uncover what has happened and what is happening feels like a ball drop for the most part, as most people looking for a casual experience will never really understand what is happening. The sheer lack of any voice acting in the game also diminishes the already minimal storytelling, as you never really feel connected to anyone in the world, only your character and the Pals you carry.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3823390797

Palworld does a lot of really positive things with its design, creating an open-world creature-collecting experience with very few walls or boundaries to hinder progress or exploration. It expertly blends the classic features of the creature-collecting genre with unique aspects such as gunplay and forced labour of your Pals in your bases across the world, having them farm, mine, and smelt metals for you while you go enjoy exploration.

[h3]Pros[/h3]
🟩 Catching Pals and training them to fight.
🟩 Levelling up your base with farmed resources and getting Pals to work in your bases.
🟩 Exploration is a huge part of this game, as the best items are found in hard-to-reach locations.
🟩 The guns and gunplay are an amazing addition to the experience.
🟩 Being able to catch humans in Pal spheres is hilarious.
🟩 Boss fights are challenging and fun encounters.
🟩 The endgame is where the game becomes a truly different experience. Opening up min-maxing Pals, farming endgame progression items and hunting for the best in-slot gear is some of the best fun I've had in this game.
[h3]Cons[/h3]
🟥Mid-game does get a bit slow and tedious, especially with the mid-game resources to farm.
🟥The arena is a bit of a bore as they focus too heavily on the grind, and not enough on making it a rewarding activity.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3823390523

Palworld is also not an amazingly beautiful experience; while the world is vast and has been designed with love and care in nearly all of its facets, many of its aspects are lost in the fact that it lacks texture diversity. Large segments of areas, especially in the latter areas of the game, are just patch-textured with the same design, and it really diminishes the look. Having a pretty janky draw distance that loads in as you fly feels like another significant oversight. The audio is in a very similar boat, failing to deliver any really unique atmosphere or soundtrack to the design, which really disappoints me, as something like Palworld would truly benefit from a chill and flowing OST.

[h2]Additional Features[/h2]

[td]There are quite a lot of achievements in Palworld, but none of them are really that difficult. Most are unlocked by simply playing the game, and most of what's left can be done fairly easily in the endgame with endgame Pals. This is a very easy 100% completion, if not a little time-consuming.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
[td]Replayability[/td]
[td]I think there's a lot of space in this game for activities to keep you occupied, but I don't think you'd want to go back and do another campaign after doing everything you can in your first one, as you'd really just be treading the same path. Better to focus on a single playthrough and do that as completely as you can.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
[td]Multiplayer[/td]
[td]Having played a majority of the game in single-player, I don't have a lot of experience with the multiplayer side of things, but from what I did try out, it seems pretty well designed for the most part; although very few of the bosses scale up with more players, most of them don't.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
[td]Technical Information[/td]
[td]I played a large majority of Palworld on PC, with the below PC build at its highest settings and had a consistent 120 FPS. I did try running it on the Steam Deck and was able to get 30-45 FPS with adjusted settings to make it perform better, sometimes having it drop to 20-30 FPS during busy locations and encounters. I would recommend playing this on PC, but the Deck capability isn't too bad.[/td]
[/tr]

[h2]Final Thoughts - Rating: GOOD[/h2]
Is Palworld going to replace Pokemon? No, not in this format at least, but it does a lot more right than it does wrong. A prettier world, with more development on using the power of gaming PC's would push this a lot further, and a greater focus on the audio-scape would help deliver that in spades. [h2]Ark meets Pokémon, and it surprisingly works[/h2]

I had my doubts about [b]Palworld[/b] and held off on playing it for a long time, but after finally being convinced to try it, I have to admit: it is a genuinely good Survival RPG and a lot of fun. 

To be completely honest, if you look at it closely, there isn't really anything revolutionary or brand new here. The mechanics are things we have all seen before in other games. However, the way they blend them together is what makes it click. It truly feels like "Ark meets Pokémon," and it executes that formula surprisingly well.

[hr][/hr]

[h3]What makes it fun:[/h3]
[list]
[*] [b]The Creature Collection & Base Management loop:[/b] Catching creatures (Pals) isn't just for show. Putting them to work at your base brings in a surprising colony-sim management layer—very reminiscent of games like [i]RimWorld[/i] or [i]Frostpunk[/i]—where you actually have to monitor, feed, and manage the sanity, health, and happiness of your "workers" to keep production running smoothly.
[*] [b]Solid Survival RPG mechanics:[/b] Exploration, building, and leveling up your character keep you constantly engaged, offering a great sense of progression as you unlock better gear and technology tiers.
[*] [b]Immediate addiction:[/b] Despite its derivative nature, it hooks you right from the start. It takes known concepts and refines them into a very addictive package that turns into an absolute time sink, whether you play solo or with friends.
[/list]

[h3]Areas for improvement:[/h3]
[list]
[*] [b]Lack of real originality:[/b] As mentioned, veterans of the survival and creature-taming genres won't find many mechanics they haven't seen elsewhere. It leans heavily on familiar formulas with many highlights here and there.
[*] [b]Performance and Polish:[/b] Like many games in this genre, optimization and technical polish can be rough around the edges, occasionally reminding you of its early development roots.
[/list]

[hr][/hr]

[h3]Final Verdict[/h3]
I had my doubts at first, but I was wrong. If you enjoy survival crafting games and monster collectors, [b]Palworld[/b] is well worth playing. It’s highly engaging, incredibly fun, and proves that you don't always need to reinvent the wheel to make a great game.

Great game, but the pacing and the base building wore me down. I can’t recommend it for solo play.

I put 37 hours into Palworld, and the start is excellent. Catching Pals and building your own base is a great premise, and I was hooked.

The problem is how fast everything comes at you. On default settings I was level 55 after about 30 hours, and I’d barely learned how to build properly. I was hoping for some real challenge to level up, but instead I got assembly lines and rocket launchers before I understood the basics. I know I could have turned the EXP down, but the default is what most people will play, and it felt way too fast.

That’s where the base building starts to hurt. Almost everything you build is rectangular, and you have to fit it all into a fairly small circular boundary ("All these squares make a circle"). You can work around it, but it never truly feels good. The only way to make everything fit is to build upwards, and the Pals’ pathfinding isn’t great with floors. Most of the more useful Pals are also huge, so the base ends up a mess where everything clips into everything else.

On top of that, I don’t like researching games before I play so I don’t spoil them, which meant I hadn’t planned a huge base from the start. So I felt constant pressure to expand. My options were to demolish everything and start over, or move somewhere new. That killed the peaceful feeling I had at the beginning.

My verdict: if you enjoy planning and optimizing a big base, you’ll probably have a great time. If you want a relaxed solo game, the pacing and the base limits will wear you down faster than you’d expect. I’d wait for a sale.

It's a creature collector but it doesn't feel like it's ripping off Pokemon in any meaningful way. I won't deny that certain aspects or designs seem like they come from it but it feels way more unique than a simple knock-off. 

Has survival elements which are pretty fun in my opinion. Standard temperature, weight, and base building mechanics. Certain Pals are more up to the task at hand than others, which encourages catching a variety to be the most efficient workforce possible. 

There's elements of perfection seeking with the pals due to passives, Luckies, Alphas, and stat changes per Pal. Breeding is a mechanic that can help with this, alongside several other features.

As far as I can tell of 54 hours played thus far (with plenty more to come), there's limits to how far you can push each stat but realistically it's good enough for what you need it for!

Playing with friends is easy enough due to room codes and servers being a thing. There's even crossplay compatibility which lets you play with your console friends!

All in all, as I said prior, one of the best games in my opinion made in recent years. Cannot recommend highly enough.

Ever since it was originally suspected months ago, Easy Anti Cheat has hit Helldivers 2, and it is honestly one of the most embarassing displays I've seen in a while put up by a Game Studio that was already disliked enough as is by many almost exclusively due to the decisions that Arrowhead has made over the course of the year.

So let me get this straight; You- An entire Company worth ~532 Million USD- cannot address basic game glitches (which you allegedly form ad-hoc development teams for, which makes this even more embarassing) and shortcomings in design. That's not okay, but it's not the end of the world objectively, because thankfully, for those who wish for Helldivers to be better, Modding was an option. Yet, in spite of it's objectively positive effect on the communities that enjoyed them at no expense of those who did not, Arrowhead chose to do everything in it's power to destroy the basis of them.

And for clarification, I'm not here to advocate for cheats, I understand live service games have their right to certain boundaries in modding, I'm here talking about this being detrimental for the countless players who went out of their way to create and use mods specifically catered to either fixing known glitches, or just making the gameplay smoother and more cohesive. Hellpod Steering Fixes, Vaulting/Climbing Fixes, AI Fixes, among others. These did not provide any sort of advantage over the average player and were almost entirely ran locally on the user's computer (unlike what Arrowhead would otherwise claim in their update post), and would only really be seen in a bad light if you interpret shortcomings in design or genuine bugs in development as the intended product (in spite of Arrowhead's own statements addressing them as 'bugs'), which is a painfully narrow perspective once you compare Helldivers' shortcomings in development to many other titles that allow or facilitate such mechanics while following similar principles in the desired gameplay envisioned by Arrowhead.

No one asked for this arbitrary removal of easy access to such fixes and the like, in fact; The majority wished for the opposite (as seen with the sheer popularity and positive endorsement these mods gained), or simply abstained, because in the end, what good could come from this other than potentially bragging rights for those in either side of the toxic ends of the game's community?

To put into a detached perspective what this is like for someone outside of the usual communities that this concerns:

Imagine that you have a series of plumbing issues in your house, and your local governing entity is supposed to provide public plumbing services for those in need like yourself. Yet, in spite of filing countless complaints and requests for the plumbing issues to be fixed in your house, the local governing entity fails to do anything about it. When they do finally send someone over, instead of fixing your plumbing, they somehow manage to break your house's heating, and after the fact, the local governing entity proudly post the work they carried out on your home that day- completely out of touch of the fact that they somehow broke a vital part of your house's ecosystem- and acredit themselves as great public service providers. With all of this having upset you, you logically turn to private plumbing providers, the local governing entity technically hasn't outlawed them, not yet, but they're unendorsed and operate outside of the usual scope of the local governing entity. You call them, and the very next day they show up, fix your plumbing and on top of that, they also fix your heating and advice you on some other things that might be wrong. You're happy, not because this private plumbing service is better than the local governing entity's, but because your plumbing is fixed, and a little extra too. So, you start advicing your neighbours having the same problems as you about this private plumbing service, some don't agree and choose to wait for the local governing entity to do their work, which is fine, but some others take you up on your recommendation, and they're equally pleased as you with the private plumbing service's work. However, the local governing entity catches wind of this from your local community, but instead of endorsing the private plumbing service, they place harsher laws in place to run them out of business and strictly enforce that plumbing may only be carried out by their public plumbing services, who to this day have made no positive change in their work ethic, of course. As if this was not bad enough, they send inspectors over to your house, and when they find that your plumbing had been fixed by private plumbing services, they break your plumbing in retaliation.

That's what is going on right now, and I cannot say for certain where the line in the sand is drawn at anymore. This isn't security against malicious cheats (such as what genuinely happens on games like early black ops titles with people being digitally attacked), this isn't moderation of unfair cheats, this is persecution of community-ran upgrade projects solely on the basis of what I can only asume to be jealousy, envy or blind hatred and prejudice. I have frankly lost all hope in Arrowhead, and I hope this helps make up your mind about who exactly you are trusting your money, time and disk drive space with.
