(I am sorry that this came out much longer and much, much less coherent (and with a few more bad words too...) than I wanted and expected, tho I think it just goes to show how much I loved this game and how badly it hurts seeing it get ripped away from everyone who loved it as well just because of some incompetent people's work and how they want you to play their game)

Now, where do I even begin with this... this GAME (emphasis on game) is an absolute masterpiece, lightning in a bottle, one of a kind work of art. Had you played this game close to a year or two ago you would have had one of the absolute best and most fun gameplay experiences ever, at least in the horde shooter genre. Shooting cool ass guns, throwing stratagems, yelling "FOR DEMOCRACY" (or whatever else you fight for (wink)) and blowing anything close to you into smithereens (with an ammount of firepower that should NEVER be given to drug fueled lunatics that the Helldivers are) is, unfortunately, really really really fun (mainly with friends). The graphics are stellar as well, truly impressive what the devs once managed to make in such an outdated piece of software (something that truly shows this studio's potential), AND also in just 23GB of space. The enemies are so cool (visually at least), I do love myself some "cosmic horror" mixed with nostalgia of things I never saw when they came out (such as Starship Troopers, Terminator, War of the Worlds, etc. etc.). One more thing I have to applaud is the voice acting, some truly amazing, visceral-sounding and sometimes comedic stuff here, and the music (the soundtrack never does get old, no matter how many times you dive). One last thing... most of the community is fantastic, making entire sub-factions of Helldivers with original lore (such as Mercdivers, Chaosdivers (haiii)), making art, mods, music. crafting original stories, creating skits... even just the players you do meet in-game feel like actual characters in a larger setting. I truly don't think I'd enjoy this game even half as much had it not had such an awesome playerbase.

Now you might be thinking "Well why would you not recommend this game? This sounds amazing!" And, admittedly, it would be - had Arrowhead not been constantly and consistently fucking everything up for nearly all of this game's life :/. Allow me to describe the perpetual cycle this game seems to be stuck in (otherwise called the "it's so over" and "we are so back" phases): Arrowhead (AH as I will call them from now because I don't feel like writing their name again) introduces some new, conntroversial, and absolutely ridiculous balance change/decision, which goes against everything that the community wants (for example the ridiculous hive guard change, THE ANTI-CHEAT CHANGE, the Coyote AR STEALTH nerf, an unplayable update that is so broken it makes you believe they never test their game (I'm staring into your empty soul, Into the Unjust), vehicles in war bonds, stealth nerfs in general (you would not believe how much they love to do this), being against any form of player creativity ("Why would you shoot into an enemy's leg? This strategy, although fully functional, makes ZERO logical sense, like why would you shoot a leg when you see the head? Are you stupid? Therefore, since it is not how we, AH, want you to play our game, we will make the head the only weak point so you shoot for the head next time, you're welcome :)"); I could go on, apologies for things you may not understand, although explaining would make this ridiculously long review even longer) -> part of the community riots, review-bomb gallore ensues, YouTubers make videos,... -> AH is silent for about one/two weeks (this is the "it's so over" phase) -> AH puts out a half-assed apology, saying they will revert the change (or do something else that will get the community off its back), that they are listening and will communicate better next time -> players satisfied for a while, have some fun with the game again (although less since the game is still a mess that AH does not feel like fixing, but they did the bare minimum and the community is having fun with the game) ("we are so back" phase) -> repeat. This cycle is draining any long-time enjoyment you can ever have with the game, that is the main reason you should not buy this game. AH is like a clingy ex that keeps promising to do better but always squanders the opportunity because of their laziness and newfound incompetence.
Why do they make decisions like this tho? Well, dear reader who is for some reason still reading. that has to do with the game they WANT to make. AH's ambition was NOT to (allegedly) "attract 6 milllion CoD players" (among others). They wanted a game with a very specific (and stupid, might I add) niche made up of realism and sci-fi, GRUNT FANTASY HORDE SHOOTER where you play as people who have the authority to rain hellfire even upon civillian architecture if it means killing even just one enemy, are able to raze entire cities with an orbital laser, can kill thousands of enemies without dying and also have unrestricted access to some magical drug that can apparently stop hemorrhaging from the chest, mend broken limbs and what not (oh yeah and then there are also the regular forces of the army who help you fight and are kind of underequipped but don't worry, you don't play as them). Then not even to attract that many players at all (they wanted a niche game like HD1 was). But they attracted "6 million CoD players", among others. So... do they change their priorities? Cater to what the vast, VAST majority of the playerbase wants? No, you silly. "A game for everyone is a game for no one," after all. AH would much rather just chase the illusion of the impossible game they want to make rather than make the game everybody wants them to make (and seriously, their "selective realism" as I've come to call it needs to be studied, they balance the players with accordance to "logic" and the enemies are basically free to do whatever they want even if it doesn't make any sense. The players really captured it with the "the enemies paid 40 Dollars to play the game too" joke). This stubborness and incapability to learn that what they want simply cannot work (even tho it has been proven to them time and time again for the past year and a half at least) is the reason I donot recommend you buy anything from them again.

Now I feel the other criticisms have already been captured by the rest of the recent reviews (such as destroying the modding community on a whim because they made AH look bad and completely incompetent, the blatant lying and deceiving, only releasing paid content (because ain't no one grinding 9+ hours for that), and many, many more), so I will just leave this as it is.

It cannot be the same Arrowhead that made this wonderful game, and I do not believe it can go back to that. I am not using any mods, I completely deleted the entire game, and reinstalled Easy Anti-Cheat multiple times. Yet, I am permanently blocked by Error Code 0xc0000142, an EAC error that means everything and nothing at this point because EAC is actively flags and fights completely bening software and files.
To make matters worse, the official GGuninst.exe does absolutely nothing. You still have to manually scrape out residual GameGuard garbage from the EAC folders after updates and force a cold boot, otherwise your system just collapses. The last time I could play normally was before the EAC patch from few days ago. It is pure irony: EAC remains utterly incapable of preventing actual cheaters, but it does everything in its power to keep legitimate players away.
You practically need the perfect "mitochondrial DNA" and a freshly wiped, naked operating system with zero drivers or peripherals just to get to the main menu. People are getting blocked simply because they have the following connected, installed, or running:
• Even the OS itself: Windows (Plus Linux, Mac, Steam Deck, handheld PCs, or even low-end hardware).
• Software & Overlays: Third-party anti-virus, standard overlays (Discord, Steam), Quality-of-Life, or Accessibility mods.
• Peripherals & Audio: Soundcards, complex audio stacks, external mixers, drawing tablets, music gear, or specific mouse/keyboard software. Even standard motherboard audio software like MSI Nahimic triggers trigger EAC.

Arrowhead's "Idgaf" Attitude & Endless Excuses
I used to want to defend Arrowhead, but at this point, it feels like they simply do not care about the game anymore. As far as i am aware of ever since the Dust Devils update (basically since i play myself), their handling of the community and balancing has been a disaster.
Arrowhead decided to completely block and delete the loading of LUA scripts just to force their anti-cheat down our throats. Instead of actual solutions, they mask their lazy development behind corporate excuses like "not enough design space" to justify terrible balance decisions and restrictions. Why fix the game when you can just restrict the players? They could have easily chosen better paths:
1. Whitelisting & Sandbox (Like Deep Rock Galactic): A proper sandbox would allow players to mess around with stats without affecting the main game, leaving visual mods, audio replacements, and UI adjustments completely untouched.
2. Server-Side Validation: A system that cross-references live data to detect if players have zero recoil, infinite ammo, or an impossible fire rate, and kicks them accordingly. UI and texture mods dont send gameplay data to the server, so they would have been safe.
3. A Dedicated Modding API: Instead of letting uncontrolled LUA scripts inject directly into the game memory, they could have provided a restricted API to safely allow custom UI, camera perspectives, and HUD elements.
4. Community Integration: They could have at least integrated the best community-made fixes and QoL improvements directly into the core game.

The Anti-Consumer Corporate Greed of Sony
But lets be honest: Arrowhead is just one side of the coin. Sony wants everything run by their rules, even on PC. Sony behaves like a crying toddler, throwing tantrums when things dont go their way while desperately trying to force a "digital-only" future. Its hilarious because they keep shooting themselves in the foot, their latest, heavily locked-down PlayStation OS version (hardened specifically because of GTA 6) was recently kinda jailbroken anyway.
They force a PSN account requirement on almost every PC release. We fought back on Helldivers 2, but the bitter truth remains: the game is still region-locked in over 170 countries on Steam because you literally cannot create a PSN account in those regions. Cross-progression is a nice marketing buzzword, but Sony will still isolate PCs from PlayStation whenever it benefits their "Player Lifetime Value" metrics.
They protect their failing Live Service model at all costs. I wouldnt be surprised if Warbonds get hit with massive price hikes soon, Im betting next year a new Warbond will cost at least 2000 SC just so Sony can recoup the millions they lost on Kojima. Speaking of which, they are petty enough to block Kojima from using their proprietary Decima Engine for future projects (even though Death Stranding was already finished), delaying game releases even further. Kojima helped build modern PlayStation, and this is how they treat him.

What "High-Quality Standards"?
Sony loyalists always brag about their "high standards." What standards? Concord, Babylon's Fall, Destruction Allstars, Knack? Never heard of them? Exactly, because they were some of the biggest multimillion-dollar flops in gaming history. Even their flagship titles like God of War, Spider-Man 2, and Horizon Forbidden West, while beautifully written, feel like slightly shinier PS4 games ported to PS5 with zero gameplay innovation. Its the Call of Duty formula wrapped in a cinematic blanket. Look at Horizon: they threw it onto PS Plus so fast it barely had a chance to sell copies, all while forcing you to pay for an overpriced subscription just to play online.
Look at Bungie, the studio Xbox willingly let go. Sony bought them for billions to teach them how to make successful Live Service games. The result? Marathon became one of the biggest disasters in Sonys history due to internal fighting, constant delays, and a catastrophic soft launch. Meanwhile, even Xbox has the decency to let studios keep their IPs and independence when they part ways instead of straight-up executing them.

Historical Arrogance Comes Full Circle
Sonys corporate arrogance isnt new. Twenty years ago, when the PS3 launched at 1,5 times the price of an Xbox 360, Sonys executive team literally told consumers: “For example, for gamers, they want to have a PlayStation 3 so much... for them, to have a second job and get more money... they want to buy it.”
Leaks show the PS6 is going to be more expensive than a high-end Steam Machine, easily breaking the 1000€/$1000 mark. If they try to force the PSN mandate onto Helldivers again, they are going to trigger another 2011-level disaster. Because when it comes to data privacy and consumer security, Sony hasnt learned a single thing in 15 years.
A once-brilliant game, ruined by restrictive developer decisions and the boundless corporate greed of a publisher that utterly despises the PC market. Not recommended.

I am a massive fan of HellDivers. While its progression is less to be desired, the power fantasy of being a soldier across basically an empire has been amazingly implemented with strong visuals, gunplay, hoardes of enemies, and missions across different planets. 
I also wanted to add: You are more than likely going to see a lot of negative reviews from people who have over 100 hours in this game. To this, I request you ask yourself this: "Can I really trust someone who played a game for over 100 hours just to say they didn't like it?". I ask myself that every single time I see a player with that many hours just to complain about one or two features a game did or didn't have, meanwhile they are absolutely enthralled by everything else. It's a lot of privilege to be able to keep playing a game they can't recommend, and it's sort of embarrassing. 

Pros:
Combat is amazing - Gunplay is top notch and weapons feel like they have some weight with every trigger fire. 
Strategems - The air drops/ships are AMAZING. I never thought of this form of special ability before and they made it seem effortless. A single soldier can carry around the equivalent of several air raids worth of bombs and strategems making most situations winnable
Enemy variety: There are HUNDREDS of enemies in each map, and the best part is they are all entirely lethal. Your helldiver is bound to die to one of these creatures and is a replaceable asset in the reach of democracy. You may find yourself play through 8 different helldiver lives in a single mission only to come out successful. It's a really interesting system instead of keeping you with the same character. 
Missions: Each planet feels diverse and different from one another. While one feels like the Bayou of a swamp, others can feel like arid desert planets where road vehicles are preferred modes of transportation. 

Cons: 
I hate the progression system. I shouldn't have to buy credits or grind for over 100 hours to get enough "Super Credits" to unlock a pack of weapons or armor that I only want one thing out of. I think this is the worst portion of the game and is only here to keep people playing. It locks WAY too much content behind extreme playtime walls to the point it forces players who want to try a new weapon to buy the stupid packs. They are only 10 dollars each, but I'm pretty sure they've released a ton of them. It's a very anti-consumer based model that is frustrating. 
I honestly can't think of another CON. This game is wonderful except for the above so I can't give it a bad review, it's just something that keeps me coming back for more so I don't have everything unlocked...it's frustrating but it works I guess?

In recent news with Helldivers 2 being review bombed I thought id add to the discourse. I assume this will be drowned out in the mountain of rightful criticism but I want to make a case and point for three points of contention for me. 

1. Lack of respect, communication, and accountability. 
Arrowhead has a track record of miscommunication when it comes to working with player expectations and responding to community concerns. A small but long-standing example is the hellpod bugs that still exist today. Before the recent update, passionate community members fixed these bugs through modding. Now, with the easy anti-cheat, that was blocked. 
On a larger scale, communication about roadmaps, timelines, and future improvements. Arrowhead recently produced a roadmap for this year. Containing 7 goals. To my understanding, they have achieved only 3-4, if you count the gloom expanding. (Which isn't related to the Devoid of Liberty focus of the squids). They now have two months left to fulfill these promises, and the company has said they will be taking breaks in the coming months. 
Of course, the community questioned this. Some more charged than others, you may ask: what was Arrowhead's  response? "Sorry lol I know the roadmap update that was supposed to come in October didn't come in October, but like, us telling you it was coming in October was just us giving you a general idea of when it would come out." This would be barely digestible in a vacuum, but Arrowhead has done this over and over again. 
The issue isn't that development takes time; it's the fact that communication isn't present, and when the community calls out this lack of communication, there is ZERO accountability, and the community is told to wait longer without question. The community shouldn't be made to feel unreasonable for holding a company accountable to its promises. 

2. The commodification of the player experience. 
A growing concern and frustration of mine is that anything that could meaningfully improve the game is consistently placed behind a paywall. 

War-bonds cost 10-20 dollars depending on if they are premium or not. War-bonds are DLC regardless of how people want to cut it; each time you buy a warbond, it's DLC. It's the only way to gain new weapons, armor, and any other gameplay add-ons besides the super store, which requires super credits as well. Again, this can be fine in a vacuum, but out of 26 warbonds, A SINGLE ONE is free. A new player will have such a limited loadout and will eventually use the Liberator Penetrator until they quit the game if they are free to play. Gaining super credits through playing is its own conversation, which I will not dive into fully, but ask anyone with more than 30 hours in the game, and they will tell you it's like collecting breadcrumbs while swimming in water. 

This begs the question of whether Arrowhead even cares. Is the company interested in improving the experience for both new and experienced players, or is it more concerned about finding ways to monetize consistent engagement? Both can be true, yes, but we as a community know where they lean predominantly. With the most recent warbond, which "answers" the community conversation about pigment changes for armor and locking it behind a $10 warbond. The community will raise a concern, and if they want the answer, they better be ready to pay that fee because $ 30 wasn't enough. You are welcome to ignore it, though!  But everyone around you will playing a completely different game with weapons and armor you have been wishing for. It's a joke. 

3. The community's suppression of criticism and their obsession with internalizing corporate interests. 
This, in my opinion, is the biggest "what ifs" in my mind. There many different divers in the community.  An insane amount if im being honest. We have the average 9-5 dad who has his kids on the mic, plays one round, and leaves (we love this guy). From there, we have fashion divers, faction divers, MO divers, explosive divers, and the list goes on. What we also have, and what is an utter plague on this community, is the Glaze Diver. These people are absolutely insufferable. A portion of the player base raises legitimate concerns. A case in point is the lack of fulfillments on the roadmap, and they are surrounded by divers that say, "All your worries will come next year, bro." "We just got a war bond? Why are you crying about it?" its insanity. On the topic of the new war bond, its main sniper was advertised as a one shot to the Hulk's eye. It isn't; it's two shots. Of course, some of the community is frustrated and raises concerns about being lied to. Then the glaze divers come in and say "skill issue" or "you cant expect it to be perfect." THIS CANNOT BE REAL. These people are the AI bots on Twitter. 
Another case of this was back in February through March: a community member challenged the devs to complete a difficulty 10 set of missions on Oshaune. They said they would donate 1k if they could extract in all 3 missions. Great challenge, and it started a conversation about how the base tools in the game don't match the game's balance. It seemed like a glimmer of hope at the time; the CEO, Shams, posted pictures of them engaging in the challenge. How do you think this concluded? Well, if you didn't guess the original community poster getting doxxed and harassed, then you guessed wrong! Oh, and of course, after the doxxing, both the community and Devs dropped the event. 
This doesn't event begin to speak too how these communities interact on the internet in spaces like TikTok or Instagram. Comments on videos are filled with shitty AI pictures and the "face the wall" memes when players are simply having fun, being called a dumbass because you dare complain even slightly.  What if we simply had a community that didnt cannibalizing itself and would hold devs accountable when they are making millions from us? 
I could go on, but I will end it here. My issue isn't with Arrowhead making simple mistakes, monetizing the game, or having struggles with development. My issue is the growing disconnect and lack of awareness Arrowhead has with its average player. Alongside the inability to call out Arrowhead from both the company perspective and a portion of the community.  

I want to enjoy this game and trust its development but Arrowhead consistently makes this less and less likely to happen. Arrowhead Making the players apologize and telling them to wait longer after breaking their own promises over and over again.

Writing this feels like telling a friend who has been around for a while that "we can't be friends anymore."
In my opinion, Helldivers 2 was the perfect PVE game that I have been wanting and waiting for the longest time. I won't lie. My 1000 hours in this game proves how much I have enjoyed playing it. Problem is, like a toxic friend, I can't recommend staying around any more. A casual glance at the leaks available on YouTube proves that this game had potential, and for some reason, the developers didn't want to expand on this potential. Instead they have shot themselves with their own gatling gun and have made something that is just "meh..."

PROS:
- "Starship Troopers-esque" political satire that is fun to roleplay.
- 4-player Coop, tactical shooter that doesn't feel like other "tactical shooters".
- Every game is coated in a liberal dose of chaos, so even though you are completing the same objectives over and over, it does not feel boring.
- Super Credit farming is boring, but easy enough to do. Makes earning warbonds feel all the better.
- 3 Unique factions with their own stories, and resembling similar factions from Helldivers 1.
- Great attention to detail to armor and weapons giving a unique feel to combat and gameplay.
- Technical requirements to play the game are more reasonable compared to other main line games today.

CONS: (strictly referring to the game.)
- Small vocal community is incredibly toxic at times. Even kicking SOS Divers from just joining missions. Big waste of time usually. (Although I also understand that those that do this are not always trying to be toxic.)
- While weapons do have a unique feel, the lack of customization for the weapons reduces much of their overall effectiveness. Meaning that meta weapons and power creep is an unfortunate result.
- Lack of customization also means that uniform loadouts are difficult if nigh impossible as color matching is a literal nightmare. (AH, WHY DO YOU HAVE SO MANY DIFFERENT VARIENTS OF WHITE???)
- Armors also have a unique feel to them, but like the weapons, the lack of customization prevents some armors from shining resulting in the meta and power creep affecting which armors get used.
- Stratagem Deployment still bounces all over the place when attempting advantageous placement resulting in the actual deployment being disadvantageous.
- While the 3 factions are unique in their own right, each subvariant lacks depth and usually only adds 1-2 new enemies (3 if we are very, very lucky). For some reason the Illuminate got the short end of the stick this past illuminate update with only 2 new enemies bringing the total number of unique enemies to I think 12? (I might be wrong with this) The Automatons and the Terminids received much more love in their updates. (With exception to the Noxious Strain. I believe more love could have been put into that.)

CONS: (Strictly with the Developers)
- I honestly cannot tell you if AH loves their game or absolutely hates it with a passion. I cannot tell you if AH loves their community or absolutely hates it with a passion. They constantly shoot themselves in the foot and look at us and ask "why is there so much backlash?"
- AH removed a lot of content from the alpha that was positive and overall exciting to look forward to. I loved the leaked cultists and what it could have done for the illuminate as it was a truly unique sub-faction, but... they just removed it from ever being content in the game, despite the cultists actually being a complete sub-faction and bringing lore and story with them. Now we just have the dollar-store pyramid head and necromorph.
- There has been a trend of not communicating with their community. They will go a few months like a binge drinking alcoholic and communicate, just to all of a sudden stop. And then they come back and say "Sorry! We will do better in the future." and it's right back into an abusive relationship with them. And, I understand that some of that is because a few of us still hope for something absolutely amazing, just like an abusive, toxic relationship.
- AH controls what major orders the helldivers are supposed to work towards, and they have not been the best Game Masters at doing this. Some of which is because even though they made the game, for some reason they don't really know how to play it. Kinda like a Dungeon Master who can't read the next few pages of their scripted scenario that they made themselves, and then they try to adlib it terribly. To their credit, I would also probably lose my mind if I had to manage 50,000 players for a DND game.
- The community has been begging AH since forever to add customization to weapons, armors and stratagems. Even though the Alpha build leak (I think it was alpha) had customization, AH has determined that it is simply impossible to include more customization in their game. So, naturally, modders did it with a few scraps in a cave and came out with something amazing. And AH just had to ruin our day with one of their recent updates and EAC, which killed the game for those who were using mods, and even some of us who weren't using mods.

I've been playing this game since release, split between PC and PS5, and it genuinely pains me to be a part of one of the most toxic communities around a live service game. Arrowhead are not perfect, but they've made a damn near perfect game, and are consistent with their support for it, despite working against Sony, China, their own playerbase, and a wider community that seemingly wants nothing more than to watch them burn to the ground.

Helldivers 2 is, for my money, the best multiplayer game ever. Above MW2, above Overwatch at it's peak, above Siege at it's peak, above even Battlefield 1. This game does not need mods, especially mods that actively change gameplay, and I think Arrowhead are in the right for their decision to add EAC, even if EAC is awful in it's own right. Review bombing this game over and over again does not fix stratagem ball bounce being wonky, or fix the odd hellpod steering, or balance the game to specifically how each negative reviewer wants.

Personally, I think the balancing of most of the enemies and weapons is great, and it's been that way for pretty much the whole lifetime of the game. I play basically exclusively difficulty 10 on all three fronts and against each subfaction, and I love all of it. I'm still waiting for them to go up to 15 like the first game so I can feel like I'm truly fighting for my life. Some guns are just bad, some enemies are just really hard, and that's okay. Vox Engines should be an oppressive force that actively get in the way of your very existence, that is their purpose. War Striders are easy to deal with even in high numbers if you're packing AT, which you should be against bots anyway. Struggling against swarms of bugs? Jump pack and Stalwart, trust me.

Also the amount of content AH add to this game on a regular basis is kind of insane, and anyone who says otherwise is literally just hating on AH for the sake of hating on them. Warbonds are easily earned, as are medals, if you just actually play the game. Some add more content than others for sure, but every one they've released in the past year has been nothing but peak. I do wish they would put out free stratagems a little more frequently, but I imagine it's a lot easier said than done. 

Arrowhead aren't the best devs out there, but they're better than every other dev team behind any game with a player count as consistent as HD2. I'm excited for their next project, and for however many years HD2 has left in it. I've never once been truly let down by an update to this game, and I don't have any reason to believe I'll ever be if AH can keep up the quality. New bug strain is fantastic btw, and terrifying. Easier than I expected, but that's a nice change of pace from the other bug strains that tend to kick my ass lol.

After six NG+ runs, I can safely say this is one of my favourite action games. The combat is easily its strongest point. You have a good number of tools to work with, and as you unlock more skills, spells, transformations, and equipment, you get even more ways to approach fights. Learning a boss's moveset, finding openings, and finally beating the shit out of something that's been kicking your ass for the past half hour never gets old.

There are a ridiculous number of bosses in this game, to the point where it can feel like one long boss rush, but most of the major encounters are fantastic. The animations, music, and presentation make some of these fights an absolute spectacle. The environments are gorgeous too, and despite the mostly linear level design, there's plenty to find if you take the time to explore. Hidden areas, secret bosses, optional quests, and useful rewards are scattered throughout the chapters. Some of the best content is tucked behind things you could easily miss, which makes exploring rewarding, even if finding everything can become a headache.

The story is interesting, but it can be pretty confusing if you're not familiar with Journey to the West. The world and its characters have plenty of depth, though I still had to look things up to understand certain parts. The animated stories at the end of each chapter are a great addition and help make sense of things that might otherwise go over your head. Some of them are among my favourite moments in the game. The soundtrack has a few fantastic tracks too, even if the whole thing isn't particularly memorable. And the visuals? The art direction, enemy designs, and environments are all bloody gorgeous (tho I hated CH4 lmao).

There are a few things that bothered me, though. The invisible walls can be ridiculous, especially when a path looks completely accessible, but the game refuses to let you through. A lot of quests, bosses, and upgrades are also easy to miss, with very little indication that you've overlooked something. I don't mind secrets being hidden, but some of these are a bit too obscure. The final chapter was also a letdown in terms of level design, and I would've liked more room to explore there. With so many boss fights, some of the regular enemy encounters can start feeling like filler. There are also occasional technical hiccups, and certain fights can be frustrating because of questionable hitboxes, input reading, and lengthy enemy attack chains. A few encounters also make it harder to stick with certain builds, which can be annoying when you've spent time putting one together.

Despite all that, I had a hell of a time with this game. It has its share of questionable design decisions, but the good far outweighs the bad. Six NG+ runs should tell you how much I enjoyed it.

Black Myth Wukong is a very good game that has plenty of interesting bosses, intense staff combat, and rewarding RPG elements to grow your powers. The game is mostly linear and you hopscotch from one boss fight to the next, while the game rewards backtracking to previous chapters to open secret paths and bosses.  Although some bosses can be defeated within a few tries, there are formidable bosses that can take hours to tackle the best strategy, stat powers, and dodging. It can be difficult to overcome especially during the beginning two chapters while you are at your weakest and still learning the game.
The story of Wukong becomes an interesting adventure and artistic journey even though I did not follow all the strange Chinese lore.
A few parts of the game are a bit cryptic as I could not figure out how to progress in the final chapter and had to peek at a guide to tell me what to do next.  I only partially enjoyed this game as it brought a bit of button fatigue on very tough fights but I really wanted to accomplish this interesting adventure.

CHAPTER AREAS
I really like that you hardly ever have to redo Chapter areas since mini-bosses remain cleared after you defeat them, and the game has generous amounts of warping "shrines" along the paths.  Almost all major bosses have a shrine right before meeting them.  When you do die, you do not lose any of your XP "Will points" and your powers are replenished without penalty.  The levels have a really good combination of common enemies, mini-bosses, and chapter bosses, that makes each area unique and surprising.  The game can be a bit cryptic and you can miss optional items that would really help on certain boss fights.

COMBAT
Fights can be intense events and you need to figure out when to hit with small attacks and charge up a stronger attack.  You need to get a feel for watching multiple gauges and cool down meters such as Spells, Focus points, Transformations, Mana; each are separate reserves of power that you will want to spend at key points in a fight. It takes experimentation to figure out how these pieces work and how they can be effective against a big enemy.  There are hidden abilities of parrying and "see-through" smashes that are really hard to get to work consistently, although you can pass the game without these super perfect timed moves.
The dodging is a constant maneuver during any fight, and it is responsive and crisp while giving you a generous window of safety.

FEW ISSUES  
There are only a few frustrating issues, such as sprinting often feels slow and is interrupted by lock on mechanics on the bosses or small inclines in the terrain. It made some fights feel frustrating and heavy like you are stuck in the mud.  The game uses invisible barriers to stop you from falling, but unpredictably other areas you can fall off ledges.  Some boss phases can be chaos on the screen and you almost cannot see what is hitting you, as well as the camera flips around.  I found it necessary to record video captures of some boss fights to analyze what actually is happening and try to see when to dodge or run or fight. The game gives you freedom to redistribute stat points, but some other items like weapons/armor are permanent and hard to know when to spend your limited materials.

DIFFICULTY - ONE MODE
The difficulty of the game cannot be adjusted.  About 14 of the bosses (of which I counted about 76 major fights) were really hard for me, each taking hours/days and some over 100 tries, while almost all the other bosses took only a few tries. I literally would memorize every move set, but would get pulverized after doing so well into a 5 to 8 minute fight and try again. Some bosses I was not sure I would ever beat but felt like I lucked out.
In retrospect, for average players, this game does not teach its systems such as Transformations, Mana, Qi, and Focus and you may flat out not realize how to use them along with juggling all the gauges and moves in a fight.
The game can be interesting and deep for people to build the most effective powers, but it can get a little cumbersome to reinvestigate all the stats when you are struggling with multiple phases of a boss.  Sometimes stacking a stat for a certain boss is the extra edge you need to get one more hit.

NEXT
For me, Black Myth Wukong is a notch too tough for the first play through.  On the most challenging bosses, you not only have to dodge amazingly well for long periods, but you need to experiment with powers and stats to find a perfect counter measure to every phase of a fight. Some players may enjoy the depth of fight options but to me there were too many combinations to keep trying something that will do more than a small sliver of damage.
I may play some of New Game Plus as a victory lap to destroy early-chapter bosses, but I am not sure I want to face the final bosses again with their punishing move sets.

# One of the Best AAA Games I’ve Ever Played

*Black Myth: Wukong* is easily one of the best AAA games I’ve played, and it has definitely earned a spot in my Top 10.

The game is heavily story-driven and draws inspiration from *Journey to the West*. I recommend learning a little about the original story beforehand if you want a deeper understanding of the game's narrative and characters. However, even if you go in completely blind, like I did, you'll still have a fantastic experience.

For me, **the combat and boss designs are among the absolute best parts of the game.** Every encounter feels exciting, and the variety of bosses keeps things interesting throughout your journey.

One thing worth mentioning is that the game isn't as punishing as many other Souls-like games. In fact, I wouldn't consider it a traditional Souls-like, despite what some people might expect. That doesn't mean it's easy, though! Certain bosses can be genuinely challenging, and you'll sometimes need to experiment with different builds, abilities, and strategies to overcome them.

The game is also packed with secrets and hidden content. There's no shame in looking things up on YouTube if you get stuck or want to discover something you missed. Even after completing the game, there's still plenty to explore, and a second playthrough can be well worth your time.

**Overall, I absolutely love this game.** It's easily one of my favourite gaming experiences and has secured a place in my personal Top 10.

I would definitely recommend *Black Myth: Wukong* if you have the patience, enjoy action RPGs, and want a game that offers fantastic combat, memorable boss fights, and a satisfying level of challenge. Absolutely worth getting!

Journey to the West is one of my favorite mythology tails, so I knew I'd been playing this sooner or later.
Sadly, 20ish hours in I just don't feel compelled to progress further.

There are many aspects I like: for one, haven't played a combat this satisfying since Ghost of Tsushima. Mastering your own evolving skills and learning enemies patterns really feels rewarding - choreography and cinematics are great and I never felt frustrated once.
Obscure lore is big plus for me in the way it's presented and delivered. Voices in the wind, riddles and a lot of hinting to Sun Wukong's myth are amazing. And visuals are really top notch.

But there are some huge problems that such bright sides can't hide for long.
There are basic upgrades hidden behind missable NPCs quest.
There are missable bosses and encounters that lock themselves until NG+ without any hint.
Most things don't have any trigger to signal the player something has changed, or that his actions had an impact - resulting in potentially missing stuff you actually unlocked or progressed towards.
Some bosses / encounters straight up negate some builds, not letting you use whatever playstyle suits you the most.

These points are straight up bad design choices that ultimately hinder the two best aspects of this game, leaving it carried by its visuals. If you like souls-inspired boss rushes, I'd suggest buying at a fairly discounted price.

[h1][b]Black Myth: Wukong[/b][/h1]
[h3][b]My Journey to the West — 130+ Hours Later[/b][/h3]

I had not anticipated that the game would take more than 130 hours. And yet, I find myself approaching the conclusion of my personal "Journey to the West." I took a methodical approach, exploring at my own pace and occasionally optimising my equipment more than was necessary. I was pleasantly surprised by the extensive range of content available. Each chapter unveils new features and storylines, consistently maintaining my interest. I was rarely bored, and best of all, I was so immersed in the activity that I did not notice the time passing. Indeed, I am still playing to increase the difficulty with highly optimised gear.

[h3][b]Gameplay, Combat & Progression[/b][/h3]

In terms of gameplay, I found the difficulty level to be fairly balanced for a first playthrough. However, the difficulty level of some bosses was notably higher than others. I particularly appreciated the variety of skills and upgrades, which allowed for customisation of combat styles.

Depending on the boss, certain stances proved more effective than others to vary their approach rather than sticking to a single strategy. The game offers a wide range of weapons that prioritise power or critical hits, as well as skills that can be developed. In addition, there are armour sets that combine to offer additional bonuses, allowing plenty of room to experiment and fine-tune your setup.

The healing system is well-designed, with various flasks to unlock and drinks to combine for bonus effects. The bestiary is also impressive, featuring creatures and bosses with meticulous designs. 

The weapons and armour are impressive, and each discovery stimulates the desire to explore new possibilities. I would also like to express my appreciation of the ability to reset my skills at will, thus allowing me to experiment with different combat styles. Furthermore, I would have appreciated greater flexibility in the use of armour upgrade resources. In my personal experience, I have sometimes held back on certain items due to concerns about wasting them on equipment that I was planning to replace. This has sometimes resulted in missing out on potentially beneficial upgrades.

[h3][b]Visuals, Art Direction & Sound[/b][/h3]

Visually, I was extremely impressed. The settings in the various chapters are stunning, but it is the animation, the creatures' movements, and the visual effects that truly set this production apart. The art direction is a complete success. Even the animated sequences are charming and well-executed. The music skilfully transitions from a supporting role to a more prominent one during the most intense scenes. The key benefit of this approach is that it does not rely on visual cues or secondary characters to guide the user.

However, it should be noted that there are some aspects that could be improved. The most significant issue I have encountered is the presence of invisible walls, which can be frustrating when attempting to navigate detailed environments.

[h3][b]Story & Lore — A Journey Worth Knowing[/b][/h3]

In terms of the storyline, Black Myth: Wukong is set in a highly detailed universe, although the narrative world is not always clearly explained. The game draws inspiration from the famous Chinese novel Journey to the West, which recounts the journey of the monk Xuanzang to India, accompanied by the iconic Monkey King, Sun Wukong. This character is renowned for his cunning, his power, and his ability to shapeshift, making him an iconic figure in Chinese mythology. In addition, he was the source of inspiration for the character [b]Son Goku[/b] in the well-known manga [b]Dragon Ball.[/b]

I found the references to Chinese mythology to be of great interest. However, it should be noted that without prior knowledge of the subject, certain events may appear confusing and difficult to understand. At times, I would have preferred the storytelling to be more immersive, so as to better grasp the story's stakes. The animated sequences are of a high standard and significantly enhance the overall appeal of the adventure.

[h2][b]Conclusion — Worth the Wait[/b][/h2]

After such a long anticipation for this game, it was only natural to have some reservations, as is often the case when expectations are set too high. However, I was incorrect. Black Myth: Wukong met my expectations and even exceeded them thanks to the richness of its content. Despite a few minor issues, these are outweighed by the significant enjoyment derived from extensive gameplay.

I therefore have no hesitation in recommending it. The memorable combat, the exceptional bestiary, the sublime art direction, and an adventure that lasted much longer than expected all contributed to making this game a worthwhile purchase. Following 130 hours of gameplay, my sole objective is to reconnect with my team members and commence the adventure once more. Finally, it appears that the Monkey King has gained a valuable life lesson: material wealth is not necessarily a prerequisite for happiness. In contrast, the key elements of happiness are a capable team and the ability to overcome challenges. If you are having difficulty following the narrative, there is no cause for concern. Simply read Journey to the West, or acknowledge that the intricacies of Son Goku's tale exceeded initial expectations.

[i]Black Myth: Wukong[/i] does enough things right that, despite my significant reservations about it, I have to recommend it. The art direction and world design create genuine moments of awe. The characters and plot pique interest (as you'd hope, given the rich source material). The combat and exploration--for the most part--feel engaging. There's an all-you-can-eat buffet of boss fights, and a surprising number of secrets for scavenger hunters. Presentation-wise, it's unquestionably a AAA game (special shout-out to the 2D and stop-motion animators who truly elevated it IMO).

But [i]Wukong[/i] also frustrated me a lot of the time:

- [b]The Combat System Feels Confused[/b]: [i]Wukong[/i] is caught between [i]Elden Ring[/i]-style dodge-six-delayed-attacks-in-a-row and [i]Nioh[/i]-style combo-all-day gameplay. When I got to the end of [i]Lies of P[/i], [i]Sekiro[/i], and [i]The First Berserker: Khazan[/i], I felt like I accumulated genuine knowledge and skill that prepared me for the late game bosses such that I could no-hit them. In [i]Wukong[/i], many victories felt cheap in comparison.

- [b]Performance, Input Queueing, etc.[/b]: I hesitate to raise this because it obviously depends heavily on one's setup. But UE5 is gonna UE5, and this game's no exception. Having the game continually hitch during traversal between areas or randomly drop frames in certain regions/boss fights was a bummer. Also had a not insignificant number of crashes. There's also the matter of just, I don't know, jank? Hitting the heal button repeatedly at a key moment and not having it register because of (I assume) how the game queues inputs? And the heal is slow enough as it is. Speaking of which...

- [b]General Tediousness[/b]: Frequent boss runbacks, including many that add no challenge whatsoever. Boss cutscenes (and other cutscenes for that matter) that you either can't skip or that take far too long to skip. Missable questlines that are extraordinarily easy to blow up. Some chapters that are poorly paced and some boss fights that feel like an ordeal. Why is the skill tree so obtuse, and why is stat buffing tied to a specific NPC who needs specific items that, again, prompt yet another cutscene animation each time you level up?

- [b]Some Actual Stinkers[/b]: Look, don't get me wrong: I think this game's great. It has a lot of truly wonderful areas and moments that genuinely made me question my [i]Astro Bot[/i] allegiance. But without getting spoilery, there were also a number of chapters/sections that weren't enjoyable at all and I never want to do them again.

On the whole, however, I'm sorry I avoided [i]Wukong[/i] for as long as I did because, despite my criticisms, it truly is a good game.

Performance was fine on my end—minor stuttering in some water-heavy boss areas, but nothing that stood out.

A dodge with 3 progressively longer animations looks cool but is impractical as hell. Self Experience and Insights:
Growing up as a child who's obsessed with Journey to the West, this is the bleakest version that matches the originally intended critique to the corrupted bureaucratic dynasty.

We idolise and even worship Wukong as a deity in Chinese's Taoism + Buddhism hybrid belief system in South East Asia, China and Taiwan, even though he's actually a fictional mythology character intended for satire.

Being a child I used to think Wukong is cool and "punk" for being a character who has no burden and care for Heaven and Earth, challenging the system that's being unfair and rigid to someone as free as him. But after playing this game, it hits a now grown-up me in a realistic level, that Wukong, an idolised figure who's deemed to be invincible and flexibly powerful, could be just another replaceable pawn to be sacrificed in a broken system manipulated by those in real power. It feels both unnerving and enlightening at the same time.

Opinion on Game itself:
1st ever 3A game by an Indie studio who has little to none prior experience in this genre and development experience. Imagine the cut content they have to give up for this game to launch as planned, and still able to keep the quality and consistency this much for players. 

- Weaving unlockable skills throughout the story is really immersive, the secrets and side stories feels equally impactful as the main one, and some even have heart-wrenching moments knowing the lore from a Chinese mythology enthusiast's perspective.
- Combats are rewarding with the monsters and boss fights, but the consistency between bosses may feel unevenly too strong or weak.

I was going to write this review weeks after the game's release, but let's just say a long Hiatus was taken and I essentially forgot about the game (reason will be said why).
So Black Myth : Wukong...is a great game, initially I was skeptical, since the more I kept playing, the more harder it got (though partially because my dumbass didn't explore enough to find out I could craft celestial medicines). Note that this Review will contain spoilers.

Gameplay 9/10 : The Fighting System is a bit of a mix from God of War but also your average Hack N Slash games. Chapter 1 : Cool Beginning
It's a great start of a game. It's beautiful, it gives you the fundamentals of combat, and the bosses are not too challenging. Especially the final boss of the Chapter, the Black Bear, it's quite epic.

Chapter 2 : A step down
I did not really enjoy it much, mainly because the Area had all these rock enemies that can really be annoying early game, but mostly cause of the bosses. All of a sudden you got a duo boss that really claps your ass into oblivion, and then the final boss of the Chapter has an unfair Tornado Wall that you can just accidentally run into, whilst the boss himself can just camp there, literally. Overall not the best.

Chapter 3 : Atrocity
I hated every second of this chapter, it's the longest of the 6, and has one of, if not, the most frustrating bosses ever made in Gaming. I despise Yellowbrow's fight with every atom of my being, due to his random non-pattern Golden Form that can just trigger mid-immobilize, and literally thanks to lightning, his attacks are just not dodgeable. Literally after I beat him, I then thought the game is just gonna get worse if I keep playing, thus why I didn't play it for a long time.

Chapter 4 : A step up
This one surprised me, it had an interesting beginning, middle, but a very bad end. The Chapter is probably the 2nd shortest, but it's the most beautiful I'd say, mainly cause of the secret area. The Final boss of the chapter though...yeah no, it's not a good one.

Chapter 5 : Redemption
This is without a shadow of a doubt, my favorite chapter of them all. I loved the area, I loved the bosses, and especially the final boss of the chapter, which was the Yaksha King, literally whoever came up with the design and fight, give em a raise.

Chapter 6 : Great Conclusion
I loved that this one you can ride the nimbus, it makes exploration be on a whole different level, but I liked the progression of the chapter, it is the shortest of them. The FInal boss was also one of the greatest fights I've ever seen in Gaming.

Issues I had with the game : For people who are playing on Laptops, yeah no fullscreen on this game, which can really be a problem. This game also suffers a bit from Input Lag, so don't be surprised if you keep trying to dodge a repeated attack but your character just doesen't or having to press the heal button twice in a row to heal. While the game has cool bosses, it also has bad one's, and they can be really bad too (I'm looking at you Cyan Loong Prince), so in short, boss Inconsistencies.

The Lore : 9/10
While it is an invented Chinese mythology story, it still references Journey to the West and I daresay even pays homage to it, whilst also having elements from Dark Souls' story a bit implemented. You, as the Destined One, gotta find 6 relics and fight what remains of Wukong to BECOME Wukong. However you will only find 5 of the relics, the 6th one is obtained from beating all major secret bosses. You fight Wukong's greatest rival, Erlang Shen, who arguably is harder. If you beat him, you get the Memories, and thus once you beat Wukong, you get the True Ending, where he finally is reborn/reincarnated, and refuses to wear the golden headband that once kept him under the Celestial Court's control.

Overall, I give this game a 8/10. For a first AAA game, I say Game Science did well, it's just that there are some inconsistencies regarding certain aspects of the game. For those who are into Chinese Mythology, and very much are Masochists/desire a Challenge to waste hours on, this game's pretty much for you.


P.S : This should've won GOTY honestly.

In a sentence: fantastic game BUT it has its flaws.

First of all, although it looks like it: this is not a Souls game. It's an action game with Souls-like elements. It has shrines where you can rest and recover your resources, along with a few other ideas borrowed from the genre, but you don't lose anything when you die, regular enemies aren't particularly difficult, and aside from a handful of bosses, the game is nowhere near as punishing as a traditional Souls game.

The skill tree is very good. There is plenty of room to customize your playstyle through skills, weapons, armor and equipment. I wouldn't call it revolutionary, but it's well designed and executed.

The bosses are probably the strongest part of the game. Each one has its own identity, design and story, which adds a lot of variety. There are a ridiculous number of them, and almost all of them have their own identity. I never felt like I was fighting the same enemy with a different skin, which I really appreciated. I beat most of them on my first try, although there were a few that made me retry several times.

The main problem with the game is the chapter structure. There are only six chapters, but the areas are quite large and can feel very long. Several times I found myself enjoying the game while also thinking, “Okay, when does this chapter end?” It's a strange feeling because I wasn't bored, but I definitely felt like the game could have been shorter. 

Personally, I think the game would have been better if it were about 10 hours shorter.

Chapter 6 is the clearest example. It's much more open, and while flying around on the cloud is spectacular, I think the level design is pretty terrible. The final fights are much better, though, and the secret ending is absolutely worth seeing.

I also really enjoyed the story. I wasn't particularly familiar with Journey to the West, so I came into the game knowing very little about it. Still, I think the way the game uses that material to build its own story works really well. The structure of moving forward, meeting characters, helping some of them and fighting others works nicely, and the story is carried more by its world and characters than by one huge central plot. The chapter bosses' backstories are also very good.

One thing that really annoyed me was the invisible walls. There are countless moments where the environment makes it look like you should be able to go somewhere, only for you to run into an invisible wall in the middle of nowhere. It happened far too many times.

Overall, I think this game is considerably better than its 81 on Metacritic. It has some design issues and is definitely longer than it needs to be, but the combat, bosses, progression, atmosphere and overall spectacle made it a game I really enjoyed.

Highly recommended, especially if you like action games with Souls-like elements. Just don't expect an actual Souls game.

[b][u]Triple-A Vaporware – A Brainless, Lifeless Tech Demo Masquerading as an Action Game[/u][/b]

Let’s strip away the corporate marketing hype and visual smoke mirrors: Black Myth: Wukong is a fundamentally broken, clunky, and utterly hollow experience. Before the fanboys rush to tell me to "get good," let's clear something up: I am no stranger to brutal difficulty. I have conquered Onimusha on Carnage mode, and I have fully beaten unforgiving high-precision games like Nine Sols. I love games that push my reflexes to the absolute limit. But those games are tough-but-fair; Wukong is just a masterclass in mechanical frustration and design incompetence.

Game Science has delivered a product that fails at basic game design on every conceivable level:
[list]
[*] [b]A "Combat" System Built on Clunky Delusions:[/b] The developers want you to think this is a precision action game. It isn't. The "See-Through" / Resolute Strike counter mechanic is a fraudulent joke. It is chained to a sluggish, unresponsive input-buffering queue that forces you to awkwardly prep a light attack before you can even attempt to parry. Worse, the invincibility frames are so pitifully brief that bosses with brainless multi-hit tracking will routinely smash you right out of your counter animation—even after the game’s own red-flash visual cue confirms you hit the frame-perfect window.

[*] [b]Abysmal Camera Work and Broken Physics:[/b] Fighting massive bosses like the Tiger Vanguard means fighting the camera, not the enemy. The perspective violently glues itself to the boss’s crotch, completely cutting off their upper body, shoulders, and arms from the screen. The game aggressively demands you react to visual cues that its own trash camera tracking refuses to let you see, leaving you staring at a blurry, zoomed-in wall of clipping pixels.

[*] [b]A Lifeless, Aggressive Theme Park:[/b] Outside of the muddy combat, the world design is a pathetic joke. The environments are completely dead, lifeless corridors padded out by a sickening amount of immersion-shattering invisible walls. You cannot explore; you can only walk down pre-baked hallways disguised as forests and deserts.

[*] [b]A Forgettable, Incoherent Narrative:[/b] For a game relying so heavily on classic mythology, the narrative delivery is entirely flat and unengaging. It gives you absolutely no compelling reason to care about the journey, dropping the ball on pacing and character motivation right out of the gate.

[*] [b]Artificial Difficulty Over Actual Balance:[/b] Lacking the talent to design genuinely fair encounters, the developers leaned entirely on magnetic, input-reading tracking. Bosses teleport across arenas and ignore spacing mechanics entirely to shut down tactical variety, forcing you into a single, rigid, utterly boring playstyle.

Black Myth: Wukong is a stunningly painted Ferrari with a lawnmower engine inside. It sacrifices crisp inputs, basic camera logic, player freedom, and world-building on the altar of visual spectacle. It is an insult to classic action games that actually respect a player’s skill and time. Do not waste your money on this overhyped tech demo. 

Uninstalling this garbage was the only satisfying part of the experience.

Rating: [b][u]Overwhelmingly Not Recommended[/u][/b]

Black Myth: Wukong has excellent animation and several genuinely great bosses. Unfortunately, after ~40 hours, I found the systems underneath the presentation surprisingly poorly thought through.

The biggest problem is not difficulty or obscure secrets. Both are great. The problem is that the game very often fails to give you the information needed to make meaningful decisions.

A good secret gives you clues without giving you the answer. Elden Ring's Purifying Crystal Tear is a good example: it tells you that it "purifies the curse of the Lord of Blood." Much later you meet Mohg, Lord of Blood. The game never tells you to connect the two. If you do, you feel clever.

Wukong frequently removes not just the answer, but the reasoning path.


Some examples ([b]SPOILERS[/b]):

[list]
[*] The entire armor-upgrade system, which is necessary to keep old set bonuses relevant, is hidden behind an optional easily missable multi-step NPC quest. Miss it and armor appears to have a completely different progression system (not a good one).
[*] Spell Binder is a whole build archetype I had wanted for most of the game. It is hidden behind another optional easily missable multi-stage quest. I found it after beating the final boss.
[*] There are many straight counter items to specific bosses, most of which do not communicate this at all. Plantain fan f.e. says smth along the lines of “good against fire” and is the hardcounter to an enemy doing pretty much no fire at all.
[*] Some quest progression consists of exhausting dialogue until an invisible flag changes, revisiting unrelated locations or performing actions whose relevance is communicated only after you already know the solution.
[*] Some crafting material is genuinely scarce while others that appear to be the same just aren’t. Most of the best weapon/ armour sets literally CANNOT be completed inside your first playthrough. You’ll be collecting material thinking you can soon craft that item but it is literally impossible unless you continue into New Game+ (which the game just isn't good enough for imo)
[*] Weapon progression is extremely uneven between stances. I really hope you like Pillar stance, because that’s the only one with a proper progression. I liked Thurst and had a weapon with a functional bonus for about 5% of my playtime as there simply aren’t any weapons or armour to support it besides one spear that immediately becomes obsolete (and can’t be upgraded…why?!?)
[/list]

None of these problems requires more handholding to fix. Quite the opposite: [b]give the player information and let them figure things out.[/b] Obscurity is fun when observation and deduction can overcome it. If the practical solution is systematically testing unrelated items or opening a wiki to find which invisible condition is missing, that isn't meaningful discovery.

Combat has a similar problem with consistency. At its best, Wukong is excellent. You have to learn Yellow Loong, Cyan Loong and especially Erlang to beat them and then it feels great.

But many other bosses substitute interaction with gimmicks, huge HP pools, excessive downtime or mechanics that invalidate parts of your build rather than challenging you to use them well. The final boss was particularly disappointing. After a game spent assembling skills and equipment, I expected a final exam of those systems. Instead, parts of the fight restrict or counter them, including interactions where certain builds can be left without an answer to a boss mechanic.

This is especially frustrating because the underlying staff combat is good. Perfect dodges feel good, charged heavies feel good, the animations are excellent and several bosses demonstrate that the system absolutely can support demanding fights.

The same pattern repeats throughout the game: [b]good individual ideas connected by surprisingly weak systems design.[/b]

There are cool armor sets, but their progression is poorly communicated. There are clever counters, but their relationships often aren't communicated. There are elaborate secrets, but many can literally just be stumbled upon by chance or looked up (no shot you’re getting the secret ending by deducing what it takes). There are specialized weapons, but progression doesn't consistently support the specialization. There are scarce materials, but scarcity doesn't consistently correspond to meaningful choices.

I don't regret playing it. There are some spectacular moments here, but spectacle was increasingly doing more of the work the longer I played. And that’s just not for me tbh.

[b]7/10. Worth buying on sale if the visuals, mythology and boss spectacle are the main attraction for you. If meaningful character progression, readable systems and mechanically coherent exploration are important to you, there are much better action RPGs.[/b]

Visual espetacular: Cenários deslumbrantes, iluminação cinematográfica e um design de personagens e chefes extremamente criativo e memorável.
Combate envolvente: Ação fluida e desafiadora, com variedade de técnicas, transformações e o cajado como arma versátil, que recompensa a habilidade e a estratégia.
Chefes marcantes: Cada batalha é um espetáculo, com identidade própria e mecânicas que testam o jogador de forma justa e empolgante.
Cultura e narrativa: Uma imersão rica na mitologia chinesa, que desperta curiosidade e apreço por uma tradição pouco explorada nos games ocidentais.
Estreia impressionante: Um feito notável para um estúdio de estreia em grandes produções, elevando a indústria de jogos da China ao cenário mundial.

Veredito: Uma experiência épica, ambiciosa e inesquecível, indispensável para fãs de ação e de jogos no estilo soulslike.

Wukong is a true masterpiece of modern gaming. Developed by Game Science, it brings the classic Chinese legend Journey to the West to life with remarkable cultural authenticity and stunning visuals.

Highlights:

Breathtaking visuals: Gorgeous environments, cinematic lighting, and wildly creative character and boss designs that stay with you long after playing.
Engaging combat: Fluid, challenging action with a variety of techniques, transformations, and a versatile staff that rewards skill and strategy.
Memorable bosses: Every fight is a spectacle, each with its own identity and mechanics that test the player in a fair and thrilling way.
Culture and storytelling: A rich immersion into Chinese mythology that sparks curiosity and appreciation for a tradition rarely explored in Western games.
Impressive debut: A remarkable achievement for a studio's first major title, putting China's game industry firmly on the world stage.

Verdict: An epic, ambitious, and unforgettable experience, a must-play for action fans and soulslike lovers alike.

Black Myth: Wukong... what to say...

it feels like a double A production, where you see a lot of attention to details... it's like looking at new developers who were ordered to place everything in detail, but upon closer inspection... you see all sorts of small issues, flying roots, trees, clipping statues, you name it. Even a plenty of stupid invisible walls, as if it were a game developed in the early 2000s...

Its gameplay is rather repetitive in nature, stamina being rather... optional, and considering it's more of a souls-like...? They could've just removed the stamina... and should've focused more on being an action adventure instead.

Additionally, there's a lot of attention to animations... only for them to be the annoying ones, like getting staggered, even by spiders doing some small attacks (if you can call them that) and that staggers you... as if you're weakest individual who could be knocked over by a light gust... which can luckily (well... most of the time) be cancelled by dodge rolls. 
There are also needless "nearly tipped over!" type of animations... which are just there for fluff... as it's only specific parts that you can fall off and die... as nearly the all areas which seems like you could fall off and die, are walled off by the invisible walls...

There isn't any sort of punishment for dying... it's just wasting your time, and you can technically only get stronger and stronger by killing the mobs.
To end off the review, I'd say the story as by itself is severely lacking, unless you've read the Journey to the West... making this feel more like a boss rush game...

Its an alright 6/10 game but it feels like at times that this game wants to be more of a hack 'n slash game with Soulslike mechanics. Like it struggles which one it wants to be at a certain time. Majority of the combat is just spamming the same 5 move light combo. There are 3 stances in the game that lets you change up the combat style depending on which types of enemies and bosses you are fighting. The heavy attacks are based on which stance you are currently using but the light combo attacks are the same literally throughout the whole game. So the combat does start to feel stale and repetitive by the time you get to chapter 3.

In chapter 4, the game drops in quality by having almost every enemy have a status effect on you such as poison. Which would be fine if it were only a couple enemies that can inflict you with it but most of the enemies inflicts you with poison and it just starts to become annoying after a while. After chapter 3, every enemy in the game, even the trash mobs gets a significant health boost. Bosses get more tedious as you are forced to spend more time fighting them due to their health. Artificially prolonging a fight by giving them more health. Resulting in the player to spam the same moves until their health reaches 0.

There are 100+ bosses in the game, majority of them being optional, but it feels annoying exploring the map at times when a boss comes out of nowhere and you're just trying to explore. Having that many bosses in the game, eventually you would fight so many bosses to the point where you start to notice the overlap between them. Who knew that adding so many can start to feel repetitive at a certain point. ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

The boss' health starting from chapter 4 and onwards are so tanky. The boss fights prior felt more polished and didn't take as long. I have a feeling that the second half of the game was rushed. The chapter 4 boss fight is so badly designed that you need a certain item in the game to counter his second phase to have a higher chance of defeating him. His second phase literally takes away half of your stamina and you move slower. The devs knew this guy was busted, that's why they added that item that you had to go to the secret chapter area and defeat the secret boss to attain it, essentially wasting your time.

Chapter 5 is a lazy chapter from the devs as the enemies within them is just reskinned enemies from previous chapters. They even have the same movesets, offering nothing new to the table except for maybe a cool looking chapter? I guarantee you that what Game Science did is open up their Substance Painter, change the colors of a few handselected enemies, change the name and lore of the "new" enemies and slap them into chapter 5 calling it a day.

Chapter 6 is the worst chapter in the whole game. Full of tanky, hyperaggressive bosses that takes away half of your health in one hit. When I reached this point, I just wanted to finish the game. I was fed up and just wanted it to end.

Can we talk about how the Supreme Inspector boss is one of the corniest bosses in the whole game where he spends most of his time flying, riding on his unicycle, constantly deflecting your attacks with their version of Rock Solid with no warning frames. This boss is so tedious because once again, hyperaggressive and once he calmed down for like a second, he starts his song and dance where you need to keep dodging until giving you a chance to attack back. Also, there is a couple of attacks where you can't react to because they're just so fast. If it is your first time fighting this boss, you will be completely blindsided at some of his attacks as they are fast.

The entirety of chapter 6 just felt low quality as the whole chapter is empty with some bosses sprinkled here and there. Ironically, the name of the chapter is "Unfinished" which basically encapsulates this whole chapter. The performance in this chapter is the worst as the framerate drops the harshest in this chapter as there are a lot of effects going on.

Invisible walls are everywhere in this game. There are so many areas in the game where it looks like you can jump on or over it, but there is a wall preventing you to do that. It is quite jarring when it happens to a normal looking platform but a wall blocks you from jumping on it. If you want players to explore, you shouldn't limit them with invisible walls. Especially with areas that looks like you should be able to explore but can't. Talking about exploration, the graphics are great and realistic, however that leads to its own downfall as everything just blends in together and it is difficult sometimes to get around without a map. A map is essential if you want to make sure that you explored everywhere. Because everything blends in, sometimes it genuinely gives me a headache just looking at the game. Pair that with the fast motion combat in this game, that gets progressivly worse the more farther you get into the game, you're just inviting a migraine to happen.

The thing that I hate the most in this game is the inconsistent hitboxes. There are so many times where it looked like I should have hit the enemy even though I am right in front of them. Many of my heavy attacks or light finishers missed alongside the terrible inputs this game has where it just refuses to heal in critical moments. Even though you are clearly pressing the heal button and nothing happens. Causing me to die in the process because the game just didn't read my input. On the receiving end, there were many times where I clearly should have not been hit, even dodging before, and still receiving damage. If you want to make a Soulslike, you cannot mess up dodging as that makes up a good chunk of a Soulslike game. The AoE attacks in this game will show you how BS the hitboxes are. You can be literally outside of its AoE and still be hit. Clearly what is happening visually on screen doesn't match up on what is actually going on. Needing the player to constantly question themselves whether or not they are far enough per the visual cue the game gives them but still being punished for it, even outside of its radius. Notorious example would be the Wandering Wight in chapter 1.

The inputs are also inconsistent as there were many times where I wanted to heal and it didn't heal. Every input in the game sometimes just does not register within the game, causing you to take damage or just outright die. Pressing dodge, it doesn't dodge, using Immobolize, it doesn't immobolize, using your transformation, it doesn't transform. Rinse and repeat until you beat the game because it doesn't go away since the problem is there since chapter 1, GG.

I know there is a lot of critic in this review but it's not all bad as the story is honestly peak along with its animations. There are several moments in this game that would take your breath away. Unfortunately, the amount of jank and unpolished BS in this game makes it frustrating to play. It says I spent around 100 hours but realistically I spent around 40 hours to beat the game after starting a new game from a long break.

If you want this game, get it on sale otherwise look somewhere else.

Black Myth: Wukong exceeded what I expected from it. What stood out most to me was how well it combines its gameplay with Chinese mythology and lore. Some areas, encounters, and boss fights are genuinely creative, and the game consistently gave me reasons to explore.

The combat is simple but satisfying. The spirits and spells offer plenty of variety, but I often found myself sticking with the starter options because they felt the most effective throughout my playthrough. Transformations, on the other hand, felt much more balanced, which encouraged me to experiment with several of them. The boss fights are where the combat really shines.. Tiger Vanguard, Yin Tiger, Erlang, and the final Monkey King fight were the most struggle happened going upto 5-10 tries yet it felt rewarding once you defeat them.

That said, I do wish the stance system had a little more depth. Smash stance became my go-to, while Pillar was something I rarely found myself using, especially against bosses. I think another layer to the stance system could have made the combat even more interesting.

My biggest issue is how some content can become permanently missable depending on the order in which you explore or trigger certain events. I don't mind secrets being hidden, but having natural exploration lock you out of bosses or areas can feel like the game is punishing you for playing without a guide.

The story kept me curious more than deeply invested, and Zhu Bajie's loyalty and emotional moments were particularly memorable. Chapter 2's music and the final boss were also standouts for me.

I ended up spending around 40–60 hours on my first playthrough and roughly 100 hours overall with NG+ and the Gauntlets. Even after finishing it, I was left wanting more... which I think says a lot.
