[b]Journey to the West meets Souls-like[/b]

+ Monkey King mythology setting with rich lore
+ Epic bosses and enemy designs
+ Stunning visuals and landscapes
+ Superb combat

Story-wise, Wukong is a reimagining of Journey to the West, with you taking the main role. Whether you're familiar with the story or not, it's easy to get drawn into this world. Every NPC and enemy has a journal entry that expands on the lore, providing crucial background information on characters, events, and locations.

Your journey takes you across a variety of landscapes, from dense forests and snowy mountains to ancient temples and forgotten ruins. The visuals are absolutely stunning, and there were plenty of moments where I simply stopped to admire the scenery. But beware, these epic visuals require strong hardware to enjoy it to the fullest.

The big highlight is the combat. There are no classes and only one main weapon. Staff. Despite that, combat never feels dull thanks to the different stances that focus on offense, defense, and mobility. It's easy to learn but difficult to master. But in the end the combat flow looks spectacular. 
Additional Wukong's abilities add a lot of variety. You can summon clones, freeze enemies in place, or even transform into defeated foes and use their unique abilities.

I highly recommend it if you're looking for a challenging action RPG with fantastic combat, and story of Sun Wukong.

Wilds is a game made for game journalists.

This game marks a step forward for the series in terms of technology, narrative, characterization, and battle dynamics. However, it fundamentally loses sight of what makes the Monster Hunter formula compelling on too many fronts.

Battles are incredible to behold. The suite of new and improved options, animations, and dynamic reactions as the hunter and monster battle look and feel amazing. Clashing with monsters with your shield or guarding against breath weapons, offsetting them with mighty blows, or dashing across the length of their spines with a flurry of attacks are all really awesome to see. But you quickly realize that the game has completely abandoned anything resembling what made Monster Hunter fun: there is no challenge here whatsoever.

The reality that begins to dawn on you as you play is that this is a complete power fantasy rather than a struggle against monsters. Massive explosions that reverberate and overwhelm the senses with their awe deal meaningless amounts of damage or can be simply avoided. Half the time you can plant yourself beneath a monster and attack it for 30+ seconds while it randomly attacks at nothing. The most powerful and intimidating attacks with the greatest visual spectacle should instill FEAR and DANGER. Instead, they mean nothing.

The mismatch between visual awe and actual game difficulty kills any sense of investment. 

This game suffers immensely from AAA disease: you frequently find yourself being literally forced to walk a glowing path, redirected by invisible walls and the like, or are just as often encouraged to let your mount auto-navigate to your hunt location. These elements add up to create a cheap and meaningless experience. Health, status effects, monster information, sharpening, and trapping are all pseudo-automated or made trivial by the amount of assistance you receive. The result is that no victory feels earned or difficult. My only deaths came from, ironically, this very thing, either dying because of an invisible wall or dying because of a monster's super cinematic attack that the game wants you to run away from to hide behind a rock. You can imagine the cringe of it, with the characters yelling out in obvious 4th wall shattering anime voices.

I have to mention stability and visuals. This game looks utterly fucking horrendous. There is a native, built-in, and unchangeable texture filter that makes everything look washed out, grainy, blurry, colorless, and just a complete eye-sore. You frequently cannot actually even visually parse what is going on because everything blends and smudges together. Water looks horrible. Assets load in before your eyes. The game's performance issues have largely been addressed since launch but the visuals of older MH games are superior for the simple fact that they possessed color and visual clarity. This is genuinely inexcusable.

Another note about the difficulty is that while certain new mechanics are interesting, the monsters have not been given enough power or agency to match the hunters. What I mean by this is, whereas in older MH games you would find yourself in an intricate dance with monsters, vying to capitalize on openings, in a sense playing a "turn-based" game, Wilds simply says "it is ALWAYS your turn to do whatever you want." Monsters can be stun-locked by all weapon types. Monsters rarely actually deal damage except with their most comically slow or choreographed moves. These factors, coupled with the ability to dodge cancel just about anything and manually aim/auto-aim at monsters and you basically get a button masher in place of the Monster Hunter everyone loves. MH is supposed to require and reward skill, careful positioning, proficiency with your weapon, manual aiming, and risk-reward assessment with attack windows.

Wilds has genuinely NONE of those things. 

Now, the DLC, Ascendance, is supposed to fix this, as Capcom has noted many of these points of complaint. Wilds requires significant changes to the feel of hunts to bring monsters on par with the new and improved hunters who have no vulnerability windows, have get-out-of-jail-free cards aplenty, don't have to manage resources, and can effortlessly keep up their damage output with the precise focus mode that trivializes monsters.

Some people may like the dynamics of the fights present in this game. And that is fine. But those people are not looking to play a Monster Hunter game. If you like this game as-is, it means you like a story-based game with trivial combat that delivers on a power fantasy and easy progression.

The Gogmazios fight is a frustrating mess, and the problems go far beyond difficulty.

First of all, the damage check is an absolutely terrible mechanic. Being forced to meet an arbitrary damage threshold just to avoid an unavoidable devastating attack is not challenging game design. It is artificial difficulty that punishes players regardless of how well they actually understand the fight. A monster hunt should reward positioning, timing, weapon mastery, and skill, not turn into a DPS race with a pass-or-fail condition.

And if that wasn't bad enough, the game crashes on the quest results screen. Imagine spending a long time fighting this monster, finally completing the hunt, only for the game to crash before you can properly enjoy your rewards. All that time and effort wasted.

These two issues make the entire experience incredibly frustrating. One is a poorly designed gameplay mechanic, and the other is a technical failure that should never happen in a finished game.

A challenging monster is fine. An unfair damage check combined with crashes at the end of a successful quest is not.

This is simply unacceptable.

Easier than World, harder than Rise, the most accessible Monster Hunter to date.
The Sixth Generation brings Focus Mode and Offsets, and faster paced gameplay while remaining visually closer to World.

Focus Mode allows you to use special Focus attacks to destroy Wounds, which will lend you a random Monster material upon destruction. They come in a few different sizes, but the most common variety is the simple Red Wound.
In Focus Mode, you may also use your weapon's Offset attack. This is a damage negating parry-and-riposte. Time it correctly, depending on the size of the Monster, and you'll stun them momentarily, giving everyone a chance to attack interrupted. Time it slightly off, and for weapons like the Greatsword, you'll be able to do a fully charged TCS on command, with the drawback of not stunning the Monster.

Every weapon is also far easier to learn in Wilds, even the Gunner weapons (LBG, HBG, Bow). Give any one of them a shot, and see what works for you.

[h1]Finally a worthy Monster Hunter[/h1]

During its Launch last year in february, we pc players had a rough time... But after a few patches, lots of postgame content and the expansion on the Horizon, Monster Hunter Wilds might finally live up to the hype (even though the Hype is long gone).

[h2]The Content[/h2]
Like any other Monster Hunter title: The content is reaaaaally lackluster. So for many people it was just another RPG after the little postgame content but since World, frequent Title Updates gave us players more content. But even Monster Hunter veterans seem to forget: It was almost always like that. Remember the time before World? Japan got its first release and we got the ultimate Variant with the Masterrank Expansion (formerly known as G-Rank) a year or so later. 

[h2]The Gameplay[/h2]
After a few stability patches, buffs and so on... Wilds feels just amazing with the gameplay! Every Weapon has its ups and downs, what perks to use with a certain weapon.. you get the idea (i hope). You can invest a long time just farming and building your Sets and try new things out and i think, this is where Monster Hunter just shines. 

Oh and don't get me started on the content that is not related to hunt Monsters in any aspect. You can quench your lust for exploring, fishing, trading... [i]You name it![/i]

[h2]The Story[/h2]
Long story short: It is a Monster Hunter Story.. What did you expect? No but seriously. The story is fine, your Main focus is hunting and gettign authorizations to hunt (looking at you Alma).

[h2]Downsides[/h2]
Well... What i dont really like is the purchasable content. BUT: It's purely cosmetic so no pay to win.
I am a long Monster Hunter Fan and i would call myself a Veteran but.. Like other reviews stated: It gets boring from time to time, not content wise tho bust just.. hunting. That's just normal Monster Hunter fatigue but Monster Hunter is just that! You hunt, you kill, you carve, repeat. This is what Monster Hunter just is. I personally wouldn't call it a real downside, just a minor thing in the gamedesign choice but still. If you are new to the franchise, you should know about this. 

[h2]The Community[/h2]
The Community is, from what i can tell, wholesome, loves to help and just wants to BONK some Monsters. Of course you have your one or two Hunters that are just questionable Human beings but overall really nice people. There are tons of good Discord or Teamspeak Server as well with Players, that are really nice and would love to help newbies getting a foot into this complex game. 
And if you are curious: Search for Veteran Lobbies ingame. A lot of Players just ask to help other People via ingame chat, out of boredom or they just like it. And i got tons of help too (Goldcrown farming is just pure grind)

[h2]Last Words[/h2]
Can i recommend this game? Yeah, totally. But keep in mind, that the very nature of Monster Hunter is repeating certain quests. Be aware of that. and on another note: Nobody tells you to run the best Meta sets: You can run anything you want and set yourself some challenges.
I can't say, if Wilds will live up to Iceborne, but let us wait for the Expansion next year and have a talk, when Wilds is finished like Iceborne.

However, do yourself a favor when playing this game: turn off the in-game minimap, try to ride your seikret (your ride) manually.

I had realized that before doing so, I was constantly looking at the minimap during the hunt, maybe like 75% of the time (outside of fighting monsters). Turning it off made me realize that I was doing a disservice towards how much love the devs put into the environment and the ecology. The world is beautiful, teeming, and alive, when you pay attention to it. With the minimap off, you're compelled to scan around the environment and learn to navigate, familiarizing yourself with the locales, like an actual hunter would. 

You'll never know which monster might linger the next corner during your hunts, unless you notice its sounds. Not only it gives another layer of excitement, you'll also unconsciously learn another thing: monster sounds/audio cues.

You'll notice the local wildlife running from the monster you're hunting when it goes to another locale, you'll notice the foliage still swaying after the monster paved its way through, you'll start relying on your scoutflies and all the residues they left behind. You'll notice the 'map' itself, rather than just looking at the map.

I also appreciate that the game doesn't sell items that directly make players more powerful. Even better, the DLC prices are quite reasonable, not just for cosmetics but also for stickers, vouchers, gestures, pendants, and other extras. It's refreshing to see a game handle monetization this way.

Suggestions for the Expansion:

- New Weapons: It would be great to see some completely new weapon types added to the series.
- Seamless Endgame: The seamless open world is one of the game's best features, but once you reach the endgame, taking quests directly from the quest board at HQ becomes much more convenient than going out and exploring the world. I hope the devs can find a way to make exploring the world just as rewarding and worthwhile in the endgame, rather than having players fall back into the usual quest-board routine.
- More Elder Dragons: I hope the expansion introduces several new Elder Dragons. Having Gogmazios as the only Elder Dragon in the base game feels a little underwhelming for such an important monster category.
- Crossover Monsters: I'd love to see more collaboration monsters like Behemoth from Monster Hunter: World. Honestly, Behemoth felt much more intimidating and fitting for Monster Hunter than Omega. I hope we get another crossover monster that feels like a true Monster Hunter hunt, with challenging mechanics and an unforgettable fight.
- A Strong Storyline: I genuinely enjoy Monster Hunter's story, not just the action. I love watching the cutscenes and following the characters, so I hope the expansion delivers an engaging storyline with memorable moments.

Overall, I'm really looking forward to the Ascendance expansion in 2027. I hope it builds on what Wilds has already done well while bringing more depth to the endgame and plenty of exciting new content. Can't wait!

I think this game is a massive step backwards for the series and indicative of an issue that many AAA games have right now, that issue being endless dumbing down and simplification of systems that made these franchises what they are. 

It's been discussed to death, but the removal of friction from the series with this game shows a massive misunderstanding of what makes this series unique. They really did make this game around getting to the monster as fast as possible, minimising or removing any gameplay that wasn't action oriented. The tracking just doesn't exist anymore, they've added story quests where you track a monster *cinematically* but this isn't the same as something like World where you have to actually look for this creature, learn its territory and engage with the environment. Of course in World's late game you basically b-lined to the monsters as well, but you had to EARN that through repeated tracking. Not to mention you still had to walk to the monster yourself instead of getting your auto-pilot Tesla bird to take you there, giving you the opportunity to put the controller down and scroll reels for a bit or some other bs that isn't playing the game you bought. 

This brings me to the maps. which kind of suck. They're all generally graphically impressive and cool on paper, but after the first three they just feel so dull. This game showers you with all the items you'll need so you never feel incentivised to actually explore the maps and farm materials, which I would argue is a pretty core part of the series' identity. I don't care if people find it tedious, IT'S A GOOD THING. Downtime between fighting monsters, preparing to fight them, is a key part of the hunting simulation, grounding you in this world and making you work for your achievements. World seems to be a game with controversial map design but I personally loved how complicated and hostile they felt. They were super vertical, full of secrets, and overall a lot of fun to explore. They felt just as important as the Monsters, and really sold the vision that these were living breathing places where you were not welcome. Not to mention, they were a lot more visually and conceptually interesting than what we got in Wilds. The first three maps are cool, the oil map is especially a standout in terms of concept even if it feels a bit too industrial (a general issue towards the end of the game) but the last two maps are truly awful. The snow map is a joke, especially compared to Iceborne's map which is one of the best snow levels in any game period. And don't even get me started on the last map. The most disappointing final zone in any MH game. It apparently has 3 different visual phases like the other maps but you could have fooled me because it looks the same throughout all of them (the map phases are also dumb, since one of them is just always ugly on every map). It's also terribly uninteresting, with such a dull colour palette and practically nothing memorable about it. The maps in this game are basically just backdrops for the monster fights, rather than being interesting spaces to inhabit on their own, and I think this is the game's greatest failing. 

You also have an awful story! Exactly what MH needed. Capcom decided that a self serious story was what this franchise needed when it has famously been pretty light hearted and silly. The biggest issue with World was its lacklustre story and characters, yet here it feels like they doubled down on that and made everyone even more obnoxious. At least in World you could ignore it most of the time and skip through dialogue, but here you have to sit through these awful "cinematic" gameplay segments where you just follow NPC's as they say nothing interesting. It's a shame, since the cutscene direction is actually pretty solid, the actions scenes are great. Everything else just sucks. Capcom games generally seem to understand that their silly premises benefit from unserious stories (resident evil, dmc, street fighter etc.), but for some reason they decided to tack on a story that adds nothing to the game here, and actively sabotages a gameplay loop that has survived for over 2 DECADES. 

This brings me to my closing thoughts. MH Wilds feels like an attempt to do something new with the series' core formula, which in some ways is commendable, but instead of doing something new and interesting they made something derivative and dumbed down. Despite the fact that World sold insanely well, Capcom thought that what the series needed was to have its systems lobotomised, its quest design dumbed down, and its challenge non existence. This feels like a game that was trying to appeal to a much wider audience and as a result has completely lost its identity in the process. It's not all bad, combat is still fun, the monster roster is super varied and creative (armour and weapon designs are also great), and the visuals can be really nice as long the maps aren't in cancer lung mode, but they can't make up for what is a fundamentally less interesting experience than what the series has offered before. 

I really hope the expansion finds a way to course correct, though many of this games' flaws are too baked in to do anything about without basically remaking the game. So ultimately I hope that whatever the next entry is, it goes back to its roots a little and brings back the friction that makes this series so unique.

This was my first entry into the Monster Hunter series, as hyped about by a friend. We played the beta together, and started right on launch day. I'm no veteran, just a casual player so I feel like my two cents might be helpful to those looking to jump in, especially as Acendance is on the horizon. Most of my thoughts come from the POV of playing with friends, but regardless I enjoy it just as much on my own.

To get the elephant out of the room, yes, at launch, there was a plethora of preformance issues. My friend and I had trouble connecting, game would crash often, visual bugs, the works. Is that the case now? No. Should it have been that way at launch? Also no, but I'm not going to begrudge a game that has had over a year of free content updates and bug fixes. Jumping in now it is seamless and beautiful, and I'm not running a NASA computer. 

Onto the game play/story itself, I thought it was really good! The story campaign isn't a slog, it's a good 10-15 hours of plot before you're let loose onto the world, but I liked the progression. The story does feel like a prolonged tutorial, but as this was my first time in the series, I didn't mind that. I love a game that has world building, and there are lots of mysteries and questions I still have and am excited for the DLC to hopefully answer. If you're planning on starting the game with a pal like I did, playing the story at the same time is a bit of a hassle. Either one of you has to have completed the quest in order to join the other, or sometimes online co-op isn't an option. Once we realized that, we figured playing together for material grinding/enviroment linking to gather ingredients was the way to go, and then save the plot missions for solo hunts. It wasn't too bad, but I will say the process of just playing together was a little tedious. You have to be in a party/on the same server to join quests, then if you wanna run around the map together, you have to link the enviroment.... I wish it was more streamlined, and moving between maps (although actually connected in solo play) means you have to redo the whole process. That being said, I'm glad that the ability is there, despite the hoops. 

Gameplay wise, straight up 10/10. After Wilds I decided to try my hand at World & Rise, and if you're coming from those games, Wilds gameplay feels like butter. I love that there isn't neccesarily a skill tree, just your ability to read a monster & rely on your equipement and gear. I played dualblades, and I feel like a human beyblade, it's awesome. My friend mains insect glaive, and I love that each weapon really has a play style for everyone. I love that a monster like Hirabami is like cutting paper for my friend and I because we main slashing-damage weapons, but put us against a Gravios and we sweat a bit to get through that hide. Each hunt is unique and I love that enviroment, team, and circumstance can really make the difference. The seikret are incredible mounts. I love my chicken raptor to bits, and the palico as a support geniunely can be the clutch between stunning a monster and getting the upper hand, or being a goner and carting. The support hunters as well, although I don't use them often, are great damage additions if you need someone like Kai for buffs, or Olivia to get head on with a monster while you chip at it's weak points. Speaking of, popping a monster's wound is a dopamine hit everytime. My ONLY complaint... Omega Planetes. I've beated 3 times, but it was truly a team effort. It was the first time this game felt like a souls game to me, we were truly punished if everyone didn't play their role well, and even then, it could be over in the first 5 minutes. I won't dwell on it, but ouch.

If you're the type to like build optimization, you really can get into the weeds with prefecting your build. Between the different armor, decorations, and Endgame weapon RNG, no two builds are the same. Now.... I don't care for RNG, I don't understand a lick of it, but eventually I came up with something that supports my playstyle, and I've stuck with it. There are loads of build tutorials and smarter hunters who get this kinda thing, but if you're like me and just wanna organically build your character, it's not difficult to learn. 

Overall, I love this game. I can play it for hours, and have, and it's the first game I've ever been invested in enough to get all achievements. I'm excited for Master Rank, and although I know the community mourns some features from previous installments (player housing comes to mind, as does actual "tracking" of a monster), I'm pumped for Ascendance. Get the game, especially if it's on sale, and of course; Happy Hunting!

Whatever anyone says - and coming from someone who was raised with Tri, spent 200h+ on MHGU and World and Rise, this is my favorite Monster Hunter game, and I really appreciate their first REAL attempt at making a more tangible story without losing gameplay or anything for it. It's... clumsy, but it shows a goodwill. Also goated move to remove the whole tickets for changing character appearance, that was... oof.

I fully recommend this game with some big caveats. If you have the ability to play it on PS5 Pro or if you have a quite beefy rig, then you will have a great time. The game has had several passes of optimization, but still is in need of work. This game, after all of its updates has tons and tons of content to do with a massive expansion on the way. The game launched in quite a poor state, and some of the core issues will mostly not be able to be fully addressed. But, again, if you have the rig to be able to handle the game, the game has given me tons of hours between PS5 and Steam. For reference, I have played Monster Hunter since Monster Hunter 3 Ultimate's demo on the Wii U and really got into it with 4 Ultimate. This is my favorite franchise, and I am biased towards this game and the devs. My hours do not reflect my actual time with the game as I had life circumstances that meant I had to effectively play in Steam Offline Mode for several hundred hours. I have roughly 1400 hours with the game between PS5 and PC. But the optimization is absolutely inexcusable. But, if you take your time to just explore the maps, engage in the free hunting aspects and dynamics of the questing system, take time to really learn your favorite weapons, and just watch the monsters, wildlife, and npcs in and outside of combat you will walk away with a deeply immersive and satisfying experience.

Personal Recommendations and Notes: 

-The devs chose for narrative reasons to set the starting weather in the game in what is called the Fallow period. It is supposed to look barren and washed out. The game has a season called the Plenty that looks absolutely gorgeous. It always comes after the stormy season in each region.
-If you have played other Monster Hunter games, the Low Rank in this game is more of a linear, story tutorial. It tries to force you to progress the story until high rank, so I recommend not trying to grind or do many hunts expecting it to be like a traditional Low Rank quest structure. Some people hate this structure, so, if you do, just know that high rank is a traditional Monster Hunter questing structure.
-AMD FSR causes tons of micro stutter
-Base preset model of DLSS has crazy artifacts in the storms of this game specifically in the Plains and Forest regions; swap to Preset M if using Nvidia card
-Only use DLSS Performance or Ultra Performance with Preset M or it has caused random crashes and Driver Error messages
-Lowering Sky/Cloud quality to low or lowest has virtually visual impact and saves performance
-Frame Generation for me also causes random stuttering
-There are performance mods that address stuttering, but Capcom does have an aggressive anti cheat to target cheating so use at your own risk or in Offline Mode

Positives:
-Music Score in this game is the best in the franchise full stop.
-Combat is the smoothest and most reactive it has ever been. Most of the hunts in this game with Switch Axe feel like I am brawling with almost every monster between the counters and offsets that send monsters reeling back. Deeply satisfying; especially in the endgame. But this comes with some negatives I will touch on below*
-Monster detail and ecology is taken to a new level with this game. Each monster is beautifully rendered and detail especially with the High Resolution Texture Pack enabled.
-Arkveld, the White Wraith, has become my new favorite fight to repeat.
-The endgame could be lost on some players for a variety of reasons, but at the end of the game after the latest updates, there are some many different monsters and quests that give you the endgame materials you need that makes it so you don't just have to farm a couple of monsters or the same quests on repeat.
-Random investigations in the maps and the monsters going in and out of regions dynamically is so immersion, and gives you technically hundreds of different quest variations at the end of the game and some interest monster match ups (specifically in the arena)
-Monster variety is much better than games such as World.
-The weapon skill ceiling is quite high
-I enjoyed the narrative being told, but do not expect exceptionally deep writing. Lots of the story is shown in the maps design and layout of the worlds.
-Gathering Hub is dynamic and has some gorgeous and fun seasonal events
-Almost all event quests are now permanent and accessible offline
-Tons of gameplay settings and toggles
-Layered Weapons and Armor in base game (transmog) tied directly to crafting the weapons and armor in High Rank
-Fun nods and direct references to some of the 3DS games
-Support Hunter NPCs are great if you are wanting to chill out offline or if you are new and preparing yourself to go into more difficult online hunts.
-Devs are very, very receptive to fan feedback

Negatives:
-The story progression is poorly communicated in low rank, and is far to easy. While it isn't as easy to me as MH Rise's village quests, I feel that it doesn't prepare hunters for the high rank adequately. The friction removed for the game allows new players to just breeze through fights without having to engage in so many deep systems the game has. This will be a problem for new players once they reach the endgame quests. The difficulty spikes up like crazy after HR 40.
-The Seikret auto pilot combined with the forced story made it so I had no idea where I was in almost any map at launch for a good 50 hours. The maps are so well designed an laid out in this game, and this system totally invalidates the need to learn and explore them.
-Combat feels buttery smooth in this game, but until the very endgame quests the wound system just obliterates every monster. The hunters are very overpowered throughout the main story.
-Performance, again, is laughably bad and far to heavy for how the game looks. It is pretty, but I should not have to spend as much time as I did with my PC to get it to not stutter or crash randomly.
-Disappointing Monster Weapon variety. I think each region's apex should have each of the 14 Weapon types. This is deeply disappointing, but doesn't directly affect gameplay necessarily
-The palico is very, very overpowered. To the point that I feel that it will become a crutch for new players, and if they go online where they don't have the palico healing or revive, they may become overwhelmed as the game doesn't prepare them for having to learn when to properly heal themselves.
-Monster gems being guaranteed in some investigations cheapens the experience to me.
-Overall there was just too much streamlining of the friction that was used to teach players about the game's systems. But, the developers have acknowledged that they did this based in the feedback that they received from world being too hard and that they will rethink the friction and the aspects people valued going forward
-9 Star Tempered Seregios (jokes). I hate him haha

In conclusion, this game is phenomenal if you can overlook some of its flaws. I, again, recommend taking your time exploring and just hunting for fun. Make a new build with some skills that you have never tried even if they aren't "meta". There are so many different builds to make and just have fun with. You don't have to do the most damage; you can just have fun with something new. The game is gorgeous and highly detailed in its ecology and animations even in the barren Fallow period. The new quest structure is an adjustment but is very immersive for me. I recommend playing with friends or in an online lobby. The MonHun community in general is one of the most welcoming and supportive communities I have ever found in a game series. Despite its technical and streamlining flaws, I have enjoyed hundreds, almost thousands, of hours in the game on PC and PS5 across all of its updates so far.

Monster Hunter! It's one of my favorite series from my childhood. I grew up with Monster Hunter Freedom Unite on the PSP and then Monster Hunter 4 Ultimate on the 3DS. This series has evolved so many times with each new entry. At first I felt a bit hesitant about Monster Hunter Wilds, although that quickly changed after finishing the main story. This game has a ton of improvements that really brings this into the modern era. Definitely liked this one more than Monster Hunter World. I'd just like to give a massive thank you shout out to all the kind folks in the Monster Hunter Discord who helped me get every small and large crown so quickly. Couldn't have done it without you all! 100%ing this game would have taken me several hundred hours otherwise. Highly recommended for any fans of action RPGs.

Here are my opinions:

Art/Visuals - Looks great, but runs poorly. I had to kick on frame gen immediately to be able to play this title at a decent frame rate. I'd still say it's quite playable as long as you can turn on frame gen. The monsters and environment are top tier for a Monster Hunter game visually in my opinion. Map design is a bit awkward in some spots!

Combat - I'm a Sword n' Shield main through and through. I think this title improved greatly upon SnS playstyles. Might be the best Monster Hunter combat aside from Monster Hunter Generations. I will always miss Prowler mode, although I understand why it didn't continue as a playstyle after MH:Generations. The monsters unique to this game feel pretty good to fight against. The only monster with some weird hitboxes is called Uth Duna, and even then it's not terrible. This game's combat in the endgame as usual comes down to either dodge everything, block everything, or run a super tanky build and lose out on a ton of damage potential. That's just the norm for these types of games.

Music - It's pretty nice. I do enjoy some of the monster themes but I think the older titles had the best village themes by far and no game really comes close. Pokke Village my beloved. At some point I did just turn off the background music and play my own tunes, but keep in mind I have played through this game for about 300 hours separately from this play through. It'll likely get repetitive after you hunt the same monsters 20+ times.

Story - Can we please not talk about this..? Okay fine, at least we can play through the story with our friends without leaving every hunt and reposting it like in Monster Hunter World. That was truly an awful story experience for co-op. This game's story leaves much to be desired, and honestly if this title didn't have any story at all I wouldn't complain in the slightest. I did listen to it all and watch every cutscene on my prior playthrough, however it's just really nothing special. Then again Monster Hunter games have never really been known for their amazing stories.

This game is definitely divisive in the same way Monster Hunter: World was. There are things that make it “easier,” but personally I think that makes this entry the most accessible Monster Hunter, well, maybe ever.

If you’re brand new to the series, this is the one to get. You’ll see a lot of noise from players saying X version from Y generation is better, but that’s all it is: noise. This game is the MCU of Monster Hunter, for better and for worse. Its systems, features, and story are all built to cater to a wider audience while still holding true to the Monster Hunter experience.

The one major difference I want to call out is support players in the form of bots. When you fire an SOS flare, instead of waiting for human players to respond, the game brings in up to 3 AI companions (from the story) to fight by your side. Once human players actually respond, the AI drops out and the players drop in. You can also turn off human players entirely and just hunt with the AI. Honestly, this is the best feature I’ve seen in the series, because it means you can do group hunts as a solo player and never have to hunt alone.

I’ve always felt Monster Hunter works best as a co-op game, and having bots stand in until real players show up is a fantastic way to keep the co-op going anytime you want. I really can’t stress enough how different (in a good way) it makes the series feel, and I hope they keep it in future games for sure.

I did have some performance issues, including one where I actually had to reinstall the game. Since that reinstall and a few settings tweaks, though, it’s been running very nicely. Just don’t expect it to play like butter out of the box.

Hello, this is my first ever review! Or at least I think it is. I'll try to be brief, but for my hunter credentials I was introduced to Monster Hunter with Freedom Unite, and finally got into it myself with Tri. I love Monster Hunter, it is my favorite ongoing franchise very close to my heart. I'm very aware of the optimization issues and I promised myself that I wouldn't write this review until I was both MR 100 and the optimization problem was fixed. While it still needs work I would consider it ultimately in a way better state than on launch and should be stable for most people even without frame gen turned on. 

What do I think about Wilds? Honestly, to start- I loved Worlds and Iceborne. However, I always knew that the combat was slower for the sake of playing it safe and keeping it grounded. Then Rise came out, and combat was super fast paced and had you, literally at times, launching yourself at the Monster. I wanted something in between, still a bit grounded but faster than Iceborne. Then Wilds came out, and it was exactly what I was asking for. I was elated, the areas looked beautiful and the monsters looked great. Rey Dau is easily one of my favorite monsters now, the sound vfx and the theme is a masterpiece. This game is nearly everything I wanted and more. I do however have one small gripe- and that is the actual hunting aspect of the game. See, back in old Monster Hunter before world you'd have to find the monster in a zone, normally in one of its preselected zones and then paint ball it to keep track. In World, you had to use the scout flies to track the monster and then only after gathering enough clues and fighting it would you be able to unlock permanent tracking for that specific Monster. In Wilds, the monster is already known on your mini map and is ready to be tracked right away. I would prefer a system where you gather clues to track the monster, and give it predictable behavior so if you know what you're doing you can predict where it will go even if you havent fully gathered the clues to track it.

The weapon designs are excellent, still some copy paste skinned on weapons like in World but no where near to the same levels and most of the monsters have their unique weapon (except lagiacrus great sword doesn't have its signature hum I'm still sad about that!) The amor is immaculate and the choice to wear male or female versions on either gender is both amazing and funny depending on the type of armor that you pick out.

All in all though, Wilds is an amazing Monster hunter and I really hope they optimize the game well enough in Ascendance that even budget or old pcs can play it. I really hope people give Wilds a try and I dearly hope you fall in love with it the same way I did way back then!

This is my first experience with the Monster Hunter franchise and I really enjoyed the variety of monsters and weapons. In case of the weapons they're similar to fighting game characters where you usually have a main character that you becomes your favorite and master them.

However, the monsters, on the other hand, are the stars of the show. Each one has unique and complex behaviors that make them interesting to fight, as well as different strengths and weaknesses that you can take advantage of. This makes preparation an important part of the experience by preparing for the hunt, crafting or upgrading your hunter's armor and weapons, stocking up on items, etc.

The hunter gear is made from monster parts, which are obviously obtained by hunting monsters. This creates a gameplay loop where you hunt monsters and use their parts to craft or upgrade more powerful gear, allowing you to hunt even more powerful monsters. I think this gameplay loop can be quite addictive and fun.

As for the story, I wasn't particularly interested in it. It's fairly simple and mainly serves as a pretext for hunting monsters, which is clearly the main focus of the game. The cinematics are really amazing, though.

I still have yet to experience the multi-player, but I think it's only going to be even more fun with friends.

Unfortunately, the one thing that bugged me throughout the whole experience was the performance, which was horrible. I couldn't get the game to run at a stable 60 FPS. I could get a higher frame rate, but that made the experience more unstable, so I locked it at 60 FPS. Regardless of the settings I used, the game never ran well. It's bearable, but absolutely not ideal.

I will keep an eye on the future of Monster Hunter, as I expect it to keep getting better and better.

This game used MH World as building blocks and added on top of it. They listened to the feedback and even though they addressed some of the things that were not working, they doubled down in some things that were not working.
I must admit that the whole design catastrophe of World has been fixed, we now have significantly better weapon designs (don't recall seeing bits on sticks this time) and the monster variety is notably distant from Dragon Hunter World; Capcom did listen, so props in that regard. Another improvement is map design, now you know were things are and everything is much simpler to traverse. 
Now, within the things that they decided to double down I cannot ignore the story. Why do we even have that? Who asked for that? It looks like the franchise is intended to pivot into a single player narrative story driven game, that is certainly not MH. Everything was much more exciting, challenging and even immersing when we were saying 'I do not know who I am, I don't why I'm here, all I know is that I must kill'. Instead, now we have annoying characters (NATA) telling an unnecessary detailed story that used to be better told when it was via text box. Who thought deviating budget towards voice acting, unnecessary cutscenes telling us some bullshit context, characters with mediocre development and moronic motivations would be more appealing than just adding more content (idk, more monsters, maps, weapons, ENDGAME, smth?). This game is kinda numb at times, you could literally drop the controller the first minutes (until you fight the first monster) and nothing would change; it plays itself! Ascendance must definitely need to address this and reduce the amount of shit nobody was asking for and that does not even belong to the franchise.
Now, you may ask 'what about performance? this fucking cunt has no idea what he's talking about, everybody knows that was utter rubbish'. My response to you, unnecessarily aggressive rando is that I never experienced issues (yes, the beta was very messy and had to fight origami monsters, but it's a beta, not the final game). So, perhaps if you have a solid enough rig nothing will hamper the performance (I don't use DLSS or FG and I never drop below 40fps at 4k; I could change the settings for better performance, but it's been a while since I've played so IDGF right now)

I love how Monster Hunter Wilds carries over many of the things I enjoyed about Monster Hunter: World, especially the combat, exploration, and the feeling of hunting monsters in a living environment. The overall performance has also improved quite a lot compared with when the game first launched.

The combat is incredibly satisfying, and I really like how fluid most of the weapons feel. The environments are also beautiful, and the dynamic weather and changing conditions make each area feel more alive.

However, I’m not a big fan of the Artian weapon system. In my opinion, it reduces some of the creativity and variety in weapon and gear building, since it can make certain crafted weapons feel less meaningful in the late game. One of the things I enjoy most about Monster Hunter is experimenting with different sets and weapon choices, so I wish there were more equally viable options.

I’m looking forward to seeing what the DLC brings next year and hopefully getting even more monsters, equipment, and build options to experiment with.

I love Monster Hunter. I have over 200 hours each in Rise and Generations Ultimate and a more modest amount in World, which makes it hurt to not recommend this game. But even after the supposed performance improvements, it runs badly, and the worst part is that the frame timings basically oscillate, which makes me nauseous. I used to play on a shitty gaming laptop, so I can tolerate low frame rates, but the stuttering and erratic frame times make me straight up nauseous.

The core combat is as fun as ever, and I think this is one of the best iterations of the Dual Blades. Everything around it is what sucks.

The story sucks ass (okay, all Monster Hunter stories suck), but this is by far the worst one, and it's the one that puts the story most front and center. There are a bunch of 10+ minute slow-walking sequences. The awful cutscenes are at least skippable, but the walking sequences are not. The characters go "wow, look how beautiful these butterflies are" and the camera does a 15-second zoom on them. This happens dozens of times. It feels like the developers didn't trust me to experience this world and find it beautiful on my own. It's patronizing, and ironically it hurts the enjoyment of the game a lot.

And while the game runs like shit, it also looks flat and just not that good. The animations are top notch like in every Monster Hunter game, and Arkveld's chains probably have more polygons than all of GenU. But the color grading looks awful, random textures look completely flat and are much lower resolution than the rest of the game, and the art style just doesn't do it for me. It might be far more technically impressive than Rise, but Rise looks better to me, and it runs at playable frame rates.

They spent a huge amount of time and effort building a massive world that the Seikret's auto-run makes completely irrelevant. I have no incentive to explore it, which isn't helped by the performance.

The QoL from Rise is basically gone. Things that took 2 button presses now take 5 to 10 for no reason.

The combat is still fun, but literally everything else is some of the worst in any Monster Hunter game I've played. If you think you can tolerate the performance and everything around the combat, which the game for some reason keeps you away from as much as it can, go ahead. Everyone else, stay away.

Facetious bit aside, I do think this is a well-made game. A bit *too* well made, in fact. The areas are perfectly designed for your new mount companion to the point where traversing any other way introduces massive friction to the experience. Your handler takes every opportunity to remind you of either a mechanic that's constantly occurring in the background or an environmental feature that you'll see dozens of times over the course of your playthrough.

I'm not arguing that this game should play *exactly* like whatever your pet Monster Hunter title is. Iteration and incremental changes are commonplace across any longstanding franchise. On top of that, fans of any entry could tell you the pain points of their particular gem are, and how they wish things were different. However, there can be *too* much change between singular titles, a fact that should be quite apparent given the variance present across the last few entries in this franchise.

I've enjoyed my time thus far with this game, and plan to participate in the expansion when that finally releases. However, it will not be taking the place of my favorite Monster Hunter. There *are* things I like about it, but there are equally as many things that I don't. I dislike needing to hold a button to keep it at a standstill. It is my get-out-of-jail free card whenever I am caught out of place during a hunt.

In my opinion, the Monster Hunter formula works for a reason. Its punishing nature teaches players about its mechanics, and to beware the monsters they hunt. The act of hunting a monster is a skill that should be slowly refined as you progress through the story and rise in hunter rank. Learning to use the environment to your advantage falls in this same category, as does learning how best to navigate this environment. This game, however, is doing its best to do all this thinking for you, from telling you about environmental features you can interact with, to your mount that does all the traversal for you so you can look cool and take in the environment without thinking.

To summarize:

Likes:
- Interconnected World
- Dual-Weapon Loadouts
- Expanded Radial Menu

Dislikes:
- Emphasis on Weak Point targeting
- Overemphasis on using your Seikret
- The "Set Piece-ification" of Monsters

If you like the things I dislike, then I'm happy for you, and I'm glad you finally got a game in this series that you can enjoy. Unfortunately for me, I think this game will never eclipse my play time in Monster Hunter World.

I've been playing monhon since the ps2 and only skipped the Wii U era, though had to wait for quite a while until Steam Machine before grabbing this entry. It's good overall, but has its problems here and there as well. Some map layouts are pretty bad, some sidequests just don't respect your time at all, the weapons feel a little dumbed down and simplified, and most egregious of all... the main story.

Monhon doesn't often cover itself in glory when it comes to the main plot of the games. But, this might be the worst of all of them. Just about every character is actively bad - especially Nata. They even somehow managed to fumble Gemma, making her more annoying than endearing when she has her little bit of limelight midway into the narrative. The Handler is boring. The side characters are bland. I never skip as a policy, but I've never been more tempted.

When the first arc of the story finished, I groaned to find Nata still in my camp instead of back with his people where he belongs. They must hate him as much as I do, quickly sending him off to be a liaison rather than take him back as they should. God, I wish they'd take him back. And now we get to look forward to him as a Hunter all grown up in the DLC? Ugh. I half expected him to come back in an Arkveld fursuit after all of that cringe.

The plus? Gameplay is excellent generally (easy mode though it may be) - it's monhon and you know what you're getting. Prepare to lose a few hundred hours of your life grinding away for talismans and decorations. It runs great on Steam Machine. The wounds and focus mode gimmick is interesting enough (though, all that free damage feels a bit like cheating sometimes, especially if you ever manage to chain 4-5 instances of the focus strike attacks).

Everyone who's a monhun fan and wanted this game probably has it already by now, so this review feels a little pointless. But I just had to get it off my chest. This story is so bad. Even for monhun, it's bad. Do yourself a favour and hold down that skip button. I regretted not doing it.

Stardew Valley is an incredible game. The care and love put into the game by the dev team is clearly seeping out from every corner of it. The gameplay is relaxing at times, and challenging at others, but is always engaging and entertaining. Whether you're farming crops, socialising in town, fishing in a lake, mining for resources in the caverns, chopping down trees to clear room or gambling your life savings in the casino. No matter what you're doing, stardew valley never fails to make even the most mundane seeming tasks of farmlife incredibly fun and rewarding.

The NPCs in this game are all highly interactable, with each one having a role in the community as well as a specific in-game event based daily routine. You can develop friendships with almost all of them, and there's even a few single NPCs that you can date and even marry later on.

There's so damn much to do in this game that you'll sink hours and hours into it and only scratch the surface of absolutely everything that can be done. The game also has great replayability, with various different farms, levelling strategies and gear upgrade orders to try out run after run. If you like the sound of a relaxing farming sim game with mountains of content, Stardew Valley is perfect for you.

I'm surprised I never wrote a review for this game.

I could just write "It's great. Buy it now." and that alone would be a valid review, but I'll go just a little further.

If you've ever played the persona games and enjoyed making the most out of your time or wanted to be rewarded for planning ahead, this game is definitely for you. There may be some things that you can't plan for on your first playthrough until you find out they exist, but odds are you'll eventually want to start a new farm anyways, whether it be to try out different stuff, be more efficient, or check out something you may have missed the first time. 

HOWEVER, if you'd say you're more intrinsically motivated and do stuff just for the sake of it, that's fun too! I find the game intrinsically fun and it's made the game very replayable as a result. Unlike real life, doing just about ANYTHING can generate you money. Not all money-making methods are created equally of course, but you have options nonetheless.

The music and atmosphere in this game is great too. The winter themes specifically are my favorites.

There's also mod support, so you can make the game more fun by getting a modded farm layout, new NPCs, QoL mods, new crops, new areas, resprite characters, etc.

Try the game out sometime, even if none of this may have sounded cool to you. There's quite a bit to do in this game with plenty of polish, and I recommend not playing with the wiki or anything until later and you've found yourself wanting to go beyond what you've already figured out. If that never happens and you just end up mining 24/7 because you find it funner than anything else, that's cool too!

Unfortunately I don't find myself having the time to write as good of a review as I'd like, but hopefully this will do.

In short, this game is well worth the money for offering a cozy farming gameplay, with a lot of optional challenges and assets that you can utilize to create your ideal country life.

As for a lengthy review however, i would like to mention about my first exposure to this game. It was around 2020 when i was watching a youtuber who playthrough of minecraft modpacks. Suddenly one day, he posted a video series about Stardew Valley. Seeing something far different from the usual contents that the youtuber made, i was pretty hooked and then watched the series myself. The vibe of the game felt so fun for me, someone who at the time still find farming flash games to pass the time, with its top-down perspective and colorful design. Sadly however, the series only lasted until summer yr 1, and the youtuber himself moved back to doing minecraft modpacks. Feeling a bit upset that i couldn't be able to see more about the game itself, and mind you, i myself back then didn't even know Steam's existence, which further makes me want to try the game myself.

Fast forward to 2022, i finally get myself a PC, and i get to know some "unusual ways" to "install" games onto my PC, so i tried to get Stardew Valley onto my desktop as quick as possible. Even though 2 years have passed, my experience with the game itself doesn't change at all. The vibrant color design, the cozy feeling of a country side farm, which further fuels my excitement to finally get an experience of the game. First time getting into the game, it was a bit tough for me to understand the story and how some buttons work. But by utilizing my experience from watching the video series, i did manage to plant some parsnips and greet all the villagers. Fast forward to day 3, i finally set my foot to the shore to meet the fisherman, and he gave me a fishing pole. And oh boy, i spent so many days fishing for extra cash. Many people in the community may consider the fishing minigame to be hard, but that's the thing that hooked me, the pain of trying to get a catfish at lvl 1 fishing was so worth it. After a while, i finally checked the mailbox after countless days of fishing, just to see that the very first event of spring, the egg hunt has already passed away. i was a bit upset over that fact, so i went to the central town to check the calendar if there're any other events coming up and slapped straight to my face was the community center cutscene with mayor himself. We went inside to see how ruined the community center was, and the mayor asked me to help repairing the community center, else he was gonna sell it to a nearby establishment. I thought to myself, "guess i should check this out after-" and right at that moment, a apple-looking creature appeared behind the mayor. My character was shocked, and so do I. Looking at how the mayor said i was probably sick or something made me so annoyed, since the creature is literally right behind him all the time, made me yelling "IT IS BEHIND YOU!!!" so loud that my mom came to check what i was doing. After some explanation to my mom, i went back to the game and checked around the community center, which was when i found a tablet that was written in whatever language that i couldnt even google translate it. After that, i went out of the community center and check the calendar to see the next event is the flower dance, which is in the 24th, and it was the 19th when i checked the calendar, so i went back to the beach to enjoy my past time with my fishing pole. The very next day, when i was about to do another fishing trip, i saw the the mail notification. I went to check it to see a letter from a wizard wanting to meet me at his hut in the forest. So instead of going to the beach, i went to the forest to check on him, The wizard was a bit rude to me, and gave me a strange brew that made me hallucinate a bunch of trees here and there. But after all that, he told me i could understand the tablet. Leaving the hut, i made my way to the community center to check the tablet again, and indeed i could read it now. The first tablet had a bundle that requires spring forageables, which i already have some at home, so i fulfilled the first bundle to unlock the next one. One by one, i get to see myself skipping so many aspects of the game. First was farming, i barely planted anything other than the first parsnips the mayor left for me to begin my farm. Second is mining, i wasnt paying attention that there is a mine i could work on. But hey, i left those all behind, because i liked fishing more than anything at the point. I  then again fished until the 24th of spring, where i participated my very first event. Seeing the villagers anticipating such a gorgeous event with beautiful flowers and happy dancing couples was fun, though it was sad that i couldnt get anyone to dance with me, since i spent all my time fishing, meaning my relationship with everything was low, aside from the fisherman himself, since i gave him some of my catches whenever he passes by. And after that event ended, i had to end my playthrough right there due to some complications within my family.

Now, moving to the year 2026, being in college with some free time and money i can spend for hobbies, i recall of Stardew Valley, so i grabbed the game on Steam when a sale happens. Even though i can buy the game and play it for however long i want, one thing that i miss having is the carefree mindset i had back in the day, to spend so much time fishing without a care of other aspects. Even though i missed the feeling, i still think that by reaching perfection and finishing the achievement tab, i have fulfilled my desire to experience the game fully back in the day.

All and all, grab the game and enjoy a cozy farming experience. 🏠

The progression can be very slow, but in some ways its good because that means even after hundreds of hours, there are things you haven't unlocked.

The side quests aren't all clear, but they do make the game more challenging. You need to learn what NPC's like to befriend them (or marry them), which is fun. 

The storyline wasn't really all that important, felt like it was something added just to give context on why your character is on a farm. (which is fair I guess, but still could have been more story related events imo)

The different seasons really make this game what it is. The mechanic of needing to go to sleep and the days progressing make you learn how important every minute of your day is. Did I replant all my crops? Did I visit all the NPC's I needed? When's the next town event? 

Definitely more of a relaxing game, but that doesn't mean its not challenging. If you're someone who struggles to manage their time and someone who puts random items in random chests when playing minecraft, you will definitely struggle here. Still worth the play.

Stardew Valley is like the epitome of a home away from home. When you first start out on your farm, everything may seem a bit too simplistic at first. The art style, the soundtrack, the atmosphere, some of the earlier quests and so on. It isn't one of those AAA titles out there, and it wasn't made with the intention of squeezing every penny out of your pockets. It is a love letter to a part of gaming that hasn't been showcased or appreciated nearly enough at the time until it came along and blew everyone out of the water. The more hours you invest into it, the more you will appreciate the beautiful craftsmanship behind every minuscule detail and how much care was really put into it. One of the most impressive aspects I found was how there really isn't a point where you couldn't be doing something productive. Somehow even handing out gifts across Pelican Town on horseback to try and increase your friendship with the townsfolk was enjoyable. I can say it with confidence that it's one of the only games where the late game holds up just as well the early game, and doesn't feel forced and repetitive. And if you aren't somehow satisfied with the base itself, or you're simply looking to freshen up your new playthrough, there are an endless amount of mods that will keep you coming back for more every time. It's ultimate comfort and the absolute crowned jewel of cozy games.

Stardew Valley is a cozy pixel art farming game where you escape the big city to live a quieter and more meaningful life.

I really enjoyed my time with it, especially so with friends. And a pretty good game becomes even better with a great modding scene which includes everything from small QoL to huge game overhauls with new characters, areas, etc.

For every strength of Stardew however, it feels like there is a matching trade off. You can be in same sex relationships, but you can only be male or female. You can rebuild a community center, but no one else in the community contributes, and you can only fully complete it by fishing. The core game path focuses on an anti-big business narrative, but the gameplay in the late game all but requires you to focus your efforts on intense money collection if you want to see all the game has to offer.

I also wish that some systems like relationships or having kids had a bit more depth to them.

But with Stardew Valley being an indie in the truest sense, it's easy to focus on the good and recommend for all the cozy evenings it has provided.

Stardew Valley is a wonderfully rewarding game that turns the simple idea of restoring an old farm into an experience full of personality, discovery, and heart. What begins with clearing weeds, planting a few seeds, and learning your way around Pelican Town gradually becomes a rich adventure in which even the smallest accomplishments feel meaningful.

The farming is satisfying because you can see the results of your effort everywhere. An overgrown patch of land becomes a vegetable garden, then a thriving farm with barns, orchards, and carefully arranged paths. Planting, watering, and harvesting create a comfortable rhythm, while new crops, tools, and crafting options keep that routine interesting. Upgrades make a noticeable difference, and getting sprinklers working or finally improving a tool feels like a real milestone. Your farm grows alongside your understanding of the game, making progress feel earned.

One of Stardew Valley’s greatest strengths is how much freedom it gives you within that daily routine. You can spend a day fishing, head into the mines for ore and combat, forage around the valley, decorate your property, or visit the townspeople. These activities connect naturally: mining provides materials for farm equipment, farming supplies ingredients for cooking, and exploring can turn up a gift for someone you want to know better. There is usually something useful or interesting to do, but you have considerable room to decide what matters most.

Pelican Town gives all of that activity an emotional center. Its residents have distinct personalities, routines, relationships, and struggles. As you get to know them, conversations and character events reveal more than their first impressions suggest. The town gradually starts to feel familiar in a lovely way—you recognize people, remember their favorite gifts, and look forward to seeing how their stories develop. Birthdays, seasonal festivals, and everyday encounters make your farm feel connected to a wider community.

The seasonal changes are particularly beautiful. Spring feels fresh and hopeful, summer is bright and busy, autumn brings warm colors and a cozy atmosphere, and winter offers a quieter change of pace. Each season introduces different crops, things to find, and events to anticipate. That gives the year a satisfying shape and makes the passage of time feel significant. The end of a season can inspire a little nostalgia even as you start planning for the next one.

The pixel art deserves enormous praise. It is expressive, colorful, and full of thoughtful details that make the valley inviting to explore. The soundtrack is equally memorable, giving each season its own mood and making ordinary moments feel special. A familiar piece of music playing while you walk through town or tend your crops adds so much warmth to the experience. The visuals, music, and ambient sounds work beautifully together.

Stardew Valley also handles long-term progression exceptionally well. Restoring the Community Center, improving your farm, reaching deeper into the mines, and building friendships all provide goals of different sizes. You might begin a session hoping to catch one particular fish and end it excited about an entirely new project. The daily clock and limited energy encourage small decisions about how to spend your time, which makes the “just one more day” feeling remarkably strong.

There is a learning curve, especially when you are first managing your energy or getting used to fishing, but discovering how things work is part of the appeal. You do not need a perfectly optimized farm to enjoy yourself. An awkward layout, a missed opportunity, or a less profitable season can simply become part of your own story.

Above all, Stardew Valley makes care and patience feel rewarding. You nurture crops, improve a neglected place, build relationships, and gradually create a life with its own familiar rhythms. It offers enough depth to support ambitious plans while preserving the pleasure of small moments: a good harvest, a rainy morning, a thoughtful gift, or a walk home after a productive day.

It is an outstanding game with charm, depth, and a remarkable sense of place. For anyone who enjoys farming, exploration, life simulation, or the satisfaction of watching something grow through steady effort, Stardew Valley is easy to love—and very difficult to put down.

I've had many farms over the years, some optimized with planners, spreadsheets, and precision - and others where I just did as I pleased. Now on my third perfection run, I've come to love just how much game knowledge I have. 

I also deeply appreciate the modding community for the game. I play with about 20 QOL mods on top of SVE. It's not because I dislike the game systems - more that I've just already seen them. Things like automate, chests anywhere, etc. - these just make sense when you're 800+ hours in. I also appreciate the modding community's commitment to, how do we say - honor Concerned Ape? There are very few mods that I feel don't belong in someone's save file. I never browse Nexus and think to myself that something is distasteful or changes the game in a terrible fashion. 

Stardew has also brought me closer with friends. Through the board game, through coop gameplay, and just always talking about it. Just like in the valley, buying Stardew for friends is like gifting a little diamond on reset. You're doing it because it's good for you, but also because it's in the spirit of the game. 

Stardew is my favorite game of all time. It's been there for me as comfort-food when I had some serious challenges in my life. I'm not ashamed to admit that some of the characters are important to me; they've taught me things about myself and what "showing up" for another looks like. Shane, Krobus, Leah, Abigail, Penny - everyone has stories that I admire in some way. All the characters feel so well written. Concerned Ape is such a talented writer, and that should never be understated. I'm excited to see his next game, as it will probably iterate on all he learned from writing over the years. 

Lastly, the community for the game is amazing. The amount of dedication from the youtube community for this game is amazing. I'm constantly watching Stardew Valley creators, even if it's just "background" while cooking or doing chores. I just love learning about the game, the world, and Concerned Ape. He's made something un-paralled in indie gaming. He is extremely kind, generous, and humble as well.

315.8 hours later, I finally decided to write a review.

I started playing Stardew Valley back in 2022, and somehow it’s already October 2026. Four years later and I’m still not entirely done with this little pixelated world.

It’s a little funny that it took me this long to write a review, considering how much time I’ve spent playing this game. But I guess some things are easier to enjoy than they are to put into words.

Stardew Valley has always been one of those games I can come back to without needing a reason. There’s something so comforting about returning to your farm, watching the seasons change, taking care of your crops, fishing by the river, and spending time with the villagers. Even after all these hours, there’s still a part of me that enjoys the simplicity of it all.

I think what makes this game so special is that it never really makes you feel like you’re running out of time. There’s no pressure to have everything figured out immediately. You can take things at your own pace, make mistakes, change your plans, or spend an entire day doing something completely pointless just because you feel like it.

Four years is a long time. A lot can change in four years, even when you don’t notice it happening day by day. And while I can’t say that I’ve spent every one of those years playing this game, it’s nice to know that there’s still a little world I can return to whenever I feel like it.

Maybe I’ll take another break someday. Maybe I’ll come back months later, start a new farm, and convince myself that this time I’ll finally organize my chests properly. We all know how that’s going to end. But that’s okay. There’s no rush.

Some games are just games. Others become little places we carry with us, even when we’re not playing them. Stardew Valley will always be one of those places for me.

There are so many positives, such as the immersive sound design and beautiful graphics that literally suck you into this world. But those times where you fully memorize the pattern of a boss after countless attempts to get the patterns and attacks locked into your brain, it feels so rewarding. I won't say anything for spoilers sake, but my favorite boss in the game and the most FUN experience I had was fighting a boss with the initials "NKG".

I could go on and on, the charm system that lets you customize your builds, the giant Kingdom of Hallownest to explore and find secrets, that all hint to the games lore and how Hallownest came to rise, fall, and then some..

Genuinely an amazing game. I hope that this review helped you urge yourself to give this a try, even if it's not your cup of tea, I'm glad there could be just one more person like me that, even though a little late, it's better that I experienced Hollow Knight.. rather than not.

I started playing Hollow Knight just over a year ago, and yet I still remember that first playthrough like it was yesterday. Before Hollow Knight I was like a sheltered toddler in terms of what kind of games I played. A lot of Nintendo. Some Minecraft. A few indie games. So when I booted up Hollow Knight for the first time, I had absolutely no idea what to expect.

The first couple hours were rough. Really, really rough. I was convinced I had finally bought a game that I simply wasn't going to enjoy. The enemies were ridiculously punishing, I had absolutely no sense of direction, and there wasn't even a clear objective of where to go next.

Then, slowly, but surely, I start to get my bearings. 3 hours later, time seems to disappear and I become fully immersed in the beauty of Hallownest. Every inch of the map was something new; the game never punished you for exploring every nook and cranny. It was so rewarding, and the more I played the more I understood just how expansive the world was.

Fast forward 217 hours, and I had every achievement and had 112% completed the game four separate times, including on Steel Soul. And I loved every second of it. This game is not one to sleep on.

The soundtrack is [i]immaculate[/i]. Often times you don't even notice it and it blends in perfectly with the environment. Other times it perfectly captures the scale of a cutscene, like Sealed Vessel.

The art direction is also phenomenal. Every little detail is accounted for, and every area has something unique about it. There are few things more rewarding than sitting down at the hidden bench in Greenpath, with a beautiful waterfall in the background to accompany you. Or walking into City of Tears for the first time. Or brutally navigating your way through Deepnest on one singular mask and finding relief at an unexpected hot spring.

The progression is done incredibly well. I would by no means describe Hollow Knight as linear, yet you can still always tell when you've made progress. The game also handles difficulty really well. Most players agree that the early game of Hollow Knight [i]feels[/i] the hardest, even though the late and end game are objectively harder. This is because by the time you make it to those sections, they don't feel unfair, as the game has already taught you how to overcome them.

I'm writing this review for my 1 year anniversary since I started playing to reminisce on what a masterpiece this game is. If you're somehow lucky enough to have never played it, PLEASE do. You will not regret it and will enjoy this game for a very long time.

Hollow knight is, like many people say, a masterpiece, but it does have a few flaws.

AWESOME STUFF : 
                                 - Great combat and movement

                                 - Beautiful map with varied ambiances and layouts

                                  - Gorgeous fighting and ambient music

                                   - Alot of content and replayability

                                   - Does NOT feel repetitive 

                                    - Multiple fun builds thanks to trinkets

                                     - The game masters the metroidvania style, bossfights, and parkour

NEGATIVES :        
                              - A few bosses are a pain to come back to if you die to them         
                                          -> Soul king, Mantis Lords, Traitor Lord, Hive Knight and 1 or 2 more i forgot
                             
                               - The first area of the game may be underwhelming for some
     
                                 - It's a metroidvania, so the game may not be so good if you REALLY dislike 
                                           -> Backtracking to get to places you couldn't reach before
                                            -> collecting items that can only be sold and Item fragments (mostly)
                                             -> Having to remember where places of interest are for later
                                              -> Restrictive travel / fast travel (not always the case)

MY BIGGEST CRITICISM : 
                                          - The hardest bosses in the game (On radiant/hitless, which is optional 
                                          endgame content) are not hard due to thoughtful game design, but because of :

                                          ->  RNG - attacks spawning on you, minions moving randomly ... 
                      
                                           -> unexpected advantages - bad hitboxes, decoration/vfx hiding attacks ...
                          
                                            -> These bosses are (for me) : Oblobble, Uumuu, Grey prince Zote, Soul 
                                                                                             Tyrant, No eyes, and of course ... 
                                                                                              FREAKIN MARKOTH (out of 47 bosses)

CONCLUSION:  - There are only nitpicks and personal taste holding this game back. Aside from that, it is
                             one of the greatest gaming experiences, and unlike what many say, it IS welcoming for        
                              people new to metroid vanias, as this is the first one i truly played
