NOTE: I wholeheartedly and unambiguously recommend that you play Hollow Knight. Regardless of whatever storefront you buy from, whichever patch you play, however much you pay for it. It [i]is[/i] an excellent game. HOWEVER, this review will be focused more on providing constructive criticism specifically to point out "yeah, there [i]will[/i] be stuff that you don't like or will otherwise piss you off." Either way, it's a factually incorrect statement to say you never got your money's worth even if it pissed you off at times.


THE GOOD
=========

* This game is an [i]extremely[/i] well-optimised Unity3D title. Almost ludicrously so. 
-> It runs phenomenally well on iGPU-only systems.
-> Earlier versions of the game, up to and including patch 1.4.3.2 support 32-bit systems.
-> The full install of the game is like <5GB tops.
-> You have the option to cap the framerate at 30fps, 60fps, all the way up to 120fps.

* This is the game that keeps on giving; you won't ever be hurting for stuff to do.
-> In-game achievement tracker (Excellent for offline sessions)
-> A well and truly expansive game world to get lost in with no shortage of secrets to uncover.
-> Combat is simple enough to pick up with a low tech skill floor and a high tech skill ceiling.
-> Platforming tech skill follows a similar curve. You'd be blown away by how much you can do with just a fireball.

* Absolutely phenomenal OST that's worth every cent you pay for regardless of storefront. To paraphrase Fukui Kenji-san from the American intro of Iron Chef: Christopher Larkin absolutely, 100%, deserves the people's fame and ovation forever. Seriously, close out your browser window, your Spotify, and just [i]vibe[/i] with the entire ordeal.

* It's a modern, indie 2D metroidvania that [i]doesn't[/i] feel highly derivative in the slightest. In fact, Hollow Knight [i]set the bar[/i] for indie studios so damn high that there's actual discourse about how Hollow Knight [i]distorted[/i] consumer expectations of indie games.


THE BAD
=======

* You don't get much latitude with build variety.
-> Wanna use something other than your default melee weapon like a club or a battleaxe? Nope. You're stuck with your broken nail (albeit with optional upgrades).
-> Does Magic have Fire/Ice/Thunder/Wind like in other RPGs? Nope. You just have fireball/ground pound/upward shriek (but with upgrades to "dark" variants later on).
-> Most charms are combat-oriented with very few (and often underwhelming) movement-based charms.
--> Want a charm that lets you stick to walls without slipping? Nope.
--> How about a charm that lets you dash upward, or otherwise extend the length of your jumps? Nope.
-> You start off with three charm notches out of a possible total of 11. 
--> Early-to-midgame is quite punishing when you can only have 1-2 charms equipped at most.
--> Some charm notches are [i]obscenely[/i] difficult to get without gitting gud (e.g. Fog Canyon behind exploding core platforming gauntlet, Trial of the Conqueror behind 17 waves)

* Death in this game is unnecessarily punishing. As in: your ghost holds all your money after you die, but your ghost can also kick your ass. And often times, your ghost will be in a genuinely inconvenient location.
-> There is a merchant who can summon your ghost for the cost of a rancid egg... but he's locked behind a keyed door, and wasting that key on him instead of access to the Royal Waterways is stupid when you can just git gud.

* The Geo economy is awful and unnecessarily punishing.
-> Enemies drop chump change for Geo, but shops sell stuff for upwards of a few hundred to a couple thousand.
-> Geo farms exist, but they're highly tedious and comparatively inefficient to equivalent money farms in other Metroid/Castlevania/Metroidvania games.
-> Even if you painstakingly clear out all the enemies, some Geo is just permanently lost to terrain hazards without specific charms equipped.
-> Relics help mitigate this, but they're finite and also it's [i]not[/i] fun when you're on the home stretch to that one merchant with 1000+ Geo, screw up and die prematurely, you go all the way back to your last bench, and then you die again right before you kill your ghost.
-> Geo costs are not proportional to the amount of progress you make in the game. Expect to see prices jump from 250, then 800, then 2500, and then 4,000 [i]just[/i] to max out your nail's upgrades... and even then, you need upwards of 60,000 or more Geo to upgrade all three fragile charms into their unbreakable forms (not required for the all charms trophy btw).

* The lategame is where you'll be spending an absurd amount of time in agonizing frustration.
-> 100% completion and the "true" ending are gated behind a late midgame, early lategame boss rush cleanup.
--> There's like seven dream warriors that you have to kill for "dream essence."
--> There's like four bosses that you can rematch in the dream world, they're much tougher, and they give "dream essence."
--> You need 1800 minimum dream essence to properly start making progress for the "true" ending.
--> Deeper reaches of Queen's Garden are gated behind a lategame platforming check
--> Expect to get off the computer or the console, go outside, and look at some birds while taking a walk after you get to the White Palace. It's a horrifically punishing platforming gauntlet
--> The "true" final boss requires you to beat the "normal" final boss, then you fight the "real" final boss... and it does 2 masks of damage (out of a maximum of 9), and has multiple stages with aerial and terrain hazards. Good luck.

* Grey Prince Zote is more fun to watch people fight than he is to actually fight. It's like playing against early Pokemon AI that already know all your inputs and makes the optimal decision every time. No, I'm not crazy enough to speedrun a gold Zote statue.

* Godhome is a fun idea. The actual boss rush itself is bitterly disappointing
-> Yeah, you get the opportunity to fight all three of the Mantis Lords at the same time... when you've successfully defeated them once within a dozen-some odd boss rush mode called a "pantheon."
-> Yeah, Grey Prince Zote is optional... unless you were stupid enough to beat him in the main game and then he hardwalls you on Pantheon 3.
-> The bosses themselves within Godhome are, for the most part, the same as their fights in the base game. Just add more health. 
--> You'd think that Hornet Protector would at least get throwing darts. Nope.
--> You'd hope that Gruz Mother gets like an acid projectile attack. Nope.
--> Pantheons 4 and 5 amp up the difficulty with double damage and variant arenas, but that's your lot
-> You don't actually need to beat Pantheon 5 to get 112% completion. You just need to beat it for the trophy.


CONCLUSION
===========

I absolutely [i]adore[/i] Hollow Knight. Genuinely one of the few times in my miserable adult life where I felt that childlike spark of joy from actually playing a video game. It [i]will[/i] require [i]some[/i] adjustment from the player. It's not meant to be a "baby's first Metroidvania," nor should we expect to to function as such. There most certainly are shortcomings that [i]can[/i] and often [i]do[/i] rub people the wrong way. I would argue that the sum of Hollow Knight's strengths significantly override its shortcomings, but I still felt the urge to highlight those shortcomings for one critical reason: this is one of those games that people play for 30-45 minutes, kinda sorta enjoy, and then never come back to. I bought it in 2020, started in 2021, but it wasn't until literally like June of this year when I made substantial progress.

Don't put this game down just because you got salty after dying a few times. Power through and seriously enjoy one of the best damn games you can buy for under $20 (under $10 if you luck out and buy it during a Steam/GOG sale).

Hollow Knight is an amazing game in almost every facet. I would absolutly recomend it to almost anyone and know that they would enjoy it. I will present how I believe it holds up in every category of gaming performance.

To begin with a smaller aspect which I feel is under represented in reviews, is the audio. The sound effects are all spot on, but thats mostly typical for any decent game, however, the ambiance/game music is what really defines whether a game has good sounds, and hollow knight does not disapoint. It has mostly area based game ambiance which is always very fitting and gives each zone a distinct vibe which adds to the enjoyment of the other aspects of gameplay in each area. I do which there was a couple of non ambiance related musical achievments, like some sweeping boss fight scores, but those are mostly not present, still far better music overall than most video games.

Next is combat and platforming, the meat of the game. The platforming is pretty precise, but not extremly so, and is more skill based, than solving puzzles like in some platformers. In some areas, it is extremely challenging but never rage quitty. Its overall a good feature. The combat, though, is absolutly amzing, its simple but perfect, and requires quite a bit of learned skill. It also allows you to aproach fights using strategy by equiping just the right charms to make the fight easier. The bosses are also some of the best in gaming, and some of the most iconic, like the hollow knight, or the three mantis lords. Overall some of the best combat in gaming. 

The story is also pretty good, this isnt the kind of game that requires a super in depth story, its pretty simple but memorable, and gives the player a driving force to continue. Finally climaxing in an epic battle to save all of the kingdom, with extra endings also available. Its not the most story focused game, but that shouldnt impede you from buying it.

The final aspect, the visuals, might be equal to the gameplay in strength. They are incredibly unique, while also being of the highest calibur for 2d gaming. It sometimes feels like you are traversing through a painting or an incredible landscape. Its also a very memorable and iconic art style, especially the look of some of the characters.

You should Definitly buy Hollow Knight its cost vs what you get for roughly sixty hours of gameplay, is very good. This also an indie game so doing so will support that community. 

Final Rating: 9/10

Hollow Knight is a fantastic introduction to the Metroidvania genre, and I can see why it's so beloved.

What I loved most was exploring Hallownest. Discovering new areas, finding hidden secrets, and gradually understanding how the world connects made exploration incredibly rewarding. Unlocking new abilities and returning to previously inaccessible areas also made progression feel satisfying.

The combat is simple but enjoyable, with boss fights that challenge you without feeling overwhelmingly difficult. I found the difficulty well-balanced enough to keep me engaged without becoming frustrating. The art style, soundtrack, and mysterious atmosphere also make the world memorable.

My main complaint is that getting lost and backtracking can occasionally become tedious, especially when you're unsure where to go next.

Overall, the more I played Hollow Knight, the more I enjoyed it. While the combat and progression were great, exploring Hallownest was what truly made the experience special for me. If you enjoy exploration, discovering secrets, and interconnected worlds, Hollow Knight is absolutely worth playing.

You must spend all this time on fights you've already won before, just to be blindsided by a new fight at the end that you've never seen before; only after you've wasted your time on the first attempt can you practice the fight. And the game has more issues. Bosses can move awkwardly off the screen which hides their telegraphs. It makes the fight harder in a way that's not fun. I also encountered a handful of glitches, like one boss's flailing slash hitbox lingering invisible after his attack was over and he got up and ran around and I died to nothing. It's such a shame that I don't see myself putting in all the time and effort required to get that last percent of completion, and getting all of the achievements, because I don't enjoy it anymore. Lethal Company is what I think really defined the "friendslop" genre of games and for it being made by a single person, its HIGH quality. It harness something very interesting as its capable of some of the most horrifying and scary moments mixed with the most absurd interactions imaginable. Proximity chat is one of the reasons its so immersive. When you are alone with an unknown horror stalking you, it can feel INCREDIBLY haunting, even if you are a professional at bashing bugs and brackens alike. However, when you are goofing off with your friends, things can get INCREDIBLY goofy incredibly quickly. Half of my time playing was essentially a mix of a youtube poop and a meme. Part of this is also from the unique variation of monsters, each one having strengths and counters, and the more monsters that are together, the more unique the solution. Having a bracken or a coilhead by themselves is easy to solve, but having them together makes it infinitely more funny and at times, heart racing and it only gets more ridiculous for each monster you add. I definite must, there is nothing like talking to your friend and hear them suddenly stop and their radio error out. 0-0

An incredibly immersive survival-horror game, for what is, honestly, a bad-looking and poorly-performing game. Sure, this is a sly against a primarily solo developer, where other games get millions in budget and hundreds across the dev team. But it's the backhanded compliment that should give you exactly the kind of awesome vibe this game has, and the reason you should jump in.

With many games attempting to artificially create a "janky but good" game, it's no surprise that those actually come together well when the concept is good and the effort is genuine. And that is the case here.
Every creature seems to have a wrinkle to add to the gameplay, even if some of them are miles easier to manage. The exploration aspect becomes boring only much later down the line. And then you find out there's a sprawling modding community for the thing!
Figuring out the dynamic in your friends group - who's happy to charge in, and who feels like sitting back and stress-reacting to every atmospheric trigger out there -, is an integral part of the fun. And it's what makes you come back, enjoy that dynamic some more, maybe ask another friend to join, maybe play with randoms.

The charm comes from being one of those quirky games. But the reason to return to play the game is its well-put together gameplay, a progression system that doesn't hate you, and a tempting world that's keen on throwing scares at you from all directions.

When reflecting on my experience with Letahl Company, I find myself in a somewhat interesting position, mainly because there are quite a few things that could be said about the experience, even if not every single one of those things necessarily needs to be said in order to arrive at a reasonable conclusion. Nevertheless, I believe that taking the time to properly consider an experience, rather than immediately reducing it to a simple positive or negative judgment, can be valuable in its own way. With that in mind, I would describe my overall impression of Letahl Company as positive, although perhaps not in an excessively enthusiastic or exaggerated sense. Rather, it is the kind of positive impression that develops through a general appreciation of what a company appears to be doing, combined with the understanding that there is always more to consider than what initially meets the eye.

First of all, I think it is important to recognize that expectations play a significant role in how we perceive almost any experience. Before interacting with a company, we naturally develop certain assumptions about what the experience might be like. These assumptions may be based on previous experiences, general impressions, or simply the expectations we have developed over time. In the case of Letahl Company, I would say that my overall experience was sufficiently positive to leave me with a good impression, which is ultimately a fairly meaningful outcome. It is not always necessary for a company to exceed every possible expectation in order to be regarded favorably. Sometimes, meeting expectations in a reasonably consistent manner is already a positive achievement, especially when one considers how difficult consistency can be to maintain over time.

This leads to a broader question about what it actually means for a company to provide a good experience. Is it the presence of one particularly impressive feature? Is it the absence of significant problems? Or is it something more difficult to define, such as the overall feeling one is left with after the experience has concluded? Personally, I tend to think that the answer lies somewhere between these different possibilities. A company can be appreciated for individual strengths, but the general impression is often influenced by many smaller details that might not seem particularly important when considered separately. When these details come together, they can create an experience that feels reasonably complete, even if it does not necessarily stand out as something extraordinary. This is one of the reasons why I consider my experience with Letahl Company to have been positive overall.

Another aspect worth considering is the importance of general competence. Although the word itself might not sound particularly exciting, competence is arguably one of the most valuable qualities a company can demonstrate. It is relatively easy to become impressed by something that is new, unusual, or presented in a particularly appealing way. It is somewhat more difficult, however, to appreciate the quieter qualities that contribute to a satisfactory overall experience. Things such as having a clear direction, maintaining a reasonable standard, and demonstrating an understanding of what the company is trying to achieve can all contribute to a favorable impression. While I would not claim that Letahl Company necessarily represents the absolute highest possible standard in every conceivable area, I do think there is enough to appreciate to justify a generally positive assessment.

In fact, the more one thinks about the concept of quality, the more complicated it becomes. Quality is often treated as though it were a single, easily measurable characteristic, but in practice it can mean different things to different people. What one person considers excellent, another person might regard as merely satisfactory. Similarly, something that appears relatively ordinary at first might become more appreciated when viewed in a broader context. This is particularly relevant when evaluating companies, since the experience of interacting with a company is rarely determined by one isolated factor. Instead, it is usually the result of a combination of expectations, circumstances, personal preferences, and the overall impression formed throughout the experience. Considering these factors, I believe that Letahl Company deserves a fair and reasonably favorable assessment.

Of course, it would be unrealistic to suggest that there is never room for improvement. In fact, I would argue that the possibility of improvement is an important part of what makes any organization interesting to evaluate in the first place. Even companies that perform well in many areas can benefit from examining their current approach and considering whether certain things could be done differently. This does not necessarily mean that something is wrong. Rather, it reflects the simple observation that most things can be refined over time. A company can be doing a decent job today while still having opportunities to do an even better job tomorrow. These two ideas are not contradictory, despite the fact that they are sometimes treated as though they are.

With this in mind, I think it is fair to say that Letahl Company has room to continue developing, just as almost any company does. I would not necessarily identify any particular area as being in urgent need of change, but I also would not suggest that everything must remain exactly as it is. There is a reasonable middle ground between excessive criticism and unquestioning praise, and I generally believe that this is where a balanced evaluation should be positioned. Recognizing the positive aspects of an experience does not require ignoring the possibility of improvement. Likewise, acknowledging potential improvements does not automatically make the overall experience a negative one. Both observations can exist at the same time, and I think that is worth remembering.

Something else that deserves a little attention is the relationship between simplicity and satisfaction. We often assume that a particularly good experience must be memorable, impressive, or somehow different from what we would normally expect. However, I am not entirely convinced that this is always the case. There is a certain value in experiences that are simply reasonable, uncomplicated, and generally satisfactory. They might not produce a particularly dramatic reaction, but they can still leave a person with the feeling that things went well enough. In some circumstances, that can be more valuable than an experience that initially appears impressive but ultimately proves inconsistent.

This is a point that might seem relatively minor, but I think it becomes more interesting when considered in relation to how we evaluate businesses in general. We tend to remember extremes. Particularly good experiences and particularly bad experiences are often easier to describe because they provide a clear emotional response. More moderate experiences, on the other hand, can be difficult to summarize. They exist somewhere in the middle, where the overall impression is favorable but not necessarily overwhelming. Yet these experiences make up a considerable part of everyday life, and they should not automatically be dismissed simply because they do not provide a dramatic story to tell afterward.

In this sense, my experience with Letahl Company falls into a category that I would describe as comfortably positive. I do not feel the need to exaggerate the experience or present it as something that completely changed my perspective. At the same time, I do not see a reason to approach it with unnecessary negativity. The experience was generally satisfactory, and the impression I was left with was favorable enough to justify saying so. So

For a long time I was looking for a game that could give me endless hours of play. When I got Skyrim Special Edition, I found far more than just high replay value.

The world is breathtaking. The mountains, snow, forests, auroras, and wildlife make Skyrim a place you want to get lost in. Every time I thought I’d seen it all, I’d find a new cave, ruin, or view that stopped me in my tracks. The Special Edition’s upgraded visuals, lighting, and effects make it even better to look at.

The rich Nordic culture is a highlight. The cities, traditions, and history made me curious, and I ended up learning more about Nordic culture just from playing. Whiterun, Windhelm, Solitude, and Riften all feel different and full of life. The different races, from Nords and Dunmer to Argonians, Khajiit, Orcs, and more, each bring their own history and place in the world.

Play it your way. Warrior, mage, thief, archer, or a mix of everything, at your own pace. Follow the main story, join a guild, or just wander and see what happens. There’s no wrong way to play.

Memorable quests and companions. The main story may not be the strongest part, but Skyrim has some of the most memorable and interesting quests I’ve come across. The companions and followers you meet make the journey better.

Fighting dragons is unforgettable. Hearing a dragon roar in the distance and then fighting it in the open is something I’ll never forget about this game.

Almost endless replayability. Mods and Creation Club content can add new quests, graphics improvements, gameplay changes, and more, so the game can feel fresh years later. If you ever run out of things to do, there’s a whole community keeping Skyrim alive.

Skyrim gives you freedom, atmosphere, and hours upon hours of content. I can see why it’s still talked about as one of the greatest video games ever made.

If you’re really into games with collecting (like - collecting is the core mechanic of the game), then you’re in for a treat. Because after downloading this game, you will spend hours on Nexusmods and other sites collecting mods. And then fixing your game. And then finding new modlists from streamers and downloading new mods.

Apart from that, this is the “canonical RPG game”. That’s it. The canonical experience of an RPG game. If someone is talking about an RPG game, or comparing other game to “RPG games”, then this is the RPG. 

Of course, they are better RPG games (in terms of RPG mechanics) or there are games with RPG mechanics and better story. But this game has a good balance in terms of gameplay, world size and freedom. You don’t feel lost, because the quests are very clear, they don’t have “wtf do i do now” moments. There’s always something to do, because there are many, MANY side quests, and many of them influence other side quests (or your character). The main story could be better, but it’s still good. 

The graphics are quite dated now, but the overall art direction and style of the game is great. For me, this is the game I like going back to because it feels kind of… cozy? Unlike other RPG games, it’s not about constant war/combat. You can just stop, forget about this whole Dragon crysis and civil war and go become a head mage. Or just go and build your house and live with your wife and children. Or just hike in the mountains to good ambient music and watch the Aurora Borealis. Or just find a mod you’d like to install.

This is the game that started it all for me. I have bought this game on the Xbox 360 when it first came out, the Nintendo Switch, and finally now I have it on Steam. I've put a lot of hours on all devices because the gameplay is so addicting and keeps bringing me back. I highly recommend this game because it has a lot of content to sink hours into, a dedicated community, and a few DLCs that add more content.

The game is old so combat may feel wonky. However the best aspect of this game (at least for me) is the soundtrack. There is a sense of escapism I feel when I wander the streets of the 9 Holds or the different environments. The gameplay and soundtrack help me truly escape from the problems of real life.

There is a good chunk of content that the game offers that encourages you to explore the world of Skyrim the way you want to. From being a mage, 2-handed warrior, or the infamous stealth archer, you can play the game however you'd like. This is what makes it addicting for me as I can complete a playthrough of the game and if I want to start a new run with a different race and upgrade a different skill tree, I can easily do that. The story is decent, but you get easily distracted by the amount of world events in the game and the different quests that are given to you. This is a good thing as you end up getting lost into another side of the game. 

The community of this game is excellent. There is a lot of modding support that adds more quests, items, and QOL content to the game. The biggest projects I am looking forward to is Beyond Skyrim, Skywind, and Skyblivion. These projects are using the engine Skyrim was built on and recreating older Elder Scrolls games. The projects are going to be free, so if you would like to avoid paying for the other titles in the franchise, you can buy Skyrim and eventually play the older games for free. 

Overall, I think this game is a necessary purchase for your Steam Library. The Anniversary edition is whatever. You don't need it to enjoy the game as the Special Edition already has enough content and all the DLCs included.

The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim Special Edition is an incredible first open world game. It's an easy game to get into if you're a beginner in the genre and want to experience a mass open world, for the first time ever. I loved how big and expansive the world was, from different biomes across the map. To the multitude of dungeons that had unique architecture to that dungeon only. For me personally there was never a boring time in the game, i was always surrounded by beautiful locations to explore, the DLC zones were no exception either, they had there own beauty too.

I loved the immense variety of weapons available, the armours and spell combinations. Not to mention all the different accessories that came with perks or enchantments to help buff your character or occasionally debuff him too. You had plenty of options and variety when it came to the playstyle and build you wanted to make for yourself as well. You could become a knightly warrior who sought out honour and evil to vanquish. It was possible to become an arcane battle mage, who sought after knowledge in tomes and magical artifacts to increase your power. If you were interested in becoming a devilish rogue who sought after wealth and riches, it was all there for your taking.

Skyrim had an incredible cast of characters and gave them fleshed out backstories, whether that was in dialogues or journals or notes laying about. There was a time when a few characters unfortunately were reused and recycled which often happens in most games. There was still enough of an incredible cast to make exploring the game all the more worth it. 

I would definitely recommend Skyrim to anyone who enjoys open world games, or anyone who has never played one before. It's an incredibly easy open world game to get into and would not be much challenging for anyone i would presume. It has a host of different difficulty levels so if it's too easy you can increase the challenge and the enemies attacking power. 

The game came out in 2011 and even now 15 years later i still think about and play Skyrim. It's always on my mind and i love going back to Skyrim occasionally and playing it in vanilla. Then getting to change or enhance certain aspects through a modded playthrough as well. The creation club content helps give it a new lease on life to and hundreds more possibilities when it comes to new companions or quests and artifacts. The nexus modding community though is where the real beauty of Skyrim and it's modding community really shine through though.

Don't worry about the negative reviews. This game is absolutely incredible. A shining example of how tropes from other games, like Prey, Skyrim, and Fallout have made it into this game, but in greater detail and variety. One minute you're busting down a GalBank transport vessel. All the staff have long since passed, it's been abandoned. A legendary vessel. The security system isn't down and the alarm is going off repeatedly. Everything is absolute chaos. Mechs and stuff. 

The next moment you're in an abandoned NASA facility, long since gone, in the underground testing and R&D department. The enemies are fewer and farther between but they are difficult to kill.

The next moment you are infiltrating a rival trade firm to Ryujin, in an attempt to hack or plant programs on their computers. 

This is a varied, psychologically deep game about space, time travel, and your place in the stars. Get it. Just even if you haven't played Bethesda games before, this is the one to get. Just get this game.

DOWN SIDE
However, that massive scope comes with a familiar caveat: the game is still noticeably buggy. While none of the glitches completely broke my experience, you will still frequently encounter technical hiccups, odd visual stuttering, companion AI pathfinding issues, and occasional menu quirks.

Building complex outposts was a total miss, instead of feeling like a rewarding sandbox feature, establishing and managing outposts turned into a tedious, exhausting grind for resources and logistics that sapped the fun right out of colonizing new worlds.

[h1]Flawed. Frustrating. Unique.[/h1]

Starfield is a game of opposites. For every great thing about the game, there is an equally frustrating or bad thing about it. I have gone through 2 playthroughs of the game, totalling close to 1000 hours,, and it is only now that I can say that I love the game, despite its flaws.

[h2]The Good[/h2]
The game has a lot to love. The worlds are genuinely beautiful. The graphics, while a bit dated, are great. It has its own aesthetic in terms of style. Gunplay is pretty good. 

It's a Bethesda Open World with all the bells and whistles. The main story is good - not great - but better than some of Bethesda's previous titles. The side quests are great though. This is very typical of Bethesda Games.

The game has a granular, adjustable difficulty, so you can tailor the experience to suit your tastes. More games should do this. I ended up creating a difficulty reminiscent of "survival" in Fallout 4.

Shipbuilding is honestly my absolute favorite part of the game. I love coming up with new ideas and making crazy ship builds come true.

[h2]The Bad[/h2]
From how Starfield came out, you can tell a couple of different things: It's clear that the game changed directions several times during development. This is evident in the systems that went into the game, only to be taken out again, but leaving behind traces. 

Fuel economy is a good example. Originally, fuel was meant to be a resource you had to manage. In order to go deeper into the unknown, you'd have to actually secure sources of fuel. The further you got away from settled space, the more this would be a challenge. This got toned down to basically nothing. Which takes us to the next system that got newtered.

Outposts were supposed to serve several purposes. Extraction of fuel and raw resources, automated processing of said resources, and enabling you to build a network of outposts, allowing you to reach the furthest corners of space. That's all still there... except, it no longer has a real purpose.

There's no actual need to ever touch the Outpost building system any more. With the de facto removal of fuel economy, and the lack of a proper place to sell bulk goods, there really isn't any reason to use these.

On top of that, the way that Bethesda has implemented procedural generation means that no matter how far out you travel, you will always run into human-built structures.

[h2]The Technical[/h2]
The technical aspect of the game deserves its own section. It's pretty much part of "The Bad", but it's all related to the engine, so I will tackle it here.

Bethesda uses their own game engine. Originally, they used an engine called "GameBryo", which was then forked, and later evolved into "Creation Engine". Starfield uses Creation Engine 2.

First, there's the loading screens. Starfield has a lot of them. This is entirely due to how the engine handles loading world spaces. Kind of. More on that later. Just know, that vanilla Starfield will have a lot of load screens, so you'll want to have it installed on an SSD.

Second, there's dialogue screens. In modern games like Cyberpunk 2077, characters will move around and emote while talking, and it adds so much to the believability of the scene. In Starfield, the game "pauses", and you zoom in on the face of whoever you're talking to, and stay there. Just like in Oblivion.

So why use an engine that's obviously old and outdated? Well, the Creation Engine does two things that other engines struggle with:

First thing: Every item in the game is simulated and has full physics. The game remembers it all. Hundreds of thousands of objects. And it actually handles it pretty well too. One of the cornerstones of Bethesda Open Worlds is being able to interact with pretty much everything in the world, and that's something that Creation Engine handles better than other engines.

Second thing: Moddability. This is quite possibly the greatest strength of the engine. It's very moddable. The process is more evolved now, but at the base level is the same as it was aaaaaaalll the way back in Morrowind from 2002. This means that there is a modding community with 24 years of experience being able to work on mods for Starfield, creating new content, stories and gameplay systems.

Which brings me to the last thing I want to mention: [b]Engine limitations are strangling the moddability of the game.[/b] Without going into detail, there's a hard-coded limit in the engine that means you can only install so many mods before the game gets wonky and unplayable. For a game that lives and dies on moddability, having this limitation is absolutely disastrous. I ran into this limit myself, and it almost caused me to quit playing.

[h2]The Saving Grace[/h2]
In a word? [b]Mods.[/b]

Every single issue that I've mentioned above? They can all be fixed with mods. Even the engine limitation on mods can be fixed with mods.

Work is currently ongoing to make landing and takeoffs from planets completely seamless. These have loading screens currently. Work is also ongoing on making... everything else seamless, including building interiors and worldspaces. The things that modders are able to do with this engine are frankly amazing.

Technical fixes aside, there are also some absolutely fantastic story mods out there. I played several of them during my latest playthrough. One of the standouts is "Watchtower" by Kinggath Creations - A mod team so good that they are routinely hired by Bethesda to make mods for them, including the universally loved FEVer Dreams mod for Fallout 4 that came out with the 40th anniversary of Bethesda.

Then there the gameplay-altering/adding mods. Remember the fuel economy I wrote about earlier? Yeah, there's a mod system for that. Want to put a little cyberpunk in your Starfield? How about a hacking system that lets you remote-hack robots, cameras and even other people's space suits? Yep, you can get that too.

[b]The possibilities are endless, and Starfield mods have now matured to the point where you can really tailor your experience to what you love, and ignore what you don't.[/b]

I played this game on PC, and used mods from both The Creation Club, and Nexusmods. This is my recommended way of playing the game. Especially since Nexusmods has something called "Collections" that will let you install curated sets of mods with a single click.

Consoles now also have mods, via Creation Club, but I don't have any personal experience with playing on console.

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
It's really taken me a while to get to this point, but I can now say that I love Starfield. Will you love it too? That heavily depends on the kind of energy you're willing to invest into it.

[b]On Steam, Starfield has a "Mixed" rating, and it fully deserves that in its vanilla state.[/b]

Add mods though, and you're looking at a different beast. With my current mod list, I have gotten my game to a state where I love playing it. With mods, the downsides of the game are outweighed by the upsides I get from all the mods I'm running - But it took time to get here.

Looking ahead, the mods coming out will be truly transformative for the game too, so this is definitely not the last time I voyage into the Starfield.

A Disappointing, Bug-Ridden and Utterly Boring Experience

Starfield is one of the most disappointing gaming experiences I've had in a long time. For a game that promised so much, it delivers remarkably little. What should have been an immersive space exploration RPG instead feels like a collection of unfinished ideas held together by loading screens, repetitive gameplay and an astonishing lack of meaningful content.

The game's technical state is frustrating, with bugs, glitches and inconsistent performance constantly getting in the way. It's hard to become immersed in a world when you're regularly reminded of how broken and unpolished parts of the game are.

The biggest disappointment, however, is the complete lack of engaging storytelling. The narratives feel uninspired, the characters are largely forgettable, and the dialogue rarely gives you a reason to care. There is very little emotional investment, very little tension and almost no sense that your choices have any meaningful impact. For an RPG, that's a pretty serious failure.

Exploration, which should be the heart and soul of a game like this, quickly becomes a tedious chore. Countless planets feel empty, repetitive and devoid of anything genuinely interesting. Quests become predictable, activities feel copy-pasted, and the constant travelling and loading screens make an already dull experience feel even longer. Things got a little better with Freelanes, but it still feels like a game that is mainly played in menus.

Ultimately, Starfield suffers from a fundamental problem: it's simply not fun enough to justify the time it demands. It has a massive universe but very little worth discovering, plenty of content but very little worth experiencing, and all the ingredients of an epic RPG without the soul to bring it to life.

A game this ambitious should inspire curiosity and excitement. Instead, Starfield mostly inspires boredom and frustration. A huge universe wasted on a painfully shallow and forgettable experience. 

Starfield has raised concerns for me regarding BGS's future and the direction the studio has taken since Skyrim, as each subsequent release appears less complex. Observing how studios such as CDPR and Warhorse have built on Bethesda's formula further emphasises areas where Bethesda falls behind. I hope the next Elder Scrolls title will mark a positive turning point for the studio.

Man this game is such a weird bummer.  I don't wanna feel like I'm just jumping on the hate bandwagon, but I really tried to give it a fair shake.  First of all, it's been 4 years since release, so they've had *plenty* of time to fix all of what I'm about to say.

The user interface itself is a masterclass in bad design.  All the game's menus are annoying and badly designed, and it doesn't feel like an accident...  stylization was overwhelmingly prioritized over functionality, down to the *main* menu with "inventory" and "missions" and such being a circle...  with labels that DON'T SHOW UP other than the currently selected option.  It took me a bit at first to even figure out that *was* a menu.  There are weird quirks like a short delay when closing the menu, that RESETS if you hit gamepad-B again, so if you spam it, you can indefinitely block the menu from actually exiting...  and you *will* be spamming B, since there are so many nested menus in menus you have to deal with.  It's incomprehensible how this UX could have come from humans who tie their own shoes in the morning.

The gunplay is probably this game's strongest aspect, and it's just bad, but like, regular amounts of bad, I guess.  Why put thin-railed handrails all throughout the game, for example, if no care is given to them having proper hitboxes?  There's also this horrific volumetric dust/fog in every indoor area, which makes it obnoxiously hard to see anything you're shooting at at any distance, and just makes the game ugly as heck.

The story and plot beats I've encountered have all been disappointing, and the dialogue writing ranges from ok to rancid.  Some situations are just complete nonsense, like the bartender who tells you that a patron of his had racked up a large bar tab before disappearing, so he wants *you* to pay the guy's tab in exchange for a lead on where to find him.  How would that even make sense?!?  Every bit of "lore" feels so haphazardly slapped together.  And then the dialogue bugs!  Everybody interrupts each other all the time!  Random NPCs, or your own followers, will just talk over active dialogues, and over each other's random babble.  It's infuriating!  I thought they had this problem solved in several prior titles!

And the art assets that make up the worldbuilding feel slapped together too.  I mean, the weapon designs are famously all random stupid nonsense, but also various items in game...  beer in juice boxes?  Does bethesda even know what carbonation is?  It feels like some executive said "you can't put all the beer in cans and bottles, that's too normal!  We need the beers to come in at least 6 different types of containers!"  There's even a beer that comes in a can, but the can is inside a plastic tube of some kind, with handles on the lid.  The lid would come off if you used those handles!  None of this has been thought through at all!  I know that's a silly nitpick, but with the variety of nonsense assets in this game, it's clear it was a big priority to make things "different" because weird = scifi, and yet it all feels so incredibly phoned in.

And then there's the fact that...  this was supposed to be a SPACE GAME!  And yet, there is no spaceflight!  You can fly your ship around a given local area, just for the purposes of having space combat, but you can't actually fly *to* anywhere...  the moment you want to so much as go from a planet to its own satellite, well, that's just a teleporty loading transition.  And the space combat itself is so much worse than even the infantry combat!  The gamepad controls went so far out of their way to make sure it *doesn't* feel like any kind of space sim, and there's absolutely no feeling of inertia to your own ship, and all the weapons just auto aim and also recharge themselves on some kind of cooldown system.

I don't know what part of this game is supposed to be the appeal.  A space game should have space travel.  A shooter should have good shooting.  An RPG should have good storytelling.  There's none of that.

This game caught a lot of static because it didn't deliver in the ways that people wanted it too. But it's as well written and as well rounded as any other Bethesda game out there. Honestly, I love it and I don't care who thinks I'm wrong.

However, there's one major problem preventing this game from being a perfect 10/10: the bugs.

### 🌌 Exploration — 9.9/10

For a space exploration game, Starfield is almost perfect.

The universe is massive, and there's an incredible amount to discover. Most of the important planets offer multiple activities, locations, and opportunities for exploration.

Yes, some planets feel empty, but I genuinely don't understand why people consider that such a massive problem.

It's space. Not every planet is supposed to be populated.

Think about it logically. Even in reality, you wouldn't expect to find civilians, settlements, or massive outposts on every extremely hot, freezing, or otherwise inhospitable planet.

Some planets being barren actually makes the universe feel more believable.

Of course, a few locations could have benefited from additional content, which is why I'm giving exploration a 9.9 rather than a perfect 10.

### 📖 Story — 10/10

The story is absolutely phenomenal.

I'll admit that I experienced some boredom during the middle portion of the main storyline. A few missions felt slower than I would have preferred.

However, as the story progressed, everything started coming together beautifully.

The later missions genuinely elevated the entire experience, making the journey worthwhile.

By the end, I was completely invested.

### ⚔️ Combat — 10/10

The combat is outstanding.

You have an enormous variety of weapons and playstyles at your disposal:

- Shotguns
- Assault rifles
- Pistols
- Sniper rifles
- Grenades
- Explosive launchers
- Laser weapons
- Special powers and abilities

There's so much variety that combat rarely gets boring.

My only criticism concerns the powers. Even after upgrading certain abilities to their maximum level, some still deal disappointingly low damage.

I believe fully upgraded powers should feel significantly more powerful, especially considering the effort required to improve them.

Nevertheless, the overall combat experience is fantastic.

### 📈 Progression & Leveling — 10/10

One of Starfield's greatest strengths is its progression system.

Leveling up feels rewarding, unlocking new skills is satisfying, and developing your character gives you a genuine sense of becoming stronger.

The progression system kept me engaged throughout the experience.

This is exactly how progression in an RPG should feel.

### 🐛 Bugs — The Biggest Problem

Now, this is where I have a serious issue with Starfield.

I cannot stress enough how frustrating the bugs are.

We're talking about bugs that can genuinely prevent you from progressing through missions.

For example, you might complete an objective, but the game refuses to register it.

Or a mission tells you to speak to a particular character, only for that character to be stuck inside a destroyed or inaccessible spaceship.

What are you supposed to do?

In some cases, your only practical solution is to use console commands to force the mission to progress.

That's unacceptable for a game of this quality.

There are also audio bugs. Sometimes you'll fire your weapon, and there's absolutely no shooting sound.

These issues completely break immersion.

And that's what makes them especially frustrating: the game itself is incredible, but technical problems repeatedly interrupt an otherwise phenomenal experience.

Many of these issues should be fixable, which makes their continued presence even more disappointing.

I really wanted to love Starfield.

I've spent hundreds of hours wandering through Skyrim and Fallout, getting completely sidetracked by random caves, strange NPCs, and stories I wasn't even looking for. Going into Starfield, I expected Bethesda's biggest and most ambitious world yet. Instead, what I found was a game that somehow feels both enormous and strangely empty at the same time.

There's no denying the scale. Thousands of planets, dozens of star systems, ship building, outposts, factions, companions, and enough content to keep you busy for hundreds of hours. On paper, it sounds incredible.

The problem is that bigger doesn't always mean better.

A lot of my time in Starfield felt like I was travelling from one objective marker to another. Talk to someone. Fly somewhere. Pick something up. Return to the original person. Repeat. Bethesda games have always had fetch quests, but previous games hid them behind engaging exploration and world design. In Starfield, I often felt like I was working through a checklist rather than going on an adventure.

The comparison to Skyrim is unavoidable. In Skyrim, I'd set off towards one objective and end up spending three hours doing something completely different because I stumbled across a ruined fort, a dragon attack, or an interesting side story. Some of my favourite moments happened by accident.

In Starfield, exploration rarely gave me that feeling. There's certainly a lot to see, but so much of it feels procedurally generated that the excitement of discovery wears off far quicker than I'd hoped. I spent more time navigating menus and fast travelling between loading screens than genuinely exploring.

That's a shame because there are things Starfield does really well.

Ship building is fantastic and easily one of the best systems in the game. Creating a ship that feels uniquely yours never gets old. Combat is also Bethesda's best to date, with gunplay that feels far more responsive than anything in Fallout 4. Visually, the game can be stunning too. Some planets genuinely made me stop and admire the view.

The faction quests are a mixed bag. The UC Vanguard storyline is probably the strongest content in the game and shows what Starfield is capable of when it focuses on storytelling rather than scale. Unfortunately, not everything reaches that standard.

The DLCs haven't really changed my opinion either.

Shattered Space finally allowed us to learn more about House Va'ruun, one of the setting's most mysterious factions. The problem is that despite the interesting setup, the story felt surprisingly restrictive. For a game built around player choice, most of the major outcomes felt largely predetermined, and my decisions never seemed to have the impact I was hoping for.

The Starborn Armada DLC was an even bigger disappointment for me. The faction itself seemed interesting enough, but the content never gave me a real reason to care about them. There was very little meaningful backstory, not much exploration of who they actually were, and most frustratingly, no real option to properly join or align with them. It felt like Bethesda introduced a potentially interesting faction and then did very little with it.

That's probably my biggest criticism of Starfield as a whole.

There are so many interesting ideas, factions, locations, and mysteries scattered throughout the game, but they often feel underdeveloped. Just when something starts getting interesting, the story moves on before you've had a chance to become invested.

In the end, Starfield is a good game, but I don't think it's a great Bethesda game.

It's one of the biggest worlds they've ever created, yet I often felt less compelled to explore it than I did Skyrim's single province. There are more planets, more systems, and more content than ever before, but somehow less wonder.

For me, that's Starfield's biggest problem.

It's a galaxy that's vast in size, but often feels empty in spirit.

I discovered Starfield in July 2026 and finally completed it after over 200 hours. I honestly don't think I've ever spent this much time playing a Bethesda game!

==========The negatives==========

-A slow start:
Compared to Fallout or The Elder Scrolls, it takes quite a while to get into the game. I spent my first 15 hours feeling a bit lost, especially when it came to managing loot, resources and money. Watching a few YouTube guides made a huge difference to my experience.

-Way too easy: 
A recurring issue with Bethesda games. You can get ridiculously powerful gear within just a few hours and breeze through even the final boss.

-Not enough space combat:
Shipbuilding is one of the game's best features, yet there are surprisingly few opportunities to actually use your ship in combat.

-Underwhelming quests:
Aside from the Crimson Fleet, UC Vanguard and main storylines, most quests felt rather forgettable. The excessive reuse of procedurally generated locations doesn't help either.

-What's the point of outposts?
Unlike Fallout 4, I struggle to see their purpose. With unlimited storage at The Lodge and resources readily available from vendors, there's very little incentive to build them beyond farming XP.. Considering outposts don't have unlimited storage.

==========The positives==========

-Freedom and exploration:
That classic Bethesda feeling of developing your character and making your own way through the universe.

-A grounded sci-fi universe:
I really appreciated Starfield's realistic approach to science fiction. The bulky spacesuits, believable technology and overall aesthetic make its universe feel like a plausible evolution of our own, rather than an over-the-top sci-fi setting filled with flashy, nonsensical designs.

-Fantastic shipbuilding:
I had a blast designing my Class B ship, followed by my first Class C ship after 100 hours, which took me around six hours to build!

-A clever New Game+ system:
It fits the universe surprisingly well. I would have loved something similar in Fallout 4 or Skyrim!

==========
Final thoughts
==========

Despite having more negatives than positives, Starfield is still a game I'd happily recommend. Not all the previous points carry the same weight, and Bethesda's open worlds remain something special.

If you've been dreaming of a game like Starfield since Wing Commander III: Heart of the Tiger in 1994, that's a 32-year wait for your ultimate space-faring fantasy to take shape

1994 — Wing Commander III

Cinematic storytelling, memorable characters, branching decisions, and the feeling that you were a pilot in a living sci-fi universe.

2023 — Starfield

Your own spaceship, distant worlds, exploration, faction storylines, and the freedom to build your own life among the stars.

What I love about that comparison is that these games scratch slightly different parts of the same itch. Wing Commander III made you feel like the star of a cinematic space opera. Starfield lets you inhabit a science-fiction universe and decide what kind of spacefarer you want to be.

And if you've spent decades imagining what you'd do if you could actually step into a universe like that, Starfield's appeal goes far beyond shooting pirates or completing quests. It's the idea of climbing into your own ship, flying into the unknown, landing on an alien world, and making the adventure yours.

I'm curious about one thing, though: what was the big dream for you back in 1994?

Was it the cinematic, character-driven space opera of Wing Commander III, the freedom to explore a vast galaxy in your own ship, or the fantasy of actually living in a believable science-fiction universe? Because those are three different dreams, and Starfield comes closest to some of them in very different ways.

I've thought about writing a long essay about all of the things this game did right and wrong, putting it in bullet points and all that, but I then figured that these sums up this game pretty well:

The core idea seems to be quite straightforward: this game is your typical Bethesda experience that was meant to be shared with the community, for the people to pour their creativity alongside what the devs made, yet it has nearly zero pull and appeal to make most of them commit to it. I'm not sure if its the creative direction or if the team lacks what the previous ones has, but everything that this game offered, outside of it's technological advancement (graphics, support for new tech, higher fps support, etc) is watered down and worse than what its predecessor has, this game has less story, less agency and less uniqueness, and due to all of that, it also has less community support.

The story is so watered down and short, the writing is safe and sterile, conflict felt fake at times and your choice doesn't matter the majority of the time, a far departure from the previous title's immersiveness and freedom. And then there's the gameplay, it's been improved but the loop is downright attrociously repetitive, majority of the things you encountered during exploration are procedurally generated, but they only made 1-2 templates for all of them, which means, everything you encountered will only have 1/2 variants, once you found an abandoned military base, you've found all of them, same enemies, same layout, same loot table. When this is all they have to offer in the base game, I can see why most people aren't necessarily interested into putting more work on it.

If they wanted to attract more talanted people to create for this game, they needed a really good hook to pull people in, yet, instead of making appealing product that allows its community to contribute their effort, they seemed to rely on the fact that people would always do so in a Bethesda game and put on a sub-par base product as a result, which then failed to appeal to a lot of those talents, it couldn't pull the old talents from their older games and doesn't garner enough interest with the newer talents either, so now, a game that had set aside some of it's canvas space for the people to work on, is left with a half-finished work, riddled with blanks spaces.

TLDR: I enjoyed Starfield enough to put a lot of hours into it and give it a thumbs up! That being said, the game also have one fundamental issue, let me try to nail it in one sentence: The concept behind Starfield is great and Bethesda designed a huge universe for it, but this huge universe is way bigger than Bethesdas ability to fill it with enough meaningful content.

Lets return to the expectation part, because I think it's important if you are thinking about getting the game. Bethesda sold the game as a huge universe full of content and exploration. I think many players were probably expecting something in the line of Skyrim where the world is packed with discoveries, distractions and surprises for almost every step you take. Starfield is obviuosly not Skyrim, but this particular difference is what I think causes most disappointment. Its a huge difference between filling a limited map with handcrafted content, and to do the same one hundreds of whole planets. This is exactly where the concept and the gaming experience collides, making the game very wide but shallow. 

Bethesda has been doing a lot of what I think they do best, which is the handcrafted exploration formula combined with often great storytelling. There is a lot of that in Starfield too but when it's stretched thin over a whole galaxy it just gets diluted. I think this game would have got way better off starting with a much smaller universe of maybe 15-20 or so explorable systems that could later have been expanded.

But again, I enjoyed the game. Not just because of lowered expectations, but also because many of Starfields individual ingredients are actually great. Some questlines like Vanguard/Crimson or Ruyjin are excellent, and some of the handcrafted locations are just as atmospheric and engaging as they come in a Bethesda game. I also found the shipbuilding challenging and fun once I got hang of it. Base building was a bit too space restricted and basic for my taste, but I somewhat enjoyed it anyway.

Personally I did not really have a problem with the loading screens or space jumps. I would say that also comes more from what you expect the game to be, and as long as I get good content at my destination, I don't mind. Some mention waiting time on loading screens, but I did not experience much of it. Hardware thing?

One sad thing is that once you are done with the handcrafted content, the game is no longer interesting. There might still be hundreds of planets left to explore, but finding identical facilities and layouts across countless planets is simply boring and eventually you just give up on it. Standard missions are also very repetetive. 

I will probably try modding next, let's see if I can squeeze a few more hours out of the game. :)

39 levels later I'm a ranger, a tracker, a pirate, a corporate fixer, a privateer and a security officer and I have super powers but most importantly I'm my own boss I fly where I want when I want and do whatever I want when I want. Piper in fallout and Sara should start a club to whine about my "crimes."

There are 4 types of NPCs in game; core who have "personalities" and back stories personal quests etc some who become followers or you deal with regularly. Generic type A can serve a function like ship or out post crew shop keeps or quest related generic B are filler exist to populate the world and not good for anything but being a crowd to enhance immersion.(the last group you can modify in settings to really make your cities come to life max it out and your computer might fry but you won't be lonely.)

Combat is good shooting someone in the face in no oxygen environments does massive crits and blinds as it should and it works both ways not pleasant but I'd call it fair.

"The skill tree" is complex(sort of) and confusing(very) and every time I add a point I feel I need 5 more before what I blew on this point makes a difference but it eventually catches up and your toon feels like its learning something useful.

It took me 3 years to finally decide to finish playing the main quest of this game. It took me this long to decide to sit down and commit to finish it because the first 15 hours is such a painful slog. 15 hours is a long time for the game to feel somewhat enjoyable. 

The first part of the main quest is a tedious, repetition of flying somewhere and mining a shiny rock out of a bigger rock after downing some mobs. I hated it. The second half the main quest does get much better and have a couple of probably the best main storyline quests they've ever made. The second half of the main storyline really saves it. I did a few of the faction questlines and I thought they were pretty good too. There's a ton of side quests, most of them are forgettable.

I felt like companions were much more fleshed out here than the previous games and even some of the dialogue was good or decent.

Lore-wise, this game is so light on lore that it never gave me the curiosity to look up anything about it. It basically feels non-existent. I think its a difficult job to live up to the vast lore of Elder Scrolls and Fallout, but it feels like they didn't even try here.

This is probably the prettiest game they've made in this genre, the art and the sounds are amazing. I have no complaints here.

Customization options are pretty great. The shipbuilder was a huge plus and unique although a bit annoying to use, and all the weapons and armor are customizable but locked behind perks and materials like Fallout 4. This felt more of a grind to get the mats though so I didn't get to customize as much as I did in Fallout 4.

Pretty good QOL features.

I was disappointed in combat the most. Special abilities are pretty cool, but they've basically haven't innovated much in this area other than that. It feels like the same-old gunplay (possibly even worse than before) and melee isn't interesting at all.

I was interested in seeing space in my customized ship and ship battles, but after a little, it got old so quickly. Most of flying around isn't interesting and the battles aren't exciting at all. It kinda feels like theres not much happening in space despite many of the systems being settled on.

In quantity, theres a lot to do in quests, outposts, grinding materials, customization, and discovery. I just think they dropped the ball on providing a good baseline of quality or enjoyment or innovating on previous gameplay elements when taking on a new IP.

I'd recommend only if you want something mildly interesting that you can sink your time on and its on sale. To me, it was mediocre.

They clearly went with quantity over quality and you can feel it after a few first hours.

The amount of planets is incredibly large but very rarely do they contain anything important on them.

Additionaly each of them is procedurally generated and it is impossible to explore them fully because of the sheer scale.

Pairing that with Bethesdas' obsession with repeatable quests it makes it uncear which ones are important and which ones are pointless fillers.

I expected a cool space exploration game, instead I got a game where 90% of planets are empty dead rocks, 9% is filled with never ending quests that feel pointless and only 1% is actually worth doing.

It's annoying and made me stop asking vendors for jobs, because I can't be sure if it will be worth my time.

I'm probably in a minority in this but if somebody is like me this is your warning.

Also don't get me wrong I'm stil going to play it because I paid for it. I'm just saying that anything beyond faction and main quests is a 50/50 to be just trash repeatable.

At first, i had my doubts about this game and was skeptical because of the backlash this game was getting but in the end i decided to give it a try.

First of all the character creation was a lot better than i expected, the sliders and options allow you to create some really good and unique characters and also some freaks if you want to, but the best part of the CC is the option to select your background and character traits, the backgrounds are quite simple, it's mostly for role playing and offers you some starting perks, you can say it's kind of like Morrowind and Oblivion classes. The more fun though has to be the traits, there's a great selection of traits that give some unique moments and interactions, Such as Dream Home that allows the player to have a house but you have to pay a weekly mortgage or pay it off in full, Or you can start by having a bounty and bounty hunters are trying to claim it or you can have your character have parents that have dialogue and unique interactions on planets and some quest lines and also provide a starting player apartment for free.

Another thing that i want to point out is that said background, traits and perks can add new dialogue options that can help with quests. Also if you decide that you no longer want a specific trait you can have them removed by certain NPCs for role-playing reasons, such as if you chose the wanted trait you can pay your bounty at a tracker alliance agent or if you have alien DNA you can get "cured" by doctors.

I am not going to talk about the main quest other than that i personally enjoy it to avoid spoilers but i will say a few things about the side quests and faction quests. 

As is typical of a Bethesda game there are a huge amount of side quest with multiple ways to complete them, you can persuade your way to completing some quests, you can find alternative ways that the game doesn't tell you or you can just do the classic and kill your way out, and some of those quests are some of my favorites in any Bethesda game for instance one of my favorites has to be the crimson fleet/sysdef questline where you work undercover to take out the pirate faction of the game while hunting for the ultimate loot in the galaxy, you can also doublecross sysdef to join the crimson fleet unlocking the pirate playstyle.

Also another that stand out to me was the UC Vanguard questline, I love the introduction, where you're introduced to the lore surrounding the Colony War and the ship Simulator. The Ryujin questline that to unlock it you need to submit a résumé to a company, after that you attend an interview and get the job, at first, it seems mundane but each mission you complete you climb the corporate ladder and the missions become more like a spy movie than a standard office job. 
Or some hidden facilities that hides some surprises that i don't want to spoil, and more. 
One thing to point out is depending on your traits, background and your factions that you joined you will get more dialogue options that may help you to proceed some quest. 

As typical Bethesda fashion there are a lot of random encounters some of those are: a dispute between a sentient ai and suits, Space shanties, a creepy woman that should be in a horror game, ship's extended warranty and more.
I also love the outpost and housing in this game i spent a lot of hours building an outpost for harvesting resources and for housing, you have access to so much junk items in this game that seem useless but can make your house or outpost be more alive, also the fact that you can rotate objects in your hand is really helpful. 

Now the shipbuilding, i have spent a lot of hours and credits in the shipbuilding trying to build ship of my own design or just ships that exist in other games and movies like the Pillar of Autumn the Millennium Falcon and Normandy, you can do a lot of things with the shipbuilding but it is difficult in the beginning and the ui is not helping. 

Another thing to note is the attention to detail put into this game like the gravity of every planet is almost accurate to how they are in real life also the gravity actually feels right and not just normal g and zero g, also the way the time passes in planets it's mostly accurate with some exceptions, also the planets, moons and sun are actual 3d objects that actually orbit and are not just a 2d skybox, that seems like a small detail but it's really nice to see for space enjoyers. 

The combat is pretty solid, nothing too fancy just fun enough i can't complain, there are some scenarios were you can utilize the physics of the game like you can grab a explosive barrel and throw it at enemies and make it explode also the zero g combat is really fun. 

Also the graphics are very beautiful and add that with the simulated 3D planets you can witness some truly beautiful sights, i have spent more than a couple of hours using the camera mode adjusting the filters and settings to capture a lot of pictures, that isn't anything new but there is something truly relaxing and therapeutic to just try to capture a really good picture  while surveying a planet. 

Of course like any game there are some negatives like i really don't like that when you shoot in public or next to NPC's they don't react at all, i also do not like the use of crowd NPC's they don't do anything just aimlessly move around say a few things and look really ugly i get that they are used to make the cities more alive but i don't like them, also i feel like the enemy ai could use an upgrade. 

Overall, I think Starfield is a pretty great game with a good selection of quests, locations, and mechanics. you can truly spend hours doing whatever you like and playing whatever kind of character you want. There are negatives, sure, but there are plenty of positives, too. If you focus only on the negatives, you're probably going to have a bad time. But if you approach it with an open mind and appreciate what it does well, you can have a truly unique experience.

I'm a big space game fan. I'm a big RPG fan. I'm a big open world fan. This game is marketed to be all 3 but it fails hard at each. I've spent a ton of time trying to like this game and modders have made massive progress making it tolerable but I cant recommend a game just because modders have worked tirelessly to polish a turd. This review is about what Bethesda put their name on. The art team, developers, and most of Bethesda are clearly talented and care; I put 100% of the blame for the lousy state of this game on awful management. 

It's an awful space game. Their latest update made space a bit more tolerable, but it's still very weak and with tons of bizarre design choices like constant loading between take off and landing when they could have easily lingered on the last frame of take off or reentry while they load the landing/space segment of the game and it wouldn't have felt broken up. They left it for modders to do their job for them. The design of the ships shows the art team cared, the modellers cared, there was thought put into everything and this was clearly meant to be a lot deeper but management rushed the game out the door before any of the depth could be added. 

It's an abysmal RPG. The world is interesting and could have really lead to some great player choices but it was artificially restricted so they could sell you DLC. Why cant you play off the tension between the various factions? Why can you join every rival group at the same time? Why is every single choice in every single mission a simple will you or wont you binary with no nuance at all? Because they cant let you make too many large choices or it would make shoehorning in DLC harder. They held back choice, then released a game so unlikable they'll likely never even get to the DLCs they ruined the game to sell in the first place. 

It's not even open world. With so many load screens in every outpost and town it's not even truly open area. Modders were able to fix a lot, but Bethesda management rushed this game out the door before their own team could complete the features they clearly wanted in the game. 

Bethesda has a very well established pattern now of releasing increasingly limited RPGs that have more and more issues they rely on modders to fix.
