Сотни пропсов, парящих в невесомости; до мелочей проработанные станции с потрясающим освещением; масштабнейшие локации для эпичных мультиплеерных зарубов, которых вы никогда не увидите; настоящий gun-porn в лучших традициях Cyberpunk 2077 с прокачкой и модификациями. А вишенкой на этом великолепию идет блочно-модульный фит кораблей, в котором можно утонуть на многие часы.

И давайте ещё раз закрепим про визуальный стиль, чтобы стало понятно, куда ушли 10 лет разработки — стилистика и исполнение выше всяких похвал. Пока другие студии делают стилизованную сай-фай мультипликацию а-ля Marathon, Bethesda проработала каждую дверную ручку.

Но... Зачем-то в перерывах между «красиво пострелять, залутать и прокачаться» завезли диалоговую РПГ. И завезли так, что лучше просмотреть пару лишних экранов загрузки, чем ритмично, с паузами, «прощёлкивать» абсолютно все диалоговые окна. 

[h1] Много загрузок, говорили они. Нет посадок на планеты, говорили они. Устаревший движок, говорили они... [/h1]

Первое, что сильно бьёт по глазам, а потом и по рукам — интерфейс. Бывает плохой UI (Grim Dawn) или сложный табличный «мониторинг всех систем» (EVE Online и 4X-стратегии), но Starfield пошёл дальше и решил не отображать ничего, а взаимодействия со звёздной картой (да и в целом навигация по меню) не оставят равнодушным даже шестипалых.

Десятки неочевидных решений перемещения по системам и посадках на планетах, невозможность следовать по простроенному маршруту неоткрытых систем — разработчики просто не понимали и явно не тестировали свой продукт. Ибо даже запутанный (визуально) интерфейс EVE Online решает самые сложные «задачи со звёздочками» в несколько кликов.

Управление — это отдельная песня, и речь о назначении и переназначении клавиш. Неотключаемые «зажатия» клавиш на клавиатуре в 50+ свободных кнопок и неразрывно связанные двойные действия на один бинд кнопки просто выше моего понимания разработки такого рода продуктов.

Это настоящая диверсия продукта. И Starfield 2.0, который якобы был, должен начинаться не с переработки игрового мира, а с переработки интерфейса.

И если вы еще не устали зажимать Escape, то геймдизайнер со сценаристами знает, как вас развлечь. Вы же любите буквы? У них «есть их много для вас». Сотни часов аудио-нарратива, лица, города, гильдии — никто и ничего не имеет никакого смысла. В какой-то момент мне начало казаться, что генерируются не планеты, а диалоги...

Ну кто играет в игры Bethesda ради сюжета, он скорее зарисовка. Прощёлкали диалоги, посмотрели цели миссии — ну дайте пострелять! Дайте мне баталии на кораблях, как в финале в Terran Armada, чтобы от обломков проседал FPS — я что, зря собрал Звезду Смерти? Дайте мне сотню солдат на станциях, да дайте мне сотню станций...

Но нет — каждый шаг, новый квест это очередная глупая просьба куда-то прилететь, что-то передать. У игры был огромный потенциал, который крайне успешно "разработали". Можно набраться сил и просто летать по Incursions или искать «заряженные» аванпосты — да, они есть. Можно прыгать по Serpentis и ваншотать Va'ruun корабли (да, на Extreme). Но всё это спрятано от вас подальше. Ведь это не шутер, а ролевая игра от Тодда Говарда. И роль ваша — петух.

[h1] Исповедь затерпевшего [/h1]

Вы хотели бы поговорить о Боге? А я скажу. Больше 20 лет назад вышла EVE Online, X4 родилась в 2018-м; десятки — нет, сотни игр, от аркад до хардкорных симуляторов, имеют более выраженный визуальный стиль каждой отдельной системы.

Даже не уходя в мягкую фантастику, а двигаясь твёрдодонаучно (так сказать, по-насапанковски), в Starfield нет даже и следа «космоса»: ни аномалий, ни чёрных дыр, ни скоплений метеоритов, космического мусора, комет, туманностей, двойных звёздных систем, пульсаров или солнечных вспышек. Нет даже «другого свечения» от красной, синей или жёлтой звезды.

Starfield — это просто деградация. Деградация идей и решений. Это прикрытие собственной безыдейности и некомпетентности «устаревшим движком», который на самом деле выдаёт очумительную картинку. Starfield — это сырой фарш, который сложно прокрутить обратно.

[h1] И тут я ей говорю — "Может разнести твою бошку к чёртовой матери?", — а она мне — "Попробуй красавчик, и за тобой будет гоняться вся Сидония". [/h1]

Ну я человек простой — "взял, да попробовал". Закрыл диалоговое окно, расстрелял её в упор, а после перестрелял весь город. Из каждого угла кто-то кашлял на карачках, периодически поднимаясь и получая очередь из Magstorm.

(Base Game only, completed main story) While I am posting a positive rating, I cannot recommend paying full price for this game (I purchased during the recent sale). With a significant discount the game was worth it for time and effort, but ultimately disappointing for a Bethesda title.

The Good:
*Beautiful world, seeing it is a visual treat
*Solid game play, very similar (see below) to other Bethesda RPG control schemes
*Detailed Character creation, as well as weapon customization
*Ship customization is brilliant, one of the best aspects of the game

The Bad:
*Writing is weak, weaker than any other Bethesda game I've played. It feels like they had a great idea, and just decided to leave it as a simple tale when it could have unfolded into so much more.
*Skills: Very annoying skill progression, particularly when so many game functions are trapped behind two sets of crafting (researching each upgrade type then crafting. Rinse and repeat for 3 tiers).
*Game economy: Earning credits feels like an extra grind between bounties and missions, with very few paying out well. You can make money from selling loot but the vendors run out of money quickly. Ships are so expensive that I used the starting ship and just built/upgraded as I went because it was significantly more cost effective. I did not purchase a single pre-fabricated ship in the game, which was a shame because some looked impressive.
*Story and replay: They make the story seem so significant early game, then as you progress it just becomes mundane, and then rather abruptly concludes with some grand philosophical concept. You can continue with a NG+ but after starting one I have found there is nothing worth the grind.
*Game mechanics: While the gameplay is sound, it's almost an EXACT copy paste of the control scheme and physics of Elder Scrolls and Fallout. For as much as they touted and advertised that this was going to be a genre defining game, all we got was Elder Scrolls V.V: Space Oblivion.

Overall: 6/10, Do not buy full priced

I've been sitting on this review for a long time, and I'm glad I did. First off, let me say that I genuinely enjoy this game, but not really in the way it was intended. I like it as a "cozy" game and a sandbox for modding and mostly messing around. I've heard all the negative talk and, honestly, a lot of it is justified. After finishing the game, I can say that the story is not only weak, but essentially pointless. It feels like there are no stakes at all, especially after finishing the game once. Most of the missions are kinda just doing what other people tell you to do, and when you ARE faced with a decision, it makes little to no difference and doesn't effect the overall outcome in any meaningful way. This game was clearly designed to be played for a LONG time, as in over and over again, as Todd Howard said, for about 10 years. The problem is, you really can't get things wrong. In a rinse-and-repeat kind of format like this, the player should be able to ruin EVERYTHING, even by accident. Maybe even wipe out the entire human race and be the sole survivor, giving reasons to play again and try to get things right. It really feels like either the writers were too afraid to take risks, or like development got so rushed and overcomplicated that they had to put the whole thing on rails to get it to the finish line. Either way, this is where I see the most room for improvement. The mechanics are fine. Some are fantastic. The gist of the story is okay, it just needs stakes, and maybe some grit. The rest of the potential improvement points have all been discussed at length here and elsewhere, so I'll leave it at that. In short, I like the game, but my recommendation is pretty much confined to those who also like to tinker with games and kinda find their own fun.

I played this game on Xbox when it released on Gamepass, and spent well over 200 hours on it. With DLCs and official support, the game is decent. It's not "Skyrim/Fallout in space", but it plays like a Bethesda RPG, so those are easy comparisons. Where the game shines is modding. Free modding resources bring life, realism, and color to the game that it was missing. Unfortunately, after the implementation of the Creation Kit, BGS locked most good mods behind a paywall, and there was really no reason for most modders to keep releasing free mods.

The story, however, leaves a lot to be desired. There's a lot of good and great depth to some stories, but also a lot of plot holes and other typical Bethesda immersion breaking details (like a 150-year-old abandoned moon base with a fresh orange on the counter). The game is designed to be played multiple times with its honestly great take on a New Game + system baked into the story, but the more you play the same missions, the more you start noticing those plot holes, and that can really break immersion quickly.

Overall, this game is worth playing, though not at full price. Mod it if you get it and get the most out of your time.

Main Story villains have absolutely nonsensical reasons to exist, an entire plotline centered around Terrormorphs is only there because, despite being studied in a lab, nobody connects the dots that one creature is remotely related to another one. (UC Vanguard questline, by the way) Freestar Collective is playing with things that big companies do TODAY and has no nuance to any of it. Despite being able to knock characters unconscious with stun guns, you HAVE to kill the final villain, and characters pretend you had no other choice. The quest won't even progress unless you hard-kill him, and then someone goes "if only we could've brought him in alive."

Beyond the story, you can make outposts. These are how you get resources to craft upgrades for guns, but inventory space is at such an insane premium that you better be doing your crafting and research out of your ship, or you'll be in inventory-management Hell. And even if you do all this in your ship, it takes about five seconds to leave any workbench so you can actually go find out where your resources are and get them in the right inventory to craft with. And don't think resources are something randomized, they're entirely mapped out by other players already. The crafting end of the game is solved, there are "best planet" guides complete with the exact pixel they suggest you click on to get the good position on the planet for easy base-building.

Combat is passable, until enemies become bulletsponges. There are hidden values that tweak enemy HP every time YOU level, and more that change values when you engage in NG+ that nerf your damage and buff enemy damage.

Your starting traits you can immediately opt out of. Some of them don't even work like they say, and often times your dialogue options that utilize these traits make you out to be a complete ignoramus. If you pick UC Native, for example, you can ask someone why you aren't a citizen already. However, it calls into question why someone who was born and raised in the United Colonies wouldn't know that the UC has Citizen-Service, a la Starship Troopers. Why is your UC Native character suddenly unaware of this? Is the writing making your character a moron so a voice actor can tell you service guarantees citizenship? Are you doing your part?

The game had potential. It needed another few years in the oven and it needed writers that don't look down their nose at you for playing their game in a way they don't plan for.

Quite possibly the most disappointing Bethesda game to date. This review is for those that have enjoyed previous games by Bethesda and are on the fence about whether this will satisfy that itch. It will not. I gave it a chance. After several dozen hours, I thought, 'Surely the end game will be fun. I'll have cool guns. The story will have opened up with cool space dragons or something wild. Maybe an intergalactic war of some kind?' No. None of those things happen. Nothing cool happens here. You will walk on a random moon and see some generic bad guys in the distance. They're oddly placed on a tower that you swear you cleared two hours before hand.

I was initially excited about Starfield's release because I appreciated the idea of the developers working on a new IP. Science fiction is a perfect setting with thousands of stories to be inspired by, but this just did not come together because of repetitive gameplay and poor storytelling. 

#1, The Story: 

You would think Bethesda would learn from previous games that their story telling is a bit weak. Characters are still the same card-board cut outs that lore dump when you talk to them, and they reveal little about their own motivations or interests. It's like reading a novel but every character is either there to move the plot forward or to speak about their time on planet I-don't-care during the alien famine era of -I-really-don't-care, so you just spam click through the monotone dialogue as the NPC's stare through you before assigning a quest to fetch the I-don't-care stone on Mars, which does nothing to change anything for you or Mars..

Honestly, it's been a couple years and I really don't remember the plot. In the first 5 minutes of gameplay, you discover a rock which does some mysterious science stuff or something, and some dude is like, 'Hey I don't know you from a hole in a wall, but here's my ship because I trust you for plot reasons.' This wouldn't be so bad if it weren't for the fact that everything is presented so seriously and cinematic. Anyway, I forgot about the rest of the plot since then. I think you develop super powers like you're space Dragon Born, and you're going to save the universe or something. 

#2, The Gameplay: 

On the surface, it wasn't so bad. I liked the combat of Fallout, and that's mostly what you get. You get lots of guns, and the fun addition of modified gravity. However, melee combat is still overly simplistic, like playing Half-life 2 with a crowbar that has a power attack. Why are we still doing melee this way? 

The skill tree..oh, dear. I don't know what happened here but it feels underwhelming. Leveling up no longer feels interesting. There are few interesting choices here. Nothing that dramatically changes your character to fit any kind of role-playing you might have in mind. 

Exploration is probably the weakest point. It's why we like Bethesda games. You love to find that random dungeon in Skyrim because there's usually something redeeming to make it worthwhile. Unfortunately, exploration falls apart here because Bethesda took the genius idea of using procedural generation and started injecting it throughout the Starfield universe. Unless you're a former crack addict with a poor memory, around hour 10 you will see the same tower of bandits with the same layout, with the same loot, on the same planet only a few feet away from the last tower you cleared. 

To make matters worse, the quests are often classic Bethesda fetch quests, like we're still in 2011. I was on a cyberpunk world on some oil rig turned into a city. I took quests from some corporation, which had me running across numerous loading zones in different buildings, all while providing me with a soulless storyline to accompany. I didn't finish the quest.

I thought they might implement a cool colony feature like Fallout 4, but it ended up being a step backward. It felt mostly cosmetic, and I didn't feel motivated to build on it. This was the most disappointing feature and felt more like a step backward from Fallout 4. 

The ship gameplay is really bad. It's basically an on-rails arcade shooter without any real strategy or tactics needed. Also, every time you send your ship into hyperspace, they show this epic cinematic of your ship blasting into space with this totally epic music, but it gets repetitive after the 300th time and you start looking through menus to toggle skipping it, but then you learn you can't, so you wonder if a developer was speaking to Todd Howard and was like, 'Todd, I don't think the players want to see this every time. Maybe we give them the option to turn this off,' and Todd Howard looked at the developer with demon eyes and didn't say a word because it was probably Todd's terrible idea, so the developer shrunk back into his seat, and that's why you have to experience this every time you go anywhere in the game, ever. 

#3, Sound & Music:

It's good. It's the one redeeming quality that makes you feel like you're in the midst of some epic sci-fi story. The music sounds like some John Williams Star Wars soundtrack. The guns and the atmosphere hit right. However, the voice acting is pretty uninspired. I feel like we're back in Oblivion with the monotone voices again, and it just encourages the player to speed through the lore dumps of planet I-really-don't-care. 


Anyway, that should be enough for a fair warning not to buy this unless you have a fetish for disappointment.

THE ENDING™ [Spoilers ahead....]

[spoiler] Call me a dumb fucking idiot if you want, call me all the names in the world. I'll only cry just a little bit. Because I love the ending of this game that much. Now you might be asking? "Alex? Are you fucking retarded? That's the worst part!" Maybe. But you've read this far, or skipped to the big block of spoilers to spite me for what I said at the start, so at least hear me out. The ending is miserable. It's lonely. It's practically invalidating. And that's why I love it. Choosing to go through The Unity to satisfy Constellation's lust for exploration is ultimately not a good thing to do. You feel it literally the moment you wake up on your Starborn ship. You feel it when you walk back into The Lodge. Fuck man you feel it on the trip there. You sacrificed everything just to see your desire through to the end. And now you have nothing and there's no point to anything. And one thing I'll say for sure is that THIS IS THE INTENDED FEELING. If you want to talk about the gameplay and how as a player it kind of sucks. Go right ahead, that's fine you play games the way you want. OR if you want to complain that the members of Constellation are weirdly pushy about it, and that there's no way to truly end the game, I have literally no defense agaisnt that, because it's stupid and there should definitely be a way to outright refuse The Unity. But I've seen people say that thinking this feeling was intended is reaching for something that's not there. Are you an idiot? The story of The Pilgrim warns you directly about this and not subtly at all. The Hunter is a living warning about where this path will lead you.  It's a huge critique about the idea of the "Frontier" and the overarching desire to have more and more and more. The Pilgrim literally tells you TO YOUR FACE (through a terminal I guess) that the best thing you can do is settle down with your flawed friends, and stare your flawed self in the face, and say "Yeah I'm fine where I am." That's not saying don't have ambition. It's saying having endless ambition is fucking stupid because then it's endless. This ending really reminded me of a time when my dumbass 10 year old self sat down and played Far Cry 3 for the first time. Gameplay and themes combining into one is something that is unique to Video Games. It's what makes them the peak of art forms in my eyes. And this ending does exactly that. When you finally take a moment to go into third person and look at your stupid ass Starborn ship in your stupid ass Starborn armor and you think to yourself: "Damn. I have nothing now. I really wanna reload back to before I used The Unity." Yeah I bet all the Starborn think that at some point. Lest they become exactly like The Hunter. Hell, if you get the alt universe where you run into the other "You?" they basically ask you if you regret using The Unity. It's absolutely intended. Games are allowed to have intentionally disappointing endings, so long as they get their message across. Now, again, if you said that you're upset about it because you grinded your outposts and maxed out your ship and your reward is deleting all that shit from your playthrough, I can't argue against that. That is an example of the gameplay and the story actively fighting each other when you look at it realistically, without your head in the metaphors. And yeah that sucks. Full stop.

To conclude my thoughts, I'll say this. When I was playing through my first NG+ universe, I was listening to Spotify and the song "The Bottomless Hole" by The Handsome Family came on auto play. And that was just damn poetic, man. If you haven't heard it, go listen to it. Even if you don't like folk music you'll get what I'm saying. It perfectly encapsulates the feeling you're rewarded with for your endless ambition and ignoring all the warnings you were given. That being said, it's fucking stupid that there's no option to outright refuse The Unity or get your companions to agree. It's like they are incapable of reading the warnings I was just talking about, and that does create a disconnect from the writers intent. Here's hoping we get that option in a future update or DLC. HOPEFULLY for free. But you know Bethesda. [/spoiler]

[h1] An Ocean of Stars, the Depth of a Puddle. [/h1]

I bought Starfield as soon as it was possible due to the promise of an RPG in a universe with over 1,000 planets to explore. What I got was a bloated, segmented simulator that trades meaningful roleplay for a Galaxy of fast travel and empty space. 

Space travel is reduced to a series of menu interactions and fast travel loading screens. Instead of flying across a seamless galaxy, you select a node, watch a jump cutscene, and land, through another cutscene. 
Once you arrive on a planet, the procedural generation reveals its limits fast. You are left running across miles of barren, low-gravity land toward the exact same recycled base layout you cleared three systems ago, populated by the exact same brain dead enemy AI. 
If you were excited, like me, with a chance of using a vehicle like the REV-8, you will quickly discover how that implementation also fell flat. 
- Zero Traction Physics: Driving feels like navigating on an endless sheet of grease. The vehicles slide uncontrollably, spin out on tiny inclines and bounce erratically off minor terrain features.
In other words, rather than offering a tight, satisfying driving loop, ground vehicles feel artifically slapped onto an engine never meant to handle vehicle physics. You spend more time fighting floaty controls and lack of grip than actually enjoying the ride.

Although I have issues with the shallow systems and dated mechanics like the Outpost Building which feels pointless because the game lacks a compelling economy or survival loop to justify them, or the Inventory Management, which added to the vendor credit limits, make selling your loot an agonizing chore, I want to focus on the RPG illusion and the quest system.

Nowhere is Starfield's identity crisis clearer than in its quest design. Bethesda marketed an RPG where you chart your own path, but in reality, you are an errand boy trapped in on-rails storytelling where your choices rarely matter. 
Take the sidequest "First Contact" as a prime, frustrating example. You discover the ECS Constant, a generation ship of human colonists which finally arrived at their destination, only to find a greedy corporation, the Paradiso Group has turned it into a luxury resort. Well, not really  "it", just a small lake with some cabins and 1 building and almost nothing to interact with. Nevertheless, it is a fantastic premise for an RPG, setting up a classic moral and political conflict. What you really get? A shockingly restrictive quest. 
You cannot use your combat skills to side with the colonists and force the corporate board of the planet. You can't use your background, traits, or high level Persuasion skills to negotiate a fair land sharing agreement. You can't even threaten the greedy CEO. The game forces you to nod along, parrot the demands of the Paradiso executives and act as their unpaid mediator. You aren't playing a character in an interactive world, you are simply carrying out rigid, pre-written scripts steps. 

Final Verdict --> Not recommended

Starfield is not a true RPG, it is an oversized action-shooter wrapped in a space aesthetic. By stripping away player agency, seamless exploration, and meaningful choices, Bethesda delivered a game that is vast in scope, but fundamentally hollow at its core.

Same with buying stuff from the Tracker's alliance vendor.

9. Lots of glitches. I got the moon jumper then had to abandon it because it kept getting stuck under my ship. Couldn't interact with objects multiple times. Got stuck between the shelf and ceiling a few times.

- The mechanics are unbalanced and broken: melee combat is awful (and unarmed combat is beyond pathetic, there aren't even brass knuckles to use as an upgrade), there's very few energy weapons compared to ballistic, and the talent tree is so obtuse and irritating to unlock that many of the top tier abilities take forever to get. For most of the game, you don't feel like you're specializing or doing anything unique. It doesn't matter what weapons or armor you use, what playstyle you want, the game feels basically the same.

- The biggest offender, by far, is the writing. I will say right now that Emil needs to either be fired or reassigned, because his "players are going to ignore the writing anyway, so quality doesn't matter" philosophy is poison, and this game is proof of what happens when your head writer is allowed to have an entire game abide by his "good writing is a waste of time" mindset. The plot holes and contrivances start right from the beginning: you don't get a say in joining the main questline. Every objection you make is countered with "Nah, you don't want to do that, go on and do the other thing", and almost no time was spent thinking through the larger ramifications of how things progress. The writing can be both cartoonishly bad and infuriatingly inflexible, and it's not just the main quest (though since you'll encounter the main quest railroading literally within your first hour, that's pretty egregious). 

The overuse of making some characters unkillable has reached its peak here: rather than deal with player choice, Bethesda just opted for sturdier guardrails. Do you want your fellow gangsters to say "Screw this, we're not making a deal to become cops" on Neon? Too bad, quest over. Do you want to put a bullet in the luxury resort CEO's head and tell the lost colonists you'll help them land wherever they damn well please? Nope, too bad, you're either going to tell them to get fucked or become indentured servants for the rich guy in charge. Do you want to not join Constellation and do your own thing? Nope, you're in Constellation, which just so happens to have no hierarchy, no presence outside one building in one city, no obligations, basically just exists in the most limited sense of the word...and you're a member. Because they gave you a spaceship. Don't like the free ship or do you feel a bit cheated that you don't earn it or get to pick your own? You can't sell it or get rid of it, ever. You don't have an option to tell them "Keep the 'free' ship, I don't want to be a part of your group, and I don't want you holding it over me,", you just always have it parked as a backup, because you're in Constellation now, just because.

The writing affects so much more than this, though, because it bleeds into everything else beyond just choices. Take your Constellation companions: they're all Lawful Good Super Nice Carebears, who get very very mad at you (not that you can tell from their tone of voice, I swear mods that use AI to replace or expand their dialogue actually work because their inflection in the vanilla game is so bland that you can't tell the difference between AI generated voiceovers and the human beings who recorded the source dialogue)....but you're told explicitly that Constellation is first and foremost basically space archaeologists but with flexible morals. They care most of all about finding relics and exploring the unknown, and you're told that your methods ultimately aren't as important as the results. This could have actually worked well and made for some interesting quests and moral quandaries, but instead you just have cookie-cutter goody two-shoes personalities who whine when you actually do anything besides The Right Thing (TM).
 
Emil believes, clearly, that every player is going to skip every line of dialogue to get back to button mashing and looting, like a drug addled spider monkey in withdrawal, and because of that expectation the writing is complete trash, inconsistent, and sometimes outright contradictory or nonsensical.

Grav drives can destroy entire atmospheres? Boy, I guess it's a good thing no terrorists who hate New Atlantis, like say some serpent worshipping extremists, have access to spaceships, or else with a few modifications they could just park some ships near the planet and destroy its atmosphere, too. 

There literally isn't the space to go on.

This game's ideas feel like people just made a list of stuff they wanted to see in the game and then shoved it in there with no thought about if it made sense or how it fit into the world. This is the perfect example of where a writing team would come in handy: they could work on the concepts, the lore and background, and think about how they fit together and why. Instead, we get a game where someone said "Let's put future fast food in there, and space cowboys because I loved Firefly, and of course we need space pirates, also smuggling needs to be a thing because Han Solo is cool, and we gotta have a robot sidekick...", and everything was dutifully shoved in without any thought whatsoever.

Don't buy Starfield. Play something else. Play anything else. Write your own sci-fi and read it to yourself. Anything is a better use of your time and your money.

Also, Bethesda, I am begging you: stop making video games. Please, I'm a huge fan of your properties, and I'm telling you it is clear you guys are much more interested in your engine than making good games, and that's fine. Do what Epic did, switch to making your engine for other companies. License the IPs you own to companies that don't think writing is for losers, and pour your hearts into the engine you love so dearly. 

If Starfield had been a demo template for a new game engine, I'd be impressed with it, and the terrible writing would be excusable as "This isn't a real game, it's a product demo for the engine".  As it is, I'm never buying another of your games again. Congratulations, Bethesda, you're getting the Ubisoft treatment from me.

[h1]This game, maybe more so then any other I know of, is proof to me the value of experiencing for oneself, over reliance on what has become of video game discourse in today's age.[/h1]

This game IS flawed, and it DOES have it’s share of legitimate issues & deficiencies. However, Starfield it is so much more then what the internet would have you believe. It legitimately saddens me how many people will not get to experience what the game DOES bring. 

[hr][/hr]

Yes, it suffers from animations that are this point are an understatement to say are outdated. But it’s also a ridiculously beautiful game that not only had the best fidelity & lighting in their entire portfolio of games (Seriously this game put a major hurting on my screenshots folder lol) but also delivered one of the best executions of that “NASA-Punk” style art direction I’ve seen in a game.

Yes, it’s writing is still very much Bethesda writing, with all the face-palms & inconsistency in quality that has historically come with that. But it’s also a game whose writing did have several really cool bright spots, with in particular it’s UC Vanguard storyline being one of the better storylines they’ve delivered since Oblivion. No, it’s not Morrowind or Oblivion quality writing, but it’s closer to Oblivion then it is to Fallout 4 quality imo.

Yes, it has load screens. Not all buildings have them, but enough certainly do. And yes, it’s a game that suffers from a reliance on procedural planetary surfaces which does deliver a hit to the traditional style of Bethesda “Wander freely” exploration. But it’s also a game whose handcrafted content (Of which there is still TONS, do not be fooled) is some of the best and most interesting environmental/level design work in the company’s history. Paired with a ridiculously fun combat system, (Including FINALLY a stealth system that’s not just “get high enough level that you become undetectable”) that’s the most enjoyable they’ve delivered in their “Gun oriented” franchises? The game is just flat out fun to play and lose yourself into. 

Yes, individually, other games do certain things better. Like NMS’ procedural exploration is more seamless. Elite Dangerous has a more in-depth flight system. Mass Effect has a much better quality story. However no one game quite has the versatility that Starfield does, it’s definitely a “Jack of all trades” ordeal, even if it doesn’t master them all of them. If you want a full fledged RPG with a character builder, variety of factions and hundreds of storylines? It’s here. If you want a super in-depth ship building and customization system to let creative juices flow? It’s here. You wanna ignore story and just go out and survey planets, scanning lifeforms and biomes? It’s here. You wanna start a mining and manufacturing operation, mining asteroids, colonizing planets and setting up factories and trade-links? It’s here. You wanna be pirate/outlaw, preying on trade ships and innocents? It’s here. Wanna be a Mandalorian style Bounty Hunter? It’s here. You wanna get into ground fights, ship fights, hell even disable enemy engines, board a ship to turn a ship fight a ground fight? It’s here. All under one roof. It really does feel like multiple games in one. For those who are only interested in one specific style or aspect out of a space game, sure that could be a weakness. 

But if you’re looking for a space setting that allows you to pursue a variety of space-related gameplay types? It’s a very short list of games that competes with the versatility of what Starfield allows you to do in one game.

[hr][/hr]

A couple other things I’d like to point out:

1) Performance was kind of shocking for a BGS game. By far, the least buggy Bethesda game I’ve ever played, with zero game breaking bugs, zero obstructive glitches, and a grand total of 3 crashes in 350+ hours of my playthrough (Admittedly 1 of these was due a mod.) It also ran at rock solid FPS at High/Ultra settings on a good but not crazy PC build (Specs should be attached).

2) The Ship-Builder system is OUTSTANDING. Piecing custom ships from scratch, piece by piece, shaping and molding it however you see fit, selectively tailoring components and then being able to fully decorate, highly customizable (and functional!) interiors is a creative players dream. Intuitive system too, that feels easy to grasp right from the jump. I've had so much fun designing ships in this game. It’s kind of a game in it’s own. Outpost Building however, while a thing in this game, felt like a step down from F04, with reduced mechanics and a building system that felt more clunky and a PITA to use. 

3) The Expansions/DLC are a mixed bag. Shattered Space is a return to their more usual approach, with the expansion taking place on a single planet, and exploration you can freely walk to and from, but it also focuses heavily on a super strict religious cult of a culture which can feel suffocating depending on your character. Terran Armada is to be blunt, short and weak. Free-Lanes update however was transformative for its positive impact on Seamless Inter-System Space Exploration & emergent gameplay moments and the game benefits massively for it. (Free-Lanes is also FREE).

4) Every BGS fan has been (or should be) aware of the gradual downward trend of RPG aspects in their games with seemingly each entry getting more and more watered down. Starfield thankfully was finally a step back in the right direction, and an improvement over their last couple games instead of another regression. Skill-Checks in dialogue made their much welcomed returned finally, as did the return of things like origin backgrounds, character traits/flaws and the game had a nice thick skill tree to dive into, with a wide variety of both combat, and non-combat skills. Don’t get it twisted, we’re nowhere near back to Morrowind/FONV/FO3 levels yet, but it’s encouraging to see them finally at least trend upwards on this again rather then ever downward like it had been. Hoping they carry that momentum to even more RPG improvements for TES6.

[hr][/hr]

[b]TLDR: Don’t get tricked by the click & headline obsessed frenzy of modern gaming media. Game isn’t perfect, and does play a bit differently then traditional BGS games, but is still a good game with a lot to offer. 

8/10, would 100% recommend for any Space Game fans or BGS fans.[/b]

Starfield is one of those games I will defend despite fully understanding why some people criticize it.

I know the reviews are mixed. I know people have criticized the exploration, loading screens, repetitive locations, technical issues and plenty of other aspects of the game. And no, I’m not going to pretend Starfield is perfect.

But I love it anyway.

There is something about its vision of space exploration that simply works for me. Building your own ship, modifying individual modules, improving its weapons and systems, hiring a crew and eventually flying something that genuinely feels like your ship is one of my favorite parts of the entire experience.

Then you have the exploration itself — jumping between star systems, landing on distant worlds, building outposts, searching abandoned facilities, encountering strange locations and simply wondering what might be waiting on the next planet.

I also really enjoy the bigger science-fiction ideas behind the story. The Unity, the Starborn and the possibility of alternate universes take what initially looks like a relatively grounded space RPG and gradually turn it into something much stranger and more philosophical.

Starfield wasn’t the first game to explore multiverses or interstellar travel, but it was Bethesda Game Studios’ first completely new universe in more than 25 years, and I think that ambition deserves some recognition.

Of course, this is still Bethesda.

There are bugs. There are glitches. Sometimes something behaves in a way that makes you stare at the screen and think, “Yep… Bethesda.” 😄

At this point, though, that almost feels like part of the package. I’m not saying those problems should be ignored, but after years of playing Bethesda games, very little of it surprises me anymore.

What matters more to me is that underneath those imperfections there is a huge science-fiction RPG with a world I genuinely enjoy spending time in.

And ship building alone can consume an absurd amount of my time. There’s something incredibly satisfying about starting with an ordinary vessel and gradually transforming it into a massive customized machine designed exactly the way you want it.

Are there better space games today in certain individual areas? Absolutely. Some games have deeper simulation, others have more seamless exploration, and others may offer stronger technical execution.

But Starfield has its own identity.

For me, it already has that distinctive Bethesda feeling — a massive world full of quests, stories, strange discoveries and moments where you completely forget what you originally planned to do three hours earlier.

It may not be perfect, but I wouldn’t trade my experience with Starfield for the opinions of people who hated it.

I had a great time with it, I love its universe, I love building ships, and I genuinely enjoyed its story.

For me, Starfield is absolutely worth playing.

Bugs, glitches and all.

The stars are calling.

I don't think anyone is reading my 3-year old review for a game as widely criticized as this so I'm not going to bother making this too comprehensive, so I'll try to keep this just to aspects or points that I haven't seen overly discussed by dozens of YouTube video essays.

Starfield will always have its detractors and it will always have its defenders, but after 180 hours I still find myself somewhat in the middle. Ultimately, I'm recommending it because I think that it deserves a closer look, even if it is still not going to be the game for many people.

Let's start first with the positive. I am someone who greatly appreciates Starfield's aesthetic and setting because I think soft sci-fi is much more prevalent in this medium than hard(ish) sci-fi and particularly the close association with NASA both visually and in the lore just hits me right. I'm an aerospace engineer myself and my most recent playthrough was right after Artemis II. I like that Starfield present a universe in a liminal space: expelled from the Earth we know and love, but not having reached the future peak of a sprawling galactic civilization.

Second, the fact that we get so few open-world sandbox RPGs where you can create your own character means that I will always have a particular affinity for Bethesda games. Look more closely at that description and think about it and think about what types of games we usually get. 

The Witcher III - open world? check. RPG? double check. sandbox? nope. create your own character? nope

RDR2 - open world? check. RPG? nope. sandbox? yep! create your own character? nope.

KCD2 - open world? check. RPG? definitely. sandbox? of course! create your own character? no again.

BG3 - open world? nope. RPG? one of the best. sandbox? not really. create your own character? yes, finally!

I love all those games above, but this particular formula just hits for me. I love having a premade character like Henry, Geralt, or Arthur because you can get a create narrative, but I really enjoy making my own backstory and roleplaying my own character as well. I get very few games that let me do that.

The third positive thing I want to say: the mod scene is pretty decent. I was able to turn the game into something more akin to what I wanted with mods. Personally, I wanted a more hardcore space survival game where planets were truly hostile environments that required preparation to explore. I was able to achieve a pretty decent experience using mods like Deadly Hazards and TN's Realistic Oxygen meter.

But let's talk about some negatives before I abruptly wrap this up. First, I haven't heard anyone criticize the class fantasy in this game and it's actually one of my biggest gripes. When I look at the skill tree in this game, I just struggle to see or imagine different compelling characters to make out of it. In Skyrim you had such distinct class opportunities: mage is different from thief is different from warrior and everything in between. They look different, play different, and feel different. I just felt like everything in Starfield boiled down to "astronaut with a gun". For example, you can spec into the tech skill tree but the game never lets you become some master engineer building robot armies and decking himself out with advanced exoskeletons (things that are feasible in the lore!). The biggest class fantasies they tried to make this game are space pirate, space cowboy, space soldier, and space explorer and none of them really play or feel too different honestly.

My other criticism related to that is that the game seems absolutely terrified of actually requiring you to invest in any particular skill. This has been an issue with all modern Bethesda games (it's the "I became the Archmage of the College of Winterhold without knowing any magic" thing), but here it's even more egregious because they actually have skill-based dialogue options! The best example of this is that there's a quest where you have to help design a spaceship for a company, but the game doesn't actually have you use the entire shipbuilding system to do that! So you literally just "design" a spaceship with a few dialogue options instead of using this incredibly fun system they built. It's similar with other major systems in the game. For example the game never really asks you to use outpost building to solve a problem with a quest or use your chef skill to make somebody a meal or anything like that. It just makes the RPG experience feel very flat compared to other games like Baldur's Gate III, where your character's stats and skills actually factor into how you solve quests. The most they could muster here is that sometimes you can talk your way out of problems.

Of course I could write about how the procedurally generated planets killed exploration and how quests lean way too heavily into fast traveling between NPCs, who for some reason don't have text or email in this universe, but those have all been discussed to death. At the end of the day I recommend buying this game if you like the aesthetic and worldbuilding, if you like sandbox RPGs and are willing to try to create your own adventure, and if you're willing to mess around with mods to fix some of the biggest gameplay issues.

I can understand why people love Starfield. If exploring space, building ships, and landing on distant planets is the main attraction, there’s a lot here.

My issue isn’t that I expected Mass Effect. I just don’t think Bethesda’s formula works as well when stretched across a huge galaxy.

Bethesda is at its best in dense, localized worlds. In Skyrim or Fallout, you head toward one objective and constantly get distracted by caves, ruins, quests, NPCs, and environmental storytelling along the way.

Starfield replaces that density with scale.

There’s technically much more to explore, but I feel less compelled to explore it. Too much of the experience becomes selecting a destination, landing, and running across relatively empty terrain toward a marker.

That’s the contradiction for me: Starfield is bigger than Bethesda’s previous games, but it often feels less alive.

Mass Effect is still the peak of space RPGs for me, and even The Outer Worlds keeps me more consistently entertained despite being much smaller.

I think Starfield would have benefited from fewer planets, fewer systems, and much more handcrafted density.

Bethesda didn’t need to make a better Mass Effect.

It needed to make a smaller Bethesda game in space.

It looks like they've tried to include here (almost) everything, but didn't have time/skills/money to bring even one of these systems to a decent level.

It is like they've tried to make a game that caters to: 
- RPG fans (but there is not much 'role playing' here' most of the time the choice is between "talk your way out" or just kill enemies), 
- action fans (but shooting is relatively stiff and there is not that much of it and the whole Borderlands inspired qualities of weapons and randomised stats does not really fit in this game),
- space sims fans (but there seems to be not much simulation going on here, everything seems to be set in stone, no dynamic market prices or territories exchanging hands),
- spacefaring fans (but ship seems to be really marginal here, it is mostly used to get from point A to B, with very little short dogfight segments)

My two cents about this game because I keep being reminded about it. My biggest issues come from the quest & world design. Why is the main hub of a major faction slapdashed together with unpaved roads and uncertain defenses? Why am I admonished for taking bad guy actions to infiltrate the bad guys in an off the books plausible deniability operation when it makes every bit of sense that they're watching my every move at that point? Why are you risking my cover frequently by requiring so many in-person debriefs at your dang flagship? Why is the entire "a murder hobo would love it here" questline the one that most discourages killing/going loud? Why does someone try to smugly meet a known killer(who's in full kit, from a faction of criminals of various stability, and may already have a bounty for killing people) alone to try to strongarm them into giving info? Can you tell what questline was my final straw?
The questions just never stop..
OH! Then there's the stuff that's been talked about to death. The ship designer is extremely limited without even being able to choose where doors/ladders spawn. Exploration feels alright until you do more than exploring around hubs you may happen across through quests, after that it's just rock after rock. Combat's OKAY, but at times enemies turn into sponges.. Only plus to this game(like any Bethesda game) is there being a lot of STUFF, but so much of that stuff is repetitive or poorly thought out.

The gripes about this game seem mostly overrated, IMHO. The game is janky- just as much so as every other Bethesda game is (and I even found some of them kind of enduring... yes, friend, DO keep walking away from me in our conversation or walk into a walk. You live your best life.). The writing is, for the most part, serviceable; I found the setting interesting enough to try to do a lore dive, so far as I could. The primary companions feel pretty developed, if at times a little flat, and I appreciated that even the secondary companions (beyond the big four) all seemed to have some personality and backstory to them. The plot didn't feel any less developed than the main Skyrim quest line, though I wish that there were more faction side quests.

Combat felt satisfying, especially when I found the guns of my dreams. Space combat was not quite what I was expecting in terms of control, but when I got used to it it felt pretty natural.

Perhaps the biggest gripe I have mechanics wise is towards the end of a playthrough: I find trying to uncover the last few temples tedious, especially since you have to wait until you are referred to one, and the internet seems to agree that any given playthrough won't have all of the temples. If they're going to do that, I'd really rather that they just dumped all remaining temple locations on you once you got to One Giant Leap, rather than having to wander systems or wait for Constellation to tell you where to go.

Overall, a solidly enjoyable Bethesda game.

I actually enjoyed this game. I'm talking about the base game. I hadn't replayed it for the DLC's yet and obviously the reviews are very mixed on those too. 

Just because I enjoyed this game, doesn't mean I disagree or invalidate the negative reviews of this game. 

Conceptually, the story is actually the thing that I enjoyed most about this game because of how niche it is. A little off-topic, but I enjoy Rick and Morty and the first season of Altered Carbon for the same reasons I enjoy this game. They involve sci-fi concepts that I could only wish were real-life. Those concepts being an either/or or a mix of:
1. Infinite universes (very dumbed down in this game and you'll know what I mean if you've beaten the game)
2. Exploring or even just simply knowing that different complex civilizations exists beyond Earth
3. A mix of Firefly and Cyber-punk aesthetics on some of the hand-crafted areas
4. A story that really captivates the idea of the unknown. What *did* you actually find out there? What does it actually do?

Before I go into spoilers, here are some things that I think are worth noting for those who just care about gameplay. These aren't listed as either pros or cons, just info for you to decide. 

- The gunplay in this game is an improvement from the Fallout franchise in my opinion. Guns also seem more entertaining to use and there's a decent variety of them. However, at the same time, since this is a sci-fi game, I do wish there were more variety in the way of laser/energy based weapons. 

-  The shipbuilding mechanic is a great addition and it's nice building your space-home how you want. My biggest gripe is that you can't build capital ships though they exist in the game and are seeming invincible and act as just placeholder locations to go to and from. It's definitely not on No Man's Sky levels. However, you can build a decently sized corvette style ship, or stick with a cozy small-crew ship. 

-  The characters are okay...I didn't really grow attached to any singular character and none of them really captured my eyes. Except my own character, who I named Starlord and gave him this 80's era hair-do unintentionally. Maybe that's why I enjoyed this game so much. Made it look like this was happening during the 80's? 

- Exploration is only really fun when you go to special area, or you go back to the Earth or Moon to look for landmarks. Other than that, it's an ocean wide, but a puddle deep. I think this is where Bethesda skimped out the most on maybe in an effort to launch the game on time. This was an ambitious IP that they should have tried to do maybe 5 years from now. 

- Quests. Again, the main quest I enjoyed, and there are some really cool side-quests in this game. I don't know what all I've done or hadn't done but there was a main quest mission where you have to go to this distressed colony and you know you're hunting a thought-extinct alien creature. That whole mission was done well even though it's very much pre-determined how it's going to go. Reminded me of Pitch Black mixed with Deadspace. 

- Lastly, that's the last thing I'll leave with. There's numerous nods or apparent nods to other sci-fi games or films that paved the way for this game. However, this game didn't have the right vehicle for pavement. Like, it was supposed to be a boat, but instead it's just trying to go on land with mechanical legs instead of wheels. Essentially, the giants propped this game on its shoulders but it didn't know how to follow in their footsteps.

What if in real-life you got to go back and re-do it knowing people and who they were before you met them, having a chance to do things differently again? That's why I enjoyed this game.

It's been 3 years, and Starfield is still a game full of nothing — that's it. There are apparently a thousand planets (IDK, never counted), and probably 85-90% of them have nothing actually there; the structures and dungeons are copy-pasted RNG. This game would have been better off with just a solar system or two packed full of content. Yes, that's the problem — the game is so vast that I don't even know what I'm doing?!?! Also, get used to loading screens along the way... Want to fast travel to a trade hub that's in another solar system? LOL! Select the solar system, plus the planet with the trader, [Loading...], wait for the contraband scan, select the trade area on the planet again, [Loading...], get out of the ship [a little bit more of [LOADING...]]!!! Oh no, the trade hub is in a separate segment of the city... time for more loading!!!!

Now for the real problem, the one that compounds all the other problems (and positives) about the game: there is stuff on these planets, but it's a copy-paste RNG dungeon system. It's the same stuff over and over and over and over... very little of the game has "unique" dungeons or places, unlike past Bethesda titles. I've tried playing this game three times now, because I thought maybe it would be fixed or improved, but no, it never was, and I just can't get myself to play this game for a long period of time. In my most recent attempt, I tried using a guide to only pursue the unique places, and even then I thought to myself: really?! I'm using a guide to help me play an open-world Bethesda game? The next journey should just be right around the corner, but no. Bethesda took the best aspect of their games and bastardized it with this one.
 
Then there's the UI and menus, almost just as atrocious as the loading screens. 

Then there's the whole question of why I'm even playing any aspect of this game. The research, skill system, and outpost building were all designed to be as tedious and annoyingly grindy as possible to distract you from the fact that the game is empty. Which is why I finally threw in the towel, why am I grinding skills to improve outposts so I can obtain resources for better gear and outposts, if the whole game is just empty RNG dungeons and locations in the first place? It feels like I'm playing a dried-out shell of a Bethesda game, where all the grind and gameplay mechanics have no meaningful purpose or end to them, unlike the other games, where they did.
Anyway...
If copy-pasted dungeons give you an adequate dopamine release then Starfield is for you, but if you're like me... you enjoy novel dungeons or places to explore, ones that could be right around the corner after fighting tooth and nail through the previous dungeon you just conquered and looted. I guess we must wait for ES6, or go back to the previous titles.

Man, Bethesda, this one rides the line between good and bad.  Enjoying myself so I'm leaning towards recommending, but not without some reservation/pontification about what could've been.  There are parts about this game that really scratch the "Bethesda Game" itch, so if you enjoy the exploration, looting, and combat aspects of Skyrim or Fallout, you'll probably enjoy this, too.  After about 50 hours, the veneer has cracked a bit, though.  Lots of weird glitches--people you can't talk to because they're "crip walking", enemies spawning inside walls in my ship so I can't fast travel, crew inside of my ship that won't GTFO the way, etc.  On top of that, a lot of the "rinse and repeat" quests like bounties lead you to, maybe, a new planet, but your target is probably in 1 of 5 or 6 building layouts you've already done.  I get there's an upper limit here, but it'd be nice if it were higher for repeatability.  Surveying is tedious in some cases, even with skills to help.  Outpost building is something I loathed in Fallout 4, and though I know it's a fan favorite, I wish it was nixed in favor of fleshing out some of the other "core" gameplay in earlier Fallout games like FO3 or NV--lusher, unique storylines; exposition where I experience it from finding clues rather than some clanker-looking dude ripping an unimpassioned monologue.  I will say I've done a LOT of sidequesting and not main questing, so maybe the main story is more enthralling and unique, but it feels a bit weird to already be seeing repeat stuff ~40 hours in.

Based on all that, sounds like I don't like the game, but harping on what I think could be improved.  Crafting, flying around, general exploration, some of the unique missions I've done so far that are more story-driven, skill diversity, and combat all feel great and pretty immersive.  I guess I just feel like there was some scope-creep to include too much that everything feels a bit sparse and repetitive rather than unique and expository--but not so much that you can't enjoy it for awhile.  Grab this on a 20% off sale and let her rip.

I really wanted to enjoy this game. I probably enjoy Bethesda titles more than the average gamer, 1000's of hours spent in elder scrolls and fallout. Skyrim in space! A recipe that can't miss right?

It misses. The game has several, fundamental issues which I'm skeptical that even the modding community can fix. Let's touch on some without getting into spoilers:

Fundamentally the game lacks depth in nearly every aspect where it feels like there should be more. Want to do base building? Enjoy the selection of buildings that's smaller than fallout 4's. Want to be a space pirate? Enjoy the 3 different repeatable missions. Want to do planet exploration? You'll get the full experience after fully surveying a single planet. Want to do faction-esque quests and get stuck into the world of Starfield? The quest lines are shorter than Skyrim's. Everything falls short.

Also, and this is bigger than it seems at first, travelling in general is just... awkward? Everything tends to be kind of far for walking on planets, so you're pressured to fast travel when you can. If you hoof it then you're hit with extended periods of just uneventful jogging. If you fast travel, you're constantly bumping into loading screens and/or menus. Jumping between star systems, for example, means charting the course and hitting a loading screen. But if you go half-meaningful distances then you need to do multiple jumps because your ship can't go far enough at once and you arbitrarily have to do multiple jumps from system to system which feels really tedious. The moment-to-moment getting around is just not good and it wears on you over time.

Specific to planet-side stuff, getting through towns is nearly as awkward as it's been in all of the previous titles. Most buildings, even basic shops, still have you running up to the location, clicking on the door, waiting for the loading screen, and then going about your business. In the year of our lord 2026 you would think Bethesda would have worked out a more elegant solution here. Hell, even open marketplaces with vendors just standing in the overworld would have been less clunky than this.

Then you have the overworld POI's... which are mostly nothing. You land in a new area, look around at things you can check out, and see POI's like you'd see in Elder Scrolls/Fallout. You wander over there, which mind you takes a long time, and arrive to find one of a few things: 1) a one-time discovered feature that just gives you XP for walking up to it 2) someone's spaceship where there's nothing for you to do 3) one of a handful of procedurally generated dungeon-style POI's 4) an underwhelming cave. That's pretty much it. The unique, hand-crafted POI's that you used to just stumble upon in previous Bethesda games simply don't exist. After doing the above several times, you'll likely find that they simply don't keep your interest when they lack true depth and variety.

And it's not subjective, the main questline really just blows. At this point I think even the most die hard Bethesda game enjoyers (like myself) have figured out Bethesda does world-building, not individual character writing. But somehow the main questline doesn't even deliver on making the Starfield universe interesting. Plus, the main quest makes you repeatedly do the same, ridiculous "mini-game" that gets old after the first time... and you're just supposed to keep doing it over and over. Nah.

There are things to enjoy about this game, but the reviews are mixed because Starfield itself is mixed. I really enjoyed the shipbuilding, but even that has issues. I enjoyed the new lockpicking mini-game more than the old Bethesda staple, but that's not a game in itself. I have fun shooting the bad guys... when their AI doesn't break and they turn into target dummies. You can certainly have some fun with Starfield but do not expect another Skyrim or Fallout here. Instead, prepare for some extremely basic offerings of a Bethesda title riddled with design issues, bugs, and questionable direction.

I really enjoyed Starfield as an open 'world' SF RPG with loads of quests, fun combat, and interesting mechanics.

I'm at just under 400 hours and have complete the DLCs as well as the main questline, but without a 1st trip through the U. At about 380 hours I installed my first 'creation' so there is a ton of content.

The assortment of side quests and interesting dialog, especially from you companions, was great fun. The RPG staples of skill tree development, loot, and story-driven reasons to do just about anything were all present and well done. Some of the 'side quests' are quite deep and involved--almost whole games.

The setting is refreshingly sci fi. I'm tired of fantasy since it's everyone from everyone and while I enjoyed the first few modern Fallout games, I've gotten tired of those. But not Starfield--so far...maybe never because there are some great 'creations' (mods) available and intentionally supported. Some add small things, other creations are game overhauls. I like that there is a compensation system in place for modders! My favorite games are often heavily modded in the end, giving me great value; so it's good to see some systematic compensation.

Disabling achievements for creations/mods is an unnecessary disappointment and own-goal reported by many.

The UI design is console-optimized and thus can be very dissatisfying on PC. Especially inventory or any table/list--everything you expect to be there is not because of some lowest-common-denominator focus on console controllers. Luckily there is a great Praxis mod that 100% fixes the poor console-focus/Xbucks controller UIs really well; I would pay for that but it was free.

Graphics are appropriate for the game although the worlds are often more empty than they should be. Important not to use the 'realism' excuse in making an SF game like this. As per Gabe Newell: "I have never thought to myself that realism is fun", a relevant reminder to devs.

Audio is good, although I near mute music in most games so can't speak to more than vocals and effects.

There is ship building and outpost building if you like that kind of activity. If you don't, it's effectively optional and non-blocking if you want to avoid it. There are ships for in-game purchase if you don't want to play [much] with the builder.

The difficulty settings are really well done. You trade off easier settings with reduced XP. It's pretty great, allowing you to jack up enemy damage and sponginess while getting some extra carrying capacity. And even with normal player damage and max enemy toughness, a mediocre player can survive most of the time especially if they plan, sneak, play ghost recon in space, use starpowers. There is an unbalanced fight in one of the DLCs where you can't do much of this, but that's it.

After hearing thousands of bad reviews about this game, reading thousands and thousands of negative words about Starfield, I still felt that despite all that, I could one day play this game and really love it. 
Somehow, that did happen and I felt the need to write this positive review as a counter action to all the unjustified hate this game seems to get, which I honestly don't understand.  
Before I get started on the actual review, I must say that I don't write reviews of games, so keep that in mind as you read this one, if it interests you. 

First and foremost, as a really important disclosure I must say that I play with a point of view of a person who actually studied a whole course of aerospace engineering, contrary to most people who might give this game a try and this is not an attempt to mock anyone, you'll see why as we go.

[Space realism]: 
I start here to connect with the previous paragraph and say that despite people not enjoying barren worlds with nothing to do/nothing in them, I need to tell people this: If people could actually travel through space, barren planets is what you'd find 99% of the time. Moreover if people could travel through space, the spaceships would end up looking a lot like these in most cases. Alien life even though possible would be weird, but mostly non intelligent 99% of time. You'd probably find aliens, which already has an insanely low chance of happening, but not necessarily intelligent. 
I encourage people to actually try to understand the concept of probabilities because this game tries, for better or worse, to give the player a compromise between the insane and harsh reality of life in space and still keep it a game with more possibilities than reality actually would offer.

[Old Bethesda feeling]: 
I need to acknowledge that, when I first started playing starfield, I struggled a lot to get hooked into it because I wasn't feeling that old pull you'd get when playing certain questlines in older games and here I give the example of skyrim dungeons. 
Yesterday was when it hit me this was the spark that made me want to write this review: When I was doing a simple side quest not even related to any faction or main quest, I found myself playing my beloved skyrim dungeon in a sense, but in a completely different setting, which never gave me any itch. So for people saying this game does not give a usual bethesda fan (older single player games) that feeling of a good quest inside a dungeon, I tell you; You're wrong. It retains that value.

Before going into the last good part of the review I will tell you about the only 'bad' part of the game, which is not even that relevant to me: I don't like this old style of character portrayal during dialogue (The issue is not the voice actors. I actually mean the movement of npcs while in dialogue). Similarly to what people say everywhere, the characters stare a lot at the main character while in dialogue with them, and I really don't like that. Nevertheless I don't weight this high enough to make it change my opinion that this game is awesome.

[Performance]
(I just remembered now that loading screens? If you really know how to make the most of your pc and I shared my specs you'll find that the vast majority of the loading screens won't take even 5 seconds, but that may be important to other people. For me it makes it so that the loading screens aren't even there).

[Replayability/Where it really shines]
The final reason for me to write this good review was something I didn't even consider when I started playing and almost no other rpg does as correctly as this one:
According to public data without any spoilers, when a player gets into ng+ the next playthrough will actually, but ACTUALLY, feel like a new experience and without trying to spoil it I encourage everyone to make a web search about this game's ng+ features because once one realizes what they're trying to do, you'll think that it is an insanely awesome idea.

So this was my honest review of Starfield, a game so miscomprehended by most, but after trying it I can't deny the feeling that it's still in the top notch levels of quality in a video game including non bethesda games. From 1 to 10 I'd give this one a 9, even if it's not a solid 9.

Thank you very much whoever makes it this far into the review because, again, I don't write these for no reason.

Very few games walk the thin line Starfield does. It does many things; space combat sim, outpost building, babysitting companions, part walking sim, lite-roleplay/rpg, illusion of choice (with a few surprises).

Anyone who has played this game for a while knows all is not perfect. But, this game blends many niche games styles into a package that isn't found elsewhere.

This game will naturally attract many comparisons to titles such as No Man's Sky, Skyrim, X4: Foundations and Elite Dangerous. I even see some Starsector and Starcom and such indie titles in Starfield. 

While No Man's Sky has a similar idea, with many planets to explore and visit. The type of gameplay, design and style really is quite far apart compared to the other games I mentioned. Some have called this Skyrim in Space; and while I can see the relation with the powers and the dragon shouts, Skyrim plays in a significantly different fashion. While Skyrim is more of an exploration/questing game, Starfield tackles the sandbox like X4, Elite Dangerous, Starsector do, but it does so while infusing its Bethesda roots (à la Daggerfall).

X4 has the economy/trading as it's main strength, Elite Dangerous has the sandbox flight sim depth, Starsector does the fleet management... so, where does Starfield sit within these space games?

It lacks the economy X4 does, but has some outpost building and very light factorio-styled building chain. While it lacks the more complex and in-depth flight mechanics of Elite Dangerous, Starfield has fully modular ships you can build from scratch, and also lets you walk in your own ships (like X4). Starsector offers a top-down retro-inspired fleet command and strategy. While Starfield lacks the fleet/wing management, it has your companions that can make your ship feel a little less lonely. Not only that, but while Officers in Starsector offer strong bonuses to the ships they command, your companions in Starfield offer up important and very useful bonuses to your ships capabilities.

So, it's a little bit of everything; while some other games push the envelope in a certain aspect (flight model, economy, trade, fleet management), Starfield takes a little bit of all those ideas and forms it into a package that also has a strong storyline and lots of very fun main side quests.

What more, Starfield does it in its very unique style that really stands out. While X4 and Elite Dangerous went the way of a sleek high-tech holographic-like future, Starfield went for its own unique look; [b]NASA-Punk[/b]. 
It's a fitting term that was coined because of Starfield. 

Everything in Starfield feels a little more grounded in a believable near future. Cockpits and bridges that still use lots of mechanical doors & latches. Buttons, knobs and switches that are 'tacticle' and 'clicky'. The use of actual material that space agencies use to line their rockets, stations and ships; from heat conservations, to padding, to exterior paneling. Bethesda has really done its research and manage to create an atmosphere that feels so grounded and not that far away. 

They didn't stop there either; they even have us relying on Helium-3, and discover other elements that are theorized to be similar to those we would eventually find if we manage to explore the galaxy. Geology AND astronomy with the table of elements to boot. It approaches these things with a touch of theory-based science, like Star Trek does.


While other games are more hardcore; they are for those who really like the aspect of economy, trade and management, or the aspects of deep flight simulation mechanics... very few games have made me dream as much as Starfield has. This is on the level of Star Trek when I was a kid. No other game has ever tied so well to my casual passion for astronomy, observing the night sky and our moon. I sometimes land on a planet simply to see if I can get a good view of the sunset/sunrise, moonset/moonrise, or landing on a moon to see the awe-inspiring gas giant, or Saturn-like planet look like a giant I can touch. 


While Starfield is far from perfect, unlike many games that can feel too hardcore, or sterile at times, Starfield feels lived-in. It feels like I'm playing out my own Firefly mini-series; a small crew of people with different backgrounds, ways of going about things, in a ship that is constantly being tweaked, changed and cared for. 

Starfield may not be a very hardcore game; but for someone like me, who plays games to relax and for escapism, Starfield hits just right! It hits the right buttons for the look I want; [u]it provides me with enough "space" stuff to make me dream and actually motivates my casual passion for astronomy and promotes my learning of it/[/u]. [b]For that fact alone, Starfield is an incredible game![/b]


But, a sandbox is just a sandbox. The reason I've had more trouble getting into games like X4 or Elite Dangerous, are because I like stories. I like movies, series, books; I enjoy playing walking simulators for their ultimate focus on story and nothing else. In all the games I've talked about in my commentary, Starfield is the only one to provide me with a storyline to follow, that I actually find interesting. I very much enjoy EVERY companion here. They all have their own style, their own approach and way of talking to you. 

There is a moment in the game where you [spoiler]lose a companion. It actually made me feel something I've never felt in any Bethesda game; there was a loss of someone on my crew, that I had grown to appreciate the banter when I walked by them. It felt like how you may have a person you see everyday at work and you exchange boring pleasantries, daily. Is it important? No. But, yes it is. The day that person stops being there, you feel that loss.[/spoiler] Something has changed.


Starfield ties this whole sandbox thing into what I call a "cohesive package". While it can be criticized for loading screens; how many games offer you the unique physics Bethesda give us? You can put items on your ship, to decorate, collect and just for fun. You can blow everything away when boarding a pirate ship. The game will remember (for the most part) where everything fell, the rotation it fell on, the height, the facing... you can exit that ship, and go back onto it, and things don't reset to where they were. You can walk into a vendor and throw all his stuff around in a fit of rage, and funny-enough, you will be reminded of your loss of control the next time you visit them.

We take it for granted, but the way items and objects react to our presence and actions are a big part of why Bethesda games can feel so immersive. The world around us, even as benign as a sandwich, will react to our actions and save that into memory the entire game. 


It is so easy to take any part of Starfield and ridicule it for how janky, unpolished or funny it may seem. But, very few games offer the player agency we are offered here, in a setting that is frankly very niche to start with. Starfield is NOT what Skyrim was, and never will be. The setting alone, the way they approached realism and space travel, means Starfield will never be a game that attracts a mass audience. Some will come and go, but those who are here to stay, stay because Starfield hits many different aspects of some hardcore games, but make it very accessible and respects your time in the process.

Starfield walks a very fine line, one that is alienating to those who expected something similar to previous Bethesda games, but one that is welcome within a genre of games that has often been reserved for the very hardcore players.


In conclusion;
[h3]Starfield, with its incredible level of detail in ship interior habs, cockpits and use of science-based (theoretical and real) technology and knowledge, with its freedom to build ships, outposts and supply-lines, offers a storied sandbox experience that makes me feel like I am living my own Firefly series. 
[b]It's an easy two thumbs up for me[/b].[/h3]
