Starfield is a massive space RPG with an incredible amount of content to explore. From flying through space and discovering new planets to completing quests, upgrading your character, and building your own ships, there’s always something else to do.

🎮 Gameplay — 9/10
A great mix of exploration, combat, quests, crafting, and RPG progression. There’s a lot of freedom in how you want to play.

🎨 Graphics — 9.5/10
The environments, planets, cities, ships, and character models can look absolutely stunning. The scale of the universe is impressive, especially when exploring new locations.

🚀 Space Exploration — 9/10
Exploring different planets and systems is a huge part of the experience. Finding new locations and discovering what’s waiting for you never gets old.

🔫 Combat — 8.5/10
Gunplay feels solid and there are plenty of weapons to experiment with. Different builds and abilities give you a good amount of freedom in combat.

🌌 Universe — 10/10
The sheer amount of content is crazy. There are countless planets, locations, factions, quests, characters, and things to discover.

🛸 Ship Building — 10/10
One of my favorite features. Being able to customize and build your own ship is incredibly fun, and spending way too much time designing the perfect ship is surprisingly easy.

🧑‍🚀 Character Progression — 9/10
Lots of skills and upgrades to unlock, allowing you to create different types of characters and playstyles.

🔊 Audio — 9/10
The soundtrack and environmental audio do a great job of creating that feeling of being out in space. Weapon and ship sounds also add a lot to the atmosphere.

⚙️ Performance — 8.5/10
Performance can vary depending on your hardware and location, but with the right settings it can run well and still look fantastic.

♻️ Replayability — 10/10
There is an enormous amount of content to go through. Different builds, quests, factions, exploration, ship building, and side activities give you plenty of reasons to keep playing.

🏆 Overall — 9.5/10
Starfield is a massive RPG with an incredible amount of freedom and content. It isn't perfect, but the scale, exploration, ship customization, and sheer amount of things to do make it a game I can easily sink hundreds of hours into.

Would recommend — especially if you love space, RPGs, exploration, and games where you can just get lost for hours. 🚀🌌🔥

[h1]Starfield Review[/h1]

[hr]
[h1]Overview[/h1]
I have never been a massive Bethesda fan. I like their games, but sometimes it feels like they expect the Bethesda formula to carry a game simply because it worked so well before.

I bought Starfield when it released in 2023 and barely stuck with it. Coming back in 2026 and playing it properly from start to finish, including both DLCs and every achievement, was a completely different experience.

The easiest way I can describe Starfield is Skyrim in space. It is huge, full of quests, factions, companions, planets, ship building, crafting, space combat, and things to grind.

After roughly 110 hours, I genuinely like Starfield. I can also completely understand why it disappointed so many people.

[hr]
[h1]Story and Characters[/h1]
The characters were one of my favorite parts of the game.

Companions have different personalities, opinions, and reactions to what you do. Some will agree with your decisions, others absolutely will not, especially when you start building relationships with them.

The voice acting is also really good. Characters rarely sounded robotic or unbelievable, and I was much more immersed in conversations than I expected.

The main story itself is much weaker. The premise is interesting enough to keep you moving, but I never found it particularly exciting. The faction questlines were honestly more interesting to me.

I also barely used the powers unless an achievement or quest required them. There are plenty with different uses, but collecting them gets repetitive fast. Find a temple, do the same floating minigame, get a power, repeat.

[hr]
[h1]World and Exploration[/h1]
Starfield has over 100 star systems and more than 1,000 planets, which sounds insane on paper.

The major locations can be really immersive. New Atlantis, Akila City, Neon, and other settlements have their own look and personality.

The problem is that exploration itself is one of Starfield's biggest weaknesses.

You can land on completely different planets, enter a structure, and realize you have already seen the exact same layout somewhere else. Same rooms, same enemies, same bodies, sometimes even the same placements.

That completely destroys the illusion of exploring a massive universe.

Planets are also often huge but empty. You can find caves, facilities, landmarks, creatures, and other points of interest, but once you notice how often everything repeats, the motivation to explore starts disappearing.

That is where Starfield really fails compared to Skyrim. In Skyrim, wandering somewhere could unexpectedly lead to a new cave, character, quest, or story. In Starfield, exploration often led me back into content I had already seen.

The menus do not help either. You spend way too much time navigating maps, inventories, planets, systems, and fast travel screens.

[hr]
[h1]Combat[/h1]
Combat is fine, but very basic.

There is a good selection of weapons and you can modify them, improve skills, use powers, or try stealth. But most fights played the same for me. I entered a room and started shooting everyone.

Enemy variety is not particularly impressive, and harder enemies often just felt like they could absorb more bullets instead of forcing me to change how I played.

Stealth was especially disappointing. Every time I tried to properly use it, it felt unreliable and frustrating.

Combat never became terrible, though. Shooting and looting stayed satisfying enough that I did not mind doing it for over 100 hours. It is just nowhere near as deep as I hoped.

[hr]
[h1]Progression and Ships[/h1]
I really liked the skill system. Skills have multiple ranks, and progressing them requires small challenges related to that skill. Most happen naturally while playing, and I liked having to actually use something before fully improving it.

Ship building is also cool. I did not go crazy with it, but upgrading weapons, shields, cargo, and grav drive was fun.

Looting kept me going too. Even when exploration became repetitive, I still enjoyed opening containers, picking locks, finding credits, and looking for better equipment.

[hr]
[h1]DLC[/h1]
The two story expansions are Shattered Space and Terran Armada.

Shattered Space was probably the stronger one for me. It feels more focused and handcrafted than a lot of the base game's exploration, with a concentrated area, story, and atmosphere.

Terran Armada was decent too. Delta was a fun addition, and it gives you more combat and progression to work through.

Neither expansion blew me away. They are not bad, but I do not think either changes how you feel about Starfield. If you already enjoy the base game, they give you more Starfield. If you hate the core loop, I doubt they will change your mind.

[hr]
[h1]Performance and Bugs[/h1]
My 2026 experience was massively better than launch.

When I first played in 2023, performance was one of the reasons I stopped. Coming back now, I had no real FPS problems and the game ran very well overall.

It is still buggy, though. I had conversations break, interactions stop working, and moments where I had to reload a save. Nothing destroyed my playthrough, but the game still does not feel as polished as I would like.

Bethesda has clearly improved it a lot since release, and the current version is in a much better place.

[hr]
[h1]100% Completion[/h1]
Getting every achievement took me roughly 110 hours.

Most are honestly pretty chill. The biggest grind for me was reaching level 100, along with some exploration and resource-related achievements.

The game currently has 82 Steam achievements. It is not a particularly difficult 100%, just a long one.

[hr]
[h1]What Works[/h1]
[list]
[*]Great companions and voice acting
[*]Enjoyable faction questlines
[*]Huge amount of content
[*]Distinct cities and settlements
[*]Satisfying shooting and looting
[*]Good skill progression
[*]Deep ship building
[*]Much better performance than at launch
[/list]

[hr]
[h1]What Falls Short[/h1]
[list]
[*]Main story is pretty average
[*]Exploration becomes extremely repetitive
[*]Too many reused locations and layouts
[*]Many planets feel huge but empty
[*]Far too much menu navigation
[*]Combat lacks depth and enemy variety
[*]Stealth feels weak
[*]Power temples get repetitive fast
[*]Bugs are still present
[/list]

[hr]
[h1]Verdict[/h1]
Starfield is not a bad game. I actually had a lot of fun with it.

It has serious problems with repetition, exploration, menus, combat depth, and a main story that never really grabbed me. But it also has memorable companions, enjoyable faction questlines, satisfying progression, tons of content, and that Bethesda charm that can keep you playing much longer than expected.

After buying it at launch, putting it down, and returning years later to complete everything, I am happy I gave Starfield another chance.

If you want a huge single-player space RPG where you can explore, build ships, complete factions, collect loot, and disappear for 100 hours, it is absolutely worth trying.

Just do not expect every one of those 1,000 planets to have something worth finding.

**Starfield gets way more hate than it deserves.**

Is it perfect? Hell no. The launch version had its problems, and I can understand why some people bounced off it. But after the updates, DLC, and all the player-created content, there’s a LOT of game here.

The exploration, ship building, quests, gunplay, and just getting lost doing random Bethesda shit can be a ton of fun. It may not have the same magic as Skyrim or Fallout for everyone, but calling Starfield a bad game is a stretch.

Give it some time, add in the DLC and Creations, and there’s a damn good space RPG underneath it all.

**8/10**

Hello fellow gamers, let me tell you a story.

It's a bit sad, a bit disappointing and a little bit tragic — much like the current state of the gaming industry as a whole (with a few exceptions).

I got this game as a birthday gift a few years ago. Curious, I started playing, and to no one's surprise I ragequit within the first few hours, outraged that a studio like Bethesda could ship something like this in 2023. Is this really the best you've got?

Years went by, and curiosity got the better of me, so I gave it another shot. I'd stopped expecting a company stuck in 2010 to feel present and self-aware in 2026. 

So what do you actually get in this 2010-era Bethesda "masterpiece"? Yes, I'm aware of the actual release date.

Picture Frankenstein's monster — stitched together, but by several different surgeons working on different schedules, and at least a few of them hammered. On paper, it could work(while you are also drunk). 

Progression and economy
There's a full upgrade system: weapons, equipment, ships, base-building and home furnishing. You can customize weapons, design your own modular ship, and push gear from standard to legendary with various mods. So far, so good — that's the pitch.

Then you actually play it. I'm level 35, I own a handful of ships, I've made exactly one ship modification (thanks, Reddit), and I've upgraded one weapon to 4-star legendary. In the process, every credit I'd saved for something meaningful evaporated — legendary stat rerolls alone can burn through hundreds of thounsands creds.

Either there's some grand plan where a few more zones and levels turn you into a millionaire, or you're signing up for an absurd grind: quests pay pennies next to what ships and gear actually cost. And even once you've farmed the loot, you still have to burn real time sitting on a bench waiting two in-game days for vendors to refill their credits, just so you can sell it.

Story and dialogue
Here's where you're really in for a treat. Want stilted persuasion conversations built on hidden stat checks that nobody bothers to explain, so sometimes they land and sometimes they flop for no clear reason? It's here. Want story that builds toward immersion and then resolve in ways that make no sense? Also here. Want to bribe a supposed millionaire with a whopping 1,000 credits, because apparently that works? Yep, that too.

Space
Now for the main event: space, ships, and planetary exploration. Jump into a system hoping to explore, and you'll find 8 planets or moons — remember the marketing? "1,000 planets." Right. Want to land somewhere? Enjoy the unskippable cutscene. Want to go somewhere else? More cutscenes. Also worth metioning that most of those planets  have nothing apart from some fauna and flora, no POI nothing.

Locations
Someone clearly put real effort into a handful of hand-crafted locations, and those are genuinely enjoyable — if only there were enough of them. For every good one, there's a pile of generated filler, and I wouldn't even mind that if there were more than a handful of prefabs in rotation. It feels like Bethesda built five templates, rotated each one a few degrees, and called it a day. Even story-critical locations sometimes don't hold together — not "confusing maze" territory, just genuinely nonsensical: ship layouts nobody with common sense would design, let alone use twice before scrapping the thing.

The best single-player space RPG on the market right now. (Especially if you're into Bethesda Sandbox.)

It’s easily one of the most polished launches Bethesda has ever had, anyone who’s played their titles before Skyrim knows exactly what I mean. Out of the box, the game runs surprisingly well, holds a steady framerate on mid-range hardware, and rarely crashes. I haven't hit a single hard crash yet, to the point where I actually turned off auto-save with full confidence.

I’ve been playing since day one and keep coming back for bite-sized sessions of pure space exploration. Bethesda has also done a great job supporting the game; updates like the vehicle patch brought massive QOL improvements alongside the Free Lanes update for free, on top of the already incredible modding scene that keeps things fresh.

It’s way too easy to get swept up in the online negativity these days and lose sight of what makes a game genuinely fun. Is the story a masterpiece? No, it can be a snooze at times. But the core gameplay loop, the gunplay, the powers, the loot, and the sheer scale of exploration, ties together into something deeply addictive.

Starfield really executes well in a lot of areas that don't get talked about enough. The gunplay is excellent with a wide variety of weapon types and playstyles. The problem this game has that its Fallout/Elder Scrolls cousins do not is the setting. While the quantity explorable planets locations is enormous, transiting between planets breaks continuity making the "world" feel small and disjointed. It's a common pitfall of open-world, space RPGs. However the post-launch addition of free lanes does a pretty good job at getting away from the "loading screen simulator" it was at launch. Bethesda really has been listening to the community and providing free quality of life updates and seems intent on supporting the title into 2027.

This is not to say I didn’t get what Starfield was trying to possibly say with its story but rather to say I don’t think it even cared what it had to say. If I had to put it rudely, it felt like Todd Howard said “I want a space game that you can play FOREVER!” but then forgot to let them make anything worthwhile to keep you playing forever.

In every Bethesda game I’ve played I feel like I’ve always had this side quest. This thing that no matter what type of play through I do I always go and visit this side quest. It could just be because it’s enjoyable, or maybe it feels like it has such a significant impact on my character’s story, the world’s story, or even the main story. In Starfield I never felt that way. Now I can understand if maybe that’s the point. Nothing you do matters because in a cosmic sense nothing you do matters and this universe can easily be left behind for a new one. But I feel like in a game like Starfield it makes it feel worthless to do anything when it feels like nothing you do matters outside the main story.

Something else that I feel hurts this game is just generally poor exploration. In The Elder Scrolls or Fallout I felt like I could go somewhere in confidence knowing I would find something, and it would be worth my time most of the time! In Starfield if I ever dared to treat this game like an open world exploration heavy RPG I would just be met with disappointment. There is virtually no point to exploring and there is often little to no reward for doing so.

I think this game should have set its sights a little lower is all. Maybe instead of every star and planet in the settled systems with uninspired and often boring point of interest we could have instead had a few solar systems with fleshed out maps and stories and factions to interact with. Something where you could actually feel like when you do something it changes things.

I love sci-fi, and I do honestly want to love this game. But I just feel disappointed is all. I hope there are other devs out there that learn a lesson from Starfield on how they should approach their game if they make something similar.

Bethesda had the misfortune of releasing Starfield shortly after the release of Baldur's Gate 3,  arguably the greatest RPG of the modern era. Although I played it a bit on GamePass, it was hard not to compare it to BG3, which I was also playing at the same time. Ultimately, I put it aside. 

Three years later, I returned to Starfield after buying it during a Steam sale, and I've found myself pleasantly surprised. No, it's not in the same league as BG3, nor is it as good as Skyrim, but it's still a great Bethesda RPG. The universe of the Settled Systems seems real and lived in, and it has some truly fantastic quests. My favorite quest involves being forced by the United Colonies government to go undercover in the pirate gang known as the Crimson Fleet. It involves a lot of duplicity, trying to earn the trust of the pirates, an expedition onto a lost spaceship, and ultimately a consequential decision that has a lasting effect on the game. Another standout moment was coming across a disabled spacecraft with a broken gravity system. As you make your way through the craft, gravity switches on and off, forcing some interesting mechanics. Also, I never tire of attacking a ship, disabling its engines, and then boarding it and stealing it. 

The ground combat system in Starfield is the best Bethesda has ever designed, easily superior to the shooting mechanics in the Fallout series. It's not a first person shooter, so pulling the trigger involves hidden dice rolls and stat checks, but the guns feel snappy and the misses don't feel quite as bad. Ship-to-ship combat is constrained by the limited orbital space maps, and although being able to target specific systems on enemy ships is a nice touch, the battles aren't quite as involved as the ground combat is. 

Bethesda crammed a lot into the game -- base building, ship construction, crew management, exploration of random planets. It's all meant to be taken in aggregate, so if you focus too long on an activity, such as base building, you realize that the systems are much shallower than they appear. They are enjoyable to experiment with, but it doesn't take much to reach the boundaries of their mechanics.

Others have complained about the necessity of menus to travel the galaxy. Unlike No Man's Sky, it's not possible to travel from planet to orbit to deep space without a load screen. This is a change from other Bethesda games, which outside of interior spaces, offer a continuous open world. Each planet is its own self-contained place, and getting on and off involves navigating the game's UI. It's clunky, but they've made some quality of life improvements since release that cut out a lot of the busy work the game used to require to go from system to system.

Finally, as with every Bethesda game, some of the writing is a bit clunky. Unlike Baldur's Gate 3 and the old Bioware games which offer a spectrum of dialogue choices, many of the options in Skyrim are variations of the same dialogue. I frequently found myself in conversations with NPCs where I wasn't given any satisfactory options.  The romance options with your party members is likewise clunky, especially when compared with the deep relationships found in games like Baldur's Gate 3 and the Mass Effect series.

Still, gripes aside, Starfield offers a well developed world, great RPG mechanics, and enjoyable immersive sim elements. I'm likely to take my current playthrough all the way to the end, which I can't say I did with Fallout 4. It is beautiful on my main gaming PC, and it's one of the few recent games that runs extremely well on Steam Machine. If you like other Bethesda games and were put off by the mixed reviews when it was released, I'd recommend giving it another try.

okay hear me out, I was a hater until I played it for a decent bit, 
Starfield is a weird game. It has all the Bethesda RPG elements & jank you would expect from a game their studio, made but it also attempts what games like Elite Dangerous, and No Mans Sky accomplished but on a WAY smaller scale.  

Those games have a very similar, repetitive game play loops. (ship/ground combat, mining, scanning, exploring, base building, trading, bounty hunting) but companied with a near infinite map these activities can satiate a gamer that likes that kind of genre.  

Starfield tries to encapsulate those same loops in sidequest and leisure gameplay form but those gameplay loops do not mesh well with how limited the in-game explorable galaxy is, and how Bethesda designs the core of their games. The overall "Skyrimness" of the main/faction mission design often feels disconnected from the typical  grindy stuff listed above you usually do in the open space sim genre. 

BUT after a dozen or so hours it started to win me over. Bethesda has a way of making your level ups and progression feel GOOD. While simultaneously raising the bar with a deadly encounter right when you are feeling at the top of your game. That kind of good ol'e Bethesda progression scaling paired with a (semi) open universe has me roped in. They also updated the game so you can freely cruise around local systems instead of fast travelling everywhere, which is honestly huge it makes everything feel much more connected. 

The games also looks pretty good graphically noting the idle facial animations. Zero G environments are impressive from a gameplay perspective, and the ship builder is actually pretty insane when you figure it all out. After nearly 3 years of updates, I can say this game is rad as hell IF you have very specific expectations. 

This is what Starfield will NOT give you:

1. Consequential choices. This isn’t New Vegas or even Skyrim. 

2. A vast handcrafted galaxy. 

3. Compelling story or moral dilemmas. Sometimes certain quests have flashes of it. That’s about it. 

Here is what you do get in Starfield:

1. The sandbox of space exploration. The “go anywhere, do anything, you never know what’s out there” feeling in Starfield is singularly excellent. Only no man’s sky does it better in my opinion. I’m confident that was NOT the case at launch, but after Free Lanes it feels way more seamless and immersive to explore systems of deep (or even uncharted) space. 

2. Difficulty options. I LOVE the way Starfield does difficulty. You can make certain things easier for an experience gain penalty and other things harder for an experience gain boost. Two huge complaints from players at launch were low carry weight and low vendor credits. Both are non-issues now with settings tweaks. 

3. Combat. Wide variety of fun weapons, and traversal options in low/0 gravity. You also get mad space magic powers. 

4. Progression. Fun hybrid between the Skyrim skills and more conventional level ups. You can spend a skill point on any skill, but you can’t upgrade that skill until you fulfill a certain challenge associated with it. Great system. 

5. Robust ship building system that you can get EXTREMELY lost in. Building the enterprise or the millennium falcon in Starfield is a special experience.

This can be completely ignored with no penalty to your gameplay whatsoever if it isn't your niche.

Properties like houses and apartments feel more like decorative sidepieces rather than places you return to over and over again, like you might with Breezehome (Skyrim)  or Megaton (Fallout 3), but they can still be functional if you allow them to be. The Lodge serves as  the only spot you ever actually need, but I always enjoy buying out every property I can in games when it's an option. That said, property is also entirely optional in Starfield.

There are plenty of loading screens, and my hardware is the ONLY reason I don't suffer from long stretches of waiting. I recognize it's a problem that genuinely causes a lot of people grief. On the other hand, I would say that expecting a game which is supposed to represent a galaxy isn't exactly prime real estate for being seamless, even if we would all like it to be.

The character models are stunning, at least to me. There's a lot more expression and animation to characters than previous Bethesda games have offered, and the world feels much more lively with NPCs wandering about in cities. That being said, they can still be stiff and sometimes a bit awkward. 

Surveying planets yields a chunk of in-game cash, but I personally wouldn't recommend surveying every planet to 100% unless that's something that you enjoy. You can get a majority of surveying done just hopping from POI to POI and scanning along the way, but it can be a time sink if you go out of your way to hunt down every last thing on every single planet.

All in all, it's a good game with its own flaws and I'm glad I bought it. I stick to things I genuinely enjoy doing and it's brought me 30 hours of good times so far. It isn't the next Skyrim or New Vegas, but if you've enjoyed Bethesda games before, you'll probably enjoy this one too. My thoughts are completely scattered, but I stand by it so far.

I’ve spent hours lost in this universe, and Starfield has genuinely hooked me. The gameplay mechanics are solid and deeply enjoyable—from the gunplay and combat to resource crafting. The map is massive, offering a constant, thrilling sense of space exploration. However, its greatest strength is undoubtedly the interactions with NPCs, which bring incredible life to every corner you visit.

To help you make the most of your journey right from the start, here are a few key recommendations:

Manage your inventory wisely: These Bethesda games are notorious for weight management struggles. I strongly recommend not picking up everything in sight—only grab what is truly valuable or useful for crafting. You aren't a moving truck!

Prioritize your early credits: At the beginning of the game, your main goal should be saving up 25,000 credits. This isn't for luxuries; it's to buy the land vehicle. It will completely change your experience by drastically reducing the massive distances you have to hoof across planets.

Look into outposts early: Don't leave crafting and base-building for the very end. Setting up a small outpost early on will supply you with rare materials and boost your economy in the long run.

Talk to your companions: Your crew's side quests feature some of the best storytelling in the game, and completing them unlocks very useful tactical perks for both combat and exploration.

It's a game with a few technical stumbles here and there, but the freedom, immersion, and scale of the adventure far outweigh them. Highly recommended!

[b]tl;dr[/b]Great amount of meh content with very little story but tons of replayability. It's buggy af however. Well it's just another Bethesda game.

[b]Who is this for[/b]
This is important and why I put "Recommend" on this!
It's purely for people who like exploring and don't mind (or actually like) grinding. Don't expect good story here or great combat or innovative gaming. If you enjoy modding your games - this has a huge potential for modding, however I am not big on mods myself. Everyone else should avoid it.

[b]The good[/b]
Good amount of content and hidden things.
A ton of replayability.
You have romance options with some characters.
Extensive skill tree and no hard limit level, so you can try all the build if you are dedicated enough.
Best gear is not necessarily locked behind difficult RNG - you can build your best gear.
Decent faction stories.
Well animated NPCs, when they don't bug out.
Really nice feeling system to build ships, guns, armor and the like. You can spend hours building the ship your want.
Plays great with controllers.

[b]The dealbreakers[/b]
Notably buggy. No crashes but many progression stopping bugs, buggy animations, buggy AI etc.
The main story and most side-stories are extremely meh. Even when voiced, I found it hard to care about it at all.
Characters in game are a bit hard to actually connect with and to care about - same as the main story essentially.
There is an immense amount of randomly generated stuff that's uninspiring and boring to do and yet you can very quickly lose yourself in it when trying to explore the main content.
The game feels primed for survival mechanics, yet they are not implemented there for those that would want them.
Stealth gameplay is clunky and not well thought out.
Worldbuilding just feels inconsistent. The universe does not follow actual set of rules and that absolutely ruins the worldbuilding.
There is a lot of missing things for quality of life things. It builds up with time and at times feels really frustrating.
Building outposts feels like a waste of time, till you learn the one and only useful thing - powerleveling.
Overall the game is a huge time-sink and has little respect for your time.

[b]Is the price right?[/b]
If this is a game for you - yes. With the amount of content you can enjoy and replayability and modding potential keeping the game alive for years - it's worth the money. It's not for everyone however and, if it sounds like you would not enjoy it, then it's not worth even your time, let alone your money.
